descs.en: He thinks her hands are broken and opens every door for her. She secretly got her surgeon’s hands back, and works nights in a basement as the family’s ghost surgeon.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Elara Lin is a final-year medical student who talks all the time, practises stitches on bananas, and on her first morning on the surgical ward tells the chief resident he’s missed a leak. She’s right. By the evening Wang Xing Yue has handed her logbook to someone else, so that he’s allowed to ask her to dinner.

She’s also the Lins’ surgeon. When the family’s people bleed somewhere a hospital can’t see, she goes. In a supply room at three in the morning she begs him not to ask, and he promises he won’t.

He keeps that promise through a knife at her father’s door, a winter when she stops talking, and the year she gets her hands back in secret and goes to work in a cellar, in a mask, as Doctor Ghost. He never asks her to stop. He restocks her bag.

He falls first · Doctors in love · Married early · Complete in four volumes, plus ten side stories

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Elara has been in the corner of every Lin book: late, in scrubs, crying at weddings, running a county hospital in her Saturday jeans. I wanted to know what that cost her, and who looks after the person who looks after everyone.

Xing Yue isn’t a nice man to anyone but her. He tracks her phone, goes through her bag and lies to his own professor without blinking, and the book doesn’t tell him off for it. The one thing he never does is ask her to be someone else.

There’s blood, because it’s a book about surgeons, but the medicine stays at story level. They get a long kitchen, two pagers and a phone in a drawer that rings at half past eleven.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

A warm, funny medical romance, with some hard moments:

• Love scenes on the page, from early on

• Knife and gunshot wounds, and surgery outside hospitals with stolen supplies

• A people-smuggling boat and its frightened survivors

• Burns after a fire

• A knife attack and a serious hand injury

• Nerve pain, withdrawal into silence, and the truth about how her birth parents died

• A fire that kills two people, and a killing at the harbour wall

• A girl’s face cut with a bottle

• A suspension at work

• A footbridge collapse with many casualties

• A partner who tracks her phone and goes through her bag, shown without judgement

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
City Hospital — the teaching hospital at the foot of the hill. Ward 9B, general surgery, is on the ninth floor of the tower; the old 1930s block stands behind it.
Harbourside General — the big hospital by the harbour, where Elara does her intern year and goes back to training in 2027.
The Crestview — the private hospital on the hill above the old racecourse, which asks no questions of people who pay, and where Ms. Cui makes her cry.
The hospital garden — behind the old block: a camphor tree older than the hospital, a koi pond, and the fourth window along on the first floor, which was her mother's ward.
14 Banyan Terrace — his flat, the top two floors and roof of a white 1950s building ten minutes downhill from City Hospital.
2 Camphor Hill — the old doctor's house above the hospital, with a long kitchen and a back room for the rig. Bought in both their names, without asking.
The Walled City — the old district where the Lins live, behind a red door with a brass fish knocker and eleven chairs that don't match.
The cellar under the rope store — the room Raiden builds next to the garage near the Docks, behind a steel door painted to look like wood.
Doctor Ghost — the name the docks give the masked surgeon who never speaks and always hums.
The rig — Jinx's steel training machine for Elara's hand: a forearm cradle, pulleys, a turntable and a fine wire that whispers until her hand is where she sent it.
The ghost phone — the line that rings only from her father's or Uncle Mok's numbers. From July 2027 it lives in the kitchen drawer.
The dot — her phone location, shared with him ‘for night shifts’ from 2023, and his with her from 2026.
The rules — what they wrote on the back of his suspension letter. Rule one: nobody does this alone.
Qu Xiaoyue — her birth name, ‘little moon’. Elara is a moon of Jupiter, so she kept a piece of it.
Qu Lighterage — her father's firm: four lighter boats between the ships and the old Walled City piers.
Plum Steps — the children's home at the top of a long flight of stone steps, closed in 2011.
Loupes — magnifying glasses surgeons wear to operate. Hers are dark red, made for her eyes, with E.L. inside the arm.
Registrar, consultant — a registrar is a mid-level surgeon in training; a consultant is the senior surgeon in charge.

chapters.title: The Student Who Told the Chief Resident He Was Wrong
chapters.desc: On her first morning in surgery, a final-year student tells the chief resident he’s missed a leak. She’s right, and he has seen her face before.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d rather be wrong about this one.”
chapters.content:
“Read it to me.”

Dr. Zang read the drug chart aloud: an antibiotic, twice a day, the usual dose. He stopped where everyone stopped.

“His kidneys work at a third of yours. It’s on the front page of his notes. Again, please. Slower. You’re not tying your shoelaces,” said Wang Xing Yue.

The old man in bed nine had put his spoon down to watch, as if it were the best thing that had happened on the ward all week. Zang went red from the collar up, read the chart a third time, and saw it.

“Oh.”

“Change it before lunch. Then find out what that drug does to a kidney and tell me tomorrow without your notes.”

It was the first Monday in September, on Ward 9B of City Hospital, and Professor Liao was at a conference across the water until Thursday, so the round was his. He’d been chief surgical resident for two months. He was thirty, and already the thing the new doctors warned each other about in the lift.

His team trailed behind him in order of fear. Dr. Rao, the junior resident, who wrote beautiful notes and never read them again. Dr. Zang, three weeks into his first job, who jumped every time his bleep went off. And four final-year students on their first morning in surgery, in white coats with the creases from the packet still in them, holding their notebooks against their chests like shields.

Sister Miao was handing over after her night, in her grey cardigan with the pager clipped to the pocket. She looked the students over the way a farmer looks at a new delivery of hens.

“Fresh ones,” she said, and went home to bed.

Three of the students were studying the floor. The fourth wasn’t. She was small and stood at the back, with her hair escaping from a plastic clip and her head on one side, and she was looking at him the way you’d look at weather coming in over the harbour: with interest, and without any fear at all. He had a ward to get round.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bed fourteen was Mr. Yin Shoucheng, seventy-one, a retired bus driver, four days after a cancer had been taken out of his bowel and the two ends joined.

He’d had a bad night. A fever in the small hours, a heart rate of a hundred and twelve, and twice the nurses had found him trying to climb out over the rails. At the bottom of his right lung there were crackles.

Xing Yue said, “Chest. He’s seventy-one, he’s had an anaesthetic, and it hurts him to breathe deeply. Sputum, a chest film, antibiotics. Physio before ten, and sit him out in the chair afterwards.”

Rao wrote it down.

“Sorry. Can I say something?”

She didn’t wait to be told she could.

“His heart rate went up first. Before the fever. It was ninety yesterday at lunchtime and a hundred and four by teatime, and his temperature didn’t climb till the night. It’s on the observation chart. And he says his tummy’s worse today, not better. I came in early to see my patients and he was awake, so I said good morning, and I sort of pressed on his belly while I was saying it.”

Mr. Yin lifted a hand off the sheet. “She did.”

“He didn’t like it. On the right. Near where the join would be.”

Nobody on the team breathed. Rao looked like a man attending his own funeral. Nobody corrected Wang Xing Yue. He never shouted. He was just almost never wrong, and when somebody told him he was, he took their argument apart in front of the patient, quite gently, while they stood there in their new coat and watched it go.

“A chest infection is the commonest cause of fever on the fourth day,” he said.

“I know. I’d still want a scan. If it’s his chest and we scan him, we’ve lost an hour and some money. If it’s a leak and we wait, Mr. Yin pays for it. I’d rather be wrong about this one.” Her face had gone pink. Her voice hadn’t moved.

“So would I, young lady,” said Mr. Yin, through his false teeth.

Xing Yue put the notes down. He rubbed his hands together to warm them, and laid one flat on the old man’s stomach, and pressed: left side, middle, low on the right. On the right the muscle went hard before he’d gone a centimetre, and Mr. Yin sucked air in through his teeth and took hold of the sheet.

“I’m sorry, Mr. Yin.”

He straightened and looked at the student. “You’re right. Book the scan.”

Then he looked at Rao. “You saw this chart at six. Why did a student find it?”

Rao’s mouth opened.

“Don’t answer that. A scan with contrast. Ring theatres and tell the coordinator I may need a slot this afternoon. Then read every chart on this ward again, and read the numbers this time instead of copying them.”

Rao went, fast. Xing Yue wrote in the notes, and watched the student out of the corner of his eye. She’d gone from pink to white. She looked as if she might be sick. She also looked as if it might be the best day of her life, and both expressions were on her small round face at once, fighting for room.

He looked at her properly then. Quick dark eyes. An impossible amount of hair. A cream cardigan under the white coat, its pocket stuffed with pens and something that crinkled. He knew that face.

June, the year before, when he’d been rotating through Harbourside General. A Saturday morning at the end of a long call, the sixth floor. A young man knocked off his feet by a van: three cracked ribs on the left, a broken wrist, a concussion, and a clean scan; nothing a surgeon was needed for. Xing Yue had been on his way to the lift when a girl in a T-shirt stepped into his path with her hair coming out of a clip and asked him, all in one breath, whether anyone had checked her brother’s spleen, because it was the left ribs, and the spleen sat right underneath them, and she’d read that it could bleed slowly and look like nothing at all for hours—

“We checked,” he’d said. “The scan’s clear.”

“Oh, good. Thank you. Sorry!” And she was past him and into the room, talking before the door had shut.

He’d gone home that morning and not slept, and blamed it on the night. He’d been blaming the night for fifteen months.

He signed the notes and moved on to bed fifteen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the round she slipped Zang something from her cardigan pocket: a boiled sweet in a twist of paper. Zang held it as if he’d been given a medal.

Later the other students caught her by the sluice. Xing Yue was coming the other way with a chart, and they didn’t see him.

“Are you out of your mind?”

“He’s going to fail you. He’s going to fail you so badly they’ll fail your parents.”

“He doesn’t fail people. He makes them stop existing,” said the tall one with the expensive haircut.

“I don’t care. It was a leak. It was, wasn’t it? Oh, no. What if it’s his chest after all?” She did care. Her voice had gone up half an octave.

“Then you’re dead, Lin.”

“Then I’m dead. Fine. Mr. Yin won’t be.”

He walked past them, and four mouths shut at once. He was almost at the lifts before he noticed that he was smiling, and stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the dark of the reporting room the radiologist scrolled through the scan and stopped. “There. A small leak at the join. And that collection’s new since Friday.”

“Theatre at one.”

He found her outside the doctors’ room eating a cereal bar standing up and reading Mr. Yin’s notes over somebody else’s shoulder.

“You found it. You’ll want to see it. Go and scrub,” he said.

She stared at him with her mouth full and swallowed. “Yes. Yes! Sorry. Yes.” She went. She came back, because she’d gone the wrong way.

She talked while she scrubbed, not to him, to herself, in a steady undertone. Where was the soap, there it was. Was this hot? It was hot. It was fine. The last time she’d done this it had been for an ingrown toenail, which wasn’t glamorous. He stood at the next sink with his arms under the water, and she glanced across and caught him watching her hands, and talked faster.

“Sorry. I’ll stop.”

“Don’t.”

They were good hands. Small, quick and sure. Every finger and every side of every finger, the backs, the wrists, in the order everybody was taught and nobody still followed after their first year. The badge clipped to her scrubs said LIN ELARA, FINAL YEAR.

Lin. Of course. The van, the private room on the sixth floor at Harbourside, the grey-haired man in the corridor with a face like the side of a building and two men standing behind him. Everyone in the city knew that family. And Xing Yue’s own name was at the top of her rotation sheet: six weeks, her logbook, the line at the bottom that said whether she was fit to be a doctor.

He held his hands up and let the water run off his elbows. She held hers up beside him, looked across, and went pink above the mask she hadn’t tied.

He made a decision there at the sink, dripping, and then he made the one that had to come before it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In theatre she held the retractor where he put it for two hours, and it didn’t move a millimetre. He took the join apart and washed Mr. Yin out until the fluid ran clear, and brought the bowel out onto the skin for a few months, until the old man was strong enough to have it put back. Ordinary work.

She murmured the whole way through. “All right. There. All right.”

Suyin, his scrub nurse, looked at her over her mask and then at him. “Does she always do that?”

“Apparently.”

“Do you want me to tell her—”

“No.”

Suyin’s eyebrows went up and stayed there. He didn’t care. If the student had stopped talking he’d have been annoyed, and that was new.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Fei Ran was eating noodles out of a plastic tub in the registrars’ office with her feet on the bin. She was the senior registrar, four years older than him and in no hurry to be anything else.

“Take one of my students. Her assessments, her logbook, all of it. Lin Elara,” he said.

Fei put her chopsticks down. “The one who found Mr. Yin’s leak? The whole floor’s heard. Why?” She squinted up at him.

He didn’t answer.

“Because she was right?”

“No.”

“Because she’s a Lin?”

“No.”

“Oh, a student you met this morning,” said Fei slowly.

“Yes.”

She looked at him, and he looked back. Then she picked up the rotation sheet, crossed out his name on one line and wrote her own, initialled it and went back to her noodles.

“I’m not going to ask. I’m going to tell everybody at Christmas,” she said with her mouth full.

✦ ✦ ✦

In recovery, in the early evening, Mr. Yin was awake, more or less, under an oxygen mask, puzzled and calm and still full of anaesthetic.

“Doctor.”

“It went well, Mr. Yin. You’ll be sore for a while. You’ll be all right.”

The old man nodded slowly. Then he turned his head on the pillow and looked past Xing Yue down the length of the ward, searching.

“Where’s the little doctor? The one who talks.”

She’d gone. Fei had sent her home after watching her eat a second cereal bar standing up.

“Tomorrow. She’s in at six,” said Xing Yue.

Mr. Yin squinted at him over the mask. “How do you know that?”

He’d read the student rota on his way down from theatre. Twice.

“Go to sleep, Mr. Yin,” he said.

chapters.title: Love at First Sight Is a Sleep-Deprivation Symptom
chapters.desc: Elara finds her logbook handed to someone else and marches into the chief resident’s office to apologise for being right. He tells her why, and it isn’t a question.
chapters.epigraph: “I can’t take you to dinner and sign your logbook. I picked dinner.”
chapters.content:
On Tuesday he didn’t look at her once. Elara knew, because she spent the whole round standing where he would have to. At the end of the bed. By the drug trolley. At bed six she got so close to his elbow that she could smell the cheap hospital soap from the dispensers on him, and tea.

He turned a page. “Potassium, Dr. Rao.”

He said it past her as if she were a coat stand. Rao got the potassium, and then Rao got everything else. Why did a man on a drip have no fluid chart? Why had nobody told the woman in bed eight that her drain had stopped? What did patient comfortable mean at four in the morning, written about a man who’d had morphine twice? Rao answered the first question, and after that he stood there going red, and by bed twelve his ears were a dark and painful colour. The woman in twelve, a big auntie with a gallstone, reached out and patted his hand once Dr. Wang had moved on.

“There, there, son.”

At the end of the round Elara found a boiled sweet in her cardigan pocket and gave it to Rao. He took it without looking at it, and then he looked at it.

“Thanks. Really,” he said, as if he’d been punched.

She went to see Mr. Yin afterwards. He was sitting up with the bag under his gown, grey and cross and alive.

“The jelly in this place tastes of shampoo.”

“I’ll tell the kitchen.”

“Don’t. They’ll make it worse. The tall one came at six and looked at my bag and didn’t say good morning.” He sniffed.

“He doesn’t say good morning.”

“You do. Are you married?” He looked her up and down.

“I’m a student!”

“That’s not an answer,” said Mr. Yin, and went to sleep in the middle of glaring at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday Dr. Fei stopped her outside the sluice with a tub of noodles in one hand. “I’m doing your logbook from now on, by the way. I’ve got your sheet. Find me on Friday and we’ll go through it.”

“Oh. All right. Thank you. Can I ask why?”

Fei was already walking away. “Ask him.”

The lift doors closed on her, and Elara stood outside the sluice and felt her whole face go hot.

Of course she knew why. On her first morning, on her first round, she’d told the chief resident he was wrong in front of his team and in front of his patient. She’d said tummy. Twice. She’d eaten a cereal bar at him in a corridor with her mouth open. And now he’d handed her logbook to somebody else because he couldn’t stand the sight of her, and for six weeks she would be invisible, and at the end someone would write fine in the last box. Fine was what you wrote about a student you’d forgotten.

She thought about it through a clinic, and on the bus, and in the shower, and at the long table in the Walled City that night, pushing rice round her bowl until Ah Sim stood over her with the ladle.

“Little sparrow. You’re eating like a bird.”

“I am a bird. You named me.”

“Then eat, bird.”

Raiden had come to dinner, which usually meant nobody else got a word in. Tonight he stopped halfway through a story about a crane and pointed his chopsticks across the table.

“What’s wrong with her?”

“Nothing’s wrong with me.”

“You’ve said nine words all evening. You usually say nine words a second. Who do I have to fight?” He leaned in.

“Nobody. It isn’t a person. It’s a surgeon.”

At the head of the table their father put his bowl down. “Which surgeon?”

“No surgeon. A hypothetical surgeon. A general surgeon, in general. I’m eating, Baba. Look. The bird is eating.” She put rice in her mouth.

Lin Jian looked at her the way he read the small print on a contract. Then he picked up his bowl again. Across the table Raiden mouthed hypothetical at her, and she kicked him under it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight the light was still on under Eliana’s door. It was always on. Her little sister was nineteen and slept from four in the morning until noon, like a bat, in a nest of hooded sweatshirts with three screens on the desk and a fourth on her knees. Elara sat on the end of the bed and told her all of it, the round and Mr. Yin and the scan and the sink and the logbook and Fei with her noodles.

“And I said tummy, Eli. To him.”

Eliana didn’t turn round. “He’s thirty. From the north. No girlfriend. Nothing online. On call he eats beef noodles at eleven at night at the place across from the ambulance bay. In July he made a registrar cry. The registrar was wrong.”

Elara stared at the back of her sister’s head. Nobody in their family ever asked Eliana how she knew things. You only got a look.

“I didn’t ask for that.”

“No,” said Eliana, typing, and Elara lasted almost four seconds.

“Is he nice?”

“He’s fair. That’s rarer,” said Eliana.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday she went to apologise.

She’d written it out on the bus in three parts, the way she wrote patient histories in her head so as not to lose anything. First, sorry for contradicting him in front of Mr. Yin, because you didn’t do that. Second, sorry about the corridor. The third had been the important one, and it had fallen out of her head somewhere near the fish market. It would come back. It always did.

His office was at the far end of the surgical corridor on the ninth floor: a cupboard with a window, a desk and two chairs, a computer older than she was, a shelf of journals. The door was half open. He was writing in a set of notes, and from the doorway his handwriting looked like a seismograph. She knocked on the frame, and he looked up and put the pen down.

“Dr. Wang. Sorry. Have you got a minute? It’ll be one minute. Possibly two. I wanted to apologise, and I’ve got three things.”

He took his glasses off and began to clean them on a folded handkerchief. She decided that meant yes.

“One. I’m sorry I contradicted you in front of Mr. Yin. You don’t correct a senior doctor in front of a patient. It undermines—well, you know what it undermines, you’re the senior doctor. Except I’d do it again, because of Mr. Yin. So I’m not sure that’s an apology. It’s more of a report. Two. The cereal bar. I’m normally quite tidy.” He went on cleaning the glasses. She could hear herself not apologising, and went on anyway.

That was a lie, and she felt it land on her face. “Very tidy. And three. Mr. Yin says the jelly’s terrible. I don’t think that’s three. But I thought you’d want to know about the jelly,” she said, to make it more convincing, and then stopped, because the third thing still hadn’t come back.

A trolley with a bad wheel went past in the corridor. He put his glasses on again.

He said, “You didn’t do anything wrong. Not on the round, and not in the corridor. You were right. You’ll be right again, and when you are, you should say so again. Don’t come and apologise for it.”

“Oh. Then why did Dr. Fei—” She blinked.

“I asked her to take your logbook because I’m taking you to dinner. I can’t take you to dinner and sign your logbook. I picked dinner.” He said it in exactly the voice he’d used for the potassium.

Elara stood in the doorway. He looked back at her and nothing on his face moved: a serious face, older than thirty, gold-rimmed glasses, dark hair swept back and kept neat, the kind of tiredness round the eyes that looked.

“That wasn’t a question,” she said.

“No.”

“You’re supposed to ask. People ask. Would you like to have dinner? And then I say yes or no.”

“You can say no.”

That was all. He sat with his hands flat on the notes and waited, and she understood with a lurch in her stomach that if she said no he would say all right and pick up his pen, and he would never mention it again, and tomorrow on the ward he would be exactly the same. She could see it so clearly that she didn’t say no.

“Oh, is it allowed? It can’t be allowed. You’re the chief resident and I’m a student on your unit. There must be a rule. There’s a rule about how long you can leave a cannula in,” she said instead, which was all she had. Then, because she was who she was, she kept going.

She got her phone out and found the student handbook, which the university had hidden inside another document inside a folder called General, and told him what she thought of anybody who would call a folder that, and read it aloud. Students shouldn’t enter into a personal relationship with any member of staff who has a role in their teaching, assessment or supervision. Where such a relationship exists or begins, the member of staff must declare it and withdraw from that role.

She read it twice and looked up. “You’ve withdrawn.”

“On Monday.”

“That’s before you asked me.”

“I still haven’t asked you.”

She opened her mouth and shut it again. He was right, which was annoying.

“Friday, after your skills session,” he said.

“I can’t on Friday. It’s banana night. All the final years suture bananas in the skills lab, it’s sort of a competition. It isn’t really a competition. Everyone treats it like one, and I won last year, so if I don’t go, Tung Kai will say I was scared.”

“Then after the bananas.”

“All right,” she heard herself say.

“I’ll wait outside the lab.”

“You don’t know when it finishes.”

“Half past eight.”

“How do you—oh. You used to teach it.”

“For three years.”

“Of course you did,” said Elara.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her to the lifts. She noticed things about him the whole way, because noticing was the one part of being a doctor she’d been good at before she knew anything else. He cleaned his glasses when he wanted time to think; he’d done it when she knocked, and again while she read the handbook. His watch was plain steel with a second hand, for taking pulses. His phone had buzzed on the desk three times and he hadn’t looked at it once. And he walked beside her, not ahead, though his legs were twice the length of hers; he’d shortened his stride without seeming to notice he’d done it.

She told him about Mr. Yin asking if she was married. “I said I’m a student, and he said that’s not an answer. It is an answer, isn’t it?”

“It’s not an answer.”

“Whose side are you on?”

“Mr. Yin’s.”

She laughed too loudly for a hospital corridor, and told him about her brother, who’d been knocked down by a van the summer before last and kept in at Harbourside, and how their father had stood in the corridor outside his room all morning until a nurse dropped a tray. He didn’t say anything to that. She looked up to see whether he was bored. He was listening the way you’d listen to a history you were going to have to present on the round: to every word.

At the lifts he pressed the button, and when the doors opened his hand went to the small of her back to steer her in, lightly, through her cardigan, for one step. Then he took it away quickly.

She turned round in the lift. He was standing in the corridor in his white shirt and dark tie with his hand in his pocket and the same serious face, and his ears had gone pink.

She didn’t think about it. She reached out of the lift and took hold of his tie. She didn’t pull. She only held it in her fist, dark blue silk, warm from him, and he went perfectly still and looked down at her, and for a second neither of them breathed.

The doors began to close. She looked down at her own hand on his tie as if a stranger had put it there, and let go, and the doors shut between them, and she rode down nine floors with both hands over her face.

Upstairs, in the corridor, he stood looking at the closed doors. Then he looked down at his tie. It was creased where she’d held it. He didn’t straighten it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the taxi she worked it out. She’d gone in with three things to apologise for, done two, lost the third, talked for a quarter of an hour about a folder called General, and come out with a dinner she hadn’t been asked to. Except that she’d said yes, somewhere between then I say yes or no and after the bananas. She hadn’t decided to. It had come out of her, the way you grab at something that’s falling. And she’d held his tie.

She put her forehead against the cold window and laughed out loud. The driver looked at her in the mirror.

“Good day?”

“I don’t know. I think so. Ask me on Friday.” She wiped her eyes.

“What’s on Friday?”

“Bananas,” said Elara, and the driver decided not to ask anything else.

The light was still on under Eliana’s door when she got home. Elara went past it into her own room and lay down on the bed with her shoes on, and her phone buzzed on her chest.

Eliana: the noodle place across from the ambulance bay shuts at 1. fyi

She hadn’t told her. She hadn’t told anyone. She stared at the ceiling, and the phone buzzed again.

Eliana: you’re welcome

The third thing came back in the middle of the night, when she was nearly asleep, and it had never been an apology at all. She’d been thinking about him since the sink.

chapters.title: Suturing Practice on a Banana
chapters.desc: She beats every student in the skills lab with a needle and a banana. At dinner she talks for three hours, and on the steps outside he stops her in the middle of a story.
chapters.epigraph: “Finish the story later.”
chapters.content:
On Friday nights in September the skills lab in the old medical building smelled of bananas.

Xing Yue wasn’t teaching. He’d taught the session for three years and handed it to a registrar this autumn, and he had no reason at all to be on that corridor. He’d driven up the hill anyway, parked, walked down past the anatomy museum and stopped at the glass panel in the door.

Thirty students sat at long benches. Each of them had a banana taped to a board with a cut down the skin, and a needle holder, forceps, scissors and a packet of suture. The point was to close the cut so neatly that you couldn’t get a fingernail into the line. The registrar at the front had a stopwatch, which wasn’t the point, but there had always been a stopwatch. They were students.

She was on the second bench by the window, talking, obviously. Her head kept turning to the boy beside her, the tall one with the expensive haircut, who looked as if he’d pay money for her to stop. Her hands didn’t care where her head was. Down the cut, in and out, the needle turning in the holder, a knot, a snip, the next. She didn’t hurry and she didn’t waste a single movement. It was like watching someone knit while they told you about their holiday.

She put her instruments down and put her hand up. The registrar checked the stopwatch, then the banana, and ran a fingernail along the line.

“Lin. Again. Unbelievable.”

The room groaned. The boy with the haircut put his head down on his arms. Xing Yue stayed at the glass with his hands in his pockets and didn’t go in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out with her bag on her shoulder and her cardigan buttoned wrong, eating the banana, and saw him and stopped dead.

“You’re faster than me,” he said.

She swallowed. “You were watching?”

“From the start.”

“Oh, no. Everyone says I talk too much to be a surgeon. Dr. Gan said it in second year in front of the whole class. Miss Lin, theatre is a quiet place. I said fine, then I’ll be quiet in it. I wasn’t. I’m still not.” She looked down at the banana. She’d eaten as far as the stitches.

“You can talk and sew at the same time. Most people can’t do either.”

The door banged behind her. The boy with the haircut came out with his board under his arm, saw who she was talking to, and rearranged his face. “Dr. Wang. Sorry. Would you mind looking at my knots? I’m never sure about the tension.”

Xing Yue looked at the banana without taking it. “Your third and fifth knots will slip by morning. In a person, that’s a bleed. You’re pulling the second throw up before the first one’s down, because you’re watching her and not your hands. Do fifty tonight. Not here.”

The boy went the colour of the banana. “Thank you, Dr. Wang.” He went down the corridor quickly.

Elara watched him go, and looked up at Xing Yue with her eyebrows somewhere in her hair. “That was Tung Kai. His father’s on the hospital board.”

“Then he’ll want his knots to hold.”

She laughed, one short startled laugh that went all the way up the corridor, and dropped the banana skin in the bin by the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Bian’s was up a steep flight of stairs above a tailor’s: eight tables, a kitchen you could see into, a calendar from a flour company on the wall, and the same plastic tablecloths it had had when Xing Yue first came south. Old Bian came out of the kitchen in his vest. He looked at Xing Yue, and at her, and at Xing Yue again, and said nothing, which from Old Bian was a speech.

Elara stood at the top of the stairs and looked down at herself. “I’m in my cardigan. There’s banana on it. You said dinner and I thought canteen, or noodles from a cart, so I didn’t change. And you’re in a coat.”

“It’s the coat I wear on the ward.”

“It’s a nice coat.”

“Sit down, Elara.”

She sat. The menu was written in chalk on the wall, and she read it the way she’d read Mr. Yin’s observation chart, every line from top to bottom, and then went back to some of it: the lamb dumplings, the cold cucumber, the noodles in chilli oil, the braised beef with eggs. When Old Bian came, Xing Yue ordered all four, and soup and flatbreads and a pot of tea.

“That’s far too much.”

“You looked at them twice.”

She went pink, and then she forgot to be pink, because the food came and she ate like someone who’d been on a ward since six in the morning, which she had. Then she began to talk.

Mr. Yin had asked for her twice today. The jelly really did taste of shampoo; she’d tried it, for science. Bananas were the closest thing to skin you could get for the price, because the peel held a stitch and tore if you were rough with it, exactly like skin. In first year they’d used chicken thighs from the market and the whole lab had smelled of it for a week and Tung Kai had been sick in a bin. “And in second year I split my jeans down the back seam at a bus stop on the way to an exam, so I went into the station toilets with my sewing kit and— No. Not that one yet. That’s a long one. Later.”

“Later.”

“You won’t forget? People forget. I’ve told that story as far as the beginning eleven times.”

“I won’t forget.”

“You say that now.”

So she told him about the Walled City instead, in pieces. A big family in a tall old house with too many stairs. Her father was in logistics; she made a face as she said it, because she knew exactly what anybody would think of that. Her big sister had a flower shop. Her brother drew buildings. Her other sister didn’t talk, and her little sister had three screens and knew everything about everyone. “She knew you eat beef noodles at eleven on call nights.”

He put his cup down. “She’s right.”

“Of course she’s right. She’s always right. It’s horrible.”

He listened to all of it, the brother and the bus stop and the chicken thighs, and found that he wanted every piece, not for anything, only to have it. He’d sat through hours of other people talking in his life: consultants, professors, his father’s board in the north saying the same six things down a long table. He’d felt that time go past like water over his hands. He didn’t feel it now. When he looked at his watch it was nearly eleven.

She caught him looking and stopped with a dumpling halfway to her mouth. “You’re doing it.”

“Doing what?”

“Listening. As if I’m a history and you’ve got to present me on the round tomorrow. Nobody listens to me like that. My family love me, but they stopped listening when I was about four. I never stop, so I’m a sort of radio.” She put the dumpling down.

“I’m not going to stop.”

“Everyone says that. Then about an hour in, their eyes go—” She did a face like a fish on ice.

“It’s been three hours.”

“It has?”

“Nearly.”

She looked at him across the plastic tablecloth for a long few seconds, and then she ate the dumpling.

Late, she remembered names. “I’m named after a moon. Did you know that? Elara is one of Jupiter’s. A small one. There are about eighty and nobody can name more than four, and I’m one of the ones nobody can name. My mother chose it. Baba says she liked the sound.” She was delighted by it.

He drank his tea and watched her get there. She’d seen his name on the rota a hundred times. She looked at the ceiling, and at the flour calendar, and back at him, and her face went red slowly from the neck all the way up.

“Star. And moon. Your name is star and moon,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Oh, no. Don’t tell anyone. If my brother finds out, he’ll put it on a cake.” She put both hands over her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

He paid while she was in the washroom. Old Bian counted out the change, looked at the door she’d gone through, and then at Xing Yue.

“She talks.”

“Yes.”

“Good. You don’t. Five years you’ve been climbing my stairs and I’ve had nine words out of you.”

“That’s not true.”

“Thirteen,” said Old Bian, as if that settled something, and went back into his kitchen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The stairs down were steep and narrow, with one bulb at the top and one at the bottom and nothing in between. She went first. On the last step but one she stopped under the bottom light and turned round, because it was story time.

“So I’m in the station toilets in my underwear with my jeans across my knees, and the sewing kit’s one of those tiny hotel ones with three colours of thread and none of them blue—”

He was on the pavement, one step below her, so that her face was almost level with his. He took his glasses off and folded them and put them in the pocket of her cardigan. She glanced down at the pocket and kept going.

“—and I’ve got eleven minutes before the exam, which is anatomy, and I’ve been up all night for it, so my hands are shaking, and I’m doing a running stitch down the whole back seam—”

He put two fingers to the side of her throat, under the angle of her jaw, where the pulse was. She stopped talking. He felt it, quick and light and hard, the way a bird’s heart feels if you’ve ever held one, and he took his time over it.

“Fast,” he said, and kissed her.

It began carefully. His fingers were still on her throat, checking that she was all right. She wasn’t all right, not in the least. She made a small sound against his mouth and took hold of his shirt in both fists, a great handful at the front on each side, and pulled him up the step into her so hard that he had to put his other hand flat on the wall beside her head. He forgot about her pulse, and the step, and the street, and Old Bian, who was certainly listening at the top of the stairs. She kissed him back. She tasted of tea and chilli oil. When he pulled her closer she went up on her toes and her clip gave up and fell, and he caught it without looking.

When they stopped she didn’t let go of his shirt. She stood on the step with her forehead nearly touching his and her breath coming quickly, her hair everywhere, laughing without any sound.

“Finish the story later,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had to get the spare glasses out of the glovebox before he could drive. She watched him do it with her hand in her cardigan pocket, and kept it there all the way down the hill. She wouldn’t let him drive into the Walled City. She made him stop at the mouth of the alley by the noodle stall, under its one streetlight.

“I’ll walk you to the door.”

“No. Not yet. If Baba sees a car he doesn’t know at the door after midnight, he’ll have the plate looked up before you’re home. I’m not joking. He has the postman checked every New Year, and it’s been the same postman for nine years.”

He didn’t like it, and kept that to himself. “All right.”

She got out and walked three steps up the alley. Then she came back, running, and bent to his open window with one hand on the roof of the car and her hair blowing across her face.

“I’ve got your glasses. In my pocket.”

“I’ve got another pair.”

“I know. I saw. But those ones are yours.”

“Keep them till Monday.”

She looked at him through the window. Then she leaned in and kissed the corner of his mouth, quickly, and straightened up and ran, up the alley and round the corner, past a red door he couldn’t quite see. She hadn’t come back for the glasses at all. He knew it, and she knew he knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana was sitting on the stairs inside the red door in a hooded sweatshirt, eating cereal out of the box.

“You’re missing a clip.”

“It fell.”

“Your hair’s down. Your cardigan’s buttoned wrong.”

“It was like that before.”

Eliana ate another handful without looking up from her phone. “His car’s still at the end of the alley. He’s waiting for your light.”

Her light was four flights up at the top of the house, the window that looked onto the alley. Elara took the stairs two at a time, all four flights, burst into her room, slapped the switch on and pressed her face to the glass. Down at the mouth of the alley, under the streetlight, a pair of headlights came on and sat there a second, and pulled away.

Nobody had ever waited for her light before. She stood at the window with her hand over her cardigan pocket, and from the bottom of the stairwell Eliana’s voice came up through the house.

“Gross.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the first red light on the hill road he found that his hand was still closed round something. Her hair clip. He opened the glovebox and put it in beside the empty glasses case, and looked at it there for longer than a grown man should look at a plastic clip. He didn’t give it back on Monday.

chapters.title: She Narrates Everything
chapters.desc: A month of noodles at eleven and slow walks to the taxi rank. Then she turns up at his flat with breakfast after his night on call, and doesn’t go home.
chapters.epigraph: “I thought it was sleep deprivation. I gave it fifteen months.”
chapters.content:
“You’ve had that drain on your list since eight.”

The registrar on the other end of the phone began to explain, high and fast, something about a blockage.

“It’s eleven o’clock. Don’t ring me to tell me it’s blocked. Ring me when you’ve been to look at it. More chilli?” He put the phone face down on the table and turned back to her.

Elara stared at him over her noodles. “That was horrible.”

“He’ll go and look at it. You were telling me about the man with the fish hook.” He pushed the chilli oil across the table.

She was, so she went back to it. What else was she going to do?

The noodle place across from the ambulance bay had four tables, a fridge full of beer nobody was allowed to drink and a television on a bracket that only showed horse racing. On call nights he came down at eleven in his scrubs with his pager clipped to his waistband, and from the second week of September she was there first. She’d moved to Dr. Fei’s team on the seventh floor by then, colorectal surgery, and they never crossed on the wards, which was the point. So she saw him here instead, and on the walk from here to the taxi rank at the main doors, which took four minutes if you were a normal person and twenty if you were her.

Tonight, outside, she took his hand. She’d never done that before. He looked down at it and didn’t say a word, and he held on the whole twenty minutes, and when the taxi came he was the one who let go last.

He kissed her in doorways. At the taxi rank against the pillar by the main doors, while the security guard studied the sky. In the porch of the old granite block, where nobody went at night. Once in the rain at the bottom of the hill, when a taxi went straight past them with its light on and she shouted after it, and he laughed and pulled her in under his coat and they got soaked anyway.

But never more than that on a call night. He’d told her so on the first one. “I don’t start anything I might have to walk away from in the middle.”

“That sounds very grand. Like a ship’s captain.”

“It isn’t grand. It’s true,” he said, and then his pager went, and he walked away in the middle. She found it maddening. She also found it sweet, which was worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Friday in October he was on call all night. She knew his rota better than her own by then: off at seven on Saturday morning, and he’d walk home down the hill, because he walked to work and only drove at night. She knew where home was, too. He’d given her the address in the second week, plainly, in case she ever needed it. She’d pretended not to write it down.

At dawn on Saturday she bought breakfast from the bakery by the hospital that opened first. Two custard buns, two egg tarts, a soy milk and a hot tea. The woman at the counter winked at her.

“Second bun for the boyfriend?”

“Yes,” said Elara, and then stood in the queue going hot. Since when? Since right now, apparently.

Fourteen Banyan Terrace was a white building from the fifties, four floors with curved balconies and a frangipani tree by the gate. His name was on the top buzzer. She stood there with the bag and her heart going, and thought that this was a terrible idea, because nobody had asked her, and he’d been up all night, and he was going to open the door and look at her like a blocked drain. She pressed the buzzer anyway.

Upstairs he was standing in the kitchen with his keys still in his hand. He’d been home four minutes and hadn’t managed to take his shoes off. When the buzzer went he looked at the little screen, and there she was, small and grainy, holding a paper bag up to the camera like a hostage note. He stood there a second longer than he needed to, looking. Then he let her in.

He opened the flat door in his scrubs and socks, with his glasses pushed up on his forehead and his face the colour of the hospital walls. He looked at her and then at the bag. “You shouldn’t have come. I’m no use to anyone. I’ve been in theatre since three.”

“I know. That’s why I came. You can tell me to go away and I’ll go away. But I’m leaving the buns.” She held up the bag.

He stood in the doorway, and then he stepped back.

It was the top of the building: two floors and a staircase going up to a roof she could see daylight coming down from. One wall was books from floor to ceiling, medical and otherwise, in no order at all. There were round flat cakes of tea stacked on a shelf by the kitchen, a long grey sofa, a low table and a good lamp, and that was all. No photographs. No plants. Her footsteps echoed.

“You live like a monk.”

“I live at work.”

She put the bag on the counter and turned round, and he was holding on to the back of the sofa. “Shower. Go on. You smell of theatre. I’ll make the tea, and then you’re eating something, and I don’t want to hear that you’re not hungry, because you’re a surgeon who’s been up all night and you’re always hungry, you just don’t notice,” she said.

He looked at her as if she’d spoken Portuguese. Then he went upstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came down in a grey T-shirt and soft trousers with his hair wet, and she sat him on the sofa and put a bun in his hand, and he ate it. Watching him do it was strangely satisfying.

“The bakery lady asked whether the second bun was for my boyfriend. I said yes before I’d thought about it. So that’s happened,” she said.

He stopped chewing, and then started again, more slowly.

She told him the jeans story at last, the whole of it: the station toilets, the hotel sewing kit, the pink thread, the anatomy exam.

“Pink?”

“There wasn’t any blue. I walked into anatomy with a pink seam all the way down the back of my jeans and I passed.”

He’d finished both buns and an egg tart, and he was leaning back against the arm of the sofa with his tea and his eyes half shut. He hadn’t looked away from her once.

He said, “I saw you before. Before the round. June last year, at Harbourside. I was rotating there. Your brother had been hit by a van, and I was called to look at his ribs, and you stopped me by the lift and asked whether anyone had checked his spleen.”

Elara stared at him. She tried. She went back through all of it: the phone at dawn, Baba’s face, the car, the corridor on six, Raiden in the bed with one eye swollen shut telling everyone he was fine in his stupid voice. The spleen, yes, she’d asked everyone about the spleen. But him? Nothing. Not his face, not the glasses, not even the height.

“Oh, no. I don’t remember you at all. I’m so sorry. That’s awful. You were there, and you were tall, and you were a doctor, and you told me about my brother, and I don’t remember a single thing about you.”

“I’d have worried if you did. You’d been up all night with your brother in a bed.”

“But you remembered me.”

“Yes. I thought it was sleep deprivation. I gave it fifteen months.” He drank some tea.

She sat with her hands round her cup and her face on fire, and opened her mouth, and nothing came out of it. Nothing came out of Elara Lin. He began to smile, which was rarer still.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him about the Lins then, because she was embarrassed, and when she was embarrassed she talked, and so far he’d only had the funny parts.

“Baba’s in logistics the way the tide’s in water. Anybody in the Walled City over fifty still goes a bit quiet when he walks down the street, even now he’s grey and frightened of his daughters.”

“Frightened of you?”

“Of Elowen. Everyone’s frightened of Elowen. I’m the fourth of five. And I’m not really any of their blood. I’m adopted. Baba brought me home from a children’s home when I was nearly three. That’s all I know. I asked once, when I was seven, and he said I’d come from a children’s home and he’d wanted me, and that was all there was to it, and he looked so sad that I never asked again.” She turned her cup round.

His jaw went tight. He was angry on her behalf at something he couldn’t see or cut out, and she could tell that he hated that more than almost anything.

“My mother died a few months after I came. Having my little sister. The house went quiet afterwards. Not for long. A month, maybe. But I remember it. All the doors shut, and nobody talking at dinner, and Baba sitting in the kitchen at night. I was three and I didn’t like it. So I talked. Somebody had to. I think I simply never stopped.” She kept her eyes on her cup. She shrugged.

She looked up, wondering whether that was too much for eight in the morning.

“Keep talking,” he said.

She laughed, a little wetly, and did. Ah Sim, who’d been with the family since before any of them were born and called her little sparrow. The noodle stall at the end of the alley. Her room at the top of the house with posters she was far too old for and refused to take down. “There’s a band on the second one. They were huge when I was twelve. The lead singer had this hair that went—”

He put his tea down and leaned across and took her chin in his fingers and tipped her face up to the window, the way you’d turn a patient to the light to look at their pupils. She kept going, naturally. “—it went up at the front like a wave, and they were called—”

He looked at her face in the morning light, checking something and finding it fine, and kissed her in the middle of the band’s name.

She laughed into his mouth, because he’d done it again, on purpose. He didn’t stop. After a while she stopped laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’ve got a rule. About call nights,” she said, a long time later, with her hands in his wet hair. He was lying back along the sofa and she was more or less on top of him. The tea had gone cold. The sun had moved round onto the books.

“That was last night. I’m off now.”

“That’s cheating.”

“It’s the rule.”

His glasses were on the table and his eyes were dark, wrecked and wide awake at once. He didn’t ask her anything. He put his hand flat on her back under her cardigan, warm through her shirt.

“Don’t go home,” he said.

She was already taking the cardigan off. His bedroom was under the slope of the roof, with a window onto the hill and the hospital tower and the harbour beyond it, and blinds that cut the morning into stripes. She talked. She’d known she would.

“You’re doing my buttons as if you’re taking out stitches. You are, though. As if you don’t want to mark the skin. I’ve watched you.” He didn’t answer. He went on, one at a time.

His mouth found her throat, the exact place his fingers had been on the steps, and stayed there.

“My pulse is probably a hundred and forty. You should write it down,” she said.

“Elara.”

“What?”

“Be quiet.”

“Make me. Oh. You’re—huh,” she said, and pulled his T-shirt over his head, and stopped with it in her hands.

“What?”

“Stronger than I thought. You’ve been hiding that under a white coat this whole time? That’s fraud.”

He laughed against her shoulder, low and startled. Then his hands were on her, warm on her ribs and her waist and the small of her back, careful and exact, learning her the way he’d learn a map he was going to be tested on. He took her shirt off. He kissed the inside of her elbow and the hollow under her collarbone and the soft skin below her breast, and every time she made a sound he stopped where he was and did it again. He was so careful that she started laughing again, and pulled him down by the back of the neck.

“I’m not going to break. I’ve watched you close an abdomen. I know you can go faster than this.”

He went still above her, and his breath went out once, hard, against her neck. “You’re sure.”

“Xing Yue.”

Then he wasn’t careful any more. She pulled him into her with her heels at the backs of his thighs and he moved in her, slow and then not slow, until there was nothing left of her but the weight of him and the heat and the stripes of light sliding up the ceiling. Somewhere in it she stopped narrating. She didn’t notice when; only afterwards. His breath ragged at her ear. Her hands on his back, holding on. Her own voice saying his name, every syllable of it. And his voice saying hers, all of it, every time; not once did he shorten it. So this was what all the talking had been for, she thought, much later: so that you’d know what it meant when you stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards he got up, and she thought he was going to the bathroom, but he pulled the sheet and blanket up over her shoulders and tucked them in firmly down both sides like a nurse on the ward, until she was a spring roll.

“What are you doing?”

“You’ve been up since dawn. Three o’clock. You’ll want to eat.” He fished her phone off the floor where it had fallen out of her cardigan, held it up to her face to unlock it and set an alarm.

“You’re the one who’s been up all night.”

“Yes,” he said, and lay down beside her on top of the blanket and went out like a light. Before he went he found her hand under the covers and turned her wrist over, and his thumb settled on the inside of it, on the pulse. She felt his hand go heavy as he fell asleep. It didn’t move.

She lay awake in the striped light looking at his face, younger asleep and less sure of itself, and thought about telling him something, and decided to keep it.

She woke at three to the alarm and an empty bed. There was a glass of water on the table, and on the pillow a note on a sheet torn off a prescription pad. His writing looked like a heart monitor having a bad day; the pharmacists at City Hospital rang him to ask what he’d written, and the nurses held his drug charts up to the window. She read it anyway. It didn’t take long.

Gone to buy food. Back by half past three. You don’t snore. You talk in your sleep. Don’t go home.

She lay back in his bed with the note on her chest and laughed until she had to put the pillow over her face.

The door went downstairs. Bags, and footsteps on the stairs. He came in with two carrier bags and stopped in the bedroom doorway.

“What did I say?” she demanded.

“When?”

“In my sleep.”

He put the bags down. “Something about Mr. Yin’s jelly.”

“I did not.”

“And my name.”

“How many times?”

“I wasn’t counting,” said Xing Yue, and when she threw the pillow at him he caught it, put it back under her head and went downstairs to cut up a mango.

chapters.title: The Family Is Not Told
chapters.desc: For her twenty-third birthday he gives her surgical loupes made for her eyes. She goes to the family dinner without him, and climbs into his car at midnight still in her dress.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re the one part of my life nobody’s ever bled on.”
chapters.content:
“It’s my birthday,” said Elara, “and you’ve bought me a pencil case.”

“Open it.”

He’d given it to her at breakfast because he couldn’t wait until the evening, and the evening wasn’t his. It was a Wednesday in the middle of November. She was sitting at his kitchen counter in his T-shirt and her own socks, eating rice porridge straight out of the pan. She stayed most nights now that weren’t call nights, and some that were; she’d sleep in his bed while he was at the hospital and leave it looking like a crime scene.

It was a hard black case, pencil-case sized, with a clasp. She put the spoon in the pan and opened it. Inside, in grey foam cut to fit, lay a pair of surgical loupes: glasses with little magnifying barrels set into the lenses, angled down for fine work. The frames were dark red. She’d said once, at Old Bian’s, that every pair she’d ever borrowed in the skills lab was black and made her look like a beetle.

She didn’t touch them. “These are through-the-lens. These are made for someone. For one person’s eyes. You can’t just buy them. You have to be measured, you have to— The eye test. In September. The email from occupational health. I went to the optician on the fourth floor of the old block and a woman measured how far apart my eyes were and made me hold a needle holder over a piece of foam at working height. I thought the university was just being strange. They once made us do a hearing test in a cupboard.” She stopped, and he watched her get there.

“I booked it.”

She took the loupes out of the foam and turned them over. Inside the left arm, tiny, in plain capitals, it said E.L. She put them on. He’d known they’d fit, and he’d still been worried. They sat exactly right on her small nose with the barrels at the angle of her eyes, and she looked down through them at the porridge pan, and at her own hands, and then, without meaning to, at his, on the counter. Then she started to cry.

“They cost more than my whole year. Fees and books and food.”

“They’re for twenty years of work. That isn’t expensive.”

“That’s not how money works.”

“It’s how mine works.”

She took them off and held them in both hands and cried on them a little, and wiped them on his T-shirt, and laid them back in the foam as if they were spun sugar, and shut the case. Then she put her arms round his neck from the stool and held on.

“You had me measured without telling me. You lied to me with an email,” she said into his collar.

“Yes.”

“That’s not normal.”

“No.” He didn’t say sorry. She wouldn’t have wanted him to. She held on tighter.

At the door, putting her shoes on, she asked him not to come to dinner. He’d known she would since the box.

“Not yet. It isn’t you. It’s Baba. You know what he’s like about the postman. If I bring a man to dinner he’ll have you looked into before the soup. City Hospital, chief resident, from the north, and then everything else. Your school, your grandmother, what you had for breakfast in 1998. Then he’ll sit at the end of the table and say nothing at you for three hours.”

“I can sit through three hours.”

“I can’t. I want to do it properly, when it’s a good time.”

“When’s a good time?”

“I don’t know yet. Soon.” She did up her laces.

He nodded, and kept the rest of what he thought to himself. She pulled him down by the collar and kissed him on the chin, which was as high as she could reach without a step, and went off down the stairs with her bag on her shoulder and the black case held against her chest like a hymn book.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the lifts that afternoon Fei caught him. “It’s your ex-student’s birthday. Lin Elara. The whole of the seventh floor sang to her at handover. The nurses made a card. Mr. Yin sent mooncakes in with his daughter, two months late, with a note.” She was watching his face hard.

“What did it say?”

“For the little doctor who talks. I thought you’d want to know.” Fei tilted her head.

“Thank you,” he said, and the lift came, and Fei got in and kept looking at him until the doors shut.

The dinner was in the Walled City, in a house he’d never seen, behind a red door he’d seen the edge of once in the dark. He sat at his desk all evening with a paper on bile leaks and read the first page four times, and then gave up and got the car keys. He drove the dark blue saloon across the city with the windows down and parked at the mouth of the alley, by the noodle stall with its shutters down, under the one streetlight, and switched the engine off and waited. He wondered whether this was what men did now, sat in cars in alleys. Apparently this one did.

Just after midnight the passenger door opened and she got in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was in a dress. He’d never seen her in one: dark green, plain, short-sleeved, to the knee, with a coat over it. Her hair was up, properly, with pins, for once, and some of it was already escaping. On her lap she had a bakery box, a bag of oranges and a paper crown from a cracker. She saw him looking and pulled the crown off.

“Raiden. He makes everyone wear them. Don’t drive yet. Let me tell you first or I’ll forget.”

She told him the whole dinner in no order whatsoever. Ah Sim had made long noodles and stood over her until she’d eaten the bowl without biting through a single one, for a long life, and she’d nearly choked. Raiden had made a six-minute toast, mostly about a crane. Elowen had brought a chestnut cake from the good bakery on Harbour Road, and her husband had stood behind her chair the whole time with his hands in his pockets like a wall. “A nice wall. A frightening wall.” Eliana had given her a memory stick and told her never to plug it into anything at the hospital, and wouldn’t say what was on it.

“Don’t plug it into anything at the hospital,” he said.

“I know.”

Then she stopped. “And Ev wasn’t there. My sister. The one who doesn’t talk. Something happened to her in October, and she won’t say what, and nobody will tell me. She’s staying up at Elowen’s house on the hill and she won’t come home. So I took her some cake on the way and sat with her for half an hour.”

“Did she talk?”

“Ev? No. So I talked for both of us. Mr. Yin. The jelly. The loupes. I told her about you. Not your name. Only that there was a you. And she looked at me. She doesn’t look at people much. She looked at me and I think she was pleased. You can’t always tell with Ev.” She turned the box a quarter turn on her knees. Her voice went odd.

He didn’t ask what had happened to her sister. He could see she didn’t know.

“And Baba asked if I was happy. At the end, when everybody was finding their coats. He doesn’t ask things. He’s learning. Elowen’s making him. He came and stood beside me by the fire and asked whether I was happy at the hospital, and I said yes, and he gave me his small-print look and said good. I didn’t say why.”

Then she went quiet. He turned in his seat to look at her, because she so rarely did.

“I’d like to be the why. Out loud. In front of them,” he said.

“I know. Soon, I promise. It’s just that everything in that house is everybody’s. Everybody knows everything and everybody’s had their hands in everything. Things come home in the middle of the night that you don’t talk about. You help, and you don’t ask, and you wash it off in the sink. You’re the one part of my life nobody’s ever bled on. I want to keep it like that for a bit.” She was looking out through the windscreen at the alley and the lamp on the wall and the corner she wouldn’t let him see round. She looked at him then.

He heard it twice. The first time it was the best thing she could think of to say about him, and she meant it, and he believed her. The second time, underneath, he heard a door being eased shut with him on the far side of it. She couldn’t hear that part at all. He let it go, for tonight.

She’d started again already: Baba at her school play when she was nine, in the front row in his coat, and the whole hall going silent, and the boy playing the king forgetting every line—

He reached across and took her hand off the bakery box and turned it palm up in the light from the streetlamp. A small wrist, blue lines under the skin. He found the pulse with his thumb, and it jumped when she felt him find it, and the king stopped. He bent his head and kissed the inside of her wrist, on the pulse, and then her mouth, hard, halfway through a word about the king.

She made a sound and grabbed his collar with her free hand. The bakery box slid off her knees and the oranges went everywhere. She came across the car at him as far as her seatbelt allowed, which wasn’t far, and swore at the belt into his mouth, and then she was laughing, and then she wasn’t. Her hand moved from his collar to the back of his neck and pulled him down, and her elbow hit the horn.

It went off down the alley like a ship. They broke apart. A shutter flew up somewhere over the noodle stall.

“Do you know what time it is?”

She clapped both hands over her mouth and shook with laughter, hair coming down, crown on the floor. Up the alley a dog started barking.

“Drive. Drive, before Baba comes out in his dressing gown,” she said through her fingers.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t let go of him all the way home. Her hand was on his knee, and then higher, and she talked quickly about nothing: the oranges rolling round the footwell, the woman over the noodle stall who’d been shouting at Raiden for twenty years. He took every bend on the hill road slower than he wanted to.

“You’re driving like a grandfather.”

“Yes.”

“On purpose?”

“Yes,” he said, and when her hand moved again he took the next bend slower still.

The green dress came off in the hall in the end. He’d meant to get her upstairs first. The zip was at the back, and she turned round on the stairs and stood with her back to him one step up, with her hair falling out of its pins.

“Please. It’s been driving me mad all night.”

He took the zip down one tooth at a time and kissed each part of her back as it came out of the green.

“Xing Yue. You’re meant to—”

“I’m doing it.”

“You’re doing it slowly.”

“Yes,” he said, and after that she gave up on the dress as a subject, and he took her up the rest of the stairs.

The first time he’d been slow because he hadn’t wanted to get anything wrong. Now he was slow because he knew how. Because it was her birthday, and because she’d shut a door on him in the car and he wanted, without a word about it, to be let back in by another.

He took her hair down one pin at a time and laid the pins in a row on the bedside table.

“Are you counting my hairpins?”

“No.”

“You are. You’ve put them in a line.”

He kissed the inside of her wrist again, and then the other wrist, and the inside of her elbow, and the hollow of her throat, and went on, and on, down the length of her, unhurried, until her talking slowed and broke and came back in a lower voice with no stories in it at all. She put her hands in his hair and held his head where she wanted it, and he let her, and stayed there until she was arching up off the bed with her heels dug into the sheet and his name coming out of her in pieces. Only then did he come up over her, and she pulled him down and in with her legs locked round him as if she’d been waiting all night to do exactly that, and he moved in her slowly, deep, his forehead on hers, watching her face in the light from the landing.

“Don’t stop. Don’t you dare—” she said.

“I won’t.”

Then it wasn’t talking any more. Only his name in the dark, again and again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on her front across the bed with her chin on her hands in the light from the landing, and he lay on his back and watched her think. Then she got up without a word and went downstairs naked and came back with the black case, and got back into bed, and opened it, and put on the loupes.

She turned and looked at him through them, close up: two little barrels pointed at his face, enormous eyes, a beetle in red glasses.

“Dr. Wang, I’m going to need to examine you more closely,” she said, in her best ward-round voice.

He laughed. Not the short sound she sometimes got out of him, half swallowed into her shoulder. He lay on his back in his own bed with his hand over his eyes and laughed out loud, helplessly, until his ribs hurt.

She sat beside him in the loupes and nothing else and stared down at him through the barrels. “I’ve never heard you do that.”

He couldn’t answer her. She took the loupes off and put them away slowly in the foam, and set the case on the table beside the row of hairpins. Then she lay down on top of him and put her ear flat to his chest.

“Do it again. I want to hear it from the inside,” she said.

chapters.title: Three in the Morning, on Speaker
chapters.desc: Her silent sister rings from a strange phone about a man with an infected knife wound who can’t go to a hospital. For three weeks Elara calls back at three every morning, and Xing Yue writes it all down and never asks who.
chapters.epigraph: “Go back to sleep. I’ve written it down.”
chapters.content:
In February she was on her student internship at Harbourside General, across the harbour: a junior doctor in everything except the pay.

She clerked and took blood and put in drips and wrote up drug charts for a registrar to sign. She did nights with her list in biro on the back of her hand. The patients adored her because she talked to them; she knew every grandchild on the surgical floor by name, and which old man wanted the window open, and which one had been a dancer and would show you his arms if you asked. She ate standing up at the nurses’ station and gave her egg tarts to whoever looked as if they needed one more, and she slept wherever she happened to be when she stopped, which was mostly his bed.

At 2:43 on the second Friday in February her phone went on the floor beside it.

She found it by feel on the fifth ring with her eyes shut. “Evangeline?”

“I need you.”

Elara was awake. Something in her changed the way it did on the wards at night, when a nurse called her name in a particular voice: the sleep went, and the warmth, and what was left was clear and cold and still. “What’s happened?”

“He’s burning. Forty. He’s not making sense. I think he’s hurt.”

The mattress moved. The lamp came on. Xing Yue was sitting up against the headboard, looking at her face; she hadn’t felt him wake. She put the phone on speaker and laid it on the duvet between them.

“Ring an ambulance now. A fever like that, and confused, with a wound: that’s an emergency. Do it now. I’ll hold,” said Elara.

They heard her sister ring, at the other end of a night, and give an address in a voice Elara had never heard her use, and say fever and confused and infected cut. Then she was back.

“Can you see it?”

“His side. The dressing’s wet. It’s red past the tape. There are stitches.”

“Don’t pull at it. Ask him when.”

A murmur. Then: “Saturday. Eleven stitches.”

It was Friday. Six days. Elara closed her eyes. “All right. When they come, you go with him. Stay with him. I’m coming.”

“It’s three hours.”

“Text me which hospital. Go,” said Elara.

The line went dead. She sat on the edge of the bed with the phone in her lap, and her hands had begun to shake, not from any old injury but from plain fright, all the way up to the shoulders.

Behind her Xing Yue was already getting dressed. He put her jeans on the bed beside her, and her jumper, and her coat. She looked up at him.

“Where are you going?”

“Wherever you’re going. It’s three in the morning and you’ve been on nights all week. I’ll drive.”

“You’ve got a list at eight.”

“Rao’s got a list at eight,” he said, and picked up his keys.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove north on the empty motorway with the heater on and the radio off, and he didn’t ask her a single question. She’d been waiting for them since the bedroom. Who is she, who is he, what kind of man has six-day-old stitches in his side and a fever of forty and a sister-in-law nobody’s met. She kept her hands in her coat pockets because she couldn’t make them stop, and watched the lights go past, and after an hour she couldn’t bear his silence any more.

“You’re not going to ask.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because you’d tell me. And then it would be mine as well as yours, and you’d have to decide whether that was all right, at three in the morning, in a car. You can decide later.” He kept his eyes on the road.

She looked at the side of his face in the green light from the dashboard. Then she put her head against the window and, for the first time since the phone went, breathed properly.

The county hospital was a low building at the edge of a market town, too bright inside. He parked where he could see the doors and switched the engine off. “I’ll be here.”

“It could be hours.”

“I’ve got a journal,” he said, and took one out of the glovebox, beside an empty glasses case and a plastic hair clip that she looked at, and then at him, and decided not to mention.

She found her sister in a plastic chair outside the treatment room with his shirt in a paper bag on her knees. Ev looked up. Elara had never seen her sister’s face so naked.

“How is he?”

“They’re treating him. He told me eleven stitches. Saturday. Six days, Elara.” Ev looked down at the bag.

“Six days. He’s in the right place now.” Elara breathed out through her nose and sat down beside her, hands in her pockets.

She stayed until the fever had begun to come down and the doctors had stopped looking at her sister. She met him once through a gap in the curtain: a big man with a white scar through one eyebrow and a drip in the back of his hand, asleep, frowning at something. Ev said his name, Jun Hyuk, the way you’d put a cup down on a table that might not hold it.

Xing Yue was where he’d said he’d be, with the journal open on the steering wheel and two cups of tea from the machine going cold on the dashboard. He put one in her hands. He started the car. He still didn’t ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

They let him out on the Monday into the back room at Nam’s, because Ev told the young doctor that someone would keep an eye on him and said it in a voice that made the young doctor write it down. On the Tuesday Elara went up again on the early bus to go through the clinic’s papers with them. On the Wednesday the stitches came out and Ev counted them. And on Thursday night, at three, Ev rang.

“The fever broke. At twenty-six minutes past two.”

That was the whole message. From Ev, it was a speech.

After that she rang every night at three. Elara never found out why three; perhaps it was the hour her sister had sat up through the worst of it and couldn’t unlearn. Every night for three weeks Elara’s phone went at three, and every night, without fail, Xing Yue was awake for it. He set an alarm on his side of the bed for five to three, low, and turned it off before it had properly started, and his hand found her shoulder in the dark.

The reports were short. The temperature. The colour round the wound. Whether he’d eaten. Whether he’d done as he was told, which mostly he hadn’t. Elara asked the questions she’d have asked on her own ward, and gave instructions, and Ev wrote them down; Elara could hear the pencil. Afterwards she’d lie awake with the questions going round, and once, at a quarter to four, she started to get up to find a pen, and his hand came across the dark and stopped her. “Go back to sleep. I’ve written it down.” He had, on the back of an envelope, by the light of his phone.

On the third night Xing Yue took the back cover off a journal, tore it off, blank side up, and handed it to her with a pen, and the next morning she found it on the kitchen counter under the teapot. He’d made it into a chart. The date, the time, the temperature, wound edges pink, no spreading redness, in a column down the left in her writing, and down the right, in square careful capitals, each letter separate, so that anyone on earth could have read them, the things to watch for and what to do if they happened. Nobody alive could read his ordinary handwriting except her. He’d written this so her sister could.

She stood in his kitchen in his shirt with the chart in her hands.

He was keeping notes on a patient he’d never been introduced to, at three in the morning, and he hadn’t asked his name.

✦ ✦ ✦

And every morning there was tea on the counter. He made it before she woke, the dark aged tea he drank, in the small brown pot under a folded cloth to keep it hot, and then he was gone to the hospital, or asleep, or at the table with a journal. He never mentioned it.

On the morning Ev said He’s eating, she came downstairs in his shirt and found him reading at the counter. She climbed onto the rung of the stool beside him to be tall enough, took his face in both hands and kissed him until he put the journal down.

“What was that for?”

“The tea. Every day. You think I don’t notice.”

His glasses had gone crooked. “I know you notice,” he said, and pulled her off the stool.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the second week he asked whether he could see where she was. He asked at breakfast, plainly, while she was looking for her other shoe.

“On your night shifts. You cross the harbour at two in the morning in taxis and walk from the ferry. If something happens, I want to know where.”

She laughed and found the shoe under the sofa, and got her phone out and did it there and then. She held the screen up so that he could watch her name appear on his: a small blue dot in his kitchen.

“There. Now you’ll know every time I go to the bakery.”

He put his phone in his pocket. He looked at it more than he’d ever have admitted: before a list, between cases, in the lift, four times before lunch on a Tuesday. It didn’t feel like a lot. It felt like taking a pulse. You didn’t stop taking a pulse because it was normal. He knew when she’d been to the bakery before she told him, and he knew when her taxi went the long way round the harbour.

“Roadworks?” he said, when she came in.

She stopped with her key in the door. “How did you—oh. The dot.”

“Were there roadworks?”

“Yes. That’s not the point. You’re supposed to pretend you don’t look.”

“Why?” he said, and she opened her mouth and couldn’t think of a single reason.

Once, on a night shift, she went down to the hospital car park at four in the morning for some air and stood by the ambulance bay in the cold for ten minutes, and her phone buzzed in her pocket.

Xing Yue: Car park?

Elara: AIR. Go to sleep.

Xing Yue: I’m on call.

She read it twice by the ambulance bay, and then she went back up to the ward smiling, and couldn’t have said why. Somebody was watching her stand in a car park at four in the morning, and she didn’t turn it off.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Thursday in March, at three, Ev asked whether he could have a shower.

“Yes. A quick one. Don’t scrub it, pat it dry, and if he’s an idiot about it I’ll know.” She hung up and lay back in the dark.

He was awake. He was always awake for the calls. His pager had gone earlier and he’d taken it in the kitchen, and she’d heard him through the floor, low and level and terrible: If you ring me about a potassium of four point one again, I’ll come in and give it to you myself. Then he’d come back up and got into bed and put his warm hand on her hip and waited with her for three.

“She’s got a man. Ev. My sister who says about ten words a month. She’s got a man, and he’s alive, and he wants a shower. He was burning on a camp bed in February and all he had was her. And I don’t know what he does that means he waits six days with an infected cut before anyone rings an ambulance—” said Elara to the ceiling.

“Elara.”

“—and Ev’s never had anybody. She’s never even let anyone sit next to her on the bus, and she rang me—”

“It’s three in the morning. You’ve got a ward round at eight.”

He brushed her hair off her face and tucked it behind her ear, and she let him, and kept talking anyway.
