“When she was little she used to sit under the kitchen table with a book while everybody shouted. She grew orchids on the windowsill and checked the roots without touching them. I always thought she’d end up alone in some tall room full of plants and be perfectly happy. I never once thought she might want—”

He leaned over her in the dark and stopped her mouth with his. She made a surprised sound, and then she stopped being surprised and got her arms round his neck and pulled him down on top of her. The duvet slid half off the bed. She felt him laugh against her mouth.

“You said sleep.”

“I changed my mind,” she said, and pushed him onto his back and came over him, and for a long while after that neither of them said anything that wasn’t the other’s name. They didn’t sleep until the blinds had gone grey.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest and watched the light come.

Three weeks of calls at three in the morning. Six hours of motorway in the dark. A man with no history and her sister in a back room somewhere. He hadn’t asked once: not who, not where, not why. He’d set alarms and made tea and sat up every night and kept a chart.

She had a world that rang in the middle of the night, and she’d always gone towards it when it did, without thinking. She’d always believed that was the part of her nobody would put up with: that one day somebody would sit her down and say, them or me.

She lifted her head. He was asleep, with his thumb on the inside of her wrist. She looked at his face for a while and wondered whether he ever would say it. Then she put her head down again. She’d stopped wondering.

chapters.title: A Bullet on the Hill
chapters.desc: Her sister’s husband crawls home with a bullet in his side, and Elara steals what she needs from the hospital. Xing Yue walks into the supply room and catches her, and she begs him not to ask.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t ask me. If you ask, I’ll tell you.”
chapters.content:
The emergency department at City Hospital on a Saturday night sounded like a market on fire, and she loved it. It was her last rotation before finals, six weeks of it, and she loved it more than anything except the bananas. A drunk man in cubicle four was singing, badly. A girl in cubicle six had put her hand through a window and was brave about it in front of her boyfriend and not brave at all once he’d gone for coffee.

“He’s an idiot,” said Elara, opening a suture pack.

“He’s not an idiot.”

“He went for coffee while you’re bleeding.”

“All right, he’s a bit of an idiot,” said the girl, and laughed, and forgot to watch the needle, and that was the job done.

Upstairs Xing Yue was in theatre with an appendix. He’d texted at midnight.

Xing Yue: Appendix. Then possibly another. Eat something.

She’d sent him a photograph of a biscuit. At twenty past three she was eating another one at the nurses’ station when her phone rang with a number she didn’t know.

“Miss Elara? It’s Peng. From the gate at your sister’s. The house on the hill. Mr. Zhao’s come back. The dogs found him at the gate. Gunshot, left side, three days, a fever. He’s been in the sea. Mrs. Zhao says bring everything. She says no hospital. She says you’ll know.” A young man’s voice, steady, saying it all in order the way he’d been told to. The voice cracked once, on three days, and steadied again.

She put the biscuit down. “I’m coming.”

She was already walking.

✦ ✦ ✦

The surgical supply room was off the corridor between the emergency department and the lifts, with a keypad on the door whose code every student knew because the nurses said it out loud. She went in and shut the door and stood with her back against it for one breath. Then she started.

Two big blue bags from the stack by the door, the ones the porters used for linen, open on the floor. Bags of fluid off the shelf: four, six; three days and a fever; eight. Giving sets. Cannulas in two sizes, a handful of each. Tape. Saline for washing, the big bottles, as many as she could lift. Gauze, a box and then another. Gloves. A green drape in its paper. Local anaesthetic, syringes, needles. A suture pack she wouldn’t use, because you didn’t close a wound like that after three days in the sea, and took anyway. On the shelf by the window were the sterile instrument sets from theatre sealed in blue wrap, and she took the top one. Antibiotics: the shelf where they should have been was empty. The emergency drug cupboard was two doors down, in front of the nurses’ station. Fine. She’d smile at Sister Kuai and say she’d been sent, and Sister Kuai would believe her, because everybody always believed her. She was planning the smile and the exact words. Her hands were quick and steady. Her heart was going so hard she could feel it in her teeth.

The door opened behind her. She spun round with a bag of fluid in each hand. It was him, in theatre scrubs and cap, his mask pulled down round his neck, his glasses on. He’d come down for a drain for a man in resus with an abscess, and he came in fast, the way he did everything, and stopped.

He looked at the blue bags on the floor and the fluid and the cannulas and the saline and the instrument set in its wrap, and at her, in her scrubs at half past three in the morning, holding a bag of fluid in each hand. The two bags knocked together. She watched him understand: everything you would need to keep someone alive on a table that wasn’t in a hospital.

His mouth opened.

“Don’t. Don’t ask me. If you ask, I’ll tell you. I’ll tell you everything, I won’t be able not to, and then it’s yours too, and you’ll have to do something about it, because you’re the chief resident, and I can’t— Please. Please don’t ask me,” she said, and it came out of her like a sob. Her voice cracked straight down the middle.

He didn’t say anything. He stood in the doorway and looked at her. Out in the corridor somebody laughed, and a trolley went past, and the drunk man in cubicle four started a new song. She never knew how long it lasted. Then he came in and shut the door behind him.

He crouched by the bag on the floor and took out the instrument set and turned it over and read the typed list from sterile services on the wrap. He put it back on the shelf.

“Take the other one. That one’s missing a needle holder. I won’t ask.” He took down the next set, read its label, and put it in her bag.

She stared at him. “Antibiotics. They’re in the drug cupboard. I have to go past the station,” she said.

“Which?”

She told him. He went out. She stood alone in the supply room with both hands over her mouth, and wondered what she’d done, and what he was doing. He came back with two boxes and put them in the top of the second bag under the gauze without a word. She found out much later that he’d signed them out to the man with the abscess.

He carried both bags down the corridor himself, past the ambulance bay and out to the taxi rank at the main doors, in his theatre scrubs, at twenty to four in the morning, as if he did it every night. He opened the back door of the first taxi and put the bags in, and they clinked, and the driver looked round and then looked hard at the windscreen. He didn’t ask her where she was going. He took his phone charger out of his scrubs pocket, cable and plug, and pushed it into the outside pocket of her bag. She didn’t know why. She’d find out at seven.

Then he put his hand on the back of her head under her hair and kissed her against the side of the taxi, hard and short, nothing like the slow kisses at the rank in the autumn: the kind you give with your mouth when there’s nothing else your hands can do. The car was cold through her scrubs. She held on to his arms. He let her go.

“Go. Ring me when you can.”

When she twisted round in the back seat he was standing on the kerb under the lights of the main doors with his hands at his sides. Then the taxi turned onto the hill road and he was gone.

“Where to, miss?”

“The hill road. Past the sea road, all the way to the top. Please hurry.”

“The hospital’s behind you, miss.”

“I know where the hospital is,” said Elara, and the driver looked at her in the mirror and drove.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went back up to theatre, where the second appendix was waiting, and scrubbed and opened, and his hands did what they always did.

“You came back from resus without the drain,” said the registrar.

“Yes.”

“Do you want me to go and—”

“I want you to watch the bleeder at your left hand. You’ve missed it twice.”

Between that case and the next he stood in the theatre corridor with his phone, and watched a small blue dot move fast along the sea road and up the hill and stop near the top. He didn’t know whose house it was. He wasn’t going to look.

Suyin came out of the changing room with her cap in her hand. “You’ve been staring at that phone for five minutes.”

“Yes.”

“Is it bad news?”

“I don’t know yet,” he said, and put the phone away, and took it out four more times before dawn.

✦ ✦ ✦

She arrived just after four, with her hair scraped back in a knot and her pearl earrings still in, and Peng ran up the drive after the taxi with the gate standing open behind him. Every light in the kitchen was on. Zhao Zhendong was on the kitchen table on a door with his shirt in rags, grey, blue at the lips, with a towel held to his side. Her sister stood at the head of the table in her nightdress with gravel cuts on her bare feet, and Raiden was at his shoulders in a T-shirt, and Elara felt her own face go white, and then still, and then become somebody else’s.

She put the bags on the counter. “Move the lamp. Clear the table. Towels, boiled water, every light in this room.”

They moved. She opened the bags.

“Where did you get all that?” said Elowen.

“Don’t ask.”

“Elara—”

“Not tonight. Later, if you like. Not tonight. Has he been awake?” She pulled on gloves.

“For a minute. At the gate.”

“Did he say anything?”

“He asked about dinner.”

Elara looked at her sister, and despite everything let out one short breath through her nose. “Of course he did.”

She cut away what was left of the shirt and lifted the towel. Three days in a fish hold and a crawl up the hill had done what three days would. She checked his pulse and his pressure and his breathing, and said what it was out loud in a flat voice so that Elowen would hear it as facts: infected; it needed opening and cleaning and every bit of dead tissue out; properly that was a theatre and an anaesthetist; she could numb the edges, but she couldn’t put him under on a kitchen table without monitoring, so it was going to hurt him a great deal.

“If his breathing changes, if he stops responding, if it bleeds faster than I can deal with, we stop pretending and he goes to a hospital, and we live with what happens. Say yes.”

“Yes.”

“Then go to his head and hold it, and talk to him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she could never put the two and a half hours in order. The long bright light over the table that Elowen had chosen for cooking. The packed shirt coming out of him in stiff black strips one at a time, and the sound he made, which she didn’t stop for. Saline running off the edge of the table onto the floor and the guards on their knees with towels, pink and red and pink. Cutting away what was dead in tiny snips with the instruments from the set he’d chosen for her. The needle holder was in it, exactly where it should have been, and she thought of him for one second, and put him away.

She didn’t talk. Everyone remembered that afterwards: Elara, silent for two hours. She didn’t know she was doing it. Only the small words under her breath. All right. There. All right.

Elowen talked. Elowen held his face between her hands and talked the whole time, the night he’d come in out of the rain and bought every flower in the shop, the registry, the dogs, the estate in the rain, and when he screamed she put her forehead against his and kept going. Raiden leaned on his shoulders. Peng kept the water coming and turned his face away every time it came back red. At some point Zhao said a number through his teeth, and Elowen laughed and cried at once, and Elara said, “He’s answering. That’s good. Keep him with you,” without looking up.

At one point she felt her sister look at her hands. Two years ago, over a teacup, they’d shaken so badly that Elara had laughed and switched to a mug. They weren’t shaking now. They hadn’t shaken for months: not since the brace a woman with grease to the elbows had machined for her in a back room by the docks, a woman Raiden had taken her to one evening in 2021 and asked her never to mention, and the hundreds of hours Elara had put in on it afterwards, alone. Elowen looked, and saw, and looked back at her husband’s face, and said nothing. Elara loved her for it so much that she had to stop for a second and breathe.

When he tried to move she said, “Hold still, you idiot,” as tenderly as she’d ever said anything.

Chen Si came in at twenty to six, soaked to the bone, and crossed the room and put his hand on his brother’s shoulder and couldn’t seem to take it off again, and then went and stood against the wall by the fridge and didn’t move.

At half past six she finished the dressing and stripped her gloves off, red to the wrist, and stood with her hands held away from herself and looked at her sister.

“That’s what I can do here. He needs a hospital,” she said.

“He can’t have one.”

“I know. Then he has me. Every day, morning and night, till he doesn’t. And you call me the minute anything changes. I don’t care what time it is.” Elara washed her hands at the kitchen sink, slowly, to the wrists.

At seven Raiden and Chen Si lifted the door between them and carried him up the stairs a step at a time, and Elara walked beside them holding a bag of fluid up in the air, and Elowen came behind with her hand on his foot because she couldn’t reach anything else. Elara hung the drip from a coat hook in the big bedroom and checked the line and his breathing and his colour, and wrote them on the back of an envelope off the dressing table with the time, the way Xing Yue would have.

Her phone was dead. She found out in the corridor: a black screen. She stood there in her ruined scrubs and stared at it. Then she remembered the outside pocket of her bag, and his charger, cable and plug, and plugged it into the wall by the stairs and sat down on the top step and put her face in her hands. He’d known. She didn’t know how he’d known, but he’d known her phone would die before the night was over.

She locked herself into the guest bathroom at the far end of the corridor and texted him.

Elara: Alive. For now.

The reply came before she’d put the phone down. He’d been holding it.

Xing Yue: Good. Eat.

She turned the bath tap on full so that it roared, and slid down onto the floor with her back against the bath and her knees up and his charger in her fist, and cried with her other hand over her mouth, so that nobody in the house would hear her over the water. Good. Eat. Who said that to someone who’d just done this? Only him. She cried harder, and didn’t know whether it was for her sister, or the man on the table, or the two words on her phone that had asked her nothing at all.

chapters.title: Fifteen Days of Drips
chapters.desc: For two weeks she changes drips and dressings on the hill, and he drives her there in the dark and waits at the bottom of the road. On the last night he asks one question.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not asking who. I only want to know if he’s alive.”
chapters.content:
“How did you know the times?”

She was blinking at him from his sofa with her shoes still on. She’d come down from the hill for two hours to shower and sleep, and had slept for forty minutes, and now her alarm was going and so was his.

He turned her wrist over and showed her. The list was on her own skin in blue biro: drips every four hours round the clock, dressings morning and evening. He’d copied the whole of it into his phone while she slept, and then into hers, with a different sound, so that if one alarm didn’t wake her the other would wake him.

She looked at her wrist and then at him, and laughed for the first time since Saturday, short and tired and cracked, and put her face against his arm. “You’re a witch.”

“I can read.”

“Nobody can read that. I wrote it in the dark with my left hand.”

“You write better with your left hand than I do with my right.”

“That isn’t hard,” she said into his sleeve.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her back. He stopped at the bottom of the hill road where it left the sea road and began to climb, two kilometres below the gate, at a bus shelter with a streetlight and nothing else. A car came down out of the dark to meet her, one of the cars from the house, with the young guard from the gate at the wheel.

She had her hand on the door. “You could take me to the top.”

“No.”

“It’s only two kilometres—”

“No,” he said again, and she looked at him and no explanation came, and she let it go. She’d asked him not to ask, and he’d said he wouldn’t. If he drove up to that gate he would see, and whatever he said afterwards, he would have seen. He’d decided that in the supply room. It was simple.

She got out. The car took her up into the dark. He switched off his engine and sat there.

On Monday she rang him in clinic. He was between patients in a small room on the third floor with a couch and a sink and a window onto the car park, and he answered on the first ring because the phone was already in his hand under the desk. At first she didn’t say anything. He heard a corridor, and breathing, and someone crying with a hand over their mouth so that a house full of people wouldn’t hear.

“Elara. Breathe first. Then tell me.”

She breathed twice, exactly as she’d have told a patient to. “It hasn’t broken. The fever. It’s the second day. It should be coming down by now. It’s thirty-nine eight.” Her voice went thin.

He didn’t ask who or where or with what. He asked what he’d have asked a registrar at two in the morning: the last dose, the heart rate, whether he was passing water, whether the wound was redder than it had been that morning. Then he told her what he’d watch for over the next six hours, and what would make him stop watching and put the patient in a hospital whatever anybody said.

“That’s what I said. That’s exactly what I said to them.” Her voice came back up.

“Then you were right. Eat something. Ring me at six.”

He turned the phone over on the desk and sat with his hand flat on it. Then he called in the next patient, a woman with a hernia, and was completely courteous to her for fifteen minutes.

The phone buzzed on his pillow in the small hours of Tuesday.

Elara: It broke

Elara: it broke!! he’s sweating through everything. heart rate down to 96

He’d been awake since one, lying on his back in the dark watching the small blue dot of her on the hill not move.

Xing Yue: Sleep now. I’ll fetch you at four.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that he drove her every morning. She’d gone back to the emergency department in the daytime, because finals were in seven weeks and she couldn’t not, so she went up the hill twice a day: in the evening by taxi after her shift to change the packing, and just before dawn, with him, to change it again before she was due on the floor.

He picked her up outside the main doors in the dark and drove across the city with the windows down so that she wouldn’t fall asleep. The bus shelter, the streetlight, the car from the house, up into the dark; engine off. He waited. Sometimes he slept in the driver’s seat with it tipped back and his glasses on the dashboard; you learned to sleep anywhere as a resident. He woke every time a car came down the hill, and it was never hers, and he went back to sleep. Then the car brought her down and turned and went back up, and she walked across in the grey light with her bag on one shoulder and a black bin bag knotted at the top in the other hand.

The first morning he got out and held his hand out for it.

“It’s clinical waste. You can’t just—”

“I know what it is.”

“And if somebody finds bloody dressings in your boot?”

“Nobody looks in my boot.”

“Somebody might.”

“Who?” he said, and she opened her mouth, and couldn’t think of anyone who’d dare.

He put it in the boot. When he went in for his day he carried it down to the waste room behind the boiler house in the basement and dropped it into the yellow bin with everyone else’s, where nobody would ever look at it again. He did that every morning for two weeks.

On the Wednesday he went down to the theatre office and asked for the stock book, an old ledger they still kept because the computer lost things. On Saturday night’s page, against the appendix he’d done, he wrote: One instrument set opened, contaminated, returned for reprocessing. Then the fluids, the dressings, the gauze, near enough to what had gone out of the supply room in two blue bags. He initialled it.

The theatre manager, who’d known him for six years, looked over his shoulder. “Busy night.”

“Yes.”

“All that for one appendix?”

“It was a difficult appendix.”

“It must have been,” she said.

He put the book back on the shelf. He’d never written anything untrue in a hospital record in his life, and he looked at his initials a second longer than he needed to. Then he went to his ward round.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday Dr. Hsu caught him at the lifts. He was the emergency department’s student lead, a good doctor and a kind man, and he actually wanted to know. “Your Miss Lin. She’s missing shifts. Leaving early. She looks as if she hasn’t slept since Christmas. Is there something I should know?”

“It’s a family emergency. It’s real. She’ll make up the hours.”

Hsu waited for more. There wasn’t any. “All right. Tell her that if she needs anything she can come to me.”

“I’ll tell her,” said Xing Yue, and meant it.

On the Friday it was Dr. Nie, an emergency registrar two years ahead of him in training and two years behind in everything else, who liked to stand at the nurses’ station and talk loudly enough for the patients to hear. Xing Yue was down for a gallbladder referral. Nie leaned on the station beside him with a coffee.

“Your little student friend’s gone walkabout again. Third time this week. Rolled in at ten yesterday. Some of us were here at eight.”

The nurses at the station went quiet. Xing Yue finished writing in the gallbladder man’s notes and signed them and put his pen in his pocket.

“Would you like to talk about your own absences instead? The two Fridays in February when you were on a course that has no record of you. The afternoon in January when you left your list to a first-year and went to the races. I can tell you which horse. Or you could go and see the man in bay three, who’s been waiting an hour and a half with a broken wrist.” He picked up the notes.

Nie put his coffee down on the station and went to bay three, and nobody in the department asked about Miss Lin again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He fed her. She didn’t eat otherwise, so he put food into her hand: rice balls in seaweed from the shop by the ferry, soy milk with the straw already in, red-bean buns from the bakery by the hospital, which opened at six, which was when he went, and he was back before she was out of the shower. There was a box on the passenger seat every morning, and she ate it on the way across the city without noticing she was eating, talking with her mouth full, and he watched it empty out of the corner of his eye.

“Is this egg?”

“Yes.”

“I hate egg.”

“You’ve eaten two.”

“I hate egg less at five in the morning.”

Between the dawn dressing and her shift she slept in his bed, and between her shift and the evening dressing she slept in his bed. He came home at lunchtime twice that week, which he never did, and both times she was face down on the duvet in her scrubs with her shoes on. He took the shoes off and put the blanket over her, and she didn’t wake. He put her shoes by his front door facing out, side by side, so that when the alarm went in the dark she could step straight into them without bending or turning on a light. On the third day she noticed. He heard her stop in the hall in the dark.

“Did you turn my shoes round?”

“Yes.”

“They look like two little dogs waiting for a walk,” she said, and laughed, and stepped into them. She kept them that way afterwards and never said why.

One morning, halfway across the city, she fell asleep in the middle of a sentence about a man in the department with a fish bone in his throat who’d insisted on keeping the bone. “—and he wanted it in a little bag, like a—”

He looked across. Her head had gone against the window, her mouth slightly open, and she was breathing slowly for the first time in a week. She was due at the bus shelter in a quarter of an hour. He drove past the turning for the hill road, on along the sea road to the roundabout at the end, round it and back, past the turning to the roundabout at the other end and round and back again, slowly, in the dark, with the sea on one side and the hill on the other. Twice. It came to twenty minutes.

When he stopped at the bus shelter she woke and saw the clock. “Oh, no. I’m late. I’m late. Did you drive round?” Then she looked at him.

“Twice.”

“You can’t just—”

“It’s a dressing, not a drip. It’ll keep twenty minutes. You won’t.”

She stared at him, and got out with her bag and went up the hill, and he didn’t regret it in the least.

On the tenth morning she came down grey. He took the bin bag, and then he took her chin and turned her face to the streetlight and drew her lower eyelid down with his thumb, gently, as he would have in clinic, looking for anaemia.

“I’m not anaemic. I’m tired. I’ve had about nine hours’ sleep in four days. You don’t need to examine me in a bus shelter—”

She was the one who kissed him, to stop him, with her hands in the front of his coat, and when he kissed her back she put her arms inside it round his waist and leaned on him with her whole weight, as if her legs had just been told they could stop. He held her up. A car came down the hill road, and its lights went over them and away.

“Fine, I’m pale,” she said into his mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fifteenth day was a Sunday. She texted at half past four in the morning.

Elara: Last one I think. Come and get me?

He was at the bus shelter early. She came down as the sky was going grey over the sea, and the car from the house left her and went back up, and she walked across slowly with her bag on her shoulder and no bin bag. He got out and stood by the car and watched her come. She stopped in front of him.

“That’s the last one. He’s on tablets. He can do his own dressings, or my sister can; I’ve shown her. He walked to the bathroom on his own yesterday and hated every step of it. I’m not going back up. Except for lunch, at home. It’s my brother’s birthday.” She was looking at his chest.

He’d promised. For fifteen days he’d driven her to the bottom of a hill in the dark, carried a stranger’s blood to a bin, written a lie in a book and taken a registrar apart in front of a whole nurses’ station, and not asked one question. He asked one now.

“I’m not asking who. I only want to know if he’s alive.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Her eyes filled. “It was my sister’s husband. Elowen’s. He’d been shot three days before and he crawled up from the sea. You didn’t ask, so I’m telling you. I wanted to.”

He put his hand against the side of her face. “I’m glad it was you up there.”

She got into the car and didn’t put her seatbelt on, and he was reaching for the key when she climbed over the gearstick into his lap. It wasn’t graceful. Her knee hit the steering wheel and her bag fell in the footwell and her elbow knocked his glasses sideways.

“Ow. Sorry. Ow—”

“Elara—”

“Be quiet,” she said, and framed his face with her hands and kissed him. He shoved the seat back blind with one hand to make room, and she followed him down with it, her hands in his hair, his mouth and his jaw and his mouth again, a small desperate sound at the back of her throat. Fifteen days, all at once. He held her and let her.

Then, slowly, she slowed. The kisses grew softer and further apart, and her forehead came down against his and stayed there, and her hands went loose in his hair and her whole weight settled on him, warm and heavy.

“Sorry. I’m so tired. I’ve got to tell you about the gauze. Ev’s got this way of folding it, in thirds, she says it’s how our mother folded towels. And I love you. And it’s so much neater than mine, I’m going to start doing it on the ward—” she said, slurring.

She was asleep. He sat in the driver’s seat at the bottom of the hill road with her face in his neck and her breath on his skin and his glasses crooked on his nose, and left them crooked. She’d never know she’d said it. He wondered whether it counted, if she was asleep, and decided that it did.

He sat there an hour without moving, while the sea went from grey to silver behind her. He’d keep it, like something a person drops without noticing, and give it back to her when she knew she’d lost it.

chapters.title: Every Wrong Answer
chapters.desc: Finals, flashcards in bed and a dare he cheats on. She graduates with her family in the hall, and on the back stairs afterwards he hands her a form already filled in, and she says yes in the middle of a sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “Get it wrong and I’ll kiss you anyway.”
chapters.content:
“Leave her. Leave her, it’s beautiful. She’s like a statue.”

Elara opened her eyes. Sunday lunch, the long table in the Walled City, a dumpling held in her chopsticks an inch from her mouth, and her arm aching. She didn’t know how long she’d been holding it there.

“The dumpling’s going cold, sparrow.”

“I’m awake, Ah Sim. I’m awake.”

She’d come straight down from the hill after the last dawn dressing and an hour asleep in a car, because Sunday lunch was Sunday lunch, and today it was her brother’s birthday and Evangeline’s too, on paper, and Ah Sim had made two cakes for the first time in fifteen years. They stood in the middle of the table, one with small yellow sugar flowers and one with a slightly drunk border of chocolate cream. Everyone was looking at Elara. Nobody was laughing except Raiden, who was also photographing the cakes for Elowen, who hadn’t come. Baba was looking at her as if she were a ship that was late.

“Night. Sorry. I’m fine,” she said.

She ate the dumpling cold.

At the end of the table Evangeline sat straight in pale blue with her black ribbon in her hair, looking at the second cake. When she reached for the vinegar Elara watched her hand cross the cloth, half asleep, and saw it: a ring, plain silver, on the fourth finger of the left hand. She looked at it, and at her sister’s face, which was doing nothing at all, as usual, and at Raiden, who had seen it too and gone still, and at their father, who had seen it and was looking at his tea.

Ev had never once asked about the phone calls at three in the morning. Elara thought she could manage not asking about a ring.

✦ ✦ ✦

Finals began in the middle of May. She revised at his flat, because the tall house had too many stairs and too many people on them and a brother who kept coming in to explain drainage. His flat had a study nobody used: a desk, a lamp and nothing else. Within a week she’d spread over the whole of it. Textbooks. Flashcards in rubber bands. Highlighters with their lids off. A skeleton hand on loan from anatomy, due back at the end of term.

He’d come in at night and find her asleep across the desk with her cheek on the brachial plexus and a highlighter in her fist, and take the highlighter and put its lid on and carry her upstairs. Sometimes, before he carried her, he stood in the doorway for a while with a tape measure, and she never knew.

“Be horrible. Be like you are on the round. Be like you are with Rao. If I get it wrong I want to feel as if I’ve been run over,” she said, at midnight in the second week. She was cross-legged in his bed in one of his shirts with a stack of flashcards in her lap.

He took the cards and read the first one. “Signs of a tension pneumothorax.”

She got most of it, and forgot one.

“Nearly.”

“Nearly? That’s what you’d say to a dog. Do the voice. The you’re-not-tying-your-shoelaces voice.”

He looked at her over the card and opened his mouth, and she watched him try. He got as far as the first word of something cutting, and then he looked at her, cross-legged in his shirt with her hair everywhere, and gave up. “I can’t.”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s you.”

She went pink and snatched the card and hit him on the arm with it. “That’s lovely, and it’s not helpful. Fine. A dare. Every one I get right, you kiss me. Every one I get wrong, you tell me something about you. Something real. Because you never tell me anything. You listen. I’ve told you everything I’ve thought since I was three, and I know about four things about you, and one of them’s your shoe size.” She put her chin on her hand, and he could see her plotting.

He thought about it for exactly long enough to make her regret it. “All right.”

She got the first one right, the causes of a raised calcium, and he leaned across and kissed the corner of her mouth, lightly, like ticking a box. The second was right as well, and that one was longer, with his hand on her knee. The third she knew was wrong while it was still coming out of her: two nerves in the hand, mixed up, which she never mixed up.

“Wrong. Go on. Something real,” she said.

He kissed her.

“That’s cheating. That was a wrong one. You don’t get to—”

“Get it wrong and I’ll kiss you anyway. I’ll pay later,” he said.

They did about a dozen cards. By the last one they were all over the floor and his shirt was half off her shoulder and his glasses were on the bedside table and she was underneath him, laughing and then not, with her hands pushing his T-shirt up his back. “You owe me three. You owe me three—” she said, against his mouth.

“I know,” he said, and didn’t stop, and she didn’t want him to.

He paid on the Thursday. She was on the sofa with her feet in his lap and a textbook on her chest, and he was reading a journal, and he didn’t look up.

“My father wanted me to run his hospitals. In the north. A group of them, private; my grandfather built them, and my father’s the chairman. I was supposed to train there and go on the board and take it over. I wanted to cut people open, not sit in a room and talk about them, so I came south, as far as I could get. That’s one. Two. I have a brother. An Yu. Three years younger. He started a company at twenty-two and earns more before breakfast than I will in my life, and he rings every Sunday to tell me I work too hard.” He turned a page.

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“What’s three?”

He put the journal on his knee and looked at her socks, which didn’t match. “Three is that I’ve never told anyone the first two. Not like that. Not because they wanted to know.”

She climbed along the sofa and put her arms round his neck, and the textbook slid off onto the floor and nobody picked it up. A few hospitals, she thought. Some clinics. A family business, like hers. She’d find out in the autumn how wrong she was.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the third week of finals her phone rang in the middle of the night with Baba’s number, which was never Baba.

“Little sister. Sorry. Sorry. It’s Ah Kuen from the boats. He’s cut his hand on a cable. It’s deep. Your father says not the hospital. But only if you can. You’ve got exams. He said to say you’ve got exams.” It was Uncle Mok, who’d driven her to school every day for twelve years.

“I’m coming. The Walled City. One of Baba’s men. A hand. I’ll get a taxi.” She was already pulling her jeans on under his shirt. He was awake beside her. She took her bag; she’d kept a few things in it since March.

He already had his keys. He stopped at the mouth of the alley under the one streetlight, because she still wouldn’t let him see the red door, and he didn’t ask to.

Ah Kuen was sitting at the long kitchen table with his hand wrapped in a tea towel and his face grey; he’d given her sugar cane when she was six. Baba stood by the stove with his arms folded and Mok by the door. She unwrapped the towel. The cable had gone across the palm, deep, and she made him bend every finger, one at a time, and every one of them moved. “Good. Good. All right.” She washed it at the sink and numbed it and sat at her father’s table a week before her surgical paper and closed it, neat and quick under the kitchen lamp, saying nothing but the small words. Baba watched the whole time.

When she’d dressed it she pointed at Ah Kuen. “Come and see me in a week. Don’t get it wet. Don’t lift anything. Come to me, not anybody else.”

“Yes, little sister.”

Baba unfolded his arms. “You’ve got exams.”

“I know.”

“I said only if you could.”

“I could,” said Elara.

He gave her the look, the small-print one, and nodded, and went to put the kettle on. From Baba that was a great deal.

The car was under the streetlight with the engine running, and he got out before she reached it. He took a folded handkerchief out of his pocket, ironed, and wiped a smear of Ah Kuen’s blood off the inside of her wrist that she hadn’t even seen. “Were you careful with your own hands?”

“Always.”

“Show me.”

She held them up under the streetlight, and he turned them over, palms and backs and fingers, and kissed her knuckles, both hands, and opened the car door for her.

“You’re very strange,” she told him, and got in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The results came out on a Thursday in the middle of June. She read them three times on her phone in his kitchen: a distinction, and a separate email, the prize in clinical surgery for her year. She screamed without meaning to, and the woman in the flat below banged on the ceiling with something, and Elara didn’t care. She rang him in the middle of his ward round and screamed down the phone.

He asked somebody on the ward for one minute, and then said to her, “Tell me again. Slowly.”

She told him again, slowly.

“Good. That’s—Elara. That’s what you are.” His voice had gone strange.

In the background, on 9B, somebody said, “Dr. Wang? Are you all right?”

Graduation was on the last Thursday in June in the Great Hall at the top of the hill: grey stone and a hammer-beam roof and windows that let in more pigeons than light. Her whole family came. Baba in the funeral suit, because it was the only suit he owned, with Uncle Mok two steps behind him. Elowen in green, with her husband beside her walking carefully. Raiden in a waistcoat he’d designed for the occasion, embroidered all over with tiny scalpels. Evangeline at the end of the row in pale blue with the silver ring on her hand. Eliana with her phone. When Elara crossed the stage they cheered so loudly that the Vice-Chancellor stopped and looked at them over his glasses. Raiden whistled through his fingers. Elowen cried, and would later deny it. Baba didn’t move at all, and when Elara looked down at him from the stage with her certificate his face was wet.

Xing Yue was at the back by the doors, in a dark grey suit, against the wall behind the last row with the photographers and the latecomers. He didn’t wave. He watched her come down the steps from the stage. None of her family knew who he was, except Eliana, who turned round in the fourth row and looked straight down the hall at him for one second, and lifted her phone and took a photograph, and turned back again, and said nothing to anybody.

✦ ✦ ✦

The back stairs ran from behind the stage to a side door by the porters’ lodge, and nobody used them but the porters and the pigeons. She took them at a run in her gown, skirt in one fist and cap in the other. He was on the landing by the old wooden banister with the carved knob at the turn. Of course he knew which way she’d come.

She didn’t slow down. She came down the last steps and took hold of his tie, and this time she pulled, and he came. She kissed him against the banister with her cap in one hand and his tie in the other and the gown sliding off her shoulders, and he got both arms round her and lifted her off the step and kissed her back, hard: two hours at the back of a hall, waiting to be allowed. The carved knob dug into her spine and she didn’t care in the least.

“Dr. Lin,” she said against his mouth. She’d never said it aloud. She wanted to hear it.

“Dr. Lin,” he said into her hair, low.

“I’m a doctor. A real one.”

“You were one in September. Bed fourteen.”

He set her down on the landing. Overhead the hall was emptying, and somewhere outside Raiden was shouting her name.

“Elara. I’d like to meet them properly. I’ve been standing at the back of rooms for nine months.”

She put her forehead on his chest. “Elowen’s getting married again, properly this time, in September, in the shop. Everyone’s going. Half the Walled City. Come to that. If I bring you to Sunday lunch, it’s you and Baba at one end of a table for three hours. At the wedding they’ll all see you at once and nobody can make a scene, because it’s Elowen’s day and she’d kill them.”

“September.”

“I promise.”

“Then I’d like to come as your husband.”

She laughed. Then she stopped, because his face hadn’t moved. He took an envelope out of his inside pocket and gave it to her.

It was a notice of intended marriage, for the registry in the old town, with every box filled in, in square block capitals, each letter separate so that any clerk on earth could read them. WANG XING YUE. And beneath it, LIN ELARA, her date of birth, her address at the tall house, her identity number.

“How do you have my identity number?”

“It’s on your logbook.”

“Fei has my logbook.”

“Fei leaves her door open.”

“You filled in my form. In capitals.”

“So the clerk can read it.”

“That’s not a question. Again. People kneel, or there’s a ring, or—”

“You’re on the step. We’re level. The rings are at the jeweller’s. Two, plain gold.” He didn’t blink.

“What size am I?”

He told her.

“How do you know that?”

“You fell asleep on the brachial plexus.”

She stared at him with her mouth open and her face wet and her cap somewhere on the floor. “We’ve known each other ten months. You’ve never met my father. My father has the postman checked. I start at Harbourside on the third of July, and I’m going to be doing fourteen-hour days, and Elowen’s wedding is in September and I’m not stealing her year, and my sisters will kill me, and—yes—and Raiden will put it on a cake, and you haven’t even— Wait. Did I say yes?”

“In the middle.”

“I did. I said yes.”

Something in her face changed, and he watched it go: the tears stopped, the pink went, and what was left was cold and clear. He’d seen it once before, in his bed, with her sister on speaker.

She said, “Rules. One. Nobody in the family. Not yet. Not Baba. Not my sisters. If Baba hears before I tell him, you’ll be looked into before the ink’s dry. Two. The old town’s good; nobody in that office owes Baba a favour. Three. I choose the witnesses.”

“Agreed.”

“Four. The date’s blank.” She held up the form. There was one box he’d left empty.

“You choose the date. I’ve chosen everything else.”

“Yes, I’d noticed. Five. Nobody bleeds on it.” She folded the form in half, and in half again, and tucked it down the front of her gown under the collar, against her skin.

He took his glasses off and folded them and put them in the pocket of her gown. Then he took her jaw in his hand and kissed her slowly on the back stairs, with her family shouting for her through two stone walls.

“Elara! Where are you? Baba’s crying again!”

She pulled back and took his glasses out of her pocket and put them on his face herself, crooked. “Don’t follow me up.”

She ran up the stairs holding her gown, with a marriage form against her heart, laughing so hard she missed a step.

chapters.title: The Flat on Banyan Terrace
chapters.desc: She starts as an intern across the harbour, living out of a bag, and he hands her the key to a room he’s already finished. She picks the date. On a Friday morning in the old town they marry in secret, with a retired bus driver and a night sister for witnesses.
chapters.epigraph: “Now that’s an answer.”
chapters.content:
On the first of July he became an associate consultant: a new badge, a better office, a parking space he’d never use, and his name in white letters on the board outside 9B instead of pencil.

On the third of July she started as an intern at Harbourside General, and he didn’t see her awake for nine days. Fourteen-hour days, out before six and back after nine, some nights to the Walled City and some to him, depending on where she fell over. She lived out of a canvas bag: scrubs, stethoscope, a banana, three chargers, a rice ball squashed flat in the back of a textbook. The form from the back stairs was in there too, folded in four, the date still blank. He didn’t ask about it. He checked her rota instead, twice a day.

When he could, he met her off the ferry. Three nights running she fell asleep mid-sentence before they’d left the car park, and on the third night he parked outside Fourteen Banyan Terrace and sat watching her breathe against the window for twenty minutes. Then he went to see an architect.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’ve got worse. You were always bad. You’ve got worse since you’ve been happy. As if you’ve got more to lose,” Fei told him in the corridor, after a lunchtime meeting at which he’d had an intern read aloud, hour by hour, the observations of a man he’d left bleeding overnight with repeat in the morning written beside them, and had waited, without raising his voice once, while the intern’s voice went somewhere around four in the morning and came back.

He didn’t answer.

“Oh, no,” said Fei. “You have got more to lose. What have you done?”

“Nothing yet.”

“Yet?” said Fei, and he got into the lift.

He gave Elara the envelope on a Sunday at the end of July, her first day off in three weeks. Inside it was a key, freshly cut, and a floor plan: an architect’s, not an estate agent’s, with every room of the top two floors of Fourteen Banyan Terrace drawn in. One of them, the small room off the big room with the window over the frangipani, had a single letter on it in his handwriting. E.

“You’ve drawn an E on the study.”

“Come and look.”

The old desk was gone. In its place was a new one, wide, pale oak, lower than he’d ever have used himself. A lamp with a long arm. A suturing board, the good kind, with a skin pad that would take a hundred hours. Shelves she could reach without a chair, with her textbooks already on them and a row of empty ones waiting. An armchair by the window, and beneath the window the frangipani in flower.

She didn’t go in. “When did you do this?”

“Over the last three weeks.”

“The desk’s the wrong height. For you.”

“It’s the right height for you.”

“How do you know what height I— May. Finals. I was asleep on the desk.”

“Your elbows. In pencil, on the wall. I’ve painted over it.”

“You measured me in my sleep?”

“Yes.”

“And downstairs, the postbox. It says WANG, and under it LIN. I thought it was a mistake.”

“It’s you.”

She was furious for an hour. She walked round and round the big room with the plan in her fist. He’d decided for her. He’d put her name on a box as if she were a parcel and shown it to her finished, like an operation, as if she’d been under the whole time. What if she hated oak? What if she didn’t want to live here at all?

“Do you?” he said.

“That isn’t the point.”

He waited until she’d run down. Then he gave her the only thing he had. “If you say no, I’ll take it all down. The desk goes back. Your name comes off the box. You keep the key for when you want to come. Nothing changes.”

She stopped walking. He meant it; he’d have had the desk out that night with a screwdriver. And she wasn’t going to say no. She’d known it in the study doorway. She’d been shouting for an hour because he’d known it first.

She went back into the study and hopped up onto the desk with her legs dangling. It was exactly the right height for that, too, which he hadn’t measured. She held her hand out, and he came, and she pulled him in by the front of his shirt until he was standing between her knees and kissed him hard with both hands on his face, still angry, quite a lot.

“It’s the right height,” she said when she let him breathe. She didn’t sound pleased.

“I measured.”

“I know you measured. That’s what I’m angry about. I’ll pay rent.” She kissed him again, more slowly.

“It’s paid for.”

She’d known that, really. She’d seen the letters from the bank that weren’t asking for anything. She’d paid for her own books since she was eighteen, on a scholarship and pride. “Then I’ll buy the groceries. All of them, every week. You’re not allowed to buy a single egg.”

“All right.”

She reached down into her bag on the floor without getting off the desk, and the form came out, soft from a month of being folded, and she smoothed it flat on the oak.

“I’m moving in on Saturday the twelfth. Uncle Mok can bring my boxes; Mok doesn’t talk. And I’m not moving in as your girlfriend. Friday the eleventh. I’m off till noon. If I’m moving in, I’m moving in married.” She took a pen out of his shirt pocket.

She wrote the date in the empty box in her own small quick handwriting.

“Witnesses?” he said, when he could.

“Mr. Yin. He asked me if I was married a year ago, and I owe him an answer. And you can choose one.”

“Sister Miao.”

“She’ll tell everyone.”

“She’s known since September and she hasn’t told anyone.”

“How do you know she knows?”

“She told me,” said Xing Yue.

✦ ✦ ✦

The registry in the old town smelled of floor polish and old paper. Mr. Yin got there first and stood on the steps in his bus driver’s jacket, dark blue, with every brass button polished. He’d had his bowel put back together in the spring and wanted everyone to know it. “Good as new. Better. That dress is too nice for a registry.” He looked Elara up and down.

“It’s the only dress I’ve got.”

It was the dark green one, from her birthday, and the alley, and the horn. His face said he remembered.

Sister Miao came straight off nights in her grey cardigan with a paper cup of coffee the size of a vase and looked at the three of them on the steps. “You have twenty minutes. Then I’m going to bed.”

Xing Yue was in the dark grey suit. He looked at Elara in the green dress on the registry steps and forgot how to do anything else.

“You’re staring,” she whispered.

“Yes.”

“Stop it. Mr. Yin’s watching.”

“Mr. Yin can watch.”

At nine the doors opened. The clerk was a small round woman with reading glasses on a chain, and she read their form with her nose almost touching it. “Oh, lovely. Lovely clear capitals. You wouldn’t believe what people hand me.”

Elara made a sound like a sneeze. He didn’t look at her, because if he looked at her she’d go.

The clerk turned the book round and handed over a pen on a chain. Elara’s hand was shaking. She’d cleaned out a gunshot wound on a kitchen table without a tremor, and now look at her. She signed, LIN ELARA, small and fast, and the pen skidded on the last letter. He signed underneath her in one stroke that nobody alive could have read. Mr. Yin signed slowly, as if he were filling in a timesheet, prouder than anything. Sister Miao signed without putting her coffee down.

“Rings?”

He took them out of his inside pocket: two plain gold bands, in no box at all, warm from him. He took her left hand and turned it over first, and his thumb went to the inside of her wrist for one second.

“You’re shaking.”

“I am not—”

He put the ring on her finger, and it went on smooth and exactly right. She pushed his ring onto his finger, and it stuck at the knuckle, and she shoved, and it went. She held his hand in both of hers. “There. Mine.”

The clerk stamped the book. “That’s you, dears. Congratulations.”

“Thank you! Thank you so much, and I’m sorry I sneezed, I didn’t sneeze, I laughed, it was the capitals, he did them so you could read them, he’s very—”

He took her jaw in his hand and turned her face up and stopped her mouth with his, in front of the clerk and the book and the stamp. She made a muffled sound and then grabbed his lapels in both fists and kissed him back on her toes with her ring hand flat on his chest.

Behind them, Mr. Yin cleared his throat loudly. “Now that’s an answer.”

Sister Miao took a photograph and finished her coffee. “Fourteen minutes. Congratulations. I’m telling nobody. I never do.”

On the steps outside he took a fine gold chain out of his other pocket, slid her ring off again and threaded it onto the chain and fastened the clasp under her hair, so that the ring lay against her collarbone where her scrubs would cover it. “You can’t wear it on the ward.”

“You bought a chain before I’d even chosen a date?”

“The day after the stairs.”

She looked at his left hand. His ring was still on it. “Aren’t you going to hide yours?”

“No.”

“People will ask.”

“Nobody asks me anything,” he said. He meant it. Wang Xing Yue was going to walk onto 9B wearing a wedding ring, and the whole department would stare at it, and nobody would dare say a word. She laughed so hard that Mr. Yin had to hold her elbow on the steps, and by noon she was on the surgical floor at Harbourside in her scrubs, taking blood, married.

Elara: my registrar just asked why I’m smiling

Xing Yue: What did you say

Elara: constipation

Xing Yue: Good.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning at seven a silver saloon stopped outside Fourteen Banyan Terrace. He watched from the top-floor window as a big grey-haired man got out and opened the boot: ELARA BOOKS. ELARA WINTER. ELARA DON’T ASK. Elara ran down in her scrubs and met him at the street door and took every box from him there; she didn’t let him in, and he didn’t try. When the last box was down, the big man stood on the pavement by the frangipani and looked up, straight at Xing Yue in the window, and at the hand on the frame, his left hand. Then he got back into the car and drove away.

“That was Uncle Mok. He’s driven me since I was six. He doesn’t talk,” said Elara, coming up the stairs behind a box.

“He saw me.”

“Mok sees everything. He doesn’t talk. He doesn’t talk!” She kissed his chin and ran for the ferry.

She worked fourteen hours. He didn’t unpack her boxes, because he wasn’t stupid; he stacked them in the study in the order she’d want them. Then he filled the fridge from a list he hadn’t meant to keep. Peach yoghurt with the bits in, not the smooth kind. The sesame paste she ate off a spoon. The small mandarins with loose skins. Old Bian’s hot sauce, which Old Bian didn’t sell, in a jam jar handed over with a look. And the terrible orange fizzy drink from the vending machine on the seventh floor, the one she drank when she was sad.

She came in after ten through the door that was hers now, talking about a gallbladder, and a man who’d tried to discharge himself in his gown. Shoes by the door, facing out. Bag on the floor. Lanyard on the counter. Stethoscope on the stairs. She opened the fridge and stopped talking.

“You said I’d buy the groceries.”

“There are no eggs.”

She looked. There was everything else in the world and not a single egg. She shut the fridge and put her forehead against the door.

“Bath. Doctor’s orders,” he said.

He ran it hotter than he liked and tested it with his wrist, and she sank in up to her chin, still talking. He knelt on the floor and took her clip out and wet her hair with the shower head with one hand over her eyes. He used his own shampoo, and she complained that it would make her smell like him and leaned her head back into his hands anyway. He took his time over it, scalp to ends, his fingers slow and firm at the back of her neck where she carried everything, until the gallbladder stopped, and there were only small sounds, and then nothing at all. The gold chain was still round her neck, and the ring sat in the hollow of her throat under the water.

He rinsed the last of the shampoo out and squeezed the ends of her hair. “I love you,” he said, plainly, on his knees on a wet floor. He’d been carrying it since April.

She opened her eyes and turned her head on the edge of the bath. “You heard that? In the car? In April? I thought I’d dreamed it. I was talking about gauze.”

“Yes.”

She sat up so fast that half the bath went over the side onto his knees, and put both wet arms round his neck. “I love you. I love you. I meant it. I was asleep, but I meant it—”

He kissed her with his hands still in her hair, and by the time he stopped there was nearly as much water on the floor as in the bath.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her to bed with her hair still wet. He dried her first, all of her, slowly, with the towel, as if it were a job worth doing properly, and she laughed at him, and then she stopped laughing, because he didn’t stop when she was dry.

“Xing Yue.”

“Mm.”

“Husband.”

He went still. “Say it again.”

“Husband. Husband, husband, husband. You did my form in capitals. You measured my elbows. You’re the worst man I’ve ever met—” She pulled him down by the back of his neck.

He kissed the inside of her wrist, where he always began, and then the chain at her throat, and the ring on it, and the skin under the ring. “Wife,” he said, and that was all he said after that.

It was slow. There was nowhere to be and nobody who’d ring, and for the first time there was no going home afterwards, because this was home. Her wet hair was cold on his arm and the rest of her was warm. He moved down the length of her with his mouth until she had both hands fisted in the pillow, and when she pulled him back up she held his face in her hands in the lamplight and looked at him, checking, the way he always checked her, while he slid into her, and watched his control go somewhere in the middle, and laughed into his shoulder because she’d felt it go, and then couldn’t laugh any more.

“Don’t you dare be careful. I’m your wife,” she breathed.

He wasn’t careful. She locked her ankles behind him and met him, and they went over together, her mouth open against his throat, his name the only word she had.

Afterwards she lay across him with her damp head on his chest and the ring on its chain between them.

“We’re married,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Nobody knows.”

“Sister Miao.”

“Sister Miao doesn’t count. She knows everything anyway. Nobody in my family knows.” She drew a circle on his chest with one finger.

“Your Uncle Mok looked at my hand.”

Her finger stopped.

“Mok doesn’t talk,” she said. She sounded less sure this time.

chapters.title: The Cake
chapters.desc: Elara makes four tiers of cake for Elowen’s wedding, and the tall doctor in glasses stands beside it all night while nobody introduces him. At midnight her father asks his name, and he tells him: her husband.
chapters.epigraph: “Sunday. One o’clock. Bring him.”
chapters.content:
“It’s relaxing.”

“It’s three in the morning.”

“Relaxing things can happen at three in the morning. Pass me the ball tool.”

He passed her the ball tool. She’d come in from Harbourside at ten, scrubbed her hands at his kitchen sink as if she were going into theatre, and sat down at the counter with a tray of sugar paste and a pair of tweezers, and that had been five hours ago. One petal at a time, rolled so thin you could see the lamp through it, for four tiers of camellias on a lemon cake for Elowen’s wedding. She’d said yes to the cake in June, before she knew about fourteen-hour days, and before she knew she’d be married.

Six weeks married now. Her ring was on its chain under her T-shirt and knocked against her collarbone every time she leaned over the tray. His was on his hand.

He’d worked out on the first night that she went faster if somebody moved the light to wherever she was looking, so he stood at her shoulder and moved it, and when she held her hand out without looking up he put the next thing into it: tweezers, brush, the dish of water for the edges.

“You’d make a terrible scrub nurse.”

“Why?”

“You keep looking at my face and not my hands.”

“Your hands don’t need watching,” he said, and she went pink and dropped a petal.

On the second night he said, “You hum.”

“I don’t hum.”

“You’ve been humming for an hour. The same tune. Three notes, and then it comes down.”

“I’d know if I hummed. Where would I even get a tune? Ah Sim only sings to fish before she kills them.” She tried to catch herself at it for ten minutes and couldn’t, because it only happened when she wasn’t listening.

He didn’t know. She forgot about it, and a minute later she was doing it again, and this time he didn’t tell her. He listened.

At two she put the tweezers down with sugar dust all over her fingers and a petal stuck to her thumb, and turned round on the stool and took his face in both pink hands and kissed him, slowly. When she let go there were pink fingerprints along his jaw.

“Don’t wipe them. You look as if you’ve been attacked by a very small flamingo.”

He left them. In the morning one was still there, faint, under his ear, and she saw it on her way out and laughed all the way down Banyan Terrace.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bottom tier was too big for his fridge, so Raiden took it on the Thursday. “I know somewhere it’ll keep level,” he said, with a face she didn’t trust, and wouldn’t say where. On the Friday night she iced the other three at the counter in Elowen’s shop among the buckets, while her sister walked round and round her asking what flavour it was.

“Chocolate?”

“No.”

“Vanilla?”

“No.”

“Lemon?”

Elara stopped with the palette knife in the air.

“It’s lemon,” said Elowen.

“I didn’t say that.”

“You stopped moving.”

“Go away,” said Elara, pink to the ears, and turned her phone off it buzzed, because it was him, and Elowen was looking.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday she came to the shop early. Raiden came at four, and the woman with him was carrying the bottom tier of her cake in a steel box she’d made to keep it level on a motorbike. At the door, before she came in, the woman took a ring out of her pocket and put it on, and Raiden broke the bit of string he wore round his neck and put his on too.

“Everyone. This is Jinx. My wife. She built Xiao Pan’s bike. Don’t touch her tools,” he said.

The shop went silent. Elara stood by the cooler with her mouth open and looked at the woman’s hands on the steel box: long and strong, grease in the creases of the knuckles that no amount of washing would shift, small shiny burn marks on the backs. She knew those hands. She’d watched them two years before in a back room by the docks, measuring her own wrists with a pair of calipers without a word, and a week later fitting a brace on her that had given her back the needle.

Jinx looked across the shop and found her, and something passed over her hard, beautiful face that might, in anyone else, have been a smile. She gave Elara the smallest nod in the world. Elara nodded back. Neither of them said anything then, or ever.

Then Elowen hit Raiden on the arm, quite hard, and put both arms round him, and the shop started breathing again, and everybody wanted to know everything, and nobody looked at Elara at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six a tall man in gold-rimmed glasses and a black turtleneck came in alone off the street, a little out of breath, and looked round once and found her, and came and stood beside her cake.

“It’s the best thing in the room,” he said.

He stood there all evening. Nobody introduced him, and he didn’t seem to expect it. Every time she walked past with a tray he looked at her, and then at nothing, and she felt it on the back of her neck like the sun.

The aunties she’d known since she was three looked at him over their paper cups. Mrs. Yung from the fish stall came to admire the cake and then looked up a long way. “And who’s this?”

“A colleague. From the hospital,” said Elara instantly.

Mrs. Yung’s eyes went to his left hand and the plain gold band, and back to Elara, and her face said married colleague in capitals. “How nice,” she said, and photographed the cake and went straight to the other aunties.

Beside her he went still, only for a second. He didn’t move away, but she felt it, like a hand taken off her back.

“I didn’t mean—”

“I know.”

“It’s what I say at work.”

“I know.”

By the roses four aunties had their heads together and weren’t even trying. Did you see his hand? Standing like that, next to Lin Jian’s girl. Elara wanted the floor to open. They thought she was standing next to some poor woman’s husband. Which she was. Her own.

“Oh. Oh, indeed,” said Aurelia, at Elowen’s elbow, looking at Elara’s throat, where the gold chain had worked its way out from under her collar.

“He’s a colleague,” said Elara, passing with a tray.

“Of course he is, darling.”

Across the shop, beside Eliana, a lanky boy with a medical textbook under one arm had seen him, and his ears had gone pink. Xing Yue looked back at him over the roses for a second, and then they both looked away.

“Do you know him?”

“My cousin. Yu Chen. He lives next door to your father.”

“Your cousin lives next door to my father and you never—”

“You never asked whether I had a cousin.”

It was true, which was infuriating. “Later. You’re telling me all of it later.”

“Yes,” he said, and reached over and fixed her lipstick at the corner with one stroke of his thumb, where she’d smudged it on a paper cup, without looking round to see who’d seen. Four aunties had.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain stopped at half past nine, and the shop was full of the last grey daylight and the smell of wet roses. Baba walked Elowen down the aisle in the black suit he’d bought for Mama’s funeral and worn to every important thing since. He was crying before they’d gone three steps, and halfway down he stopped and asked, across the whole silent shop, how the lemon tree was, and Zhao Zhendong, under the arch of old shipyard timber, who’d crawled up a hill with a bullet in him in March and lain on a kitchen table under Elara’s hands without once asking her to stop, said, “Nine lemons,” and his face opened like a door.

Elara cried. She cried at weddings and graduations and dogs on the news, and she stood by her cake and cried with her mouth open. Without looking, he put something into her hand: a white cotton handkerchief, ironed into a square with a sharp crease.

“You iron your handkerchiefs?” she whispered wetly.

“Yes.”

She blew her nose on it during the vows, loudly, and he didn’t flinch. Elowen said something about ordinary mornings and Zhao said something about learning to ask, and Elara put the whole handkerchief over her face.

At exactly nine forty-one Eliana turned the lights on, and the whole shop went gold at once, every beam and shelf and thread of green. Everyone looked up. Elara looked up at the lights and then sideways at her husband, who wasn’t looking at them at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later Zhao came for cake. He ate two pieces off a paper plate with his fingers, with her sugar camellia still in his lapel, uneaten, and then he looked up at the man beside her, and Elara knew that look. She’d seen men in the Walled City go grey under it.

Xing Yue looked back. “How’s the side?”

Zhao didn’t answer. She wondered what he’d worked out from the bags she’d carried up the hill in March, the hospital labels, the instrument set with the needle holder exactly where it should be. His eyes went down to Xing Yue’s left hand and up again.

“Hm,” said Zhao, and took a third piece, and went back to his wife.

Nobody else came near them all night. The whole family was busy with Raiden, and Raiden was busy telling everyone about Raiden. He swung past at eleven with a paper cup in each hand. “Elara! Have you met my wife? Isn’t she terrifying? Hello, tall person. Two years next Saturday!”

“Two years?” But he’d gone.

“Two years,” she hissed. “Since 2021. He hid a wife from all of us. Who does that?”

Her husband looked down at her.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

Baba had gone out to stand on the step for ten minutes after the word wife. Everybody was talking about Raiden. Her brother’s secret was so big and so loud that hers slid by underneath it, and she had never loved him more.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight, when most of the guests had gone and the floor was petals and there were glasses everywhere, she was crossing the shop with a stack of plates when she saw her father go over to the very tall man still standing beside the ruins of her cake.

“I don’t think we’ve been introduced,” said Lin Jian.

“No, sir.”

“Your name?”

Xing Yue looked across the room at her, with her stack of plates, for one second. She felt her mouth want to do it again: colleague, a friend, Baba, this is. She didn’t let it. She only looked back at him.

Then he looked at her father. “Wang Xing Yue, her husband,” he said.

Elara dropped a plate.

It broke on the tiles with a sound like a shot, and the people still in the shop turned round. Her father looked at Xing Yue, reading the small print, the way she’d seen him read men twice that size before they left the city. Then he looked at his daughter, standing in a drift of rose petals with the other plates held to her chest and the gold chain out of her collar and the ring on it swinging in the light.

His eyes went past her to the door, where Uncle Mok was leaning on the frame, looking at the sky.

“Mok,” said Lin Jian.

Mok went on looking at the sky. Her father made a sound that wasn’t a laugh and wasn’t not one. He turned back to the tall man by the cake.

“Sunday, one o’clock. Bring him,” he said.

He went to find his coat. Under the arch, Zhao had his arms round Elowen from behind, and Elara could see both their shoulders shaking. She stood among the petals with the plates.

“Did my father just invite my husband to lunch?” she said.

Xing Yue came across the shop and took the plates out of her arms, and set them down on the counter, and crouched to pick up the pieces of the one she’d dropped.

“Yes,” he said.

“Oh, no,” said Elara, and started laughing, and couldn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Out on the pavement the air smelled of rain and frangipani from somebody’s courtyard, and the street was empty except for Uncle Mok’s silver car at the kerb with Mok inside it, reading a newspaper by the light of the dashboard.

She stopped under the shop’s awning. She undid the clasp of the gold chain at the back of her neck with fingers that didn’t want to work, and slid the ring off it into her palm, and stood looking at it.

She said, “I’ve never worn it. Not once. Not since the registry. It’s been on the chain the whole time, under my scrubs, under my dress. Six weeks.”

“I know.”

She held it out to him on her palm. “You do it. You did it the first time and then you took it off again on the steps. I want it put on properly.”

He took her left hand and turned it over first, the way he always did, and his thumb found the inside of her wrist and stayed there. Her pulse was going like a bird’s. Then he turned her hand back and put the ring on her finger, and this time he didn’t take it off again.

She looked at it in the light from the shop window, gold on her hand where anyone could see.

“There. Now Mrs. Yung can say what she likes,” she said. Her voice wobbled.

Behind them, through the glass, her father was standing in the gold light of the shop with his coat over his arm, watching them. He didn’t come out. After a moment he lifted one hand, slightly, and turned away.

chapters.title: Sunday Lunch in the Walled City
chapters.desc: The red door, eleven chairs and a father who has learned to ask things. Raiden asks his intentions, and Xing Yue tells the whole table he’s already married her.
chapters.epigraph: “Does she eat when she’s on nights?”
chapters.content:
The week after the wedding Elara’s phone didn’t stop.

Elowen rang at seven on the Sunday morning, and Xing Yue could hear her from the kitchen with the phone on the other side of the room. A registry? On a Friday? With a bus driver? Elara ended up face down in a cushion saying “I know, I know, I know” for twenty minutes, and defending Mr. Yin, who had driven the number nine for forty years and was a good bus driver, and pointing out that her sister had a husband and two dogs and was supposed to be on her honeymoon.

Eliana sent one message.

Eliana: I know. since the 11th. you were in green

Elara: HOW

Eliana: spreadsheet

Evangeline sent nothing at all. Raiden sent a photograph of two steel washers on a napkin with the caption TWINS, and Elara threw her phone across the sofa.

The first Sunday he was on call, and she rang her father to say so, and he heard her side of it from the kitchen: the rota, the ward, the general unfairness of surgery, and then a silence. “Yes, Baba. The next one. I’ll tell him. He said a surgeon on call is a surgeon on call. He said he doesn’t mind waiting. He’s never said that in his life. Elowen’s been teaching him things. It’s frightening.” She came out with the phone in her hand and a strange look on her face. She stared at the phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Sunday they took the ferry over.

“Don’t mention the north. Don’t mention money. Don’t mention the hospitals. Don’t sit in the carved chair, that’s Baba’s, and don’t sit in the high chair, nobody sits in the high chair.”

“What do I mention?”

“Nothing. I’ll talk.”

“I know you’ll talk.”

“Don’t say it like that.”

The red door was at the top of the alley past the noodle stall, round the corner he’d never been allowed to turn: deep lacquer red, with a brass knocker shaped like a fish rubbed gold in the middle by sixty years of hands. She didn’t knock. She opened it, because it was her house, and went in talking, and he followed her into a hall that went straight up into the dark, all stairs, smelling of soup and woodsmoke.

“Don’t be nervous.”

“I’m not.”

“You’ve cleaned your glasses twice since the ferry.”

He put his handkerchief away.

The kitchen was long and low with a fire at one end and a table down the middle with eleven chairs round it, none of them matching: a carved one at the head, a bentwood one, a child’s high chair nobody had sat in for years and nobody had moved. The whole family looked up. A woman the size of a child came out of the scullery with a ladle and looked at him from his shoes to his hair and back.

“Too thin. Sit,” said Ah Sim.

He sat where the ladle pointed.

He knew who they all were; she’d told him a hundred times, and he’d listened every time. Lin Jian at the head in the carved chair, grey and enormous, in a cardigan, with his hands flat on the table on either side of his bowl. Elowen on his right, cool and sharp, in green. Her husband beside her in black, who looked at Xing Yue across the table and didn’t stop. Raiden opposite with a plaster on his thumb and his chair tipped back, delighted with everything. Eliana halfway down with her laptop open beside her soup, not looking at him at all, which he didn’t believe for a second. And Evangeline at the far end by the fire, straight and silent, with a silver ring on her left hand, not blinking much.

Elara talked for both of them. She talked through the soup: the ward, the ferry, Mr. Yin, who’d sent a card to say he was back on his bus pass. “He was at the registry. He polished his buttons. Baba, did I say about the buttons?”

“You said.”

“And Xing Yue once made a registrar cry in three sentences, and the registrar sent him a thank-you card at Christmas, which tells you—”

She was frightened. He could hear it, and he didn’t think she could. She was doing for him what she’d done in the past for her silent sister: filling every gap before anything else could get into it. He put his arm along the back of her chair, and she went on talking, but her voice dropped half a tone.

Lin Jian let her go on. He ate his soup and listened to his daughter with his eyes on her husband, and when she stopped to breathe he put his spoon down.

“Does she eat when she’s on nights?”

The table went quiet. Even Raiden’s chair came down onto four legs.

It wasn’t the question Xing Yue had prepared for. He’d prepared for the north, his family, his salary, you married my daughter in secret at a registry with a bus driver, and had answers ready for all of it. He looked down the table at Lin Jian and saw a man who’d brought a three-year-old home from a children’s home and listened to her talk for twenty years, who’d watched her fall asleep over a dumpling at this table in April, and who wanted to know one thing.

“Not unless someone puts it in her hand.”

“Do you?”

“Every time.”

Lin Jian looked at him a few seconds longer. Then he picked up his spoon again. “Good.”

Beside him Elara let out a breath she’d been holding since the alley.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fish came, steamed whole with ginger and spring onion, and Ah Sim put the best piece of the belly in Elara’s bowl without asking anyone. Elara reached for it.

“Wait,” said Xing Yue.

He took her bowl and picked the bones out of the belly with his chopsticks, every one, small and quick, and lined them up on the side of his own plate, and put the bowl back in front of her. Nobody said anything. Ah Sim had stopped with the ladle in the air.

“He does that. At home. He does that at home,” whispered Elara, scarlet.

“Does he,” said Elowen.

“I choke on them otherwise. I’ve always choked on them. I choked on one at my sixth birthday and Baba had to—”

“I remember,” said Lin Jian.

Raiden was grinning so hard it looked painful, and to make up for it Elara picked up a dumpling and put it straight into her husband’s mouth with her own chopsticks in front of everyone.

“I’m going to be sick,” said Raiden.

“Good. Be sick. Ah Sim, he’s going to be sick.”

“Not at my table,” said Ah Sim, without turning round from the stove.

✦ ✦ ✦

Of course it was Raiden who asked. Over the fish, with his chopsticks waving.

“So. Dr. Wang.”

“Raiden,” said Elowen, without looking up.

“No, I have to. I’m the only son. It’s in the rules. Baba, it’s in the rules, isn’t it? You married my little sister in secret without asking anybody.” He pointed his chopsticks across the table.

“You were married for two years before—”

“I’m in no position. I’m aware. I’m asking anyway. What are your intentions?” He leaned in.

Xing Yue put his chopsticks down. “To have married her. In August. I’d like your blessing for the rest of it.” He turned his head, not to Raiden but to the head of the table.

Elara had just taken a mouthful of soup. She choked on it so badly that she had to put the bowl down and put her head between her knees. He laid his hand flat on her back without looking at her and kept his eyes on Lin Jian, and Lin Jian said nothing.

Raiden stared, and then he laughed. All of him went, tipped back in his chair with his hands on his stomach, and the laugh went up the stairwell and round the house until Ah Sim came out of the scullery to see what had died. “The rest of it. Baba, did you hear him? He wants a blessing for the rest of it—”

Lin Jian had heard him. He still said nothing at all. But at the head of the table his eyes had gone wet at the corners, and at the far end Evangeline looked at her sister bent double with a napkin over her face, and the corner of her mouth moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch Zhao stood up and looked at him and went out, and Xing Yue followed him through the red door into the alley. It was a grey afternoon, and the noodle stall at the bottom had its shutters up and its steam going. Zhao stood by the wall with his hands in his pockets: big and broad, with a face that didn’t move. Xing Yue had stood beside the cake with him the Saturday before last and had thought every day since about the scar he’d never seen: a wound left open to drain, packed morning and evening for two weeks by a final-year student with stolen gauze.

“You saw her bags,” said Zhao.

“Yes.”

“You didn’t ask.”

“No.”
