Zhao looked at him in the grey light, and at the ring on his hand, and back up. Then he nodded, once, the smallest movement a head could make, and went back in through the red door and left him in the alley alone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara caught him at the bottom of the stairs. “Come and see my room. Quick, before Raiden finds us. He’ll want to show you his drawings of the house. He’s got drawings of every house.”

She pulled him up four flights, each narrower than the last, past a landing window over the roofs of the Walled City with a cat asleep on the sill, to a room at the very top under the roof. A sloping ceiling. A bed with a faded quilt. And the posters; she hadn’t been joking. Five boys with a great deal of hair. A film. A heart cut out of a magazine with arrows added in pen. A map of the moons of Jupiter.

“That’s the band, I liked the one with the fringe, don’t judge me. That’s the film, I saw it four times in one weekend when I was fourteen and cried every time at the same bit, the dog bit. And that’s the heart, and there’s a mistake in one of the arrows, look, there, I never fixed it, I was going to fix it when I got into medicine and then I got into medicine and I thought it was funnier to leave it—”

It was too fast, much too fast. She was nervous of him in her old bedroom in a way she had never once been in his. He shut the door.

“Elara.”

She turned round and looked at him standing with his back against her bedroom door and his hand still on the handle. He crossed the little room in two steps and took her chin and tipped her face to the light from the window, and she opened her mouth to say what, and he kissed her against the door. She tugged him down into it at once. Her hands went into his hair. Five boys watched from the wall. The whole house came up the stairwell, dishes and Ah Sim’s voice and Raiden laughing at something, and he kissed her until they were both breathing as if they’d run the four flights, until she was tugging the back of his shirt loose and her hands had found the skin of his back.

He stopped first, with his forehead against hers and his eyes shut and his hands flat on the door on either side of her head.

“Not in your father’s house.”

She opened her eyes, flushed to the collar. “That’s a rule?”

“It is now.”

“We’re married. It’s allowed. It’s practically compulsory.”

“Not in your father’s house. Ask me again at home,” he said, and she looked so outraged and so pink and so pleased at once that he nearly broke the rule inside a minute. He stepped back and straightened his glasses.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left at five. Ah Sim gave him a bag of leftover dumplings and a look. Raiden shook his hand and said “The rest of it” and began laughing all over again until Elowen steered him away by the arm. Lin Jian stood at the bottom of the stairs and nodded to him once, the way Zhao had in the alley.

“Next Sunday,” he said, and went back into the kitchen.

Elara grabbed Xing Yue’s sleeve so hard she nearly tore it. “That’s it. That’s yes. That’s the blessing. He’s never said next Sunday to anyone.”

Evangeline was holding the red door open for them. She looked at him as he went past, steadily, her face doing nothing.

“Good,” she said.

Elara burst into tears on the step. She cried in the car for ten minutes and talked for twenty: her father’s eyes, Raiden’s laugh, Zhao in the alley, which she’d watched from the landing window, and Ev, Ev, Ev. “She said good. She says about ten words a year, and one of them was to you.”

When they got home she put her shoes by the door facing out and stood in the hall in her coat and looked at him. “I’m asking you again. We’re home.”

He’d been waiting since the top of her father’s house. She took hold of the lapels of his coat and walked backwards up the stairs pulling him with her, a step at a time, and kissed him on every third one, and halfway up she took his glasses off and put them in her own pocket, and he heard himself laugh. At the top she dropped her coat on the landing, and then his, and took his hand and turned it over and kissed the inside of his wrist, watching him, doing his own move back to him.

“I pay attention,” she said against his pulse.

He forgot about rules. She’d been frightened all day, and now it came out of her in a different shape, eager and laughing and greedy. She pushed him down onto the bed and undressed him herself, slowly, taking her time over every button, and told him the whole way through exactly what she’d wanted to do in the room at the top of the house, in detail, and then she did it, sitting astride him with her hair coming down and her hands braced on his chest, until he pulled her down by the back of the neck and stopped her mouth with his, and she laughed into it, and then she didn’t, and neither of them said anything that made sense.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his shoulder in the dark with his hand in her hair.

“To have married her. In August.”

“I meant it.”

“I know you meant it. That’s why I choked.”

“You choked on soup.”

“I choked on my husband asking my father for a blessing for the rest of it in front of Raiden, who will never, ever let it go.”

“He said next Sunday.”

She went quiet. “He did. He did say that,” she said.

chapters.title: His Brother Comes for Tea
chapters.desc: Elara finds out her silent sister got married before she did, and told nobody either. Then his brother flies down for one cup of tea, notices everything, and lets slip how rich the Wangs really are.
chapters.epigraph: “He rang me to ask whether love at first sight was in the literature.”
chapters.content:
Elowen never rang at eleven at night. On the Tuesday after Elara’s twenty-fourth birthday she did.

Elara was at the kitchen counter in her scrubs eating peach yoghurt out of the pot after a late shift, and she answered with the spoon in her mouth.

“Ev’s married.”

Elara took the spoon out. “What?”

“Married. Since April. A registry in a border town. She told me in July and made me promise. I’ve been dying. The man from February, the one you— He went to see Baba on Thursday, in his office. Your birthday. You were on nights. There was a knife. Nobody’s hurt. Baba’s fine. And on Saturday he asked her again, at the orchid stall in the flower market, to marry him properly, in front of us. And she said yes. Out loud. In front of the orchid woman.” Elowen’s voice was doing something strange. She stopped, because nobody in their family said certain things on a phone.

Elara put the yoghurt pot down on the counter upside down.

“Yes. Out loud.”

“The orchid woman gave them a plant,” said Elowen, and Elara started to cry.

She stood at the counter with the phone against her ear and her hand over her eyes while her sister told her the rest: his name, which she knew; that he was enormous, which she knew; that he talked all the time to everyone except about himself, and couldn’t cook, and would have walked into the sea for Ev without being asked.

“April. April. I saw the ring at Sunday lunch. I was half asleep over a dumpling and I saw it, and I didn’t—” said Elara.

“Why didn’t you ask?”

“Because she never once asked me about the phone calls. And she was married. She did it first. She beat me by four months.”

“Elara. It’s good news.”

“I know it’s good news. That’s why.”

“And you’re one to talk.”

“I know,” said Elara, and Elowen laughed down the phone, which Elowen almost never did.

When she put the phone down Xing Yue was standing in the kitchen doorway in his reading glasses with a journal.

“Evangeline,” he said.

“She’s married. Since April. To the man in February. Nobody knew except Elowen, she just went and did it at a registry, like a— Like me.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t say yes like that. I’m fine. I’m happy. I’m crying because I’m happy.” She wiped her face on her sleeve.

He came over and took the yoghurt pot out of her hand, because she’d picked it up again upside down. “You cry at everything good. Dogs on the news. The banana prize. My handkerchief. Mr. Yin’s card. Your father saying next Sunday.”

She opened her mouth and couldn’t argue with a single one. “Two sisters. Two secret weddings in a year. Baba must be having a heart attack.”

“Three. Raiden.”

“Three,” said Elara.

✦ ✦ ✦

His brother came on the Saturday, between two flights.

Xing Yue told her on the Thursday, as if it were a change to the rota. An Yu was flying south for a meeting and back north the same evening, and would come for tea at three. He said it while cleaning his glasses, and he’d been working out how to say it for two days.

“Your brother. The one who rings on Sundays. The one who earns more before breakfast than you do in your life. He’s coming here. To our flat. And you’ve told me on Thursday.”

“He told me on Wednesday.”

“Does he know about me?”

“He knows. I rang him from the registry steps.”

“You rang your brother from our wedding and didn’t tell me you rang your brother from our wedding?”

“You were laughing at Mr. Yin.”

She spent Friday evening cleaning, which she never did. She moved her things into piles, and he moved the piles into rows, and she moved them back. She bought a cake from the good bakery on Harbour Road and then panicked that it was the wrong sort of cake and bought another one. She asked him four times what An Yu was like and got the same answer four times, like An Yu, and threw a cushion at him.

An Yu came at three exactly. He was shorter than his brother and broader, with the same serious face closed in a different way, like a door with a better lock, and a coat that probably cost as much as a small car over a suit that probably cost as much as a larger one.

“Elara.” He shook her hand, dry and brief, and gave his brother a cake of old aged tea in a paper wrapper at the door, the way other people gave wine.

Xing Yue made it in the small brown pot, and An Yu sat on the grey sofa with his cup and his back straight and let her talk. She couldn’t help it. The two cakes and why there were two; the ferry; the man on her ward who’d swallowed a key; Mr. Yin’s card. She heard herself doing it and couldn’t stop. An Yu said yes once and I see once.

But his eyes moved. She watched them go round the room while she talked, the way Eliana’s went over a screen. Her shoes by the door facing out. The study through the open door with the low oak desk and the suturing board. The little heap of taxi receipts on the counter, because she always took a receipt and never knew what to do with it. Her lanyard on the stairs. The second toothbrush mug by the bathroom door. His brother’s left hand. Then his brother.

Halfway through the man with the key, Xing Yue laughed, a short sound under his breath at the part where the man asked for the key back. An Yu turned his head and looked at his brother laughing, and his face didn’t change at all, and he looked down into his tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

“He rang me to ask whether love at first sight was in the literature,” he said.

It was the first thing he’d said that wasn’t yes or I see, and he said it to Elara, and put his cup down.

“Two summers ago. June. A Saturday night. He doesn’t ring me; I ring him, on Sundays, to tell him he works too hard. Eleven at night. He wanted to know if anybody had studied it,” he said.

Elara’s mouth fell open.

“Medical, he said. Psychiatric. Neurological. Anything with a reference. He’d seen someone on a ward and hadn’t slept, and he wanted to know whether there was a documented mechanism or whether it was simply tiredness. I sent him three papers. One was about voles.” An Yu picked his cup up again.

“Voles.”

“Pair-bonding in prairie voles. It’s a well-known paper. He read all three and rang back to say the voles were the only useful one.”

Elara turned round on the sofa. Xing Yue had his glasses off and was cleaning them on his handkerchief, every corner of every lens, slowly, and his ears had gone dark red. She laughed until she had to put her tea down, and laughed until she was crying, which apparently she did at everything, and An Yu watched her with his closed face, and the corner of his mouth moved once, exactly like his brother’s.

It came out sideways after that. She asked him, to be polite, what his meeting had been about, and he told her, and she understood about a third of it. The numbers she understood perfectly well. They had a great many noughts in them, and he said them.

“Xing Yue said your father has some hospitals.”

An Yu looked at his brother. “Some.”

“In the north. Your grandfather built them.”

“Fourteen. And the medical school that trains the doctors for them. And the land they stand on. And the port the equipment comes in through. And the house in the hills where our grandmother lives and writes to him every month to tell him to come home and get married. Some.” He set his cup down. He looked at Elara.

Nobody said anything.

Elara was a Lin. Money came in the back door of her house at night in envelopes and went out of the front in her father’s coat; men stood up when her father walked down the street; there’d been a car and a driver her whole life. She’d thought she knew what rich was. This was a different size. She didn’t have a word for this size. What were you supposed to say to a port?

She looked at her husband. He’d put his glasses back on, and there was no apology on his face and no worry either. He looked as if he were waiting to see which way she’d go.

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu left at a quarter to four. He put his coat on in the hall and shook her hand again, dry and brief. “Thank you for the cake. Both of them.”

She went red. She’d thought he hadn’t noticed there were two.

“Sister-in-law,” he said, with a nod, and she couldn’t tell whether it was a joke or a welcome, and decided later that from An Yu it was both.

She was in the kitchen with the cups when she heard them at the front door behind her, low.

“Nainai will ask at New Year when you’re bringing your wife home.”

A short silence. “I am home.”

She stood at the sink with a cup in each hand and didn’t move. The door shut. His footsteps came back across the big room, and she turned the tap on fast so that he wouldn’t know she’d been standing there, and he came into the kitchen and looked at the tap running into an empty sink and knew anyway.

She waited until she’d dried the cups. Then she began.

“Fourteen. Fourteen hospitals. And a medical school. And a port. You told me in May your father had some hospitals and I thought you meant clinics. I told Elowen your family was in healthcare. I said it as if it were a dentist’s.”

“You never asked.”

“Don’t you dare. You said that about your cousin. You can’t keep not telling me things and then saying I never asked, as if it’s my fault for not guessing you’ve got a medical school—”

“You’re right.”

She stopped. He never said you’re right in an argument. He said it on ward rounds, about scans.

“I didn’t tell you because I didn’t want it to be the thing about me. It’s been the thing about me my whole life, and I came here so that it wouldn’t be. That isn’t a good enough reason.”

He told her the rest standing in the kitchen, plainly, like a history. His grandfather’s trust, which had come to him at twenty-five. The top of this building, bought in 2019. The rest of it put somewhere and not looked at since. A consultant’s salary he hardly spent. He would never run anything in the north; his father knew that and didn’t believe it, and his grandmother knew it and was the only one who did.

“None of it changes where I live. Or who with,” he said.

She’d stopped being angry somewhere in the middle without noticing, and that annoyed her, so she started again. “We’re married. I haven’t even said it out loud at Harbourside yet. I find out on a Saturday afternoon from your brother that I’ve married a port—”

He looked at his watch.

“Are you timing me?”

“I’m giving you five more minutes. Then I’m going to kiss you.”

She stared at him, and then went on louder, because nobody was going to tell her when she’d finished: his coat, which probably cost more than her loupes; the second cake; cleaning all Friday night for a man who’d read her taxi receipts. She was halfway through the receipts when she saw his eyes drop to the second hand.

“You’re early. That’s four, that’s not five—”

He took her wrist and turned it over with two fingers on the pulse, as if he were going to count it against the second hand, and kissed her in the middle of the word, against the counter, with her back to the clean cups. She made a furious sound into his mouth and grabbed his shirt in both fists and kissed him back, still furious, then less, then not at all, until she’d pulled the shirt out of his trousers and he’d lifted her onto the counter beside the cups, and the argument went somewhere neither of them bothered to look for.

“That was four,” she said, much later, when she could.

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the card on the Wednesday. She was at the hospital kiosk in his coat, which she’d taken that morning because hers was in the wash, and she opened her wallet to pay for a coffee, and there it was in the slot behind her identity card, where it hadn’t been on Tuesday: a plain dark grey card from the green taxi company with LIN ELARA on it and an account number.

She rang him from the kiosk. “What is this?”

“An account in your name. Every taxi you take goes on it. Anywhere, any time.”

“Who gets the bill?”

“I do.”

“So you’ll see every taxi. Where from, where to, what time. You’ll get a list of everywhere I go.”

“I already know where you go.”

She started to answer and didn’t. He did. He’d had her on his phone since February, a small blue dot, and she’d watched him check it and never once told him to stop. She didn’t tell him now. She hung up on him instead, and was furious for an hour, the way you are furious about something you know perfectly well you’re going to keep.

At two in the morning she came out of Harbourside after a shift that had run six hours over, into rain, with no cash and no bus and her feet screaming. There was a green taxi at the rank. She got in and handed over the card, and the driver swiped it.

“Banyan Terrace, Dr. Lin?”

It was already on the account. She sat in the back of the warm car with the rain on the windows and the harbour going past, and got her phone out.

Elara: Fine.

He was asleep. He answered anyway, inside a minute.

Xing Yue: Good.

chapters.title: He Is Bad at Holidays
chapters.desc: He works every holiday so other people can go home. On Lunar New Year’s Eve his wife brings dumplings to Ward 9B, and he breaks his own rule.
chapters.epigraph: “I said not in the hospital. I’m allowed to be wrong.”
chapters.content:
On the last Sunday in January Raiden took his wife through the red door for the first time, and Xing Yue was in theatre with a perforated duodenum, and Elara wasn’t there either. She heard it from Raiden at nine that night, in a call that lasted forty minutes and was mostly him laughing, and then she rang her husband.

His phone went in the pocket of his scrubs while he stood at the end of a theatre table watching a registrar close. He let it ring twice, then nodded to Suyin, who took it out of his pocket and held it to his ear. She’d been doing that for four years and knew who rang at this hour.

“She went in.”

No hello.

“Jinx. She went in the house. Married to him for over two years and she’d never once been through the door, and today she went, and Ah Sim opened it before Raiden touched the handle and took both her hands, grease and all, and said she was the one who’d taught him to cook properly.”

“I’m glad.”

“And Baba offered to have his lawyer deal with somebody who’s trying to cheat her father over some land, and she said no. To Baba. In the kitchen. And then she told him it was one of the conditions, and Baba said he’d read the napkin—I don’t know what the napkin is, Raiden wouldn’t say—and then he laughed. The big one. Raiden said it nearly took the windows out. He said nobody had said no to him in his own kitchen since 1987.”

On the table the registrar had put a stitch in the wrong place. The third one. Xing Yue had watched the first two and said nothing, because the first two had been the man’s own to get wrong.

“I’ve heard Baba laugh like that about four times in my whole life, and I wasn’t there—”

“Wait.”

She stopped. He never said wait to her. He turned his head an inch from the phone.

“Dr. Zou.”

The registrar’s hands stopped.

“Take that out. And the one before it. You’re closing skin, not wrapping a parcel. If you close a wound like that on anyone of mine again, you can go and work in a shoe shop, where it won’t matter what the stitches look like. Again. Slowly.” His voice didn’t go up; it went down.

Dr. Zou took them out. Nobody in theatre breathed. The anaesthetist found something urgent on her machine. He turned back to the phone. “Sorry. Go on. He laughed.”

There was a long pause on the line, and he waited to find out whether she was angry.

“You just told somebody to go and work in a shoe shop. In that voice.”

“He’ll do it properly now.”

Another pause, and then she laughed, low, somewhere on the floor of their study with her feet on the armchair. “Poor man. I’ll bring him a sweet tomorrow. Which one’s Zou? The one with the eyebrows?”

“Yes.”

“I’ll bring him two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that week she asked him why he always took the holidays. Not as a complaint. She was lying on the floor of the study again with the phone on her chest, and he was on call, walking an empty ninth-floor corridor in the small hours, and he could hear she’d already guessed half of it.

He stopped by the window at the end. The harbour was black down there, and a ship was going across with all its lights on.

“The ones with children should go home. Fei has two. Rao has a little girl. If I’m here, they’re not. That’s most of it. The rest is that I don’t like them. At home they were dinners. Thirty people at my grandfather’s long table, and my father at the end of it talking about the hospitals: how many beds, how many new ones, which son would take over which. An Yu used to hide under the table with a book. I used to sit and wait for the courses to end.” He could have stopped there. He always had, with everyone.

“Oh,” she said, small.

“Here something happens.”

“Every Christmas? Every New Year?”

“Yes.”

“You told me that without my asking. You’ve never once done that. I always have to dare you, or drag it out of you with a broom.”

He thought about it. She was right. “Don’t get used to it.”

She laughed so loudly on the floor of the study that he had to hold the phone away from his ear. Then she said, “Baba said the Eve. One o’clock is for Sundays. The Eve is six. He said bring him, the way he said it in September.”

He stood by the black window for a while.

“Rao can have the evening. I’ll take the night,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

So on Lunar New Year’s Eve, which fell on a Friday, he went to the red door at six in a dark suit with a bag of mandarins and a tin of green tea biscuits for Eliana, and Elara went in ahead of him in a red dress she’d bought for it, talking.

The house was full of everybody. Elowen and Zhao, with the dogs shut in the yard. Evangeline in grey, and the enormous man she’d married, who’d come up the alley with a kumquat tree on his shoulder and set it down in the hall as if it weighed nothing. Raiden and Jinx, who sat at the end of the table with her hand on the back of his chair, and Eliana beside Jinx asking what her lathe could cut and writing the answers on a napkin. Ah Sim fed them until nobody could move and said nobody was eating.

He’d sat at long tables all his childhood. This one had eleven chairs that didn’t match and more people than chairs, and nobody talked about beds. Raiden called Evangeline’s husband the wardrobe four times. The wardrobe talked to Elara about wound packing for twenty-five minutes and knew a great deal about it, and when she told him he had better technique than half her registrars he went red, all of him, which took a while. Lin Jian and the wardrobe stood by the window for an hour with their hands in their pockets talking about tides, until Ah Sim said that if they didn’t sit down she’d give their soup to the dog. There was no dog.

Halfway through the fish Xing Yue looked down the table and found Lin Jian looking at him. Neither of them looked away. Then Lin Jian put a piece of the belly into his bowl, without a word, the way Ah Sim did for Elara, and went back to the wardrobe and the tides.

At the end of dinner Lin Jian lifted his glass. “To the ones who came home,” he said, and looked at Raiden, and at Jinx, and drank. Elara’s hand found her husband’s under the table and held on hard.

At ten he stood up. Ah Sim met him in the hall with a cardboard box tied with string and put it into Elara’s arms instead of his. “He’s working. You take it to him. Later. Not now. Let him go first, he’s got a face like a man who hasn’t eaten,” she said. And she pushed him out of the red door into the cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

From half past ten his phone buzzed in his pocket on the ward and didn’t stop.

Elara: eliana just threw a bag of dumplings over the wall to the boy next door. your cousin. i saw. she doesn’t know i saw

Elara: ev let the wardrobe hold her hand on the sofa IN FRONT OF BABA

Elara: jinx and baba are drying up in the kitchen. alone. nobody is allowed in. raiden is pacing

Elara: baba laughed again!! twice in two weeks!! what is happening to him

He read them at the nurses’ station between patients with his face perfectly straight. Sister Miao watched him read them and pretended not to. At eleven he sent one back.

Xing Yue: Eat something.

Elara: i’ve eaten FOUR bowls. ah sim’s counting

At twenty to twelve he was at the station writing up a man with a bowel obstruction when the lift doors opened at the end of the corridor and she came out of them. Red dress, coat over it, hair coming out of its pins. Ah Sim’s box in her arms and a string bag of oranges off her wrist. Her cheeks pink from the cold. She came down the corridor past the dark bays where the patients were asleep, and every nurse on the ward looked up, and Sister Miao put down her pen.

“Happy New Year. Ah Sim’s dumplings. Chicken and cabbage. There’s a coin in one, she says, but she won’t say which, and if you get it you have to tell her. And oranges. You have to have oranges. I got a taxi. On the card. I thought you’d want to know,” Elara whispered at the station. She put the box down in front of him.

He looked at her, and at the box, and at the red dress under her coat, and put his pen down.

“Sister Miao. I’ll be in the on-call room. Bleep me.”

Sister Miao looked at Elara, and at him, and at the dumplings. “Of course, Dr. Wang. Happy New Year, Dr. Wang.” She picked her pen up again and said, without looking up, “Leave me two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The surgical on-call room on nine was narrow: a bed, a chair, a desk, a sink, and a window looking west over the hospital garden and the roofs all the way to the Walled City. They ate off the bed with the box between them and the chopsticks Ah Sim had tucked under the string, and she talked with her mouth full.

“It was so loud. The loudest New Year we’ve ever had.”

“I liked it.”

She stopped with a dumpling halfway to her mouth. “You did?”

“Nobody counted anything.”

“Ah Sim counted my bowls.”

“That’s different,” he said, and she looked at him and then put the dumpling in his mouth instead of her own. His teeth hit something hard. He took it out: an old coin, wiped clean, warm from the dumpling.

She stared at it and put both hands over her mouth and laughed into them until her eyes ran. “You have to ring her. Tomorrow. She’ll be furious. She’ll say I gave it to you on purpose. I didn’t.”

He put the coin in the pocket of his scrubs. He wasn’t giving it back to anyone.

The fireworks went up over the Walled City at midnight. They stood at the window with the light off, red and gold and green a long way off over the old piers and the roofs, each bang a second late through the glass. Somewhere under them, on a roof, her whole family was standing in the cold. She stood with her back against his chest and he had his arms round her and his chin on the top of her head.

“Happy New Year.”

“Happy New Year.”

The last of them went up and the sky went smoky and quiet. She turned round in his arms and looked up at him, and he watched her decide to be wicked.

He’d made the rule in the autumn, the first time she’d come up to 9B with his lunch and a nurse had found them in his office with the door half open and gone away with her eyebrows in her hair. Not in the hospital, not where his team were, not where his patients were. Outside the doors was outside. Inside was work.

She backed away from him slowly until her shoulders met the door, and leaned on it, and folded her arms. “Not in the hospital. That’s what you said. I’m in the hospital. You’re in the hospital. It’s strict. I’d hate you to break it. You’d never forgive yourself. You’d have to go and work in a shoe shop—”

He crossed the room and put his hand flat on the door beside her head and pushed it shut the last inch and turned the lock.

“I said not in the hospital. I’m allowed to be wrong.”

He tipped her face up to the light from the window and kissed her in the middle of whatever she’d been going to say next. She made a sound of pure triumph into his mouth. Her arms came uncrossed and took hold of him, and she tasted of oranges, and her coat went somewhere, and her hands were cold from the window and she put them up under his scrubs on his back on purpose, and he made a sound he had never made in this building. She laughed.

He lifted her off her feet and carried her the two steps to the bed and sat down with her in his lap, and she kissed him as if it were a holiday, which it was, slowly and then not slowly, her knees on either side of him on the narrow bed and his hands on her back through the thin red dress, until she was kissing his throat and he had his eyes shut and couldn’t have said which building he was in.

His pager went off on his waistband, loud, right between them. She jumped. He opened his eyes, and she was a few centimetres away, flushed and furious.

He read it with her still in his lap, and reached for the phone on the wall. “Wang. Yes. Coming. Bed eight’s pressure is dropping.” Her forehead dropped onto his shoulder and she shook with silent laughter into his neck. He put the phone down.

“Go. Go, save bed eight. I’ll wait. I’ll eat your dumplings,” she said into his neck, still laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bed eight took two hours. When he came back she was asleep on the narrow bed in her coat and red dress, curled on her side with her shoes on, the empty box on the floor and an orange in her hand. He sat on the chair and watched her for a while, then took off her shoes and put them side by side under the bed, facing the door.

At three he walked her down to the taxi rank at the main doors. It was cold and clear and the air smelled of fireworks, and she was shivering, so he took off his jacket and put it on her over her coat and did up one button at her chest.

“Now I’m wearing a surgeon.”

A green taxi pulled in. She turned on the kerb and put something in his hand: a small red envelope with a gold character on it, folded flat.

“I’m married. Married people give red packets,” he said.

“Ah Sim doesn’t believe in registry offices. Until there’s a banquet you still get one. And anyone who works on New Year’s Eve gets one. That’s an old rule. She might have made it up. Don’t open it till I’ve gone.” She closed his fingers over it.

She got into the taxi in his jacket, and he watched it go down the hill, and opened it. There was no money in it. Only a slip of paper folded in four, in her round quick handwriting that anybody on earth could read.

Come home for breakfast.

He stood on the kerb in his scrubs in the cold and read it twice, and put it in his pocket with Ah Sim’s coin, and went back up to his ward.

Sister Miao looked up from the station. “My two dumplings, Dr. Wang?”

He’d forgotten. There had been an orange in Elara’s hand and nothing else in the box.

“Tomorrow.”

“Mm-hm,” said Sister Miao, and went back to her notes, smiling at them.

chapters.title: Ring Me First
chapters.desc: Her sister shoots a man in a noodle shop, and Elara runs across the road from the bakery and takes over a county hospital. She gets home at midnight and shakes on the hall floor, and her husband asks for names.
chapters.epigraph: “Next time ring me first. I’ll drive. I’ll wait in the car.”
chapters.content:
On the Saturday in the middle of June Elara was off, which happened about once a month, and her husband was on, which happened every other day, so at half past one she took a taxi over the river to the bakery on River Bridge Road, because Nuo had passed her first exams in May and wanted to show her the marks, and because at three they were going across the road to Nam’s for a slice of the birthday cake Ev had baked that morning in the bakery’s oven.

Nuo had the paper folded in her apron pocket and unfolded it four times. Elara read it four times and said look at that every time, and they ate a custard tart each at the back counter among the flour sacks, and Elara was licking the last of it off her thumb when the noise came across the road.

She’d grown up in the Walled City. She knew what it was before Nuo did.

She was out of the door before the third one. A van was pulling away from the kerb outside Nam’s with its side door still open, and somebody inside it was shouting, and the glass in Nam’s front window was all over the pavement in pieces. Then the van was gone round the corner, and there was nothing in the street but a dropped umbrella and an old man on the bakery step with his hand over his heart.

“Stay there,” Elara told Nuo, and Nuo didn’t, and came after her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nam’s front room looked as if a lorry had gone through it. The tables were over. The duck cabinet had a hole in the glass the size of a fist, and the duck that had hung in it for twenty years was on the floor. A young man was sitting against the wall with a constable’s hand pressed over his shoulder, grey in the face. A man in a pale shirt lay face down by the counter with Sergeant Chiu, out of uniform, kneeling on his back, and he turned his head on the wet tiles and watched her come in with no expression at all.

And on the floor of the kitchen, in a lake of broth, lay Nam on his side, holding his arm against his chest, telling the ceiling she’d no business in his kitchen.

“Oh, Nam,” said Elara, and swore once and knelt down in the broth.

Then she was a doctor.

His wrist was broken, she could see that from the shape of it, and he had a cut over his temple that was bleeding into his collar, and he was furious, which was good. “Don’t talk,” she told him.

“I own a shop.”

“You can own it quietly. Where’s Ev?” She sent Nuo for clean tea towels and a bag of frozen peas from the bakery and showed her how to hold the towel against his head.

Nam rolled his eyes towards the back door. Her sister was in the yard, on her knees in the wet, with her husband’s head in her lap. Blood down his face and broth in his hair, and his eyes open, going slowly round the yard. Evangeline’s hand was on his cheek. On the stone step by the back door, a pistol lay pointing at the wall.

Elara didn’t look at it. She knelt and parted his hair with her fingers and looked.

“It’s long. Down to the bone. Did he lose consciousness?”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“I don’t know. A minute. Twice.” Ev’s voice was perfectly level, which was how Elara knew.

“Has he been sick?”

“Not yet.”

Elara looked down at him. “Do you know where you are?”

“Nam’s. In the yard. In the broth. Your sister shot somebody.” His eyes found her.

“He’s oriented. Rude, but oriented. Like that. Hard. Don’t let go till I say,” said Elara. She folded a tea towel into a pad and put Ev’s hand on it, and pressed it down.

The ambulances took nearly twenty minutes to come over the bridge.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone went in her pocket in the back of the second ambulance, with Jun Hyuk on the stretcher and Ev holding his hand.

Xing Yue: ?

One question mark. He’d watched the dot sit in the bakery for half an hour, which was where she’d said she’d be, and then go across the road, and then go over the bridge to the county hospital at forty miles an hour. What was she supposed to say? Ev shot someone, home for dinner? She put the phone back in her pocket without answering.

The county hospital on the far side of the bridge had four treatment bays, and that afternoon three of them were full of people from Nam’s Noodles. She’d been a doctor for eleven months, which on paper made her the most junior person in the building, and she took it over, because the registrar on duty had been up since Thursday and looked at her the way a drowning man looks at a boat.

“Nobody touches the yard till the police have photographed it. Somebody find me his scans from the last time. And why does my sister’s husband have broth in his hair?”

“Nam threw it,” said Ev.

“Of course he did.”

In the next bay Nam lay with his arm in a splint, asking a nurse for his own spoon. He caught Ev’s sleeve as she passed and asked whether she’d brought the cake, and Elara watched her sister’s face when she said yes, and remembered the box on the floor of the shop crushed down one side.

“Seventy-two,” said Elara, “and still giving orders.”

“Seventy-one,” said Nam.

The boy Ev had shot was in the third bay with a policeman outside the curtain, and he was about twenty, and when the curtain moved and he saw Evangeline he said, “You shot me. You could have killed me,” and Ev said, “Yes,” to both, and they looked at each other.

“That’s enough. Both of you,” said Elara, coming round behind her sister.

The registrar put the staples in Jun Hyuk’s head while Ev held his hand. Elara checked the dressing afterwards and stepped back. “That’s that. He’s still going for a scan.”

“No,” said Jun Hyuk.

“That wasn’t a question. Not here. Crestview. I want the good machine and somebody I trust reading it.”

He looked at Ev, and Ev nodded, and he said, “You’re both enjoying this.”

“Immensely,” said Elara.

At twenty-seven minutes past four a tall policeman with black hair falling over his forehead came in with two officers and a thin folder. She knew who he was; everybody in her family knew who Song was. He looked at her across the bay, in her Saturday jeans with broth to the knees and a stethoscope she’d borrowed from the drowning registrar.

“Dr. Wang.”

“Inspector.”

She smiled at him, the smile she’d been giving policemen her whole life, and went and washed her hands at the sink in the corner and listened to none of what came next.

✦ ✦ ✦

Crestview looked like a hotel: carpet, soft lights, a receptionist who whispered when there was nobody to whisper to. They scanned his head at six. A concussion and a small fracture of the skull, not displaced, the bone where it should be, and no bleeding inside. They’d keep him for the night.

Elowen came, and Raiden with Jinx, and Elara gave them the scan in plain words in the corridor and then sat on a chair nicer than her sofa while her family held onto each other. At some point she heard Jun Hyuk through the door start on Ev about a sandwich and stop in the middle of the word and not start again, and she smiled into her coffee. At eleven Raiden put her in a green taxi and told the driver to go carefully, and she laughed at all the driver’s jokes the whole way home.

She got as far as the inside of the front door. She shut it and hung her keys on the hook and stood in the dark hall at Banyan Terrace in her ruined jeans, and began to shake.

It came from nowhere, up from her knees. She’d been fine at Nam’s and fine at the county hospital and fine at Crestview and fine in the taxi, and now her teeth went and her hands went, and she put her back to the wall and slid down it onto the floor by the shoe rack, with her own shoes in front of her still pointing out, and sat with her arms round her knees, rattling like a cup on a train.

The light came on upstairs. He didn’t say anything. He came down in a T-shirt and soft trousers and sat on the hall floor beside her and pulled her against his side so that her head was on his chest, and held on. She talked, of course.

“The window was broken. The duck had a hole in it. There was a boy against the wall, and Nam in the broth with his wrist, and a man on the floor watching me, he watched me the whole time. And Ev’s husband’s head was open—”

“Elara.”

“—and the policeman, and the registrar who’d been up since Thursday—”

“Breathe.”

She breathed. It came out in pieces. “My sister shot someone. Ev. She had a gun and she knew how to use it, and then she sat in the yard holding Jun Hyuk’s head as calm as anything. I’ve known her my whole life. I didn’t know she could.” Her voice went.

He went still against her. Not his thinking stillness: something colder, that went through him like ice through water. She lifted her head and looked at his face in the light from the stairs and didn’t know it.

“Who?”

“Who what?”

“Who came into the noodle shop. Who’s on the floor with a sergeant’s knee in his back. Who sent them. I’d like the names.” Perfectly level.

“No.”

He looked at her.

“No. I’m not giving you names. You’ll do something. I can see you’ll do something. And it isn’t yours. It’s Ev’s, and Jun Hyuk’s, and Song’s. Song was there. He’s dealing with it.” She grabbed his T-shirt in her fist.

“Elara—”

“That world raised me. That’s my family. Things come in the back door at night and you help and you don’t ask, and I’m not going to stop going when they ring. Don’t ask me to.”

He didn’t. She watched him take in the whole of it, and put the names away somewhere, and the ice with them, and come back.

“I won’t. Next time ring me first. I’ll drive. I’ll wait in the car. I won’t come in, and I won’t ask who.”

She stared at him. “You’d hate that.”

“Yes. But I’m not finding out from a dot on a map. The bakery, and then the road, and then a county hospital at forty miles an hour, and then the hill, and then nothing. For nine hours. I didn’t know whether it was you that was hurt.” His voice was steady, and then it wasn’t. It cracked.

She hadn’t thought of that. She’d thought of everything else in the world and not that.

“Yes, I’ll ring you first,” she whispered.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she’d stopped shaking he stood and pulled her up by both hands, and she thought he was taking her upstairs. He put her against the wall of the hall with his hands on either side of her face and kissed her, glasses still on, hard, his whole body holding her to the wall, steady, not letting up, like pressure on a bleed. She held onto the back of his T-shirt with both fists and kissed him back with her mouth still wet from crying. Under her hands his heart was going much faster than his face had let her see.

When he stopped he kept his forehead on hers. “You’re having a bath.”

He ran it. She sat on the edge in her jeans and talked about staples: that on a scalp you want the wide ones because of the hair, that she’d once seen a registrar try skin glue on a scalp and glue the man’s hair to his own glove so that he had to be cut free. She got in and sank to her chin and kept going. He knelt on the tiles beside the bath with his elbows on the edge and listened, and didn’t look away from her once.

She stopped. He was kneeling there, dry, glasses on, serious face, being sensible. She took the front of his T-shirt in one wet hand and pulled.

He came over the side before he knew it was happening, all his clothes on, glasses and all, and a wave went over the edge and across the floor. He landed with one knee on the bottom of the bath and his elbow in the soap dish and came up gasping with water pouring off his hair, and she laughed so much she slid under. He hauled her up by the arms, and he was laughing too, out loud, the real laugh she’d heard perhaps six times in her life, in a bath, in his trousers. He threw his glasses out onto the bathmat and tried to get his T-shirt off and got stuck in it, and she helped, badly.

Then it wasn’t funny. She didn’t know when it changed. She was holding his face, and he had both arms round her in the water as though she might go somewhere, and she kissed him slowly, for the first time all day without any hurry or fear in it. He kissed her back the same way, and under her hands he was shaking a little, and it wasn’t the cold. She held him tighter. He got the rest of his clothes off in the end, and the bath was too small and neither of them cared, and she took him into her there in the cooling water with her arms round his neck and her face in his wet hair, slowly, so that they could both feel every second of being alive.

Afterwards he sat her on the closed lid of the toilet in a towel and dried her hair, the towel first, rough and thorough, then the dryer on low, his fingers working through it section by section while she leaned her head against his stomach with her eyes shut.

“You’re very good at this.”

“I’ve watched you do it badly for a year.”

“Rude.”

“Oriented.”

She laughed into his T-shirt. In bed she lay along his side with her damp head on his shoulder, and his thumb found the inside of her wrist and stayed on her pulse, counting it, probably. When he moved once she caught his arm.

“Where are you going?”

“The light.”

“Leave it.”

He left it.

chapters.title: The Vow at Dawn
chapters.desc: On the morning she finishes her intern year he meets her in the old garden at City Hospital and asks his wife to marry him again, in front of everyone this time. She’s talking about fish, and says yes in the middle of a sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “Sorry, what? Say it again. I was talking.”
chapters.content:
He’d walked past the window for five years on his way to the ferry: a broken necklace on black velvet with every break mended in a thin line of gold, no price, no label. In the second week of June he went in.

“Dr. Wang. Elara’s husband,” said Aurelia Chen, coming out from the back of the shop herself, in grey, with her hair up. She looked at him from his shoes to his glasses exactly as she’d looked at him across Elowen’s shop in September, like a stone she hadn’t yet decided whether to set.

“I’d like a ring made.”

“Of course you would. You married her with a plain band from a shop on Harbour Road that isn’t mine. I saw the chain at the wedding, under her collar.” She sat down on the other side of the glass counter and folded her hands.

“I know you did.”

“I’ve decided to forgive you. Go on, then.” She opened a drawer.

He’d had it in his head for a year. A star sapphire, not large, the grey-blue kind with the star that slides across it under a light. A narrow plain gold band. Nothing that could catch in a glove; small enough for a surgeon’s hand.

“A star,” said Aurelia.

He didn’t explain, and he watched her work it out the way Elara had at Old Bian’s, and the corner of her mouth went. “Star and moon. Elara told Elowen what your name meant, and Elowen told me, and we both agreed it was the most nauseating thing we’d ever heard. Enzo will set it. He’s the best goldsmith in the city and he’ll make you wait three weeks.” She put a tray of stones in front of him.

“I need it in two.”

“Then it’ll cost you double, for rushing a genius. I shan’t tell Elowen. Not because you asked. Because it’s the only time in ten years I’ll have known something about her family before she did, and I intend to enjoy it for as long as it lasts. And when you do it again in front of everybody, I’m making the bands. Both of them. Don’t argue.” She named a figure. He didn’t blink; he’d known she would, and that she’d enjoy it. She ran his card.

He didn’t argue.

✦ ✦ ✦

He carried it for nine days in a small box covered in grey silk in the inside pocket of his jacket: on the ward, in his locker in theatre, in the car at night picking her up from the ferry. He didn’t give it to her, because the day wasn’t right yet, and he knew which day was.

On the first of July she’d start as a surgical resident at City Hospital, on Professor Liao’s team, colorectal and general on seven. Not his team and not his unit. She’d applied knowing that. He’d sat on no panels and signed no papers. Liao had read her Harbourside reports and her prize and her logbook and taken her in a week, and then cornered Xing Yue in the lift, sucking a boiled sweet. “I don’t want to hear one word from you about her, Wang. Not one. Good or bad.”

“You won’t.”

“I know I won’t. I’m telling you anyway.”

On the last night of June she’d come off her last shift at Harbourside, and the intern year would be over. That was the day.

“I want to see it when nobody’s there,” she’d said, a week before. “The old part of the hospital. The garden behind it. Two years I’ve been coming and going and I’ve never once been in, because I’ve always been running. I want to see it before it’s mine.”

“I’ll meet you.”

“You’re never off on a Sunday.”

“I’ll meet you.”

At five to seven on the Sunday morning he stood at the garden gate behind the old block and watched her dot cross the bridge and come up the harbour road and turn up the hill, and put his phone away when the taxi turned into the lane.

It had rained in the night, and everything was grey and soft and dripping, warm the way late June always was. A camphor tree older than the hospital, and under it a round pond with a low stone edge and koi going round, orange and white and gold. Benches. Two floors of tall arched windows on the back of the old block, with the paint coming off the frames.

She got out of the taxi in scrubs with a cardigan over them and a canvas bag on her shoulder, her hair falling out of its clip and night-shift shadows under her eyes, and saw him at the gate, and her whole face lit up.

“You came. At seven on a Sunday.”

“I swapped.”

“You never swap. Oh. Oh, it’s beautiful. Nobody told me. Look at the tree. Look at the fish.” She came through the gate and stopped dead.

She took one step and her trainer lace flicked out across the wet path, and he was down on one knee in the puddle and tying it before she could tell him to leave it, a double knot, with her hand on his shoulder and her laughing at him. He stood up. She didn’t notice that his knee was soaked through.

✦ ✦ ✦

She walked round the pond and talked. Her last patient, an old woman who’d had her gallbladder out on the Thursday and given her a knitted bookmark at four in the morning with a crooked cat on it. “It’s got three ears. I think it’s meant to have two. I love it more than anything I own.” The whole year: the ferry, the floor, the porters, the eighty-four-year-old who’d wanted a third pudding. She’d miss it, and her voice went wobbly. Then tomorrow.

“I’m scared. Not of the work. Of Professor Liao. Everyone says he’s lovely. He eats sweets on the round. They say he can tell from how you hold a pen whether you’ll be any good. What if I’ve been holding pens wrong my whole life and nobody’s ever told me?”

“You don’t.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I’ve watched you hold a pen for two years.”

She knelt on the stone edge and looked down at the koi. “Do koi sleep? They haven’t got eyelids, so how would you know? Maybe they’re all asleep now and moving out of habit. That one, the big gold one, I think that one’s asleep, it’s sort of drifting, look, by the stone—”

“Marry me again.”

“—and they live for ages, don’t they, I read somewhere they live longer than people, there was one in a pond somewhere that was two hundred—”

She stopped, and turned her head and looked at him over her shoulder.

He was on one knee on the wet path behind her. The same knee; he hadn’t planned that. His glasses had fogged at the edges in the warm wet air and he could only see her through the middle of them, kneeling on the edge of the pond in her scrubs with her mouth open. He held out the grey silk box, open.

“Sorry, what? Say it again. I was talking.”

“Marry me again. In front of everyone.”

“We’re already married.”

“In front of everyone.”

She stared at the ring and then at him. “Yes. Yes, but I was saying about the koi, there was one in a pond in—oh. Oh. Yes. I said yes in the middle of the fish. That doesn’t count, I want to say it properly—”

He stood and put his wet hand to the side of her throat, two fingers where her pulse was going like a bird’s, and stopped the rest of it with his mouth. She made a sound that was half a laugh and half a sob and grabbed his shirt and stood up on the stone edge to reach him better and nearly went in, and he held her, and she kissed him back with both hands in his collar while the camphor tree dripped on them and the fish went round underneath.

When she let go she said it again, standing on the stone so that her eyes were level with his and both her hands flat on his chest. “Yes. I’m saying it properly now. Yes.”

Then she cried, all at once, with her whole face, and was still doing it when she pulled the chain out of her collar, where she’d moved the ring for the night shift, and slid the plain band off it with shaking fingers and put it back on her own hand, and held her hand out to him.

He put the star on above it. It fitted; he’d measured her finger with a piece of thread in April, while she was asleep. She held her hand up to the grey light and turned it, and six thin lines of light slid across the blue-grey stone.

“It’s a star.”

“Yes.”

“You put a star on me. Star and moon. That’s the most embarrassing thing anyone has ever done. This is Aurelia’s, I can tell, look at the setting, that’s Enzo.” She laughed through it.

“She charged me double. She says she’s going to enjoy not telling Elowen.”

Elara laughed until she had to sit down on the bench under the tree, and he sat beside her, wet at the knee, while she held her hand out in front of them both and turned it so the star moved, over and over.

“They come off for theatre. Every day. Where do I put them? I lose everything. I’ll put them in a pocket and the pocket will go in the wash, and some poor woman in the laundry will find a star sapphire in a pair of scrubs—” she said, frowning at them.

“There’s a hook. In your locker. The residents’ changing room on seven, third from the end on the left. A small gold hook inside the door at the top, where you’ll see it. I asked the porters on Friday.” He looked at the koi.

She was quiet for one second. “On Friday. Before you’d asked me. You had a hook put in my locker. What if I’d said no?”

He turned his head and looked at her. “You didn’t.”

She hit him with her bag, quite hard, on the arm: knitted bookmark, stethoscope, three phone chargers. He let her. She hit him again, then put the bag down and put her face in his shoulder and laughed until she was crying again. She kept the hook.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fell asleep in the car before they were out of the lane, with her left hand held up in front of her face, looking at it, sinking slowly into her lap. He carried her up the stairs and she woke on the landing.

“Did I say yes?”

“Twice. Once in the middle of a fish.”

“Good,” she said, and went back to sleep on his shoulder.

He woke at three to stripes of sun through the blinds. She was awake beside him, propped on one elbow, looking at her hand in the light, and she saw him wake and put her hand flat on his chest, rings and all, and looked at it there.

“I want to tell you something before anybody else gets to say anything about it. I love you. That’s all. I wanted to say it first today, before Raiden makes a joke.”

He took her hand off his chest and turned it over and kissed the inside of her wrist, and her palm, and the rings, and then he sat up and held her face and looked at her.

“What?” she whispered.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking.”

“Yes.”

She went pink from the collarbones up, and he didn’t stop.

The whole afternoon was slow. Nowhere to be, nobody to ring, nothing tomorrow that mattered as much as this. She lay back in the striped light and let him take his time, and he undressed her as if he had never done it before and had to learn the way, the cardigan, the scrubs, the clip out of her hair, and kissed every part of her he uncovered until she was arching off the sheet and holding the headboard with the hand that wore his rings. For once she didn’t talk. Then she did: his name, and yes, over and over, as though now that she’d started she couldn’t stop. When she pulled him down into her the rings were cool against the back of his neck, and he felt them there the whole time, and moved in her so slowly that she began to laugh and then to beg, and he held out until she came apart under him with her face turned into his shoulder, and then he stopped holding out at all.

Afterwards she lay on her front with her chin on his chest and her hand beside her face. “I’m going to be so annoying about this.”

“I know.”

That evening she sent the family chat a photograph of her hand on his knee with the rings on it and no words, and put the phone down on the cushion and both hands over her face. It buzzed, and buzzed, and didn’t stop, and she turned it over and read them to him one at a time.

Elowen: ELARA

Elowen: Why didn’t Aurelia tell me

Eliana: spreadsheet updated

Raiden: First try? Show-off. I needed thirty-one napkins

Evangeline: Good.

Then the phone buzzed once more. Not the chat. A number that never texted anyone.

Baba: Bring him on Sunday.

She read it twice. “He comes every Sunday anyway. Baba knows he comes every Sunday. Why’s he saying bring him?”

“Because he wanted to say something.”

She looked at him, and at the phone, and put her face in his shoulder and cried again, at another good thing.

chapters.title: The Seventh Guest
chapters.desc: Elara kneels in a noodle shop’s back room by the river after midnight while her husband waits in the car, then runs late up a lane in scrubs to her sister’s garden wedding. That night she says she doesn’t know who her own mother was.
chapters.epigraph: “Ev knows who her mother was now.”
chapters.content:
“You hold your pen like a scalpel.”

Elara froze with the pen in mid-air. It was her second day on Professor Liao’s team, and the whole round turned to look.

“Is that bad?”

“It’s correct. Lemon or ginger?” Liao held out a paper bag.

So he could tell. Everyone had been right.

The rest of the autumn went past her in pieces. One Sunday in October the whole family drove up to Ev’s new house on Fig Tree Lane in three cars, the first time they’d all gone up the lane at once, and the neighbours watched over the wall, and a ginger cat with white feet walked along the top of it as if he’d been sent to count them. In November Elowen bought both the buildings beside her shop and put one in Raiden’s name without telling him, and he found out from the deeds and rang Elara and shouted for ten minutes, mostly with joy. Xing Yue was at neither. He was on call for one and in theatre for the other.

“Tell me,” he said on the phone, both times, and she told him all of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Saturday in December, late, her phone buzzed on the arm of the sofa.

Evangeline: Nam’s. Tonight. About thirty people off a boat. Cold. Some hurt. Song is bringing some of them to the back room. Bring your bag.

She read it twice and looked up. He was at the other end of the sofa with a journal and her feet in his lap, and he’d looked up when the phone went and seen her face change.

“Ev?”

“Ev.”

She held the phone up so that he could see it. Then she took it back and rang him. He was sitting a metre away. His phone went in his pocket, and he looked at it, and at her.

“You said ring you first. I’m ringing you first,” she said.

He answered it. “I’ll drive. Get your bag,” he said into the phone, looking at her down the length of the sofa.

The green bag lived in the hall cupboard now. She restocked it herself, a bit at a time, from places she didn’t think about too hard. He’d been through it; she knew he had. One night in October she’d packed it in a hurry with the scissors on top, and in the morning they’d been in the side pocket where they belonged, and the out-of-date saline she’d been meaning to throw away was gone. She’d never said a word about it, and nor had he.

In the hall he took her coat off the hook and held it out, and when she’d put her arms in he zipped it to her chin, all the way.

“I can zip my own coat.”

“It’s cold at the river.”

“How do you know it’s cold at the river?”

“It’s December. It’s a river.”

She opened her mouth, then closed it and went down the stairs with her chin buried in her collar.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove over the bridge with the black water under them and the lights of the old market district coming up on the far side. She opened the glovebox for a tissue and found green tea biscuits, three packets, the ones from the ferry shop.

“When did these get here?”

“October.”

“I’ve been in this car fifty times since October.”

“You never open the glovebox.”

She ate one and stopped talking, and held the bag on her knees the rest of the way.

He pulled in at the kerb across the road from Nam’s, outside the dark bakery, and turned the engine off.

“I’ll be here.”

“You can’t sit in the car all night.”

“I said I’d wait in the car.”

She looked at him. He’d said it on the floor of the hall in June, and he was going to do exactly that. Nothing she could say would get him out of the car and through that door, because she’d told him it wasn’t his, and he’d listened. She leaned over and kissed him, hard, once, and got out with her bag and crossed the road.

At 11:38 Nam was still on his feet. She’d told him twice to sit down and let somebody else carry the blankets, and he’d told her twice that his back room was his back room. He had thirty clean blankets on the shelves and a big pot of broth on the stove and rice and the kettle on, and he’d pushed the tables against the walls and put clean cloths over the cats’ baskets and set a plate of biscuits by the door.

“For the children,” he said.

“There may not be any children.”

“There might be,” said Nam, as if that settled it.

Ev came in just before midnight with Raiden behind her carrying two bags of clean clothes, her hair tied back and her face pale under the fluorescent tube. She stood in the back-room doorway and counted the blankets, and took out her phone and looked at it and put it away, and Elara didn’t ask her anything, because she knew that face from the yard in June.

The first of them came in a little after one, in police blankets, with a constable: twelve of the thirty, because Song had no better room within an hour of the river and Nam had told him so. A woman with a little girl who wouldn’t let go of her mother’s sleeve. A man with a cut leg from the deck. A girl of about fifteen who sat with her hands clamped together in her lap. An old woman with blue lips and short breath and her hand flat on her chest, whose name was Lian.

Elara knelt on Nam’s floor and opened the bag and didn’t think. She never did, once she’d started. Warm and cheerful and clear. “I’m Elara. I’m a doctor. Auntie Lian, I’m going to listen to your chest. My hands are cold, sorry—”

“Cold,” the old woman agreed.

“Mine are worse than yours. We’ll warm each other up.”

She counted the breathing and wrapped her in a second blanket under the first and held the old woman’s hands between her own until they started to warm. Then the next one, and the next. The man’s leg, cleaned and closed. A boy with an ankle up like a balloon. An old man who was only cold and frightened and wanted to tell her where he’d come from, and she let him: a village, a river much smaller than this one, a brother who wasn’t here. She wrapped him up and held his hand a minute longer than she had to.

A little after three the back door opened, and Ev’s husband came in out of the dark, enormous and wet to the knees, and Nam looked him up and down from behind the counter and said, “You’re late. You’re not bleeding. Good. Sit down.”

Ev was by the kitchen door. She’d been standing there for three hours. When she saw him she stopped, and then she crossed the room in front of thirty strangers and a police constable and walked straight into his arms, and he held her with his face in her hair, and Elara, on her knees beside Auntie Lian, had to look at the blood pressure cuff hard for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her home at four with the sky going grey over the roofs. She talked at first, about the thirty, the cold, the girl with her hands, Auntie Lian, whose breathing had come back to normal by three and who’d held Elara’s face in both hands and said something in a dialect Elara didn’t know. All in pieces, too fast. Then she stopped and sat beside him in the dark and said nothing at all. In two years she had never once been quiet in his car for longer than a minute.

A long way further on she said, “Ev walked across the room to him. In front of everyone. She was so frightened she’d been standing in one place for three hours, and she let everybody see it.”

“Yes.”

“I didn’t know she could do that either.”

She reached over in the dark and took his left hand off the gearstick and held it in both of hers in her lap. Then she lifted it and pressed her mouth into the middle of his palm and held it there against her face with her eyes shut, for a long way along the harbour road. He drove one-handed all the way home and didn’t ask for it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ev had her wedding two weeks later, on the shortest day of the year, in the garden at Fig Tree Lane, with six guests and her father to give her away, a year and eight months after a registry office in a border town. Elara was meant to be the seventh.

She was on a twelve-hour night. She couldn’t swap; she’d begged, and nobody would. At four in the morning she messaged the family from the doctors’ room.

Elara: on a twelve-hour. two crash calls already. will come when I can. start without me. DON’T START WITHOUT ME

Raiden: we will NOT start without you

Raiden: (we will)

She came off at eight, and then didn’t, because a man she was handing over wouldn’t stop bleeding and she stayed with him until he did, and that was two. At half past two she got a taxi on the card from the main doors in her scrubs with her pass still clipped on, and fell asleep in the back, and woke on the reservoir road with the hills going past.

“Stop at the bottom. I’ll run. It’ll be quicker.”

It wasn’t. Her hair came out of its clip halfway up the lane. She came through the green gate a little before four in navy scrubs under an open coat, out of breath.

“I know. I’m late,” she said.

They were eating outside under the lights in the fig tree, Nam’s bread beside the neighbour’s sponge, and everyone looked up. Elara looked at the chairs and the lights and the bundle of herbs tied with white ribbon on the table, and at her sister in her dress, with an aquamarine on her hand beside the old silver ring, and at the man beside her who couldn’t stop looking at her, and her face crumpled.

“I was going to come in and be normal.”

“You’ve never been very good at normal,” said Evangeline, and got up and held her.

“You started.”

“We waited till one,” said Elowen, not even looking guilty.

“One isn’t waiting, one is lunch.”

“Sit down. Eat. She laughed. Out loud. At the cat. Head back, the whole thing. You missed it,” said Jinx.

“Don’t tell me that,” wailed Elara, and sat, and ate Nam’s bread with tears running into it, and nobody minded.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got home at seven with a jar of salted lemons Ev had pushed into her hands at the gate and a container of noodles from Ah Sim, and her eyes swollen half shut. He was home, a whole weekend off, the first in months. He took the jar and the noodles and put them on the counter, and she sat on the stool and told him.

“There was frost on the garden. She carried herbs. From her own glasshouse, not flowers, tied with white ribbon. And the neighbours watched over the wall, and the cat went up in the air when Raiden cheered and landed in the rosemary, and that’s when she laughed, and I missed it—”

“And the music?”

“Her mother’s viola. Somebody played it from the upstairs window during the vows. Her real mother’s. Ev found out about her this year, who she was, what she looked like, a photograph by a lake. And now she’s learning to play it. Ev knows who her mother was now.” She was turning the jar of lemons round on the counter, round and round.

He waited.

“I don’t know who mine was.”

She heard herself say it. She’d never said it. Not to Baba, not to her sisters, not out loud in an empty room.

“I don’t even know her name. I don’t know what she looked like. Whether she was alive when they took me to the children’s home. Whether she gave me away, or somebody took me. What if she talked? What if I talk because she did? That’s so stupid. That’s the stupidest—” The jar stopped.

He came round the counter and took the jar off her before she dropped it.

“I never wanted to know. I always thought, I’ve got the Lins, I’ve got Baba, that’s enough, it’s greedy to want another one. And then I watched Ev’s face when the viola started, and I wanted it so much I couldn’t breathe.” Her eyes filled again.

“What do you know?”

“Nothing. That’s what I’m saying. Baba brought me home from a children’s home when I was nearly three. That’s all there’s ever been.”

He didn’t say anything to that. He put his arms round her on the stool, and she put her face in his shirt and cried, for Ev and for herself and for a woman she couldn’t picture, until she was hiccupping.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine she said she was going to sleep for a week. Thirty-six hours awake. She lay down on the long grey sofa with her head in his lap, and he pulled the blanket off the back and put it over her and tucked it under her feet, and stroked her hair, and after a while his hand stopped.

“Please,” he said.

She opened her eyes. He never said please. Perhaps once in two years, to a porter, in extreme circumstances. He was looking down at her in the lamplight, glasses on, serious, and he didn’t say anything else. He’d sat beside her all evening while she cried for something he couldn’t give her.

She gave in at once; she hadn’t been going to hold out anyway. She sat up and took his glasses off and put them on the arm of the sofa and kissed him, slow and sleepy and warm. They didn’t get as far as the stairs and didn’t try. She was so tired she was clumsy and laughed at herself, and he didn’t laugh. He held onto her as if she were the thing he’d asked for and he wasn’t going to waste a second of it, his hands slow on her back under the scrubs top she’d never changed out of, his mouth slow at her throat.

“I’m too tired to be any good,” she mumbled.

“Then don’t be.”

She pulled him down onto the cushions and wound herself round him, and he drew the scrubs over her head and the blanket over them both, and moved in her so slowly and so deep that she stopped thinking about anything, everything soft and heavy and close, the lamp low, the frangipani tapping at the study window, his breath on her neck and his name in her mouth. She felt as if she were being held together, and she let him do it.

Afterwards she lay on top of him under the blanket with her ear on his chest, not sleepy at all.

She said, “I want ours outdoors. When we do it in front of everyone. Ev’s was in a garden in the frost, and it was the best one I’ve ever been to. I want ours outside, early, when the light’s coming. Somewhere with trees. Somewhere nobody’s ever bled.”

“All right.”

“You’re not allowed to organise it.”

“All right.”

“You are a bit,” she said, and fell asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she came downstairs at seven, and he was already at the counter, dressed, with a cup of tea and his prescription pad, writing something. When she came in he tore the sheet off and folded it and put it in his shirt pocket.

“Patient?” she said, yawning.

“Something I need to look up.”

“On a Sunday?”

“It’ll keep.”

He made her tea, and spring onion pancakes with the hot sauce, because she hated eggs, and she sat on the stool in his T-shirt eating a slice of Ev’s salted lemon with honey and didn’t think about the sheet of paper again. It was a year before she saw it, in an envelope: her birthday, and children’s home?, and under that, underlined twice, in handwriting only she could read:

Find her.

chapters.title: A Name in a Ledger
chapters.desc: He finds the old matron of the children’s home and the birth name his wife has never heard. He decides to keep it for their garden day, and she catches him hiding something.
chapters.epigraph: “They called her the bell girl. She never stopped.”
chapters.content:
A birthday. The words children’s home. The age of nearly three. That was what he had, and a tall house behind a red door, and a man who had his postman looked into every New Year. He kept the sheet from the prescription pad in his wallet behind his driving licence, and on the nights when she was on call and he wasn’t, he sat at the kitchen counter with his laptop and looked.

He rang the children’s homes that were still open from his office between clinics, and the women who answered were kind. “I’m sorry, doctor. Records of a child placed with a family are closed. To anyone but the child.”

“I understand.”

“Is it for a patient?”

“No.”

The ones that had shut had sent their files to the welfare archive behind the courts, and he went on a Saturday in January: a grey building, an index card for Plum Steps Children’s Home, closed 2011, and boxes of files he wasn’t allowed to open. What he found in the end was a newspaper, a short piece from the week the home closed, with a photograph of a small woman in a cardigan at an iron gate with a bag of keys, looking at the camera as though she didn’t think much of it. Matron Sima, who has run Plum Steps for thirty-one years. He found her through the church on the steps below the old home, where she still did the flowers, and it took three weeks for her to agree to see him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took a Friday off in March. He never took Fridays off.

“Dentist,” he told Elara.

“Open.”

“What?”

“Open your mouth.”

She looked at his teeth, all of them, with a torch. “Very clean.”

“Thank you.”

Fourth floor, no lift, two rooms that smelled of camphor and cooking oil, and her husband’s photograph on the wall in a black frame with a dish of oranges in front of it. She was eighty-one and tiny. She made him take his shoes off and sit on a stool too low for him, and poured his tea and not hers.

“You’re a doctor.”

“A surgeon. City Hospital.”

“And you want a child.”

“I want to know about one. She doesn’t know I’m here. She came to you in the autumn of 2002. Nearly three. She went to a family that November. Her birthday’s the sixteenth of November.” He put the cup down.

“Lots of children.”

“She talks.”

Matron Sima looked at him with small hard eyes. “Why should I tell you anything?”

He had a story ready, and he didn’t use it. “She told me she doesn’t know who her mother was.”

“Plenty don’t.”

“She’s never said it to anyone else. She said she wanted it so much she couldn’t breathe. I’m her husband. I’m going to marry her again in front of everyone, and I’d like to be able to give it to her.” He kept his hands flat on his knees.

The old woman didn’t answer. She got up and went into the other room, and a cupboard opened, and a great many things got moved, and something heavy went down. She came back with a ledger bound in red cloth with the corners worn through and put it on the table between them, and sat, and didn’t open it.

“They called her the bell girl. She never stopped. The girls in the kitchen named her. She talked from the minute she woke to the minute she went to sleep.” Something that might have been a smile went over the old face.

“She still does.”

“In her sleep too?”

“Yes.”

“Followed you round all day like a bell on a cat. You always knew where she was. She asked the boy fixing the roof whether his ladder had a name.”

“Did it?”

“She gave it one. She never cried. All those weeks. The others who came from fires cried at night, or wouldn’t eat. That one talked. She sat on the end of my bed and told me about the boats.” The smile went.

“Boats.”

“Her father’s boats. The little ones that go out to the ships.” She opened the ledger.

✦ ✦ ✦

He read it upside down at first, and then she turned it round for him: every child who’d come through the iron gate in thirty-one years, in the same small upright hand in blue ink. “The official files went to the archive. The government can keep them. This one’s mine. I wrote in it every night.”

October 2002, a line near the bottom of the page.

Qu Xiaoyue. Little moon. Born 16 Nov 1999. Brought by police 12 Oct from the fire at Qu Lighterage, Walled City piers. Found in a laundry basket under wet towels. Father Qu Mingde, lighterage, deceased. Mother Shi Yuning, nurse, deceased. No relatives found.

And under it, in the same hand and different ink: 4 Nov. Gone to a family. Papers came back with another name. He read it three times.

“The papers came back with another name, so I wrote the first one down. I always did. If somebody’s going to take a child’s name away, somebody should keep it.” She tapped the line.

“Who took her?”

“A man came in a black car. He paid for the roof. Six years it had leaked and the government never paid, and he paid for all of it, in cash, and the next week he came back for her. I don’t know his name. I never asked. You didn’t, then. She went down the steps holding his hand and talking, and he didn’t say a word. He looked as if he’d been hit.” Her mouth shut tight on whatever else she knew.

He didn’t say anything.

“Can I photograph the page?”

“No.”

“Can I copy it?”

She looked at him a long time, and then fetched a pencil and a sheet of paper from a drawer, and he copied it at her table on the low stool, every word, in square block capitals that anybody could read.

At the door she held onto his sleeve. “Does she still talk?”

“All the time.”

The old woman nodded and let him go.

✦ ✦ ✦

The newspaper turned up that afternoon in the reading room at the central library, on a machine with a screen that flickered. Saturday, 12 October 2002, page nine. Fire at Walled City lighter office kills two. Four short paragraphs: a small lighterage company by the old piers, and the flat above it; the owner and his wife found dead by firemen; the boats undamaged; police suspected the fire had been set; no one charged. No child in it. Nobody had told the paper about a basket. No other names, and nothing pointing anywhere at all.

He paid the man at the desk for a printout and sat in his car outside the library with it on the passenger seat beside the pencilled page, and didn’t start the engine. Her mother had been a nurse. Her father had run boats out to the ships. Somebody had put a child in a laundry basket under wet towels while the building burned, and it had worked. And three weeks later a woman behind a red door had looked at a girl called little moon and named her Elara, because Elara was a moon too, so that she’d keep a piece of it without knowing.

My mother chose it, she’d told him at Old Bian’s, delighted. Baba says she liked the sound.

He put the papers in a brown envelope in the glovebox, beside her hair clip. He’d give it to her on their garden day, in the morning, before anybody else was up: her mother’s name in her hands on the day she married him again, and nobody else’s voice in the room when she read it.

Whether he had the right to choose the day, he didn’t ask himself. Not then.

✦ ✦ ✦

That week she set the date. On the Wednesday she came in from a long day on Liao’s list and sat at the counter with a bowl of his noodles and announced it.
