“The hospital garden. Where you asked me. Under the tree, by the fish. It’s the only place I can think of that’s outdoors and has trees and where nobody’s ever bled. I checked. I asked Sister Miao. Thirty years and nobody’s ever bled in the garden except a porter who fell off a bench, and that was his nose, and it doesn’t count.”

“You’ll have the windows full of patients.”

“Good. They can wave.”

He reached over and took a mouthful of noodles off her fork while she was talking, and she stared at the empty fork. “Thief.”

“They’re my noodles.”

“It’s my fork.”

She wanted May, after her first surgical exams, because she’d cry at both and couldn’t be expected to cry that much in one month. She held her phone up across the counter and scrolled, and he watched her finger go through the rest of 2025 and into 2026 and stop.

“The ninth of May. A Saturday. Next year. That’s fourteen months. Is that too long?”

He thought of the envelope in the glovebox. “No. It’s good.”

She put it in her calendar, and then in his, by taking his phone out of his pocket while he ate. GARDEN WEDDING in capitals, and under it, DON’T BOOK ANY LISTS.

✦ ✦ ✦

The driver came in on a Thursday night at the end of March. Xing Yue was the consultant on call and had been down to resus for an old man with a twisted bowel, and he was writing up the notes at the station when he saw her across the department in cubicle eleven, with the curtain half open. She was the surgical resident on call, sent down to see a hand.

He knew the man. Not his name; his face. A face you’d seen at the bottom of a hill road at four in the morning: one of Zhao’s drivers, a thick quiet man who’d sometimes brought the car down from the house to the bus shelter and looked at nothing. He was on the trolley now with his left hand on a pillow in a towel that had been white, and his face was the same colour as the towel. A young constable with a notebook stood at the curtain, and Elara was talking to him the way she talked to everybody, warm and cheerful, with a boiled sweet in her cheek. She unwrapped the towel and looked at the hand.

For one second there was nothing on her face at all. Nothing warm, nothing cheerful: a cold, clear, flat attention that went to the wound and the man’s face and the constable’s notebook, and back.

Then it was gone. She said something to the constable that made him laugh. She closed it at the trolley, fast, and talked the constable through every bit of it, tendons and luck and a man she’d once seen fire a nail through his own boot. “Through his boot. And he wanted to keep the boot.”

The constable had stopped writing. In the morning, before the round, Xing Yue read her notes. Nail-gun injury, building site. Through and through, left hand, between second and third metacarpals. Tendons intact. Washed out and closed. PC present at assessment. Patient declined to give a statement. Underneath it, as consultant on call, he wrote Seen and agreed, and signed it.

On the round Dr. Zou leaned over his shoulder at the screen. “Funny kind of nail gun. That’s a big hole for a nail.”

Xing Yue didn’t look up. “Did you see him?”

“No, I was—”

“Then you don’t know what size the hole was. Bed four’s drain chart has nothing on it since midnight. Go and find out why. Then find out why you didn’t know at six.”

Dr. Zou went. The nurse with the drug trolley looked at the floor.

That night Elara was asleep on the sofa when he came in, with one foot hanging off the edge, and he stood and looked at her for a while and thought about her face in cubicle eleven, and whether he wanted her any different, and he didn’t, not by one hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

She caught him on the first Sunday in April. He’d never been good at hiding things. The Friday at the dentist. The Saturdays. He cleaned his glasses every time she asked him where he’d been, and she’d started asking just to watch him do it.

That evening she sat on the sofa beside him, and then on the arm of it, and then she took the journal out of his hands and dropped it on the floor and climbed onto his lap and sat across it with her hands on his shoulders and looked down at him like a chart she didn’t trust.

“You’re hiding something. Since Christmas. Saturdays. A Friday off. An envelope in the car next to my hair clip, which I’ve known about for two years, by the way—”

He reached for his glasses. She got there first and held them up out of reach.

“No cleaning. One. Is it bad?”

“It’s not bad.”

“Two. Is it about the hospital? Three—”

“Elara.”

“Three is the important one. Is it about me? Because if it’s about me—”

He put his hand flat on her back between her shoulder blades under her jumper and pulled her down and stopped her mouth with his. She made a sound of pure outrage against his lips and kept hold of the glasses and kept kissing him too, one hand on his shoulder, hard. He slid his other hand up under the jumper and found she’d nothing on under it, and she pressed herself into his palm and bit his lip, still furious, and for a while neither of them argued about anything.

When she pulled back she was pink to the ears. “That’s cheating. You do that to stop me talking.”

“It works.”

“It works because I let it. Is it about me?” She sat back on his knees.

“It’s a wedding present. You can have it on the day. In the garden, in the morning, before anybody else is up.”

He watched her want it. She opened birthday presents on the bus home; she’d once read the end of a crime novel in a bookshop and put it back on the shelf. Then he watched her get annoyed, properly, and that was harder.

“You’ve decided when I get to know something. It’s mine, isn’t it? Whatever it is. It’s mine, and you’ve got it, and you’ve picked a day for me to have it.”

He had no good answer, and didn’t want to give her a bad one.

“I hate that.”

“I know.”

She sat on him frowning, with his glasses in her hand, and then she folded them and put them on the table the way he did, and cupped his jaw. “Fine. Keep it. But it had better be good. Better than the loupes. The loupes were the best present anyone’s ever given me, so you’ve made it very hard for yourself. And I’m writing down that I hate it. So that on the day, when I cry, you’ll remember I was cross first.” She kissed his forehead.

She got up and wrote it on the fridge list, under peach yoghurt and above sesame paste. XY’S SECRET — CROSS ABOUT IT.

Then she came back and sat in his lap and kissed him until he’d forgotten the envelope was anywhere at all, and took him upstairs by the hand, and was still a little cross the whole time, and showed him exactly how much. It stayed on the fridge for months. He read it every morning while the tea brewed.

chapters.title: Again?
chapters.desc: At five in the morning her brother and his wife come in from a fire with burned hands. For six weeks she spends her days off fixing switches in the rebuilt shop, humming, and her husband catches her on a ladder.
chapters.epigraph: “You’ve got good hands. Steady. I’d hire you.”
chapters.content:
In June Liao sent her back to Harbourside for three months to cover the surgical floors, and on the second Thursday of the month, at ten past three in the morning, she had a biscuit halfway to her mouth for the first time since midnight when the phone went.

“Dr. Wang? It’s the ED. Your brother’s down here. And his wife. Smoke, and his hands. They’re both all right. I thought you’d want to know before somebody else told you.” The nurse had known her since she was a student and knew whose sister she was.

Elara put the biscuit down.

She didn’t remember the stairs. She remembered the doors at the bottom, and the corridor, and coming through the curtain of the end bay in her scrubs with her hair pinned up, and her brother on one trolley with both hands in dressings like two white boxing gloves, and Jinx on the next with an oxygen tube under her nose and a blanket round her shoulders and soot still in her hair and in the lines round her eyes. Four years ago, almost to the week, he’d been on the sixth floor of this building after a van.

“Again?” she said.

It went right up the corridor. A porter looked round. Raiden turned his head on the pillow and looked at her, and his eyes creased, and the idiot was grinning.

She checked everything. She couldn’t not. She read their notes and lifted the edge of Raiden’s dressings and looked at his palms and put them back, and kept her face nice, because he was watching it. She listened to both their chests. She asked the nurse what Jinx’s oxygen had been when she came in, and what it was now, and then asked again.

“Same as I just said, Dr. Wang.”

“Right. Yes. Good.”

“There was a shutter. Locked from inside. He didn’t know I’d gone down the back stair,” said Jinx. Her voice was a rasp.

“Of course it was locked. He pulled on a burning shutter.” Elara looked at her brother’s hands, and then at Jinx.

“I didn’t ask him to.”

Elara said, “No, you never have to ask him for anything. That’s rather the problem with my brother. I’m not going to shout at either of you tonight. I reserve the right to do it on Saturday.” She stood up and pulled Jinx’s blanket straight.

Jinx looked at her, and one corner of her mouth went up. Nearly.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five she’d sent him three words, Raiden. Fire. Fine., and at six her husband walked into the Harbourside ED in his coat with his bag on his shoulder and two teas from the bakery by the ferry, on his way to his own hospital on the far side of the river, which was nowhere near on the way. He found her against the wall outside the bay and stopped beside her and held one out.

She took it in both hands and just held it. He didn’t ask whether they were all right. He’d have read the board on the way past. He stood next to her against the wall with his own tea and looked at the trolleys, with his shoulder against hers, and after a while she leaned her head on his arm.

“His hands. He draws with his hands. It’s all he does.”

“Partial thickness. I looked. They’ll heal.”

“You looked? On your way past? I know they’ll heal. I’m a doctor. It’s just that it’s the second time I’ve come down a corridor in this building and found him on a trolley.” Her voice went up.

He put his hand on the back of her neck under her hair and left it there, in the corridor, in front of the whole department.

“Drink the tea. Then eat something. You’ve two hours left, and somebody upstairs is going to need you, and you’re no use to them on one biscuit.”

“I didn’t even eat the biscuit.”

“Then on no biscuit.”

She wanted to argue and drank the tea instead. He’d put sugar in it. He never put sugar in anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

They rebuilt the shop in six weeks.

On the first Saturday Eliana came with her laptop and her tool roll and a box of cable and rewired the back wall herself with an electrician checking behind her, and refused to be paid, and told Jinx she’d been waiting three months to say I told you so about the camera. Elara came on her days off. She’d told Elowen she would and then lay awake wondering what use she’d be, and on the first day she found out: nobody wanted the small jobs. Switch plates, light fittings, little brackets for the shelves, hooks for the tools, the hundred fiddly things that went back on the walls once the paint was dry. She did all of them, and liked it, up a stepladder with a screwdriver in her teeth and a bag of fixings in her pocket, her hands knowing what to do the way they did with a suture. She hummed. She didn’t know she was doing it.

On the Monday she stood on the tall ladder holding the new shelf brackets against the back wall while Jinx drilled, and her hands didn’t move a millimetre. Neither of them said anything about why. When the last one was up Elara came down the ladder and looked at her own hands, and then at Jinx, and said, “Good,” and that was all.

On the fourth day Jinx’s father came with a broom, and Elara’s father was already there, in shirtsleeves, which she’d never seen in her life, shovelling wet ash into a skip with a borrowed shovel. The two old men nodded at each other and worked side by side for an hour without a word. Then Jinx’s father said the floor drain at the back was blocked, and Lin Jian asked whether he knew how to clear it, and Jinx’s father said he’d been clearing drains since before Lin Jian could walk, and they got down on their knees and cleared it together, arguing.

Elara was on the mezzanine stairs with a box of switch plates. She put the box down on the step and went out into the street and stood on the cobbles with her back to the shop and her hands over her face. She didn’t know what had happened between those two men, years ago, under a flyover. Something had. And her father was on his knees in the ash beside him.

Later in the week Jinx came and stood at the bottom of the stepladder in her overalls, black to the wrists from a machine she’d been under all morning, and watched Elara put up a bracket, and then another. They’d been sisters-in-law since a flower shop and spoken perhaps forty sentences, most of them about burns.

“You’ve got good hands. Steady. I’d hire you.”

Elara stopped with the screwdriver in the air. “I’m a surgeon.”

“I know. I’d still hire you. That’s level. Nobody does them level. Eliana’s are all a degree off and she says it’s the wall.” Jinx looked up at the bracket.

“It isn’t the wall.”

“No.”

That was the first real conversation, and it went on, off and on, all afternoon. Jinx told her what each bracket was for. Elara told her about bananas.

“Bananas?”

“For suturing. They’re the closest thing to skin for the price.”

Jinx thought about it. “Do they complain?”

“No.”

“Better than people,” said Jinx, and they ate noodles sitting on a crate, and Jinx said nothing else nice all day, and it was plenty.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth of July Eliana and Yu Chen graduated on the same afternoon in the Great Hall, in two different gowns. Xing Yue sat near the front beside his wife in his dark grey suit with his back straight. He’d been Yu Chen’s mentor for four years and had been asked to come, and when Yu Chen went up he clapped exactly as hard as everybody else, and Elara looked at him sideways and saw that his jaw was tight.

“You’re proud,” she whispered.

“I’m clapping.”

“You’re proud.”

“Elara.”

Afterwards on the steps Eliana kissed Yu Chen in front of everyone, and Elara burst into tears and went and hugged her little sister so hard her cap fell off and rolled down two steps, and Eliana stood stiffly with her arms out and said, “You can stop now. Elara. You can stop.” Yu Chen came over with his ears red and shook his cousin’s hand.

“Emergency. You’ll be good at it. You don’t panic and you don’t like being thanked,” said Xing Yue.

Yu Chen looked at him as if he’d been handed something heavy and didn’t know where to put it down. “Thank you.”

“That’s what I mean.”

On the way down the steps Elara put her arm through her husband’s and didn’t say a single thing about his jaw.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ladder was on a Tuesday afternoon in the last week of the rebuild. She was off, and he’d had a clinic in the morning and nothing after, which happened about twice a year, and he came down to the shop because he wanted, he said, to see what she’d been doing with her days off for a month.

She was at the top of the tall ladder by the back wall with her hair tied up in one of Jinx’s scarves, putting up the last of the tool hooks, when the ladder went still under her. She looked down. He was at the bottom in his work shirt with the sleeves rolled up, one hand on the ladder and the other round her ankle.

“Let go. I’m fine. I’ve done about two hundred of these.”

“You’re humming and leaning out to the left, and the left foot of the ladder’s on a drain cover.”

She looked. It was. She went red and finished the hook anyway, and he didn’t let go of her ankle the whole time, his hand warm round it above her trainer and his thumb on the bone, and she felt it all the way up.

When she came down he didn’t move out of the way. On the rung above the bottom she caught the back of her thumb on the edge of the last bracket and said a word Ah Sim would have washed out of her mouth, and he took her hand and turned it over and held it to the light from the new window, frowning at a thin red line.

“It’s nothing. It’s a scratch. Don’t you dare put a plaster on it, I’ll never hear the end of it from Jinx—”

He kissed it, the back of her thumb, and then, before she’d finished telling him it was nothing, her mouth. She came off the last rung into his arms, and the screwdriver hit the floor, and she got her arms round his neck and kissed him back in the middle of the half-built shop with sawdust in the air, her feet off the floor, laughing into his mouth without stopping.

Somebody coughed. Raiden, in the arched doorway, with a tray of coffees balanced on his healing hands and a face of enormous innocence. “I’ll come back. In ten minutes. Or tomorrow. Jinx says the hooks are level.” He backed away.

That night she had plaster dust in her hair and her eyebrows and down the back of her neck. She sat on the bathroom counter in her vest while the shower ran hot, picking it out of her fringe and talking, and he stood in the doorway with his arms folded in a clean shirt, being sensible. She hooked two fingers into his belt and pulled him in between her knees, and turned him by the belt to the mirror, and there was a grey streak through one of his eyebrows from where her hands had been in his hair at the shop. She laughed until she nearly fell off the counter, and he caught her, and she was still laughing when she started on his buttons.

The dust wouldn’t come out of her hair, so she made him wash it under the shower, standing behind her, and he got shampoo in her eyes and she swore at him and he laughed against her shoulder. She soaped his face with enormous care. They knocked the bottle off the shelf. The water ran grey and then clear, and he turned her round and lifted her against the wet tiles with her legs round his waist and kissed her with the water running down both their faces, and she stopped laughing, and held onto his shoulders, and said his name into the steam until there was no breath left to say it with.

Later, in bed, she lay across him with her wet hair all over his chest. “You held my ankle all afternoon.”

“Ten minutes.”

“It felt like all afternoon. Don’t do that on a ladder again. I couldn’t think. I nearly put a hook in upside down.”

He reached down under the sheet and put his hand round her ankle. The same one, thumb on the bone. She put her face back on his chest and gave up.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Friday before they reopened she put up the last bracket, a small brass one by the new stair door for a fire blanket, which Jinx had saved for her. Everyone else had gone. Eliana’s cameras blinked in the corners of the ceiling, and Raiden was upstairs behind the new glass with his hands unwrapped at last, drawing.

She put in the screws and tested the bracket with her hand, and it didn’t move, and she turned round, and her father was at the bottom of the step in his good coat. She hadn’t heard him come in. He was looking at her hands.

“You have your mother’s hands,” he said.

Elara laughed and came down off the step with the screwdriver in her pocket. “Mama’s? Ah Sim says Mama couldn’t sew a button. She says she burned rice. She says she was the worst cook in the Walled City and you married her anyway.”

He didn’t say anything. He was still looking at her hands, and his face had gone the grey it went sometimes when someone brought up the old days at the table.

“She did burn rice,” he said.

That was all. He put his hand on her shoulder, heavy and brief, which he almost never did, and went out to the black car where Mok was waiting. She watched him go. He looked tired. She’d tell Elowen he looked tired.

“What did he say to you?” Jinx was leaning over the mezzanine rail.

“Mama burned rice.”

Jinx considered that. “Coffee,” she said, and Elara went up, and forgot.

chapters.title: The Knife at the Red Door
chapters.desc: After Sunday lunch a man in a seaman’s jacket comes for her father with a knife. Elara gets in the way, and her husband keeps her alive on the stones of the alley, then stands in the corner of theatre with empty hands.
chapters.epigraph: “Stop diagnosing yourself. I know what’s cut.”
chapters.content:
Sunday lunch was soup: the beef bone one with lotus root that took Ah Sim two days. It was the end of November, the first cold week, and Elara had turned twenty-six a fortnight before, and Ah Sim still thought she was too thin.

“Eat.”

“I’m eating.”

“Eat more.”

Elowen and Zhao had come for the soup and gone again by two. Nam had come up from the river on the bus with a bag of his own ginger because he didn’t trust Ah Sim’s, and the two of them had argued about it in the scullery for twenty minutes like a pair of cats, and now he sat at the end of the table beside Raiden and Jinx, who were arguing about a carburettor. Evangeline sat beside Jun Hyuk, who was explaining lotus root to Lin Jian, who had been eating lotus root his whole life.

“—it’s the holes, you see, the holes are for air, it grows in mud, it has to breathe somehow—”

“Yes,” said Lin Jian, and went on eating.

Elara talked about the garden. It was five months away and she had a dress now, and nobody was allowed to see it. “Not even you. Especially not you. You’d measure it.” She pointed her spoon at her husband.

He would have. He let it go.

“I asked Sister Miao whether the koi would mind, and she said the koi have seen worse. And his grandmother’s coming from the north. With a stick. She points it at people.”

“I’d like to see her try it on Baba,” said Raiden, delighted, and Lin Jian laughed, the big rusty one, straight into his soup, and Xing Yue watched his wife laugh at her father laughing and put another piece of beef in her bowl while she wasn’t looking.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three everyone got their coats.

“We’ll get a taxi.”

“No. Mok has the car at the bottom. I’ll walk you down.” Lin Jian was already at the hook by the stairs for his good coat.

Ah Sim pushed a box into Xing Yue’s hands, leftover soup with three dumplings on top. “Make her eat them.”

“I will.”

“You say that. Make her.”

Elara was on the step buttoning her coat with one hand and talking with the other, and she missed the top button, as she always did, and he reached over and did it up for her.

“I can do my own—”

“You can’t.”

Lin Jian opened the red door. Grey alley, cold, the light already going. The noodle stall at the mouth had its shutters half down, and beyond it the black car waited at the kerb with Mok at the wheel. A man was standing by the stall.

Xing Yue noticed him because there was nobody else. Sixty, perhaps. Thin and weathered, in an old navy jacket with a high collar, the kind men wore on deck, with his hands in his pockets, looking at the red door. When it opened he took his hands out.

“Lin Jian,” he said. “Do you remember the Qu boats?”

Lin Jian stopped on the step. His face went grey all at once, the way a patient’s does when the pressure goes. And something in Xing Yue’s head caught on the name like a foot on a stair in the dark.

Then there was a knife, and the man was coming up the alley.

He didn’t run. He walked fast, straight at the old man on the step, with the knife held low and his face perfectly calm. And Lin Jian didn’t move. He stood in his own doorway in his good coat and watched him come and didn’t lift a hand, as if he’d been waiting twenty years for this and had decided long ago that when it came he would let it.

Elara was closest, on the step below her father. She didn’t think. Xing Yue saw her not think. She put up her right arm and grabbed at the man’s wrist, the way you put a hand out for something falling.

The blade went across the inside of her wrist.

✦ ✦ ✦

He dropped the box. He heard it hit the stones and the soup go everywhere, and he was already there, both hands round her forearm before she’d begun to fall, hard, and the blood came through his fingers anyway, bright, too bright, in spurts that kept time with her heart.

He knew exactly what that meant, and put it away.

“Lie down. Elara, lie back for me. Keep it up.”

He got her down on the stones with her back against the step and her arm straight up over her head and his hands locked round it above the wrist. She was looking at her own hand with great interest.

Behind him somebody shouted. A body hit the ground. Mok’s voice, Mok who never said anything, saying something low and terrible. The red door banged open and there was a sound like a wardrobe falling over, and when he glanced up for half a second the man in the seaman’s jacket was face down on the stones with Mok’s knee in his back and Jun Hyuk sitting on top of both of them, holding his arms, and the knife was skittering into the gutter. There was blood on Lin Jian’s coat. None of it was his.

“Belt. Someone hold her arm.”

Feet at a run, out of the gate of the house next door. Yu Chen, tall and thin in a grey jumper, knelt on the stones without asking anything and put his big careful hands round her forearm exactly where Xing Yue showed him and held it up, hard, while Xing Yue pulled his own belt out of his trousers in one movement and put it high on her upper arm, as tight as it would go, and held it. The spurting slowed and then stopped. He looked at his watch and said the time aloud so that Yu Chen would remember it if he didn’t.

“Car. Get the car into the alley.”

“I’ll clear it,” said Eliana, in a hoodie at the gate next door, already walking to the mouth of the alley, where people had begun coming out of their doors to stare. She said something to them, and they went back in.

Elara was talking. Of course she was. White to the lips, coat soaked down one side, sitting on the cold stones of her father’s alley with her arm in the air, held by two men.

“It’s the ulnar. The artery. That’s why it’s spurting like that. You’ve stopped it. Good. And the tendons, it went deep, I felt it go deep, it’s the flexors, three at least, I can’t bend my fingers— And I can’t feel my little finger, or half the next one, so that’s the ulnar nerve, and the thumb’s numb, so that’s the median, it’s both of them, Xing Yue, it’s both—” She tried, and he watched her see it.

“Stop diagnosing yourself. I know what’s cut.”

She stopped. His voice was calm, calmer than he had ever heard it in his life, slow and level, coming from somewhere a long way below his chest where nothing at all was happening.

“I’ve got you. I know what’s cut. Keep your arm up. Look at me.”

She looked at him. Her pupils were huge, and there was blood on her chin. Her mouth shook once, and then she pressed it shut and nodded.

Raiden came out of the red door and didn’t make a single joke. He looked at his sister on the stones and went white, and then he bent and lifted her, soaked coat and all, as if she weighed nothing, while Xing Yue kept the arm up and Yu Chen let go, and carried her down the alley at a fast walk with her head on his shoulder, past the noodle stall, past the doors Eliana had shut, to the black car with its engine running and its back door open.

Xing Yue got in first, and Raiden laid her across his lap, and he held her arm up against the roof with one hand and the belt with the other. Mok got behind the wheel with his trousers torn at the knee and somebody else’s blood on his hands, and said nothing, and drove. He went through every light between the Walled City and the hill, red or not, and never once touched the horn, and the old car got to the ambulance bay faster than any ambulance could have.

She talked the whole way. About the soup. About Ah Sim, who’d be furious about the box. “She’ll say I did it on purpose. She’ll say I didn’t want the dumplings.”

“I’ll tell her you wanted them.”

He’d never talked back to her like this, about nothing, a box, some soup, and he kept on doing it. Her voice was getting slower, and as long as he talked, she’d go on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Resus at City Hospital on a Sunday afternoon was Dr. Sha’s. They ran her in on a trolley with his hands still on her arm, and the registrar on duty met them at bay two: a young man, competent; Xing Yue had watched him run an arrest and been satisfied. The registrar looked down at the trolley and saw who it was and stopped with his gloved hands up, staring. Dr. Wang from the surgical floor, who brought sweets to the department at New Year and asked after his girlfriend by name, white on a trolley with her coat soaked through. He looked two seconds too long.

“Get out of my resus.”

“It’s not your—”

“Two large lines. Blood for cross-match, six units. Get Dr. Meng from plastics on the phone, and if she’s at home, get her out of it. Then go and stand somewhere I can’t see you.” He didn’t look up.

The registrar went. A nurse had a line in Elara’s left arm before he’d finished, and glanced at the left hand. “Rings.”

He took them off himself, the plain gold band and the star, and slid them off his wife’s finger onto his own little finger beside his ring without taking his other hand off her arm.

Dr. Sha came in from the next bay, small and brisk, and looked at the trolley and at him. “Wang. This is my department.”

“Then you can tell me if I’ve missed anything.”

She looked at him, and then went round the other side of the trolley and checked everything he’d done from the top, and didn’t send him out. Professor Liao came before four; somebody had rung him at home. He came into the bay in a cardigan with his car keys still in his hand and looked at Elara, and his face went still.

“Step back, Wang. You can’t treat her. You know you can’t. She’s your wife. Step back and let the department do it.”

“When Meng’s here.”

Liao looked at him across the trolley and didn’t say it again. Dr. Meng came a few minutes after four in a tracksuit with her hair still wet from the shower and pushed through the curtain and looked at the wrist, all of it, fast, turning it in her hands.

“Theatre. Now. I’ll take it.”

He took his hands off her arm and stood back from the trolley and held them up in front of him, and they shook. They hadn’t shaken in the alley or the car or the bay. Now they shook so hard that he had to jam them under his arms and stand there while the trolley went out past him and down the corridor to the lifts.

✦ ✦ ✦

The repair took five hours. He shouldn’t have been in the room, and everybody in it knew that; he was her husband and he was a surgeon, and there were rules about both. Meng looked at him when he came in scrubbed and gowned and gloved.

“I won’t touch anything.”

She looked a moment longer, then nodded at the corner by the anaesthetic machine and went back to her microscope. He stood in the corner with his empty gloved hands held up in front of his chest and watched. Meng did the tendons first, one by one. Then the artery, and the hand went pink. Then the microscope came down for the nerves, and she spent most of three hours on them, with stitches finer than a hair, so slow that the scrub nurse shifted her feet. Nobody spoke. The theatre was cold. On the board he could see Elara’s hand, small and pale and still, with nothing on it. Her rings were on his finger under his glove.

Nobody hummed.

After nine Meng sat back and took off her loupes and rubbed her eyes, and came over to the corner, stripping her gloves. “The repair’s good. As good as I can make it. It was a clean cut, she’s young, and you got her here fast. She’ll keep the hand. Whether she keeps the surgeon’s hand, nobody can tell you for a year.” She looked at him.

He nodded. He’d known all of it on the stones. “Thank you.”

“Go and sit with her. She’ll want you when she wakes.” Meng put her hand on his arm the way you would with a relative, and went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke in recovery at ten. He was on a stool beside the trolley and had been watching her face for forty minutes. Her right arm was in a thick splint to the elbow, raised on pillows. Her eyes opened and wandered over the ceiling and the monitor and found him.

“Oh. It’s you. You look terrible. Has somebody died? You’ve got your bad face. The one for registrars. Is it me? I don’t think I died. If I’d died I’d be cross about the soup.” Thick and slow. She frowned. Her eyes half closed and opened again.

“You didn’t die.”

“Good.”

She tried to lift her right hand, and the splint wouldn’t let her, and she looked at it, and he watched her remember. Her face went still. Then she said something he didn’t understand to the ceiling.

“Second time,” she said.

“What?”

But she’d looked back at him and made her mouth smile, crooked, with the drugs in it. “Well. At least it wasn’t my talking hand.”

He couldn’t answer that, and she saw that he couldn’t, and her eyes swam.

“Xing Yue,” she said. Only his name.

He stood and bent over the trolley and kissed her forehead and kept his mouth there, on her cold skin under the edge of the paper cap, for as long as he could. Then he took her left hand and worked the rings off his little finger and put them back on hers, the band and then the star. It took him two tries; his hands still weren’t right. He turned the hand over and kissed the inside of her wrist where the pulse was, slow and steady and there.

“I’m here.”

She was already asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song came up to the ward at midnight. Xing Yue was in the chair beside her bed in a side room on the plastics floor. Lin Jian sat in the corridor outside on a plastic chair, where he’d been since six, with her blood dried on his coat; he wouldn’t go home and he wouldn’t come in. Raiden had taken Jinx home. Ev and Jun Hyuk were in the relatives’ room, and every hour Jun Hyuk put his head round the door and asked if there was anything, and was told asleep, and said “Good. Ev says good,” and went away.

Song stood in the doorway in his long black coat and looked at the splint, and then at Xing Yue, and tipped his head towards the window at the far end of the corridor, away from her father. He’d grown up in the Wang house beside the Lin estate. He’d raised Yu Chen. He knew whose wife was in the bed and whose daughter, and it was in his face that he wished he didn’t.

“He’s not saying much. He isn’t denying anything, either. He came for Lin Jian. He says he never meant to touch anyone else. He keeps asking whether she’s all right.” Song’s face didn’t move.

“Who is he?”

“Qu Wenjun. Fifty-seven. Merchant seaman, thirty years. A prison term in the middle for a fight. He says Lin Jian burned his brother’s boats in 2002, and killed his brother and his brother’s wife. He says Lin Jian killed the child too. He says the whole family died.” Song watched him.

Xing Yue looked out at the dark car park.

Qu. Qu Lighterage, Walled City piers. Qu Mingde. Shi Yuning, nurse. A child in a laundry basket under wet towels. A man in a black car who’d paid for a roof in cash, and come back the next week, and gone down the steps without a word, looking. No relatives found.

He went cold. It started in his hands, where her blood had been, and went up his arms and into his chest, and he stood at the window and let it.

“Wang.”

“I’m all right.”

“You don’t look it.”

“I need to go back in. She wakes and talks. I don’t want her to wake and find nobody there.”

He went back down the corridor past Lin Jian on his plastic chair. The old man lifted his head and looked at him, and Xing Yue looked back. He’d guessed. The old man didn’t know yet that he had.

He went in and sat down by her bed and took her left hand, rings and all, and put his thumb on her pulse, and kept it there until the window went grey.

chapters.title: The House Is Too Quiet
chapters.desc: Lin Jian tells her where she came from and what he did. She finds out Xing Yue has known her name for nine months, and stops talking to everyone.
chapters.epigraph: “It was mine. You picked the day.”
chapters.content:
The first thing she learned about nerve pain was that it had no respect for sleep. It came when it liked: a thin electric thread from the wrist into the tips of the fingers, or a burning under the dressing as if somebody had laid a hot wire along the inside of her hand, or something worse, sharp and bright, that made her whole arm jump before she could stop it.

On the Tuesday after they let her home she sat up in bed at three in the morning with a notebook on her knee and a pencil in her wrong hand and worked it out. Tendons, six weeks protected. Nerves, a millimetre a day, if they grew at all, from the wrist to the fingertips. Months before anyone could say what the hand would do. Months after that before anyone would let it hold a needle. She wrote down how old she’d be, and crossed it out, and wrote it again.

He woke when the pencil fell. He put the lamp on and held out his hand, and after a while she gave him the notebook. Her sums were careful and her assumptions were reasonable, and at the bottom of the page, in letters that sloped the wrong way, she’d written If I can’t operate, what am I?

He read it twice and closed the notebook. “That isn’t a medical calculation.”

“It’s a practical one.”

“It’s a frightened one. You don’t have to decide your whole life in the first week.”

She dropped a spoon on the Thursday, at breakfast, and stared at it on the tiles, and when he bent to pick it up she said “Leave it” so sharply that he left it. She said sorry. He said she didn’t have to be. She looked at her hand in the splint and said she used to be able to hold things, and he didn’t tell her she would again, because he didn’t know, and she’d have heard it if he lied.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Saturday in December they went to the red door for lunch, and she ate almost nothing, because the alley made her think of the stones. When Xing Yue went out to take a call from the ward, her father stood up from the carved chair and said, “Come upstairs,” and she went.

His office was at the back of the house, with the account books and the boxes nobody had opened in years. He shut the door. She sat. He stayed standing, and for a while he looked.

He said, “The man who came for me. Qu Wenjun. His brother was Qu Mingde. Mingde ran four lighters off the old piers, out to the ships at anchor and back. Honest work. The only honest boats on the piers, very nearly. There was a man called Zuo Hanlin who wanted those berths and that contract, and I owed Zuo Hanlin. In 2002 I owed him for most of what I had. He asked me which nights the Qu boats would be out and the office shut. I knew. I knew everybody’s nights. I told him.” He looked at his hands.

Elara didn’t move.

“I told myself he’d burn the boats. I knew he wouldn’t burn the boats. The boats were what he wanted. Qu lived over the office with his wife and his little girl, who talked to every boatman on the pier. Everybody knew that. I knew it. I didn’t ask Zuo what he meant to do, because in our world, not asking is the same as knowing, and I wanted to be able to say I hadn’t.” Her father’s voice didn’t change.

“My parents,” said Elara.

“Your father and your mother. Your mother was a nurse. On the old wards at City Hospital, on nights. On her nights off she sewed up my men at her kitchen table over the office, for nothing, when no hospital would have them. I watched her do it. I knew her hands. I told you in July you had your mother’s hands. I wasn’t talking about Mama.” He made himself look at her. His mouth moved.

The room was quiet. Somewhere below them Ah Sim was singing to a fish.

“A policeman I paid told me there’d been a child. A neighbour had put her in the laundry basket under wet towels and carried her down the outside stair. They’d taken her up to Plum Steps. I went. I stood at the gate and listened to you tell a man fixing the roof what his ladder was called. I couldn’t give you your parents back. I could give you a roof. So I paid for theirs, and I came back the next week for you.”

“And Mama?”

“Your mother knew you came from a fire. She never knew whose. She read the name on your papers, Xiaoyue, and said, Then she’s Elara. It’s a moon. She’ll keep a piece of it. She didn’t know what I’d done. I never told her. I never told anyone.”

“Zuo Hanlin,” said Elara. “Where is he?”

“In the harbour. Since the spring of 2003. I put him there myself. It didn’t give anybody back.” He said it the way he’d have said in the north.

She looked at him, this man who had walked her down every aisle she’d ever been afraid of, who’d sat on a plastic chair in a corridor with her blood on his coat for twelve hours. She found she couldn’t feel anything at all. Somebody had taken every feeling she had and put it on a high shelf where she couldn’t reach.

“Did you ever think of telling me?”

“Every day.”

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

She stood up. The splint knocked the edge of the chair and the pain went up her arm like a struck match, and he moved towards her at once and she said “Don’t,” and he stopped where he was.

“I need to go,” she said, and went downstairs past Ah Sim and out through the red door, and her husband was at the bottom of the alley with his phone in his hand, and she walked past him to the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

She opened the glovebox for a tissue on the harbour road.

Green tea biscuits. Her hair clip from the steps, two years old. A brown envelope with a single letter on the front in his square hand. E.

She’d known about the envelope since spring. She’d promised not to look, and she’d written on the fridge that she was cross about it, and she’d kept her promise every day since April. She looked at it now with the splint in her lap and her father’s voice still in her ears, and took it out with her left hand, and opened it with her teeth.

A sheet of paper in pencilled capitals. QU XIAOYUE. LITTLE MOON. BORN 16 NOV 1999. BROUGHT BY POLICE 12 OCT FROM THE FIRE AT QU LIGHTERAGE, WALLED CITY PIERS. Her father’s name, and her mother’s: SHI YUNING, NURSE. A printout from a newspaper with a date on it. A sheet torn off a prescription pad, a year old, with her birthday on it and children’s home? and Find her. And across the top of the pencilled page, in the same square hand, the day he’d copied it. 14 March 2025.

He’d seen her open it. He kept driving. She heard his breathing change.

“How long?” she said.

“Since March.”

“Nine months.”

“Yes.”

“You knew my name.”

“Yes.”

“You knew they died in a fire.”

“Yes.”

“Every time I said I didn’t know who my mother was.”

“Yes.”

“You were going to give it to me in the garden. In May. On the day. It was mine. You picked the day.” Her voice was perfectly steady, which frightened her more than anything.

“Yes, I was wrong,” he said.

She put the papers back in the envelope with her one good hand and held it in her lap, and looked out of the window at the harbour going past, and didn’t say anything else. She didn’t say anything else for eleven days.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was too quiet.

He had never heard the flat without her in it. Even asleep she talked. Now she came down in the morning and took the tablets he put by her cup and nodded or shook her head. She wrote what she needed on the pad by the kettle in her sloping wrong-handed letters, Medication, Water, Appointment at three, Leave the light on, and after the third day she stopped writing too, and pointed. She went to her appointments and answered Meng’s questions in as few words as a question could be answered in, and came home and lay on the sofa with her face to the back of it.

On the fridge, under peach yoghurt, she’d taken the marker in her left hand and drawn a line through XY’S SECRET — CROSS ABOUT IT, and written underneath, crooked: NOT CROSS.

He read it every morning while the tea brewed.

He didn’t ask her to speak. He’d taken one choice out of her hands already, and he wasn’t going to take another. He put the food in front of her and the water where she could reach it with her left hand. He slept beside her, and some nights she lay facing the wall and some nights facing the ceiling, and either way he lay still. He told her things, not because he expected an answer but because he thought she’d want to know when she was ready. Your father went to see Song today. Meng’s moved you to Thursday. Ah Sim sent soup and says you’re to eat all of it. She nodded at the soup.

Her father came twice. The first time Xing Yue opened the door to him and Lin Jian stood on the landing in his good coat with his hat in his hands and asked whether he could see her, and Xing Yue said, “Not today,” and the old man looked past him up the stairs and said, “Does she hate me?” Xing Yue didn’t answer, because it wasn’t his to answer. The second time Lin Jian didn’t ask. He left a box of the sesame biscuits she’d liked when she was six on the mat and went down again, and she put them in a cupboard without opening them.

Raiden rang and she didn’t answer. Eliana sent a photograph of the cats sitting on the step of the red door. Elowen came and sat with her for an hour, talking, and went away with her eyes red.

On the seventh day Evangeline came. She took her coat off and sat down at the other end of the sofa and said nothing, and Elara said nothing, and they sat there through the whole of a grey afternoon while the rain came and went on the windows. At five Ev got up and touched her sister’s hair, once, and put her coat on and left, and that evening, for the first time in a week, Elara ate everything on her plate.

He understood that. Ev had been silent for years in the next room of a house that talked all the time. She knew what silence was for. He’d never had to learn it, and he sat at the kitchen counter after midnight with the envelope in front of him and learned it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Christmas Eve he cooked, because she’d once said that Christmas was the only foreign holiday she approved of, on account of the food, and because the flat was so quiet that he could hear the fridge.

He made her the chicken with ginger she liked and the greens and rice, and because she still couldn’t hold a knife, he cut her chicken for her at the counter before he brought the plate, the way he’d done every night for three weeks. Without thinking, he cut it the way he did everything. Into squares. Exact ones, a centimetre and a half, in rows.

He put it down in front of her. She looked at it.

“You’ve cut it into squares,” she said.

Her voice was rough from not being used, and it went through him like the pager in the on-call room, right between the ribs.

“Yes.”

“Exact squares.”

“Yes.”

“You measured my dinner. That’s the most you thing anybody’s ever done. I’m so angry with you I could throw it at the wall, and you’ve cut my dinner into a grid.” She picked up the fork in her left hand and put it down again.

He didn’t say anything. He stood on the other side of the counter and waited, and after a while she looked up.

She said, “I want everything. Not what you think I should know. Not the version that makes it easier. Everything. The matron. The library. What Song told you in the corridor. What my father’s face did. All of it, tonight, and then whatever you find out after this, the day you find it out, even if it’s three in the morning, even if I’m in theatre, even if it’s the worst thing in the world.”

“Yes.”

“I want to see Matron Sima myself. I want the police papers. I’ll decide who I see and when.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t say yes like that.”

“I don’t know another way to say it.”

She looked down at the squares. “I’m still angry.”

“You should be.”

“I don’t know when I’ll stop.”

“You don’t have to.”

She ate one square. Then another. He told her everything, standing at the counter, from the women on the telephone at the children’s homes to the old man lifting his head on the plastic chair, and she listened without interrupting once, which she had never done in her life. When he’d finished she put down her fork.

“You thought you were giving me something. You were. You were also keeping it. Both. You don’t get to only remember the first one,” she said.

“I won’t.”

She got down off the stool and came round the counter and stood in front of him, close enough to touch, and didn’t. He didn’t either. She looked up at him in the light from the cooker hood, and then she leaned her forehead against his chest, and stayed there, and he put one hand carefully on the back of her head and kept it there, and neither of them moved until the rice had gone cold.

“Merry Christmas,” she said into his shirt.

It was the second thing she’d said in eleven days. He’d remember both of them for the rest of his life.

chapters.title: She Gives the Ring Back
chapters.desc: Out of the splint, Elara puts the ring in his hand and goes to stay with the sister who knows what it is to learn why you were kept. He sits on the porch step every night for five weeks.
chapters.epigraph: “Keep it safe. I’m not giving it to anybody else.”
chapters.content:
The splint came off on the first Monday in January.

She’d imagined it so often that she expected to feel something when Dr. Meng undid the last strap: relief, or freedom, or at least the satisfaction of seeing her own arm again. What she felt was cold. The skin under the splint was pale and dry and peeling. The wrist was thinner than she remembered, the muscle gone off it. The scar ran across the inside, pink and raised, with the marks of the stitches still on either side like a railway on a map.

Meng turned it gently in both hands. “Tell me when it hurts.”

“Now. Along the inside. And the base of the thumb, when you pull it back.”

“Numbness?”

“The thumb and the first finger are better. The little finger isn’t mine.”

“Pins and needles?”

“When they feel like it.”

Meng tested every finger against her own, and wrote, and looked up. “There’s progress.”

“It’s not much.”

“It’s progress. Therapy now, properly. The splint off for the exercises, on between them. Nothing forced. Nothing to prove. You’re a surgeon. That doesn’t make you a good patient.” She looked at Elara over her glasses.

“When can I go back to theatre?”

Meng didn’t look away. “I can’t give you a date. Not three months. Possibly not six. We’ll know more by the summer, and I won’t guess before then.”

Outside the room he was waiting, and he stood up when she came out, and his eyes went straight to the wrist, to the scar and the thinness and the small movements she was making with the fingers without knowing it. He didn’t reach for it.

“Can I carry your bag?”

“No.”

“All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The therapy was worse than she’d expected, not because it was hard but because it was simple. Bend one finger and hold it. Slide the fingertips towards the palm without letting the wrist help. Shut your eyes and say whether that’s silk or sandpaper. Move a wooden peg from one hole to the next. Things a child could do. Things she had done without thinking for twenty-six years, and now she had to think about every one, and the fingers shook when she tried to move them one at a time, and some feelings came late and some came much too sharp, and when the therapist worked the scar she had to turn her face to the wall.

“Breathe.”

“I am.”

“You’re holding it.”

She gave him the ring on the Thursday.

It was in the bedroom, in the quiet between dinner and the evening tablets. He was putting clean shirts away and she was sitting on the end of the bed with her right hand on a pillow, turning the plain band on her finger with her thumb. She’d taken the star off that morning because it pressed on the swelling. She thought about the old town and Mr. Yin’s buttons, and the steps, and the chain under her collar for six weeks, and the koi. She thought about the alley, and the envelope, and since March.

She slid the band off and held it out.

He stopped with a shirt in his hands. “Elara.”

“I need to give this back.”

He didn’t move.

“I can’t wear it now. That’s not— I don’t mean I don’t want it. I mean I can’t look at it every morning and remember that you knew. I love you. I don’t want a divorce. I don’t want to stop loving you. I need to be somewhere I don’t wake up next to the person who kept it, every single day, while I work out what any of it means.”

“Where?”

“Ev’s.”

He put the shirt down and came and took the ring off her palm, and his fingers closed over it.

“You’re not going to ask me to stay?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because you’ve told me what you need.”

She looked at his closed hand. She’d thought it would be a small thing to give back. It wasn’t.

“Keep it safe. I’m not giving it to anybody else,” she said.

“I know.”

He helped her pack. She put the star in its little silk box in her bag, and he watched her do it and didn’t say anything about that either.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her up to Fig Tree Lane on the Friday morning. Evangeline opened the green gate before they’d got out of the car, looked at her sister’s bag and at the man behind it, and didn’t ask a single question in the lane.

“Come in. Your room’s ready.”

“I only told you last night.”

“I have a spare room. It’s a useful room. People need it,” said Ev.

At the door Xing Yue stopped. “Your tablets at six. Therapy’s Monday at ten. It’s in your phone.”

“I know.”

“Meng said—”

“I know, Xing Yue.”

He stopped. She looked at him on the step with his hands at his sides.

“Thank you,” she said, and he nodded and went back down the path to the car, and Ev shut the door, and Elara stood in her sister’s hall among the plants and said, “I don’t know what I’m doing.”

“Nor did I,” said Evangeline, “when I came here.”

He came back that night after dinner. He didn’t ring the bell. He sent one message. I’m outside. You don’t have to come down.

She read it at the upstairs window and didn’t answer. He was sitting on the bottom step under the porch light in his coat, with his hands clasped between his knees, looking at the fig tree.

Ev went out to him after half an hour with a blanket. Elara watched through the glass. She couldn’t hear what her sister said. She saw him take the blanket, and saw Ev sit down beside him for a minute, and go in again. He stayed until the light in Elara’s window went out. Then he folded the blanket and left it on the mat and drove home.

He came the next night, and the night after that. By the second week the house had made room for him. He came after work, sometimes early with a journal, sometimes at ten with his hair still wet from the theatre showers. He never rang. He never asked Ev to make her come down. The messages he sent were practical. Meng’s moved you to ten. Your prescription’s ready at the pharmacy by the gate. It’s raining; I’ve left the umbrella in the porch.

She knew the shape of his shoulders in the dark. She knew how he lifted his head every time a door went inside the house. It made her angry, and then sad, and then it made her want to go downstairs, and she did none of those things, and Ev never once told her to.

One evening Jun Hyuk came out with a pot of rosemary and set it down on the step beside him.

“It’s in the wrong place. The wind takes it by the wall. People think rosemary’s tough. Everybody says it is. It is, but people misunderstand tough. They think it means it’ll survive anything. It won’t. Too much water kills it. Too little kills it. Bad drainage. Too much shade. You have to know what it needs and give it that, not what you’d want if you were a rosemary. People are the same,” he explained. He crouched to look at the leaves.

Xing Yue looked at him.

“You’re not going to say anything?” said Jun Hyuk.

“I was listening.”

Jun Hyuk considered this, and appeared to find it acceptable, and explained rosemary for nearly an hour: root rot, pruning, frost, the right kind of grit. At some point Xing Yue asked how often it should be watered, and Jun Hyuk’s whole face lit up. When Ev came out with two cups of tea she looked at the pot, and at her husband, and at Xing Yue.

“Are you still talking about rosemary?”

“Yes,” said Jun Hyuk.

“Of course you are,” said Ev, and handed the tea down, and went in.

Upstairs, at the window, Elara laughed out loud for the first time in a month and put her hand over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

The pegs got harder. Textures with her eyes shut. Separating rice from lentils with two fingers. The first time she dropped the wooden peg in front of the therapist she stared at it on the floor.

“Try again?”

She tried again, and dropped it, and tried again.

“That’s enough for today.”

“One more.”

“Dr. Wang, it isn’t a race.”

In the car Ev asked how it had gone, and Elara said, “I dropped a peg fourteen times,” and Ev drove for a while and said, “Did you pick it up fifteen?”

“Yes.”

“Then I think it was a good day.”

On the fourth Friday he left a paper bag on the step. Inside it was a soft sleeve for her wrist, the kind that stopped clothes catching on a new scar. Nothing clever. She ran her left hand over it at the kitchen table, and put it on, and didn’t send him a message. The next evening she looked down from the window as he sat down on the step, and saw him look at the empty bag still lying by the door, and knew he knew she’d kept it.

In the fifth week a cold snap came in off the hills and the step stayed cold long after dark. He came late, from theatre, tired, with no blanket, and Ev brought one out anyway and said something to him that made him look up at the window. Elara stepped back from the glass.

She came down just after ten in her cardigan, with the sleeve on her wrist, and opened the door. He stood up.

“It’s cold. You should go home,” she said.

“I will.”

She stayed in the doorway. Then she came down one step, and another, and stopped beside him. “Have you been here every night?”

“Yes.”

“Did you sleep?”

“Enough.”

“That’s not an answer.” She looked at him and then sat down on the cold step, and he sat down beside her and left a space between them.

“Have you still got it?”

He took a small box out of his coat pocket and opened it. The plain band lay inside.

“You’ve been carrying it?”

“It’s in my coat most days.”

“Why?”

“Because you gave it to me.”

She looked away. “I don’t know when I’ll be ready.”

“I know.”

“I might be angry for a long time.”

“You’re allowed.”

“Stop saying that. I still can’t hold a pen properly.” The old irritation came up into her face, and he nearly smiled.

“How was therapy?”

“Horrible. I finished it.”

“Good.”

“I hate that word.”

“Excellent?”

“Worse. I missed you. I don’t know what to do with that.” She looked at him in the porch light.

“Neither do I.”

“Did you think I’d leave you? Properly?”

“Yes. When you gave me the ring.”

“Did you think I’d come back?”

“I hoped you would.”

“That’s different.”

“Yes.”

She looked down at her hands, the scarred one and the other. “I don’t know how to be close to you without remembering.”

“I remember too. The envelope on your knee. The date. Knowing you were asking me something I should have answered in March. I don’t want you to forget it. I want to be somebody who doesn’t do it again.” He looked at her.

The cold came across the garden from the stream. After a while he said, “May I kiss you?”

She looked at his mouth, and back at his eyes. “Yes.”

He put his hand to her cheek, not her wrist, and kissed her slowly, and didn’t pull her closer than she came, and let her be the one to end it. When she drew back she kept her forehead against his.

“Come inside. Not to—just to sleep. I don’t want you driving home tonight,” she whispered.

He slept in her sister’s spare room with his arm across her and his face in her hair, and nothing more, and for the first time in five weeks she slept the whole night through.

✦ ✦ ✦

They had Lunar New Year at Fig Tree Lane, because Elara couldn’t face the red door yet and her father said that if she couldn’t come to the table, the table would come to her. Red lanterns in the fig tree. Ah Sim in Ev’s kitchen, criticising the stove.

Her father was in the doorway when she came in. He looked older than he had in December. He didn’t reach for her.

“Happy New Year,” he said.

She looked at him. “Happy New Year, Baba.”

It was the first time she’d called him that since the office. His face did something, and he looked down, and nodded once, and stepped aside.

Jun Hyuk had made the dumplings, which nobody could explain, since he couldn’t cook. Some were too thick and some had split and one was shaped like a small animal. Raiden picked it up and asked what it was, and Jun Hyuk said it was a traditional shape, and Raiden asked from where, and Jun Hyuk said, “Somewhere traditional,” and Jinx was laughing too much and had to put her head on the table. Jun Hyuk put another on Elara’s plate. “That one’s better.”

She bit it, and chewed, and swallowed, and looked at him. “It’s terrible.”

“It’s handmade.”

“That isn’t a defence. I’m a doctor. I know a medical emergency when I eat one.”

The whole table went, Ah Sim included, and across it her husband watched her laugh as if he wanted to make sure the sound was real before he let himself smile.

She picked up her chopsticks in her right hand. The grip was wrong and the tips shook. She tried again, and lifted a dumpling, and it slipped, and she caught it against the side of the bowl and lifted it again and looked straight at him. He nodded.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were thinking it.”

After the oranges Jinx put a canvas roll on the table and undid it: calipers, a steel rule, a notebook, a pencil. She didn’t say what it was for. Elara knew. She’d sat on a stool in a back room by the docks in 2021 and held her wrists out while those hands measured them without a word.

“Second time,” said Jinx, low, so that only Elara heard.

“Yes.”

Jinx measured. The wrist, the palm, every finger, how far each one went before the scar pulled, where it hurt and where it didn’t feel anything at all, and wrote it all down in small neat figures. “I’ll build it to what your therapist allows and nothing past it. You’ll show her the drawing before you touch it. And you won’t turn it up because you’re cross,” she said.

“I’m always cross.”

“I know. That’s why I said it,” said Jinx.

Later Elara went out into the garden under the lanterns, and he came and stood beside her.

“I don’t want to set a date. For the garden. Not yet. May’s going to come and go and I’m going to let it,” she said.

“All right.”

“But I don’t want it to disappear.”

“It won’t.”

“And you tell me things. All of them. Even when it’ll hurt.”

“Especially then.”

She held out her left hand, and he took it, and they stood under the red lanterns while Jun Hyuk promised the kitchen that the next batch would be better and Ev said nobody was letting him near it again.

“I want to come home. Not tonight. Soon,” she said.

He didn’t ask how soon. He held her hand. The ring stayed in his pocket.

chapters.title: The Machine Before the Garage Opens
chapters.desc: At five every morning, before the garage opens, Elara works her ruined hand on a steel rig Jinx built for her. Her uncle pleads guilty, and she watches from the gallery.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m writing so that you know I survived. I’m here.”
chapters.content:
The first morning she was home at Banyan Terrace she woke at twenty to five without an alarm and lay still in the dark. The pale curtains. Her books on the bedside table in two leaning piles. The little dish where her rings had always gone at night, with nothing in it. Beside her he was asleep on his back with one hand open on the sheet in the place where she usually lay.

She slid out from under the covers and dressed in the bathroom without the light, and went down the stairs with her shoes in her hand, and at the bottom of Banyan Terrace a green taxi was already waiting, because she’d booked it on the card the night before.

Tai Hing didn’t open until seven. At five in the morning the back room belonged to her, and to the machine.

Jinx had built it in three weeks from the numbers she’d taken at Ev’s kitchen table: a steel frame bolted to the end of the long bench, with an adjustable cradle for the forearm and a row of small pulleys and a turntable and a set of interchangeable pieces for the fingers, each one machined to the millimetre. A fine wire ran through a tension block and whispered against its guide whenever she moved. It wasn’t built to make her strong. “Strength comes later. This is for movement that doesn’t cheat,” Jinx had said, and tapped the drawing. The therapist had been through every part of it with her reading glasses on, and set the stops, and written the limits on a card that was taped to the frame, and Jinx had made her promise not to touch them because she was cross.

She’d promised. She hadn’t promised to be sensible. She put the light on and washed her hands at the sink in the corner, and opened the notebook.

5:00. Pain before: 2. Thumb comes and goes. First finger dull. Middle patchy. Little finger not mine.

Then she put her forearm in the cradle and began. A small movement, against almost nothing, stopping before the wrist tried to help. Back. Again. The wire whispered. Her first finger lagged behind the others. The little one curled too early. When she tried to correct them the wrist tightened, and she stopped and breathed and started over. At twenty past five she changed the piece. At twenty to six she had to rest. By ten to six her hand was trembling and there was sweat running down the side of her face, though the back room at Tai Hing was always cold, and she took her arm out and wrote the numbers down and sat looking at the steel frame.

Unimpressive, nowhere near enough, and hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found out on the third morning, not because he woke, though he did, but because the green taxi company sent the account to his phone every Monday, and there it was in a column. Banyan Terrace to Tai Hing, 04:41. Tai Hing to Banyan Terrace, 06:18. Three mornings running.

He read it at the kitchen counter and put the phone away.

When she came in at twenty-five past six with her hair tied back and her sleeves pushed up unevenly and red marks on her forearm from the cradle straps, there was a warm towel folded by the kitchen sink and a cup of tea on the counter with the steam still coming off it. She looked at the towel and at him.

“Did you do your exercises?” he said.

“Some.”

“Jinx’s machine.”

“Yes. The therapist went through all of it. The stops are hers.” She waited for the rest of it.

“Did you keep to them?”

“Mostly.”

“Elara.”

“I did.”

He looked at her a moment longer. “You could have told me.”

“I didn’t want to wake you.”

“I wake when you’re not there. That’s all.” He wasn’t scolding her, and that was somehow worse.

“I wanted something I did myself. Something you didn’t manage,” she said.

He nodded slowly, and pushed the tea across the counter, and didn’t ask again. After that there was a warm towel by the sink every morning, and she never thanked him for it, and he never mentioned it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Monday in March she began teaching.

It wasn’t surgery. The medical school had asked whether she’d take small groups of first-years in the anatomy rooms two mornings a week, and she’d said yes before the dean had finished the sentence. She arrived early. A boy at the front looked at her wrist and then quickly away.

“Today’s the flexor compartment of the forearm,” she told them. “Before we start: what’s the point of knowing the name of a thing if you can’t say what happens when it stops working?”

They looked at each other.

“Anatomy isn’t a list you learn for an exam. It’s a map of what a person can and can’t do.” She drew a forearm on the board with her left hand, the wrist and the flexor tendons and the two nerves, and the lines were good until she reached for a small detail and stopped, and then went on. “A man comes in with a knife wound to the front of the wrist. He can still move some of his fingers. What does that tell you?”

A girl at the back said, slowly, “It doesn’t mean all the tendons are intact.”

“Exactly. One finger moving doesn’t rule out the one beside it. Test each one. Test the feeling. Test the circulation. Know your anatomy well enough to know what you haven’t ruled out. And know when you need help.” She put the pen down.

They wrote it down. She looked at the diagram on the board, and something settled in her that had been loose since November. The hand was injured. She wasn’t.

He was outside the building at noon with two coffees, and she came down the steps towards him trying not to look pleased, and failed.

“How was it?”

“Good. Very good. I made them tell me why one finger moving doesn’t mean the tendon beside it isn’t cut.” She took the coffee.

He glanced at her wrist.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You looked.”

“I’m allowed to look,” he said, and she held out her left hand instead of her right, and he took it, and she let him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time she kissed him over the kitchen counter that spring was a Wednesday. She’d come back from teaching with a headache and an exercise sheet she didn’t want to discuss, and he’d looked at the sheet and at her and at the bowl he’d put in front of her.

“Have you eaten today?”

“Breakfast.”

“And?”

“Coffee. A biscuit.”

“Elara. You’re still laying down collagen in that wrist. You’ve therapy this afternoon. You can’t keep missing meals and expect the tissue to—”

She leaned over the counter and kissed him, and he stopped.

“What was that for?”

“To end the lecture.”

“I wasn’t lecturing.”

“You were about to explain protein to me.”

He put both hands flat on the counter on either side of the bowl and looked at her. “Would you like me to go on?”

“No.”

“Will you eat?”

“Maybe.”

He leaned across and kissed her again, longer, until she’d forgotten the headache, and then straightened up. “Eat.”

At night he’d begun kissing her fingertips. Neither of them noticed when it started. She’d be reading, or half asleep, with the bad arm on a pillow, and he’d take the hand and kiss each finger in turn, thumb to little finger, without counting. One night when he got to the middle finger she said, “Can you feel that?”

He lifted his head. He understood that she wasn’t asking about him. He kissed the fingertip again, lightly, and she watched, and shook her head.

“Not properly. It’s there and then it isn’t. Sometimes I can tell something’s touching it but not what. I hate it. I hate that you can kiss my hand and I can’t tell which finger.” Her face went before she could stop it.

“I know.”

“I know it’s one hand. I know people lose far more. I know I ought to be grateful that the repair—”

“Don’t. You don’t have to make it smaller by putting someone else’s next to it.”

“What if it never comes back?”

“Then we’ll find out what that means when we know it. We don’t know it yet. I’ll keep on doing it.” He kissed the palm, away from the scar.

“Even if I can’t feel it?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I can,” he said, and she put her forehead against his shoulder and cried until she’d finished, and then he kissed every fingertip again, and didn’t skip any.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the third week of March the mornings had a shape. The taxi at twenty to five. The back room. The light, the notebook, the cradle, the wire. Her first finger was moving better; the therapist said the tendons were gliding, and the feeling was no better. She didn’t tell him every number. She told Jinx.

Jinx came in one morning at half past six in her overalls with a coffee and looked at the notebook and then at the machine.

“Every morning?”

“Most.”

Jinx looked at her.

“Every morning,” said Elara.

“Turned it up?”

“No.”

“Moved the stops?”

“No.”

Jinx went on looking at her, and then at the stops, which hadn’t moved, and nodded, and took a key out of her pocket and moved one of them herself, two millimetres. “She says you can have a bit more range here. Not more weight. Range.”

“Do you think I’ll get back to where I was?”

Jinx tightened the screw. “I think you let your hand tell you what it can do before you tell it what it can’t.”

“That’s an annoying answer.”

“I got it off your husband. And if you break my machine you’re helping me fix it,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Friday in March she went to court.

Her uncle was pleading guilty. The room was smaller than she’d expected, with wooden benches and a raised bench and a narrow public gallery at the side, and Song had arranged for her to come in by a door that didn’t share a corridor with anyone else’s. She sat in the gallery beside her husband with her wrist in her lap in its sleeve.

She’d told herself for a week that she didn’t need to come. The plea was enough. The sentence would be what it was. But she wanted to see the man who’d come up the alley. She wanted to know whether he’d look at her.

They brought him in. He was thinner than in November and his hair was shorter, and he stood beside his lawyer in a plain shirt with his eyes on the floor. When at last he looked up, his eyes went along the faces and stopped at hers, and stayed there, and she didn’t look away.

The charges were read: the knife, the attack on Lin Jian, the injury to Lin Jian’s daughter. The judge asked whether he understood his plea and whether it was his own, and he said yes, and yes. Then the judge asked whether he wished to say anything, and he stood up.

He said, “I believed Lin Jian killed my brother. I believed the child died in the fire with him. I didn’t know she was alive. Nobody told me. I came back from the sea last summer and heard the Lins had a daughter who was a doctor, adopted, the right age, and I thought he’d taken everything we had and kept the child as well. I brought the knife for him.” His voice was rough.

“And when your niece stepped in front of him?”

Qu Wenjun looked at the floor. “I didn’t stop.”

That was the part she’d come for. Not that he’d been angry, or wrong, or grieving. He’d seen her hand go up and the blade go across it, and he hadn’t stopped.

Beside her Xing Yue’s hand lay on the bench an inch from hers, and didn’t move, and let her decide. She didn’t take it. She didn’t need to.

They sentenced him that afternoon. Six years. He turned once at the door as they took him down, and looked up at the gallery, and she watched him until the door had closed and didn’t nod and didn’t look away.

Outside on the steps Song was waiting in his long coat. “He’s asked if he can write to you. He wants you to know he didn’t think you were alive. You don’t have to answer. If you want to send anything, it comes through me.”

“Thank you,” said Elara.

In the car she sat with her hands in her lap. “He thought I was dead. And then he saw me on the step and knew who I was, and he still didn’t stop. He wanted my father to pay, and I paid,” she said. She turned the bad wrist over.

“Yes.”

“I’m not asking you to do anything. I don’t want you finding people. I don’t want you to make it worse.”

“I won’t. I told you I wouldn’t decide things for you.”

She looked at him. “I want to write to him.”

The letter took three days. She wrote it with her right hand, because she wanted the words to come out of the hand he’d cut, slowly, with the lines leaning, stopping when the wrist got tired and going on later. She didn’t ask him to read it. She took out every sentence that sounded like a question and every one that sounded like forgiveness, and in the end what was left was short.

Qu Wenjun,

I know you thought I died in the fire. I didn’t. I was three. I didn’t know my parents’ names until this winter. I grew up thinking the family that raised me was the only one I had.

You came to the red door with a knife. You saw me, and you knew who I was, and you didn’t stop.

My hand is still healing. Nobody knows yet what it will be able to do. I’m working on it every morning before it’s light.

I’m not writing to forgive you. I’m writing so that you know I survived. I’m here.

Elara Wang

She gave it to Song on the Monday. That night she went to bed early, because the taxi was at twenty to five, and he came up later and found her awake with the bad hand on the pillow.

“Kiss my fingers,” she said.

He took her hand and did it, thumb to little finger, and didn’t ask whether she could feel it. When he’d finished she looked at her hand on the sheet.

“Tomorrow I’m going to Tai Hing at five. You can sleep,” she said.

“I’ll probably wake.”

“Then don’t come down.”

“All right.”

At four forty the next morning he heard the bedroom door, and her feet on the stairs, and the front door, and the taxi pulling away at the bottom of the terrace. He lay still in the dark. Down by the docks a light came on in the back room at Tai Hing, and a fine steel wire began to whisper against its guide, and his wife asked her hand for one more movement, and then one more.

chapters.title: Her Mother’s Window
chapters.desc: In a prison visiting room her uncle gives her the only photographs of her parents. She finds her mother’s ward window over the hospital garden, and Xing Yue asks her again.
chapters.epigraph: “She sang. When she was doing things.”
chapters.content:
Song rang on a Tuesday afternoon in April. “He’s had your letter. He read it, he says, a great many times. He hasn’t asked for an address. He’s asked whether you’d visit.”

Elara was at the kitchen counter sorting the post with her left hand. “Did he say why?”

“He says he has something that should have been yours a long time ago. He wouldn’t say what on the phone.”

She looked at the envelopes for a while. “Can you arrange it?”

“I’ll send you the details.”

He was at the table with a report and had looked up when the phone went. “Qu Wenjun.”

“He wants me to visit.”

“Do you want to?”

“I think so.”

“Then I’ll drive you.”

“You don’t have to come in.”

“I know.”

“I might not want to talk about it afterwards.”

“I know that too.”

She looked at him. “You’re being very agreeable.”

“I’m trying not to make your decision about mine,” he said, and she came round the table and kissed his cheek, and he turned his head and caught the corner of her mouth.

She’d been to Plum Steps already, in February, from Ev’s, with Ev beside her. Matron Sima had opened the door of the fourth-floor flat and looked up at her and then taken her face in two small dry hands and said, “Still talking,” and Elara had cried on the low stool for an hour and the old woman had let her, and poured her tea, and not her own.

✦ ✦ ✦

The visiting room smelled of disinfectant and old coffee. The tables were bolted to the floor. She sat with the bad wrist in her lap in its sleeve and waited eleven minutes, and then the door opened and an officer brought him in.

He stopped when he saw her. Then he sat down across the table.

“Xiaoyue,” he said.

Her fingers tightened in her lap. She’d seen the name in pencilled capitals and in Matron Sima’s red ledger, but she had never once heard it said by somebody who’d known her before she was Elara.

“Don’t call me that. Not yet. My name’s Elara,” she said.

He lowered his eyes. “Elara.”

He looked at her wrist. “Is it healing?”

“Slowly.”

“Can you use it?”

“Some things.”

He nodded as if he’d expected nothing more. Then he looked at the officer, and the officer took a small brown envelope out of a bag and put it on the table, and her uncle pushed it across to her with one finger without touching anything else.

He said, “My brother sent these to me at sea, the year before. I was on a tanker. He wrote to me every month, and twice he put in a photograph so I’d see how fat everybody was getting. They’ve been in my sea-bag ever since. I thought you’d died. I didn’t know who else to give them to.”

She opened it with her left hand.

The first was a man and a woman outside a low building on a pier with QU LIGHTERAGE painted over the door. He had a serious face and was trying to smile and not managing; she was laughing at something outside the frame with her head back, and Elara looked at the way her eyes went when she laughed and knew it from the mirror.
