The second was the woman alone. She was sitting on a wide sill in a nurse’s uniform with a cardigan over it, with her hair tied up and a cup in her hands, looking out of a tall arched window at something below. Behind her, through the glass, there were the tops of trees.

Her uncle said, “She was on nights. My brother took that on her break. He used to bring her dinner up the back stairs at midnight because the canteen was terrible.”

Elara couldn’t look away from it.

He said, “She sang. When she was doing things. Cooking. Folding. Putting you down when you wouldn’t go down. There was a tune. I don’t remember the words. Three notes and then it came down.” He shut his eyes and hummed it, badly, in the visiting room, under his breath.

Three notes, and then it came down. She’d been humming it all her life. At the sink. On the bus. Over sugar petals at three in the morning while her husband moved the lamp. She’d thought it was something she’d made up.

“You know it,” he said, watching her face.

“I hum it. I always have. I didn’t know where it came from.” Her voice had gone small.

He looked at her, and then down at the table. “She’d have liked that.”

Elara said, “You knew I’d been alive. Since the summer. You’d heard. And you didn’t go to the children’s home and ask. You didn’t find out anything. You came with a knife.”

“Yes.”

“You could have found out I was alive before you came up the alley.”

“Yes, I know,” he said.

She put the photographs back in the envelope. She’d wanted to ask him so many things: whether her mother liked rain, what she ate, whether she was ever afraid on the night wards. None of it would come.

“I can’t give you back anything,” he said.

“No.”

When the officer came for him he stood up and looked at her once more. “Your mother loved you,” he said, and nothing else, and they took him out.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was by the car in the car park with his hands in his coat pockets, and he straightened when he saw her, and didn’t ask anything. He opened the door for her and put a bottle of water in the holder and waited until she was settled before he shut it.

“He called me Xiaoyue,” she said, a long way down the road.

“How did it feel?”

“Strange. These are my parents.” She took the photographs out and held them in her lap.

He looked, at a red light, and didn’t take them from her. “She had your eyes.”

“She sang the tune. The one I hum. He hummed it for me and I knew it before he’d finished.”

He put his hand over hers on the photographs and kept it there until the lights changed.

She asked him to take the coast road, and he did, and at a lay-by over the water he pulled in and they got out and stood by the car in the wind with the sea going past in long silver strips. She held the envelope against her chest.

She said, “I keep thinking she sat at a window somewhere and looked at a garden. And I’ll never know whether it was raining, or what she was thinking, or whether she was tired, or wanted to go home.”

“No.”

“And whether she knew I’d remember her somehow.”

“You did. Not her face. The song.”

She took the front of his coat in her left hand and kissed him, slowly, twice, with the envelope between them, and when she drew back he kept his forehead against hers.

“Are you all right?”

“No. But I want to be here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she put the photographs side by side on the study desk where she’d see them every time she sat down. He brought her tea and stood behind her chair, and he looked at the second one for longer than at the first, and she felt him go still.

“What?”

He didn’t say. Then he said, carefully, “There’s something in the window. I think I know where it is. Do you want me to tell you, or do you want to look first?”

She turned round in the chair and looked up at him. He’d asked. He’d stood there behind her knowing something about her and asked whether she wanted it, and she saw what it cost him to stand still and wait for the answer.

“Tell me.”

He leaned over her shoulder and put his finger on the glass in the photograph, on the tops of the trees, and on the curve of something pale below them that might have been a stone edge. “That’s a camphor. The pond’s under it. The window’s arched, with the bar across the top. It’s the old block at City Hospital. The first floor. They were the night wards until 2009. It’s the window over the garden.” He took his hand away.

She didn’t say anything at all.

On Saturday they went. It had rained in the night and everything was grey and soft and dripping, the way it had been on a morning in June two years before. The camphor tree. The pond with the low stone edge and the koi going round, orange and white and gold. The bench. And above it, on the back of the old block, the row of tall arched windows with the paint coming off the frames.

She held the photograph up in her left hand and looked from it to the wall, and found it: the fourth from the end, with the bar across the top and the sill wide enough to sit on.

“That one,” she said.

“Yes.”

She sat down on the bench under it. She’d stood here in her scrubs talking about whether fish slept while he knelt in a puddle behind her. She’d chosen this garden to be married in because it was the only place she could think of where nobody had ever bled. And her mother had sat on that sill on her break at midnight with a cup in her hands and looked straight down at it.

“She looked at this,” said Elara.

“Yes.”

“Maybe she could see that tree.”

“Possibly.”

“You don’t know.”

“No.”

“Good. Don’t pretend.”

“I won’t.”

She sat with the photograph on her knee. Her right thumb lay along its edge. And something happened there, so faint that she thought at first it was the paper moving in the wind. A coolness. A distinct, particular edge against the pad of her thumb, where for five months there’d been nothing but a dull pressure that might have been anything.

She went still. She moved the photograph a millimetre. It was there again. Paper. The edge of paper, against her own skin, in her own hand. Her eyes filled. She blinked them clear.

“Elara?”

“Nothing.”

“Does it hurt?”

“No.” She kept her thumb exactly where it was. She didn’t tell him. She wanted to know that it was real before she gave it a name, and she wanted one thing, for a little while, that was only hers.

They stayed until the light changed. At the car she looked up at the fourth window from the end. “Can we come back?”

“Whenever you want.”

“Not just once.”

“Not just once.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he went up to the study and came down with the small box, and sat down beside her on the sofa, and opened it. The plain band was inside.

“I’ve kept it here. Not because I thought you’d take it back. I wanted you to know it was still yours,” he said.

She looked at it.

“I’m not asking you to forget anything. I wanted to look after you and I used that to decide what you were allowed to know, and I won’t do it again. Coming home doesn’t mean it’s mended. I’m not asking you to marry me. You did that. I don’t want to keep making you prove it. I’m asking whether you’ll let me be your husband again. Not the one who decides when you can know things. Not the one who watches every door. The one you come home to when you’re angry with him. The one who sits beside you while you find out what that hand can do. The one who goes back to that garden with you as many times as you want.” He closed the box halfway and looked at her.

He opened the box again. “Will you take it back?”

She lifted the band out with her right hand, slowly, and turned it in her fingers.

“I can’t promise I’ll never be angry again.”

“I don’t need that.”

“I’ll remember all of it.”

“I expect you to.”

“I’ll need to leave the room sometimes.”

“Then I’ll let you.”

“And you won’t come after me?”

“Not unless you ask.”

She held the ring. “Then yes.”

He breathed out. It was almost nothing, a small sound, and she heard it. She gave him the ring and held out her left hand, and he put it back on her finger beside the star.

“I don’t want another proposal. I want this one,” she said.

“Then this one.”

She stood up and held her hand out to him, and he took it, and she led him upstairs.

In the bedroom he stopped by the bed and looked at her, and she knew the look: he was trying to decide whether she was sure.

“Don’t. I’m sure. Not because the ring’s back on. Not because I feel better today. I want you,” she said.

For five months he’d been careful of her. Careful of the wrist, of the places it hurt, of the way a sudden touch could put the alley back in her face. She came close and put his hand on her waist herself, away from the wrist, and kissed him, and when he began to be careful she smiled against his mouth.

“You can touch me.”

“I know.”

“Then stop being frightened of me.”

“I’m not frightened of you. I’m frightened of hurting you.”

“You won’t hurt me by loving me,” she said, and he shut his eyes for a second, and then he kissed her.

She pulled his shirt loose and laughed when he caught his foot on the edge of the rug, and he laid her down and undressed her slowly, and kissed the scar on the inside of her wrist, the whole length of it, lightly, and then her palm, and then moved down her, unhurried. She guided his hands where she wanted them. She pulled him close whenever he began to draw back into caution, and when he came into her she held his face with her left hand and watched him, and he moved in her so slowly that she could feel every second of it, and she didn’t look away from him once, until she couldn’t help it, and said his name into his shoulder, and he followed her with hers.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest in the light of the bedside lamp. “Don’t go anywhere.”

“I’m here.”

Much later she woke. He was asleep beside her. The ring was on her finger, and the star caught a little light from the street. She turned her right hand over on the blanket and brushed the tip of her thumb along the side of her first finger, and felt the warmth of her own skin. She did it again. Small, imperfect, hers.

Her first thought was to wake him and put his hand against hers and make him feel how enormous so small a thing could be. She didn’t. Not because she meant to hide it for ever. Because it was hers first.

In the dark she hummed three notes, and then the little tune that came down, and this time she could feel the weave of the blanket under her fingertip as she held it.

chapters.title: A Surgeon Who Doesn’t Exist
chapters.desc: At one in the morning her father rings for the first time in eight months: his driver’s grandson is bleeding on the kitchen table. Elara picks up the instruments herself, and her hands don’t shake.
chapters.epigraph: “I won’t forget your rules.”
chapters.content:
The wire went silent at seventeen minutes past five on a Tuesday in May.

For ten weeks it had whispered against its guide every time she moved, a thin uneven hiss that she’d come to hate, because it was the sound of her hand not being quite where she’d told it to be. That morning she moved her first finger through the range and back, and there was nothing. She did it again. Nothing. She moved the wrist a degree in the cradle and did the whole set, thumb to little finger, and the wire ran through the block without a sound, and her fingers went where she sent them, and stayed.

She took her arm out of the cradle and picked up a paperclip off the bench. Turned it over. Put it down. Picked it up again, and held it out in front of her in the cold light of the back room at Tai Hing, and watched the end of it for a full minute, and it didn’t tremble. She opened the notebook.

5:17. Wire silent.

After a while she wrote underneath it, Repeat with therapist. Don’t turn it up. And then she switched the light off and sat in the dark among the engines until the taxi came, and didn’t ring anyone.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ninth of May was a Saturday, and it went by without a wedding.

It had been circled on the kitchen calendar since last spring, with a small camellia drawn beside it in her hand. In the morning he made breakfast, and she sat at the counter and watched him cut a mango into exact pieces, and said, “Do you remember what today was supposed to be?”

He didn’t pretend not to. “Yes.”

“I thought I’d feel worse.”

“Do you?”

She thought about it. “No. Not exactly.”

“We don’t have to decide anything today.”

“You love that sentence.”

“It’s been useful.”

She ate the mango. In the evening she took a pen and drew one line through the date, not angrily, only enough to mark that it had gone, and left the camellia.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday after, he came home late and stood in the kitchen doorway with his keys still in his hand, and said, “I went to see Meng today. Twice. I asked her for your therapy notes.”

Elara put down the chopsticks she’d been practising with. Ordinary ones, no loop, a piece of tofu moved from one side of a plate to the other and back. She let her hand drop into her lap.

“What did she say?”

“No. Both times. She said you’d tell me what you wanted me to know, and that being worried didn’t give me the right to any of it. She was right. I’m telling you because I said I’d tell you everything, and this is a thing.” He put the keys down.

She looked at him. “Good. She should have said no,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you ask me?”

“I do ask you. You tell me better. I wanted the numbers. I’ll ask you.” He came and kissed her temple.

She didn’t tell him about the wire.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first lie was small. On a Sunday in July he asked whether she’d been to see Ah Sim, and she said, with her eyes on her book, “She’s been poorly. Tired. I said I’d look in on her this week,” and he asked whether she’d seen a doctor, and Elara said she thought so, and he said he’d ring her, and Elara said, much too quickly, “Don’t, she’ll be cross if everyone starts ringing,” and he looked at her and let it go.

Ah Sim wasn’t poorly. Elara had seen her on the Friday complaining about the price of fish. But she’d needed somewhere she might plausibly have gone at night without a taxi on an account, and she hated herself for choosing the one person in the world he’d never think to check, and she hated how easily the words came out.

The call came a little after one on the second Saturday in July.

He was asleep. She wasn’t. Her phone buzzed on the bedside table and she looked at the screen, and it said Baba, and her heart did something she didn’t recognise. He hadn’t rung her in eight months. They’d sat at the same table at New Year and in the spring, and he’d asked about her hand and she’d answered, and he’d sent messages, short ones, about the weather. He had never once rung in the middle of the night.

She took it out onto the landing. “Baba?”

“Xiaoyue.”

He’d never called her that. Nobody had, except an old man in a prison visiting room.

“What’s happened?”

“Jiale. Mok’s grandson. He’s on my kitchen table. A knife. His arm. He put it up. He’s on bail for something stupid with some stupid boys, and if he goes into a hospital with a knife wound they’ll take the bail off him and he’ll be inside by Monday with the boys who did it. He’s seventeen. He’s bleeding. Mok’s holding it. I don’t know how hard to hold it. I’ve never known.” Her father’s voice was level, which was how she knew.

“Call an ambulance.”

“He won’t let us. Mok won’t make him.”

“Baba, a kitchen isn’t a hospital.”

“I know. He’s a child to me. I can’t watch him bleed to death on my table. There’s a car at the bottom of your road. Not a taxi. Come or don’t. Either way I won’t ring you again tonight.” She heard him breathe.

She stood on the dark landing with the phone against her ear. Through the bedroom door her husband was asleep on his side with one arm across the place where she’d been.

“I’m coming,” she said.

She dressed in the bathroom without the light, her left hand doing the buttons. She took the green bag out of the hall cupboard and the loupes he’d given her on her twenty-third birthday out of the drawer in the study, where they’d lain in their case since November. She stood beside the bed and looked at him. Then she went down the stairs with her shoes in her hand, and at the bottom of Banyan Terrace there was a dark car with one of her father’s men at the wheel, and he didn’t say a word all the way to the Walled City.

✦ ✦ ✦

The kitchen was too bright. Somebody had put every light on. A tea towel on the floor, soaked. A chair pushed back against the wall. The boy on the long table with his face grey and his eyes too wide, and Mok standing over him with both hands clamped round the boy’s forearm and blood between his fingers, and her father by the sink in his shirtsleeves.

Her father looked at her when she came in, and stepped aside.

“Doctor,” he said.

“Don’t.”

Jiale turned his head on the table. She’d known him since he was six and used to follow her round Mok’s car in the alley asking whether doctors were allowed to mend bicycles. “Dr. Elara. I’m sorry.”

“You can be sorry when you’ve stopped bleeding. Keep still.”

She put the green bag on the table and opened it and washed her hands at Ah Sim’s sink with Ah Sim’s soap, which smelled of ginger, and gloved, and put the loupes on. “Mok. Don’t let go until I say. Baba, I want the big lamp from your office and every clean towel in the house and a pan of water on to boil. Then stand where I can see you.”

She looked at the arm.

It was the inside of the left forearm, just above the wrist. He’d put his arm up the way she’d put hers up on the step. The cut was long and deep and she could see, when Mok eased his grip on her word for a count of two, that it had opened the radial artery and gone into the tendons beside it. Bright blood came up in a spurt, and she said “Hold,” and Mok held.

The same wound. Nearly the same. On the other arm. She waited for her hand to shake. It didn’t.

She checked the hand first, because that was what you did, and pressed the boy’s fingertips and watched the colour come back, and pressed on the ulnar side at the wrist with her own thumb and watched it again. The hand would live on the other artery. She told him so. Then she took the needle holder out of the bag in her right hand, the bad one, the one Meng had put back together with stitches finer than a hair, and it closed round the instrument as it had closed round instruments since she was eighteen, and held.

The room narrowed to the lamp and the wound and her own breathing. She found the cut ends of the artery and tied them, one and then the other, and the bleeding stopped. She washed the wound out with the boiled water, a great deal of it, while Mok held the boy’s shoulders and the boy swore at her in a voice that was getting stronger. She looked at the tendons under the loupes. Two cut, cleanly. She could do those. The nerve was bruised but whole, and she’d have bet her life on it, and in a way she did. She repaired the tendons one at a time, slowly, the way Meng had done hers, with the boy’s fingers held exactly where she put them, and every stitch went where she sent it.

“Can I sleep?” said Jiale, at some point.

“No.”

“Bossy.”

“Very. Tell me about the bicycle.”

He told her about a bicycle. She closed the skin. She splinted the wrist with the fingers flexed as they had to be, from a roll in her bag and two of Ah Sim’s wooden spoons. She gave him the antibiotics from the bag and wrote down for Mok, in capitals, what he was to take and when, and what it would look like if it went wrong.

“If his hand goes cold, or white, or he gets a fever, or the bleeding starts again, he goes to the ED the same minute, bail or no bail, and I’ll take him myself. That isn’t a question. And he goes to someone for the nerve within the week. Someone good. Crestview. They don’t ask people who pay.” She looked at her father.

“He’ll go.”

She took the gloves off and dropped them in the bin and washed her hands again at the sink. The water ran over her fingertips. She looked down at them. No tremor. Nothing.

“You didn’t shake,” said her father behind her.

She didn’t turn round.

“I watched your hand. In December you couldn’t hold a spoon. In February you dropped dumplings. I saw you,” he said.

“I know.”

“How long?”

“Not everything. Not yet. Some things.”

“I didn’t ask everything. How long?”

She looked at the water. “Since May.”

“And your husband?”

She shook her head.

He was quiet. Then he said, “You were very good.”

She flinched, and he saw it.

“Don’t praise me for it. The boys who did this.” She dried her hands on one of Ah Sim’s towels.

“Will be dealt with.”

“I don’t want to know how.”

“No, you don’t,” said Lin Jian.

She turned round then, and looked at him, this man who’d put a man in the harbour in the spring of 2003 and told her about it in the same voice he used for the tides.

“Will you come again? If someone needs you. If someone can’t go to a hospital,” he said.

“I’m not your doctor.”

“I know.”

“If I come, I decide what can be done and what can’t. I decide when I leave. Nobody is ever stopped from going to a hospital because they’re frightened, not by you, not by anyone. And you tell me everything, the whole of it, before I’m through the door. No more hiding it in case I say no.”

“Yes.”

“You have to mean it.”

“I mean it.”

She looked at the boy asleep on the kitchen table with his arm on a pillow, and at Mok sitting beside him on the bench with his head in his hands.

“Then you can ring me. Those are my rules,” she said.

“Your rules. Xiaoyue.” Her father picked up her bag and held it out to her.

She took it.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Tell Mok I’ll come on Tuesday to look at the dressing,” she said, and went out through the red door without looking back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car left her at the bottom of Banyan Terrace at half past four. She let herself in without a sound and put the bag back in the cupboard and the loupes back in the drawer, and went up the stairs, and he was sitting on the bed with the lamp on.

“Where have you been?”

She took her coat off. “Ah Sim.”

He stood up. “What’s happened?”

“She wasn’t well. She didn’t want to wake anyone else.”

“At one in the morning?”

“She rang me.”

“Is she all right?”

“Yes. She was frightened, that’s all. She’s asleep.”

He looked at her, and then he held out his hand. “Come here.”

She went. He touched her cheek, and then her shoulder. “You’re cold. You’ve been out three hours.”

“Time goes.”

“Were you frightened?”

That nearly broke her. She had been frightened. Not of the blood, and not of the knife wound, and not of failing. She’d been frightened of how easily her hand had worked. Of how familiar it had all felt, and how much she’d wanted to keep going. And now she was frightened of him, not because he’d ever hurt her, but because he’d look at her hand in the lamplight and know.

So she kissed him. Hard, all at once, so that he took a step back against the chest of drawers, and she held his shirt in both fists and didn’t let the space come back between them. He kissed her back. When she let go his eyes went over her face.

“Elara.”

She kissed him again.

He put his forehead against hers. “What’s happened?”

“Nothing.”

“Don’t say that if it isn’t true.”

“I’m tired,” she said, and that, at least, was true, and he looked at her a moment longer and then put his hand on her hair and gave up asking. He knelt and took her shoes off, and brought her water, and helped her into bed, careful of the wrist, and put the lamp out and drew her close in the dark.

“I’m here,” he said into her hair.

She wanted to tell him. The words were all there, in a row, ready. My hand worked. I held a needle holder and it didn’t shake. I tied off an artery on my father’s kitchen table and mended two tendons with your loupes on. But the lie was already out of the door, and the truth was too big to come in after it, and she put her face against his chest and listened to his heart instead.

At half past seven he woke first and lifted her right hand off the pillow, and kissed the fingertips, thumb to little finger, the way he did. She stirred.

“Go back to sleep,” he said.

She knew exactly what he was doing, and for the first time she wished he’d stop. Not because she didn’t want it. Because she could feel it. Every single one.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing,” she said, and turned over to face the window, and lay with her fingertips pressed into the blanket, feeling every thread of the weave, and cried without making a sound.

At nine her phone buzzed. Jiale is sitting up. Hand warm. Mok is with him. And then, a minute later: I won’t forget your rules.

She looked at it while the shower ran next door. Then she opened her notebook.

Saturday 11 July. Right hand under load, two hours. No tremor.

And under it:

I haven’t told my husband.

She shut the notebook when the bathroom door opened. He came out drying his hair. “Hungry?”

“Yes.”

“Good. I’ll make breakfast.” He kissed her hair and went downstairs.

She could have followed him and said all of it at the counter while the kettle boiled. She didn’t. Not that morning. And somewhere between the back room at Tai Hing and her father’s kitchen table, between the wire and the lie, a surgeon who didn’t exist had gone back to work.

chapters.title: The Cellar Under the Rope Store
chapters.desc: Raiden opens a room under the old rope store next to the garage, and Evangeline comes to hand her the instruments. The ghost never says a word.
chapters.epigraph: “Then I won’t. Not down here. Not one word.”
chapters.content:
The building next door to Tai Hing had been empty for eleven years. It had been the rope store when Tai Hing still made rope, and the ground floor was full of what nobody had wanted to throw away: coils of old tarred rope hanging from the rafters, crates under a skin of dust, a sign over the door whose letters had long since gone back to rust. Raiden had bought it in Jinx’s name with Tai Hing in the winter of 2021, along with everything else that leaked.

On the Tuesday after the kitchen table, Raiden came to the back room at a quarter to seven with two coffees and said, “Baba told me.” On the Wednesday he took up the boards in the middle of the rope store floor. By the Saturday Elara was standing at the edge of a square black hole with a ladder going down into it.

“What’s that?”

“A cellar. They kept the tarred rope down there. It’s dry. It’s the only dry thing on this street.”

“I can see it’s a cellar.”

“Then why did you ask?”

She turned to Jinx, who was kneeling on the floor beside a roll of drawings with a pencil behind her ear. “Why is he like this?”

“I married his personality,” said Jinx.

“You married my money,” said Raiden.

“The money came with the personality.”

“I’m going home,” said Elara.

“No, you’re not. Come down and look.” Raiden held out his hand.

Jinx stood up and wiped her hands and unrolled the drawing on a crate before Elara could argue. It wasn’t large. Sealed walls, a poured floor with a drain, proper light and proper air, a steel table that could be scrubbed, a sink, a cupboard that locked, a shelf. And two ways in: the ladder from the rope store, and a second door at the far end that went up three steps into the service lane behind the building, with a lamp over it. Neither of them went anywhere near the garage.

“It’s a clinic,” said Elara.

Jinx said, “It’s a clean room with two doors. It isn’t a theatre and it isn’t a hospital, and anyone who needs a hospital goes to one. I’ve written that on the drawing so nobody can say they didn’t know.”

“How long have you been thinking about this?”

Raiden didn’t smile. For once in his life he didn’t. “Since Baba told me you did it on his kitchen table with two of Ah Sim’s wooden spoons. I’m not telling you what to do with it. But if you’re going to be rung at one in the morning, you’re not doing it on anybody’s kitchen table again. That’s all.”

She looked down the ladder into the dark, and at the second door on the drawing, and at Jinx.

“Does Xing Yue know?”

Raiden and Jinx looked at each other. “No,” said Raiden.

“Wonderful,” said Elara, and went down the ladder.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took three weeks. Raiden did the structure with a builder from Ms. Bok’s office who’d once put a pigeon loft on a roof and asked no questions about anything. Jinx did everything that had to be cleaned or plugged in, and wouldn’t let Raiden buy a single thing until she’d read the specification, and he complained, and she didn’t listen. Elara came most afternoons after teaching and wasn’t allowed to lift anything, which she found insulting.

“You sound like Xing Yue,” she told Jinx.

“Then listen to both of us.”

They argued about the walls. Raiden wanted grey and Jinx wanted white, and Elara chose a pale warm colour like the inside of a shell that neither of them liked, and kept it.

Eliana came on a Sunday with a black telephone in a padded case, old-fashioned and heavy, and a box of cable. “Don’t touch the wiring,” she told Raiden.

“I know how to put in a phone.”

“You know how to break a phone. You dropped mine in a bucket.”

“It was already broken.”

“It was not already broken. Two people can ring this. Baba and Mok. Nobody else has the number and nobody can ring out on it. No names on it anywhere. When that one rings, this one rings. Wherever you are. Keep it somewhere he doesn’t open.” Eliana knelt and connected it, and it rang once and stopped. She took a small grey phone out of her pocket and put it in Elara’s hand.

Elara looked at the little grey phone. “Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. It’s a bit creepy.” Eliana looked round the shell-coloured room.

“It’s a cellar.”

“It’s a secret cellar.”

“Now you’re getting it,” said Raiden, and Eliana pointed at him and said, “Don’t encourage her.”

On the last day her father came down the ladder in his good coat with a folder, and put it on the steel table. Inside, typed, were her rules, the ones she’d said to him at his own sink with the boy asleep on his table, set out in plain words with headings by someone who’d once written a list of conditions on a napkin and had it framed. The doctor decides whether to come. The doctor decides what can safely be done here and what can’t. Nobody may demand treatment, hide how an injury happened, or stop anyone from going to a hospital. At the bottom there was a line for a signature.

“Jinx wrote it. I’ll sign it,” said Lin Jian.

“You can’t ask me to treat somebody because you know them.”

“I won’t.”

“You can’t bring somebody here and tell me I have to.”

“I won’t.”

“Then sign,” said Elara, and he did, and pushed it across the table to her, and climbed the ladder again, and stopped halfway with his head in the rope store and said, without looking down, “Don’t stay down here too late.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Evangeline came on the first Friday in August, in the evening, with a hard grey case.

She put it on the steel table and opened it. Instruments, a full small set, each one wrapped and laid in its place, clean and good and chosen by someone who’d asked somebody who knew. Elara didn’t ask where they’d come from. Ev’s husband had spent nine years in places where people needed things that couldn’t be bought in shops.

“These are yours?”

Ev nodded.

“You’re giving them to me?”

Ev shook her head. She closed the lid and put her own hand flat on it, and then she took a folded paper mask and a plain cap out of her coat pocket and put them on the table beside it, two of each, and looked at her sister.

Elara understood. Ev wasn’t giving her the instruments. Ev was going to stand on the other side of the table and hand them to her.

“You’ll faint.”

Ev raised one eyebrow. She had sat in a yard in a puddle of broth with her husband’s head in her lap and a pistol on the step.

“You won’t faint. All right,” said Elara.

Then she thought about it. Who would come down the ladder, or up the three steps from the lane. Men who’d know her father’s face, and might know his daughters’. A doctor at City Hospital who talked to everybody about everything and whose voice half the Walled City had heard at its noodle stalls since she was three.

“If I talk,” she said slowly, “they’ll know me.”

Ev looked at her.

“Then I won’t. Not down here. Not one word,” said Elara.

Her sister, who had spent most of her childhood in the next room not speaking, put out her hand and touched Elara’s cheek, lightly, the way she’d touched her hair in December. Then she went up the steps into the lane. And the ghost never said a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

The grey phone rang at twelve forty-one on the following Thursday, in her bag on the hall floor at Banyan Terrace, under her scarf, while her husband slept upstairs.

The man was sitting on the steel table when she came in by the lane door with her hair under the cap and the mask on: a dock worker in a wet singlet, holding his left hand against his chest, with Raiden beside him and Mok by the ladder. He’d caught it between a container and a quay wall. Nobody seemed sure what name he’d been working under. He had no papers, no address he’d give, and no wish to meet a policeman.

She didn’t say anything. She washed and gloved and took the hand in hers and turned it in the light. Two fingers. The skin torn back off the middle one like a sleeve, and the end bone of it broken, and the nail gone. She looked at it. Then she wrote on the pad on the shelf, in capitals, and held it up for Raiden.

I CAN CLOSE IT. IT NEEDS AN X-RAY TOMORROW. IF IT GOES HOT OR RED HE GOES TO A HOSPITAL.

Raiden read it out. The man looked at her, and then at Lin Jian’s man by the ladder, and nodded.

Ev was already across the table with the case open. Elara held out her right hand without looking, and Ev put the first instrument into it, and the next, and the next, without a word, at exactly the moment she wanted each one, as if she’d been doing it for years. Elara washed the hand out and cleaned the bone and laid the skin back where it belonged and stitched it, small, under the loupes, and splinted the finger, and while she worked she didn’t speak, and after a while she found she was humming, under the mask, three notes and the little tune that came down, the way she always did when her hands were busy.

The man watched her the whole time. When she’d finished he looked at the splint, and at her eyes over the mask, and said something to Mok in a language she didn’t know. Mok laughed.

“He wants to know your name,” said Mok.

She said nothing.

The man said it again, in their own language this time, slowly, trying it out. “Doctor Ghost.”

“That’s terrible,” said Jinx, from the top of the ladder.

Mok was grinning. “Doctor Ghost.”

Elara pointed a gloved finger at him, and he laughed so much he had to sit on the bottom rung.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second came three nights later: a girl of seventeen with a long cut across her cheekbone from a bottle outside a restaurant, and a friend holding her hand. The girl kept asking whether it would scar. Elara looked at it under the light, and at the eye above it, which was whole, and closed it in fine stitches so close together that the friend had to look away, humming the whole time. When she’d finished the girl touched the dressing and said, “Are you really a doctor?”

Elara nodded.

“What’s your name?”

She didn’t answer.

“They said you’re the Ghost,” said the girl, and laughed nervously, and Elara wrote the instructions for the stitches on a card and gave it to her, and Ev showed them out by the lane.

The third came in the rain, through the lane door, held up by two men who’d run a long way: a young man with a bullet in the top of his thigh and a face like paper. She knelt and put her fingers on the top of his foot, and then on the inside of his ankle, and felt almost nothing there. She looked at the wound, and at the swelling coming up round it, and wrote on the pad in letters so big they took the whole page.

HOSPITAL. NOW. ARTERY. HE’LL DIE HERE.

“He can’t. He’s wanted,” said one of the men.

She held the pad up to Mok and pointed at the bottom of it, at the line her father had signed. Then she put both hands on the wound and leaned her whole weight on it, and looked at Mok, and didn’t move.

Mok went up the ladder. Five minutes later the black car was in the lane with its engine running, and they carried the young man up the three steps on a door taken off its hinges, with her kneeling on it beside him, pressing, all the way to the car and into the back seat, and Mok drove to the ED at City Hospital through every red light between the docks and the hill, and left him on the ramp outside the ambulance doors with the porters running, and drove away.

She was in the cellar again before he was in theatre. She washed her hands and sat down on the floor with her back against the shell-coloured wall, and Raiden came down the ladder and sat beside her.

“You all right?”

She nodded.

“You know what they’re calling you.”

“Don’t.”

“It’s catching on.”

She leaned her head back against the wall and shut her eyes, and in the morning the little grey phone buzzed once in her bag with a message from a number with no name. Thigh boy alive. Vascular kept him. Didn’t ask how he got there.

✦ ✦ ✦

He noticed the nights. Of course he did.

At first he thought it was the rig. She said it was the rig, the extra sessions Jinx had let her have in the evening, and he wanted to believe her, and so he did, for a while. But the pattern was wrong. She went out at odd hours and came back with her hair tied up and washed her hands twice at the kitchen sink before she came upstairs. She was sleeping less. There were no taxis on the account. When he asked whether the machine was still helping she said yes, and whether Jinx had changed anything she said no, and whether she was keeping to the therapist’s limits she said yes, and each time the lie came more easily, and that frightened her more than anything in the cellar.

On the first Saturday in August she came in at twenty past three and he was in the big room on the grey sofa with a book open on his knee that he wasn’t reading.

“Why are you awake?”

“Waiting.”

“For me?”

“Yes. You’re exhausted.” He shut the book and came and looked at her: her eyes, her colour, the way she was holding her right hand.

“I’m all right.”

“Tomorrow you’re taking a nap. That’s a medical order.”

“From whom?”

“Your husband.”

“That’s not a recognised qualification.”

“I’m making an exception,” he said, and she laughed, and the laugh hurt somewhere under her ribs.

The next afternoon he shut the curtains and put water by the bed and a plate of cut fruit, and stood over her while she got under the cover, like a ward sister.

“Sleep for an hour. I’ve got work.”

She caught his hand as he turned. “Wait. Come here.”

“You’re the one who needs the nap.”

“It’s a prescription. I’ll sleep better if you’re here. Please.” She lifted the cover.

That changed his face. He took his watch off and put it by the water and got in, and she came into his arms at once and lay with her face against his chest.

“You smell of the hospital.”

“You smell of the garage.”

“That’s very romantic.”

“I thought so.”

She lifted her head and kissed him, and kept kissing him, and when he said her name in the voice that meant sleep she put her hand on his belt and said, “Afterwards.” He didn’t argue. She undressed him in the striped dim light with her left hand, slowly, and let him undress her, and pulled him over her and held him there with both arms round his back and her bad hand flat between his shoulder blades, where she could feel the long muscles moving under it, every one, in a hand he still thought couldn’t feel anything at all. He moved in her slowly, and then not, and she turned her face into his neck so that he wouldn’t see it when it came over her, and said his name, and didn’t say anything else, because everything else she might have said was a lie or the truth, and she couldn’t bear either.

Afterwards she slept, properly, for three hours, with his arm across her. He thought she was tired. He didn’t know she’d spent the night before on the floor of a cellar under the rope store with her whole weight on a stranger’s thigh. He didn’t know about the black phone, or the grey one in her bag, or the second door, or the name.

At seventeen minutes past five on the Sunday morning she woke. He was still asleep. She slid out from under his arm and sat down on the bed and flexed her right hand in the grey light, and the fingers went where she sent them, every one, and when she touched the side of the bedside table the wood was cool under her fingertip and she knew exactly which finger it was.

She leaned down and kissed his forehead, so lightly he didn’t stir.

Then she went down the stairs with her shoes in her hand. Down by the docks the rope store was dark, and below it the black phone sat on its shelf, and the lamp over the lane door was waiting, and the ghost had work to do.

chapters.title: The Pillowcase
chapters.desc: He wakes at two in the morning to find her sewing up a torn pillowcase by the light of her phone. He knows a surgeon’s hands when he sees them, and a week later he follows her to a steel door.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s a pillowcase. Don’t look at it like a specimen.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past two in the morning he woke to the sound of thread being drawn through cloth.

It was a small sound, soft and regular, like someone breathing out through their teeth. Her side of the bed was empty. He thought she’d gone down for water. Then he saw the light.

She was sitting on the floor beside the bed with her back against the bedside table and her phone face up on the rug, its torch pointed at her lap. One of his pillowcases was spread across her knees. The corner had torn along the seam, and she was mending it with a needle and white thread from the tin she kept for buttons, her hair tied loosely at the back of her neck.

She was humming. Three notes, and then the little tune that came down. He didn’t move.

She held the cloth with her left hand and worked the needle with her right. In, through, and out. She drew the thread until the tension was exactly right, eased the fabric a millimetre along, and went in again. She didn’t look at the phone. She didn’t look at her hand. She knew where the needle was. When the thread caught she stopped, freed it with a fingernail, and went on.

He had spent his whole working life watching other people’s hands. He knew the difference between a hand trying to make a movement and a hand that knew where the movement ended: the small pause before pressure, the way the fingers held something delicate without crushing it, the way the wrist stayed quiet while the work happened at the tips. He knew those hands. He had watched them hold a retractor for two hours on a September morning when he’d had no right to remember them at all.

She tied off with a knot so small it disappeared into the seam, ran her thumb along the stitches, turned the pillowcase over, and folded it. Only then did she look up and see him.

“Oh,” she said. “Why are you awake?”

“My pillowcase was being attacked.”

“It tore. I didn’t want to wake you.”

“It’s two in the morning.”

“It would have bothered me.” She held it out when he put out his hand. The stitches were even, every one the same length, the thread pulled neither loose enough to gap nor tight enough to pucker. He turned it over.

“That’s good work.”

“It’s a pillowcase. Don’t look at it like a specimen.”

He gave it back. She put the needle in the tin, point away from him, and said, “Go back to sleep, I’ll come in a minute,” and he lifted the cover and said, “Come here,” and she climbed in against his chest, still humming, and fell asleep before he’d decided what to do with his hands.

He didn’t sleep again.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning the pillowcase was back on his pillow with the mended corner underneath. He turned it over and touched the knot, and listened to her brushing her teeth in the bathroom, humming, and sat at the foot of the bed.

He’d heard that tune in the car, in the kitchen, in the corridor on nine, for four years. He’d thought it was something she did when she was nervous. Now he knew it had been her mother’s.

He thought about the photographs on the study desk. He thought about the nights she said she was going to Jinx’s machine and came back with her hair tied up and washed her hands twice at the kitchen sink. The faint smell of antiseptic on her coat. The night in July when she’d come in at half past four from Ah Sim, who’d never been ill in her life, and kissed him too hard against the chest of drawers so that he wouldn’t ask anything.

Relief came first. Her hand was working. Not perfectly; he knew nerves well enough to know that one good night with a needle didn’t make a surgeon. But she could hold cloth and guide a stitch and tie a knot she couldn’t see, and he’d spent nine months trying not to hope too loudly, and now he’d seen it.

Then fear, because she hadn’t told him. Because she’d been doing it alone, and might have been pushing harder than anyone knew, and there was a reason she’d hidden it, and he didn’t know whether the reason was him.

Then the quieter thing. He had sat beside her while she cried because she couldn’t feel his mouth on her fingertips. He’d kissed every one of them anyway, every night. And she’d let him go on believing that her hand was too weak for the things she was doing with it. He understood wanting something that was only yours. He also understood, sitting there with the pillowcase, that she’d chosen him as the one person who wouldn’t know.

He put the pillowcase back the way it had been.

He wouldn’t ask. He’d taken her name away from her once and given it back on a day he’d chosen, and she’d stopped speaking for eleven days. He wasn’t going to make her hand into one more thing she had to account for to him. But he wasn’t going to leave her alone with it either.

✦ ✦ ✦

Over the next days he noticed things and said nothing about any of them. She’d stopped using her left hand to lift the kettle and then, if she saw him looking, changed hands. She turned the pages of a book without dragging them over the edge of the table first. She held a pen the old way, like a scalpel. And when he came into a room her right hand went back into her lap, a small inward turn of the wrist, a pause before she picked something up.

He asked whether she wanted tea. He listened to her complain about a first-year who’d confused the radial and ulnar arteries for the third time in a week. He kissed her when he left for the hospital. At night he held her, and didn’t ask about the pillowcase, or Tai Hing, or where she went.

On the Thursday she woke to find him watching her with her right hand held between both of his and his thumb near the scar.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re staring.”

“I married you.”

“That doesn’t give you the right to stare at me while I’m asleep.”

“It gives me a reasonable allowance,” he said, and kissed the base of her thumb, and then the scar, and she looked away, and he saw her do it.

“You’ve been doing that a lot.”

“Do you want me to stop?”

She thought about it. “No.”

That evening she came home early from teaching and he came home before dinner, which never happened, and they ate at the counter talking about nothing, and went upstairs while the flat was still full of the last of the light. She reached for him first. When his hand went towards her wrist and stopped, she caught it and put it there herself.

“It’s all right.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t be frightened of touching me.”

He undressed her slowly in the gold light and laid her down, and then he took her right hand and kissed the whole length of the scar, from one end to the other, the place where the blade had crossed her, so slowly that her eyes stung. She guided his fingers across her palm. He lay with his cheek against her hand as if it were the most precious thing he’d ever been given, and she put her other hand in his hair and pulled him up to her mouth, and he came into her with his forehead on hers and his eyes open, and moved in her as if he were learning the way back, not to an injured woman who needed protecting but to his wife, who was coming home to herself one finger at a time. She held his back with both hands. She could feel every muscle under the right one, and didn’t tell him, and arched under him and said his name into his throat until the light had gone.

“I love you,” she said afterwards, in the dark, with her hand on his chest.

He held it there. “I love you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later, at twelve forty-six on a Thursday night, he was awake when she got up.

He’d been awake for an hour. He watched her dress in the bathroom without the light and pick up her bag in the hall, and heard the front door, and went to the window. At the bottom of Banyan Terrace a dark car was waiting with its engine running and no light on in the cab. It wasn’t a taxi. It wasn’t on any account he’d ever see.

He knew that following his wife was a terrible idea. He did it anyway.

He kept three cars back through the empty streets: down the hill, along the harbour road, past the shuttered fish market and the old warehouses, into the narrow streets by the docks where Jinx had her garage. The dark car stopped in a lane behind a row of buildings. Elara got out and walked along the backs of them to a door with no sign, three steps down from the lane, with a small lamp burning over it. She opened it and went in, and it shut.

He parked across the end of the lane and turned the engine off.

Every part of him wanted to cross the cobbles and knock. To demand, from whoever opened it, why his wife was going into a locked building by the docks at one in the morning. He sat with his hands on the wheel. Then he got out and walked down the lane and stood on the bottom step under the lamp.

The door was steel, painted to look like old wood, heavy, with a small panel beside the handle. Through it he could hear almost nothing. A man’s breathing, uneven, catching. The small bright click of an instrument laid down on steel. Another. Nobody spoke. Nobody said a single word, the whole time he stood there, not her and not whoever else was with her.

And under it, faint through the steel, she was humming. Three notes, and then the tune that came down. He closed his eyes.

He knew that rhythm. Pause, click, the breath of the patient, pause. He knew what it sounded like when a surgeon was closing and somebody across the table was handing her each thing a second before she reached for it. It wasn’t a rig. It wasn’t a back room where she practised. His wife was working, in silence, with her mother’s song in her mouth, on someone he couldn’t see, and her hands were steady enough to do it.

He put his hand flat on the cold steel, just above the handle.

Then he took it away and stepped back up into the lane. He’d promised himself he wouldn’t make her defend this. If he opened that door, she’d spend the rest of her life defending it. He walked back to the car and drove home without the radio and got into bed on his side, and lay on his back in the dark with his eyes open.

At twenty past three he heard the front door, and the tap running in the kitchen, twice, and her feet on the stairs. She got in beside him carefully, smelling of soap and, under it of something else. He kept his breathing slow. After a while she put her right hand flat on his chest, over his heart, and left it there.

He didn’t move. He thought she could probably feel it going.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he made breakfast. He cut a mango into exact pieces on the board and put them in front of her, and she sat at the counter in his T-shirt with shadows under her eyes and ate them one at a time with her fingers.

“You were out late,” he said. It cost him a great deal to say it in that voice, the one for weather.

“Tai Hing. Jinx let me have the rig after closing. I couldn’t sleep.” She didn’t look up.

“How was it?”

“Good.”

He nodded and poured her tea. He’d heard her tell that lie in exactly that tone for six weeks and had believed it every time because he’d wanted to. This morning he heard all of it: the small pause before good, the way she said Jinx’s name a little too clearly. She was a terrible liar. She’d always been a terrible liar. It was one of the things he loved most about her, and he’d never once been glad of it before.

“Eat the rest. You’ve got first-years at ten,” he said.

“You sound like Ah Sim.”

“Ah Sim’s usually right.”

She laughed, and finished the mango, and kissed him at the door with her bag on her shoulder, and went down Banyan Terrace in the bright morning humming. He stood at the window and watched her go. Then he went to the sink, where she’d washed her hands twice in the night, and found that he’d already folded a clean towel and laid it there without thinking, warm from the airing cupboard, the way he’d done every morning since March. He left it where it was, and went to work, and was civil to every registrar he met all day, which frightened them more than anything he’d ever said.

chapters.title: Notes in the Margins
chapters.desc: He starts leaving surgical journals open on the kitchen table at the hardest cases. She can’t resist writing in the margins, and he answers.
chapters.epigraph: “Good. I like who I’m turning into.”
chapters.content:
The first journal appeared on a Tuesday in September, on the kitchen table beside her tea, open, with a paper bookmark halfway through. An old trauma journal with the corners gone soft. The article was about complex injuries of the forearm after penetrating trauma: two photographs, a diagram, and four pages on how hands did after nerve repair.

She looked at the stove, where he was making her rice porridge, because she hated eggs.

“Is this yours?”

“Yes.”

“You left it open.”

“I’m told that’s generally how journals are read.”

She narrowed her eyes at his back. He put the bowl in front of her and sat down with his tea and the news on his phone, and didn’t look at her. She ate. Then she picked up the pencil lying beside the journal and circled a sentence, Anatomical continuity doesn’t necessarily translate into functional recovery, and wrote in the margin, in her small quick hand: Obviously. A repaired structure isn’t a recovered person. She looked at that and added, You of all people should know that, and put the pencil down.

He turned a page of the news. “Your porridge is getting cold.”

The next morning there was another. Decision-making in patients with multiple injuries, an article she’d been given in final year, with a faint pencil mark beside one line: The surgeon must distinguish between what can be done and what should be done. Underneath it she wrote, Very convenient sentence for people who don’t have to decide while someone’s bleeding in front of them, and left the pencil across the page. When she came in from teaching there was an answer underneath in his square capitals, the ones anybody could read. CONVENIENT SENTENCES ARE USUALLY WRITTEN AFTER THE DIFFICULT DECISIONS.

She read it twice and smiled at the kitchen table, alone.

It became a habit. Not every day; he was too careful for that, and she was too sharp not to notice if it had been. Sometimes the journal was there when she came down. Sometimes it appeared on the sofa, or by the fruit bowl, or once on the edge of the bath. He never mentioned them. She never asked. They began to talk in the margins, in two hands, about other people’s patients.

You’ve ignored the man’s age.

I’ve judged it irrelevant to this conclusion.

It isn’t. Read the next page.

This is a poor study. Twenty patients, no control, and the conclusion is twice the size of the data.

You sound like Liao.

TAKE THAT BACK.

No.

Halfway through the month he left an article about fatigue in long operations open at a paragraph on how judgement fails after the fourteenth hour, and beside it he’d written, There is a point at which experience stops compensating for exhaustion. She wrote underneath, You once operated for twenty hours. The next morning: THAT WAS DIFFERENT. And under that, in hers: It wasn’t. And then his: I HAD A GOOD TEAM. And hers: You had a good team and a terrible decision-maker. He drew a small line under her sentence and wrote nothing else at all, and when she came and stood behind the sofa that evening and said, “You’re not going to defend yourself?” he looked up from his book and said, “Would it change your mind?”

“No.”

“Then there’s very little value in it.”

She leaned over the back of the sofa and kissed his cheek, and he caught her wrist before she could go and pulled her round and down into his lap, and said, “You’ve been writing in my journals,” and she said, “You left them open,” and he said, “I did,” and kissed her, and the book slid onto the floor and stayed there.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the second week the margins stopped being about other people.

He left a case open of a man who’d refused an operation, and she wrote, The surgeon’s treating consent as an obstacle instead of a decision. He wrote: YOU’RE ASSUMING THE MAN UNDERSTOOD WHAT HE WAS REFUSING. She wrote: Then explain it again. He wrote: AND IF HE STILL SAYS NO? She wrote: Then the answer’s still no. He wrote: EVEN IF IT’S THE WRONG ANSWER? She wrote: Especially then.

He left that page open for two days. On the third morning there was one more line under hers. YOU HAVEN’T CHANGED. She stood at the counter with it.

“Do you think I haven’t changed?” she said at breakfast.

“No.”

“Not at all?”

“You’re kinder to students. You’ve stopped correcting people halfway through their sentences.”

“That’s because they get frightened.”

“You let me choose the restaurant.”

“That’s because you order too much. I’m not the same as before.” She looked at her bowl.

“I know.”

“Then why write that?”

He put down his cup. “I meant that I’d know you anywhere. The way you think. The way you decide a sentence is wrong and won’t leave it alone until it admits what it means.”

“That’s a terrible description of a person.”

“It’s accurate,” he said, and reached across the table and moved a piece of hair off her cheek, and she said, “Good,”, “I’m glad you’d know me,” and he didn’t say anything else.

The next one was about peripheral nerve injuries. Beside a paragraph on how movement returns before sensation does, he’d written, ONE SHOULD NOT CONFUSE THE RETURN OF MOVEMENT WITH THE RETURN OF CONFIDENCE. She wrote, Confidence isn’t a clinical measurement. That evening: NO. BUT ITS ABSENCE CAN BE OBSERVED. Her pencil went in hard: Are you saying I haven’t got any? His: I’M SAYING YOU’RE VERY GOOD AT PRETENDING NOT TO BE FRIGHTENED. Hers: You’re not qualified to make that assessment. His: I’VE BEEN OBSERVING YOU FOR FOUR YEARS. And hers, underneath, That sounds suspiciously like surveillance, and his, IT PROBABLY IS, and she laughed out loud in the empty kitchen so that he came to the doorway.

“You’ve admitted to surveillance,” she said, holding up the journal.

“I’ve admitted to observation.”

“It’s the same thing.”

He came round the table and stood behind her chair and looked over her shoulder at the page, and took the pencil out of her fingers. “There’s a mistake here. Suspiciously. Too many syllables.”

“It’s the correct word.”

“It’s an inefficient one.”

She turned her head to argue, and he bent over the back of the chair until his face was upside down above hers and kissed her mouth, and she laughed against him with one hand up round the back of his neck. “Your neck—”

“It’s fine.”

“You’ll hurt yourself.”

“Worth it,” he said, upside down, and kissed her again until she’d forgotten what she’d been arguing about.

When he straightened up she was smiling. He picked up the journal and informed her that her argument remained unconvincing, and that she was avoiding the question.

“What question?”

“Are you frightened?”

She took the pencil back and wrote one word in the margin. Sometimes.

He read it, and didn’t write anything under it. He bent and kissed her hair instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was one note she found that he hadn’t meant her to see.

She came home early on a Monday with a bag of pears and a stack of anatomy papers to mark, and he was in the shower, and a journal lay open on the dining table at an article about long-term outcomes after hand injuries. In the margin beside a paragraph on what patients themselves reported, there was a line in his ordinary handwriting, the heart-monitor scrawl only she could read.

I think she can feel paper now. She turns the pages without wetting her finger first.

And under it, half a line more, I think she wants to know it’s real before she—and then a dark pencil line through all of it, rubbed at so hard that the paper had gone thin.

She stood still with the pears against her chest.

She thought of the garden, and the edge of a photograph under her thumb, and lying awake afterwards feeling the weave of the blanket. She hadn’t told anyone. She’d been so sure that nobody could know.

The shower went off upstairs. She shut the journal.

When he came down she was putting pears in the bowl one at a time. He glanced at the table. “Did you read the article?”

“Some of it.”

“Anything interesting?”

She put a pear in the bowl. “Not particularly.”

He looked at her, and she looked back, and for a second she wondered whether he’d ask. He didn’t. He took the next pear out of her hand and put it with the others and kissed her cheek and said he was going in, and she said, “Come home early,” and he said he’d try, and she asked whether that was a clinical promise, and he said no, and went, and she stood in the kitchen after the door had shut.

✦ ✦ ✦

On a Wednesday, in his office on nine, over a rota that had become more complicated than it deserved, Yu Chen put down his pen and said, “Can I ask you something?”

“No.”

“I’m going to anyway.”

“I know.”

“How did you know? With Elara. That she was the one you’d—” Yu Chen gestured at the general idea of the rest of a life.

Xing Yue went on reading the rota. “I didn’t know. I knew I wanted to marry her.”

“That’s not the same.”

“In practice it is.”

“Wasn’t there a moment?”

“Several. The first time she told me I was wrong, in front of my whole team, on her first morning. She’d been awake since five. Her hair was coming out of its clip. She was holding a retractor as if the operation depended on her not moving, and she looked straight at me and said I’d missed a leak.” He turned a page.

“And you fell in love.”

“I’d seen her once before, a year earlier. That morning I knew why I’d remembered.”

“Why?”

“Because she minded more about the patient than about whether I liked her. Then she brought me breakfast after a night on call, and I thought she’d go home after I’d eaten. She didn’t.” He put the rota down.

Yu Chen waited for the rest.

“That was enough,” said Xing Yue, and picked his pen up again.

“And if she’d said no to you? On the back stairs?”

“She wouldn’t have owed me a yes. I’d have gone on loving her anyway,” said Xing Yue.

Yu Chen looked at the rota for a while. “You could have told me that years ago.”

“You didn’t ask.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Sunday in October she went back to lunch at the red door for the first time since July. She hadn’t announced it. She came down that morning in a pale blouse and a blue skirt, with her hair pinned back in the plastic clip he’d kept in the glovebox for four years and given back to her on her last birthday, and he was waiting by the door.

He looked at her for a moment at the bottom of the stairs. “You look beautiful.”

She held out her right hand for him to take, and he took it, and didn’t comment.

Her father opened the red door himself and looked at her face, and then at the hand in her husband’s, and said, “You’re late.”

“It’s two minutes to twelve.”

“Exactly,” said Lin Jian, and stood aside.

Nobody made a speech. Ah Sim put a ladle in her hand and told her the soup needed stirring. Raiden and Jinx were arguing at the end of the table about a gear ratio. Jun Hyuk stole a dumpling off the plate and denied it with his mouth full. Eliana and Yu Chen sat with their knees touching under the table and pretended they weren’t. Her father pulled out the chair beside his own, at the head of the table, and said, “Sit here,” and put rice in her bowl, and didn’t ask about her hand, or whether she was working, or anything at all. “Eat.”

She ate, and across the table her husband looked down at his tea, and his mouth went soft at the corner.

Halfway through the fish Evangeline passed her the greens across the table, and as the dish went from her hand to Elara’s she lifted two fingers off the rim, slightly, the way she did in the cellar when she’d laid out the last instrument and was ready. Nobody else at the table could have seen it. Elara put two fingers on the rim as she took it, and that was all.

Xing Yue saw it. He’d never seen the gesture before, but he knew a scrub nurse’s signal when he saw one: the last instrument laid out, the tray ready, go. He looked down at his bowl and ate his rice, and Ev’s grey eyes rested on him over the steam, steadily, and then moved on, and he had the strong and uncomfortable feeling that the silent sister-in-law had known for weeks exactly who had been standing on the bottom step that night, and had decided to say nothing about it either.

That evening there was a journal on the kitchen table when they got home. A paper on rehabilitation after complex hand trauma, open at a section about returning to meaningful activity, and he’d underlined a single sentence. Recovery isn’t complete when the patient can perform a task, but when the patient can choose what to do with that ability.

She picked up the pencil and wrote beside it, Who decides what counts as meaningful?

He came down from changing and read it, and took the pencil from her, and wrote: THE PATIENT. And then, under it: ALWAYS.

She read it twice. Then she turned to the last page of the article, where there was a blank space at the bottom, and saw that he’d already written something there, small, in capitals, before he’d gone upstairs. I AM NOT ASKING YOU TO COME BACK TO WHO YOU WERE.

She wrote under it, Good. I like who I’m turning into.

He read it over her shoulder. Then he closed the journal carefully, and took the pencil out of her hand, and took his wife upstairs.

chapters.title: Doctor Ghost
chapters.desc: A young man on a trolley hears Elara humming and calls her Doctor Ghost. Xing Yue frightens him quiet, lies in the notes, goes through her black bag in the night, and buys her instruments she thanks her sister for.
chapters.epigraph: “Then make it somewhere she can tell you things.”
chapters.content:
On the third Tuesday in October he was on call, and she brought him dinner, the way she had once brought dumplings to 9B: a tin of Ah Sim’s chicken and rice in a cloth bag, carried up the hill on foot at eleven at night because she liked the walk. He was down in the ED reviewing a perforated ulcer, so she sat on the plastic chair by the end of the resus corridor to wait for him, with the tin on her knees, and hummed.

She didn’t know she was doing it. She never did.

On the trolley nearest the wall a young man was lying with a fresh dressing on his forearm and his other arm over his eyes. He took the arm away and turned his head and looked at her, and then at her hands round the tin, and his face changed.

“Doctor Ghost,” he said. Not.

She stopped humming. She knew him. It took her a second because the last time she’d seen him it had been under the lamp in the cellar, holding a girl’s hand while Elara closed the girl’s cheek, and Elara had been in a mask and a cap. He’d never seen her face. He’d only heard the tune.

“You. You’re her. That’s the song. You’re the Ghost,” he said, half sitting up, delighted, as if he’d found a coin in the street.

A nurse at the station looked up. Elara made her face do what it had done for policemen her whole life: pleasant, puzzled, kind. “I think you’ve got me mixed up with somebody, love. Lie back, you’ve got a drip in.”

“I haven’t. I’d know that anywhere. You hummed it the whole time you were doing Lili’s face—”

“Is there a problem?” said a voice at the end of the corridor.

Her husband was standing there in scrubs with a set of notes under his arm. She had no idea how long he’d been there. He came down the corridor without hurrying and stopped at the foot of the boy’s trolley and looked at the dressing, and then at the boy, and the boy lay back down without being asked.

“Your arm,” said Xing Yue. “What happened to it?”

“Glass.”

“And this.”

He lifted the boy’s other wrist and turned it to the light. There was a thin white scar across the back of the hand, neat, the stitches so fine you’d have needed to know what you were looking at.

“Somebody closed that. Recently. Not here,” he said.

The boy’s eyes went past him to Elara, and back.

“A clinic,” said the boy.

“A clinic,” said Xing Yue, and let go of the wrist, and Elara stood up and said brightly that she’d leave his dinner at the station, and walked away down the corridor with her heart going like a bird’s, and didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He pulled the curtain round the trolley.

He said, “Listen to me. You’ve had a fright, and you’ve lost some blood, and you’re seeing faces. That woman is a teacher at the medical school. She’s my wife. She has never been anywhere near your friend’s face.” He didn’t raise his voice. He never had to.

“But I heard—”

“You heard a tune. Half the city hums it. If you say that name in this building again, to anybody, the people who brought you in tonight will want to know where your hand was stitched, and who stitched it, and who else was there, and they’ll keep asking until somebody answers. I don’t think you want that. I don’t think your friend Lili wants that. I don’t think the people who rang the person who stitched you want it either. Do you understand?” He looked at the boy until the boy looked away.

The boy looked at him. “You’d do that to her?”

“I’d do a great deal worse than that to anyone who made her easier to find,” said Xing Yue, and something in his voice made the boy pull the blanket up. “Do you understand?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Someone will review your arm.”

He went to the station and sat down and opened the boy’s notes. Under past history the triage nurse had written, Healed laceration dorsum R hand, sutured elsewhere, pt vague. He looked at it for a while. Then he added, under his own name, Reviewed. Sutured at a private clinic two months ago; well healed. No concerns. He signed it.

He had spent fifteen years telling registrars that the notes were the one place in a hospital where you never wrote what was convenient. He’d just done exactly that, at a quarter to midnight, with his wife’s dinner going cold beside his elbow. He ate the dinner. It was good.

✦ ✦ ✦

“What did you say to that boy?” she asked the next evening, on the stairs at Banyan Terrace, coming down as he came up. She’d been waiting all day to ask it in a voice that sounded like nothing.

“That he shouldn’t shout nonsense at strangers in my department.”

“He was frightened. You frightened him more.”

“He was talking about ghosts.”

She searched his face for a second, and found nothing there but the irritation of a consultant with a difficult patient, and relief went through her so hard that she had to hold the banister. He hadn’t understood. He’d heard a boy with a drip in raving about a ghost and been rude to him, which he was to everybody.

“You can’t go round terrifying people because they’ve said something odd,” she said.

“I can, actually. It’s most of my job.”

“Xing Yue.”

He came up the last two stairs until he was level with her and put one hand on the wall beside her head. “Are we having an argument?”

“Yes.”

“What about?”

She opened her mouth, and found that she couldn’t tell him what it was about without telling him everything, and took the front of his shirt in her fist instead and kissed him, hard, on the stairs, to stop it, the way he’d always stopped her. He made a sound against her mouth and put her back against the wall and kissed her the same way, and she held on until her lungs hurt.

“That’s cheating,” he said, when he could.

“I learned it from you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday she saw the girl from the cellar at the flower market under the viaduct, buying gerberas with her mother. The cheek had healed into a fine pale line along the bone that you’d only have seen if you’d known where to look, and the girl was laughing at something her mother had said, and turned her head to the light without thinking about it at all.

Elara stood behind a bucket of lilies and watched her for longer than she should have. The girl didn’t look at her. Why would she? She’d never seen her face.

That was the whole point, and it was the first time it had hurt. She’d made a thing as good as anything she’d ever made in a theatre, and the person wearing it would never know who’d made it, and neither would anyone else. Nobody would ever say nice work to her about it the way the grey woman at Crestview had once said it about a scalp.

She bought a bunch of the gerberas herself, orange ones, and took them home and put them in a jar on the counter, and when he asked where they’d come from she said, “The market. I liked them,” which was true, and he looked at them and at her and said, “So do I.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At three in the morning, ten days later, he opened her black bag.

It was on the chair in their bedroom with its straps folded over each other. She was asleep with her face turned to his side of the bed. He stood beside the bag for nearly a minute. He told himself he needed to know what she was carrying, whether she had enough, whether there was anything dangerous in it that he could make safer. The truth was less respectable. He wanted to know what she’d been doing without him.

He unzipped it. Packed pouches, each one labelled in her round hand. Gloves, dressings, a penlight, sutures, a folded clean scrub top. Ev’s instrument case, worn now at the corners. And a notebook with nothing on the cover.

Dates. Times. Male, 30s, crush injury L middle finger, degloving, distal phalanx #. Washed out, closed, splinted. X-ray next day (R. arranged). Seen day 5: healing. Female, 17, bottle laceration R cheek, 6 cm, eye spared. Closed. Card given. Male, 20s, GSW R thigh, foot pulses absent. NOT HERE. Pressure. Mok to ED. Page after page. He read what she’d done and, more slowly, what she hadn’t; every case she’d sent away, every one she’d written NOT HERE beside and underlined. Her rules, kept, in her own hand, at two in the morning, on her own.

At the back there were pages that weren’t about patients. He read one before he understood what they were, and then he shut the notebook.

He put everything back exactly where it had been, the straps folded the same way, and perched on the end of the bed in the dark and looked at her hand lying on the cover beside her face.

He’d promised himself, in August, that he wouldn’t make her defend her recovery to him. He had just gone through her bag while she slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two days later he went to the instrument maker in the old town that City Hospital had used since the fifties, and chose a set himself: a small one, the best they made, for exactly the kind of work the notebook said she did and nothing beyond it, in a slim steel case that would fit the bag. He paid for it from his own account, so that there’d be no hospital stock book anywhere with his name on it for this. When it came he put it in the black bag, behind Ev’s case, and didn’t leave a note.

“Did Ev put something in my bag?” she called down from the bedroom that evening, and came down with the steel case open in her hands.

“What is it?”

“Instruments. New ones. Beautiful ones. Ev doesn’t usually buy things without telling me.” She turned the case over.

“Perhaps she wanted to surprise you.”

She looked at him. He kept his face exactly as it was.

“Do you know where they came from?”

“No.”

She ran her thumb along the edge of the case, and her face went soft. “Tell her thank you. When you see her. I’ll forget.”

“I will.”

She went back up to put them away. He stood in the kitchen with the tea towel in his hands. He’d wanted to give her something she could use. He’d given her one more reason to believe that he knew nothing at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

His brother came on the Saturday between flights, the way he always did, and found him in the study with a report he hadn’t turned a page of in half an hour.

“You look terrible.”

“Thank you.”

An Yu put down his tea and sat. “What’s happened?”

So Xing Yue told him. Not all of it; not the back of the notebook. The pillowcase. The steel door. The boy on the trolley, and what he’d said to him behind the curtain, and what he’d written in the notes. The bag. The instruments.

An Yu listened without interrupting once. When it was finished he leaned back. “So you know. And she doesn’t know you know.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t know how to say it without it sounding like an accusation.”

“Then don’t accuse her.”

“It isn’t that simple.”

“It rarely is. You followed her. You searched her bag. You’re very good at finding reasons for the things you already want to do. You always have been. You want her to trust you with the truth. You can’t ask for that while you’re sitting on yours.” An Yu’s closed face did something unusual.

Xing Yue didn’t answer. Then he said, “I don’t want her to stop coming home.”

“Then make it somewhere she can tell you things,” said An Yu, and finished his tea, and went to catch his plane.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Friday in November she came in at ten past three with her hair under a cap she’d forgotten to take off, and he was on the sofa with a book.

“Why are you up?”

“Waiting.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be. Have you eaten?” He looked at her face, and then her hands, and stood up.

“Not really.”

“I made something.”

“You always make something.”

“It’s a habit.” He took the cap off her head, gently, and put it in his pocket without looking at it, and she was too tired to notice what he’d done. She leaned into him and he held her, standing in the middle of the big room, and didn’t ask anything.

At dawn she woke with his mouth against her forehead. He was lying on his side with one arm under her pillow, watching her.

“Why are you kissing me?”

“Because you’re here.”

“I’m always here.”

There were a great many things he could have said then. That he’d stood on the bottom step under the lamp with his hand on the steel. That he’d read her notebook, every page, including the ones at the back. That he was frightened and proud and hurt and grateful all at once, in ways he couldn’t yet arrange into a single sentence.

“I love you,” he said instead.

She smiled with her eyes shut. “I love you too.”

He’d promised himself he would tell her. He’d promised himself he wouldn’t leave her alone with it. Lying there in the grey light with her breath on his wrist, he still didn’t know how to do both without making the same mistake again.

chapters.title: Two Surgeons, One Table
chapters.desc: Zhao’s guard is shot at the armoury gate and is bleeding faster than one surgeon can stop. Elara writes the call she swore she’d never make, and her husband comes down the steps in thirteen minutes with two units of blood in his own name.
chapters.epigraph: “He says he knows where it is. He says thirteen minutes.”
chapters.content:
The grey phone rang at eleven thirty-eight on the last Saturday in November, in her bag on the hall floor, and she was on the stairs with her coat half on before it had rung twice. He was on the sofa. He looked up.

“Jinx, the rig. She’s had an idea about the stops,” she said.

“At half past eleven.”

“You know what she’s like.”

He looked at her for one second longer than he needed to.
