Then he said, “Take a coat,” and went back to his book, and she went down the stairs to the dark car at the bottom of the terrace with her heart going and didn’t see him close the book behind her and sit still with his hand flat on the cover.

Her father’s voice in the car, on the black phone’s line through to the grey one: “Peng. At the armoury gate on the hill. Two men on a motorbike. Zhao’s bringing him to you himself. It’s high in the leg. He says it’s bad. He says it’s very bad, Xiaoyue.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao came down the three steps from the lane twelve minutes later with the boy over his shoulder, and his shirt was black with blood to the waist.

She’d known Peng since he was twenty-four and ran up a dark drive behind her taxi with the gate standing open, the night she’d come to a kitchen table on the hill with everything she could steal. He was grey now, on the steel table in the shell-coloured room, with his eyes going round the ceiling without finding anything, and somebody’s belt cinched round the top of his right thigh, and a towel under it that had stopped being a towel.

She didn’t speak. She was the ghost. She had her cap on and her mask on, and Ev was across the table already with the case open and her gloved hands flat on the steel either side of the tray, and Jinx was at the door, and Raiden was at the top of the ladder, and Zhao stood at the head of the table with one hand on the boy’s hair and his face like a shut door.

She took the towel away. Groin. Low, just below the fold, where the big vessel came out from under the ligament into the thigh. A small hole in front and a ragged one behind, and when she loosened the belt for a count of one, bright blood came up out of the front hole in a pulse that hit the light. She tightened it again.

She knew exactly what it was the moment she saw it, and the knowing went through her like cold water.

The femoral. Torn, not cut through, or he’d have been dead on the hill. She could get to it. She could open it and find it and get a clamp above and a clamp below and repair the hole in the wall of it with the finest thread in Ev’s case, if her hand held. She’d done it. She’d done it once with Liao standing over her and a vascular registrar holding the vessel up for her in a loop.

But somebody had to hold the vessel up. Somebody had to keep the pressure off while she found the top of it under the ligament with her fingers, somebody with surgeon’s hands, not a scrub nurse’s, and Ev’s hands, however steady, didn’t know what an artery felt like when it slipped. And he’d lost so much already. He had no colour at all. Even if she stopped the bleeding, there was nothing in the room to put back into him, and he wouldn’t last the drive to anywhere that had any.

One surgeon wasn’t enough, and there was only one in the room.

She looked at Zhao. Zhao looked back. She saw him understand that she was going to say something, in a room where the ghost never spoke, and saw him wait.

She pulled the pad off the shelf with her clean left hand, and wrote on it in letters that took the whole page, and held it up to Raiden at the top of the ladder.

CALL XING YUE. O NEGATIVE. TWO UNITS. TELL HIM THE ROPE STORE.

It was the call she’d sworn to herself in August she would never make.

Raiden had the phone out before she’d lowered the pad. She heard him say, “It’s Raiden. It’s Peng, Zhao’s man, a gunshot high in the leg, it’s bad, she’s asking for you, she says O negative, two units, she says the rope store—” and then stop.

“He says he knows where it is. He says thirteen minutes,” said Raiden slowly, looking at her.

She didn’t let herself think about that. There wasn’t room. She put her hand back on the boy’s groin and leaned her weight on it above the hole, through the towel, and started counting his breaths out loud in her head.

✦ ✦ ✦

The blood bank at City Hospital was on the ground floor of the old block, at the end of a corridor that smelled of floor polish, and at five to midnight on a Saturday there was one technician in it, a young man with headphones round his neck who stood up when the consultant from nine came through the door in a coat with his car keys still in his hand.

“Two units of O negative. Now,” said Xing Yue.

“Which patient, Dr. Wang?”

“Emergency. Unknown. I’ll do the paperwork when I’m back.”

The technician hesitated for exactly as long as it took to look at his face, and then went to the fridge. Xing Yue took the pen and signed the release strip on each bag in his own name, in the square capitals anybody on earth could read, and the date, and the time, 23:56, and put them in the cool box, and was gone before the young man had sat down again.

He knew what he’d just done. There’d be no patient on any ward with those two units against their number tomorrow, or the day after, and in a month or two somebody in an office would put the fridge log beside the transfusion records and find two lines that didn’t match, with his name at the end of both. He’d spent fifteen years making sure that every line he signed matched.

He drove down the hill with the box on the passenger seat and his hand on it at the lights, the way she’d once held his on the harbour road. Eleven minutes. He’d already known the way for three months.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came down the three steps from the lane in thirteen minutes, in his coat, with a blood bank cool box in one hand and his own bag in the other.

He looked at Peng first. Then at her. There was no surprise in his face at all. No question, no reproach. Only a kind of recognition, as if he’d come down those steps a hundred times. He put the cool box on the shelf and opened it, and the two dark bags were there with the labels on them and the blood bank’s signature strip, and his own name on the strip, in his own hand.

He took his coat off and washed at the sink without a word, and put on the gloves Ev had already laid out for him, two sizes bigger than hers.

Then he came to the table and stood on the other side of it from his wife.

Jinx hung the first unit from the hook in the ceiling that Raiden had put there for a lamp, and ran it in through the line Elara had already got into the back of Peng’s hand. Xing Yue put two fingers on the boy’s neck and looked at her over the table, and she understood that he was asking her what she wanted. Not telling her. Asking.

She pointed at the top of the thigh, at the fold, and made a fist and pressed down with it once in the air. You. Above. Hold it.

He nodded. He put his hand flat on the groin above the wound, where she’d been leaning, and pressed, and the boy’s whole body arched under it and fell back. She opened the thigh.

She worked the way she’d always worked, fast and clean, and the whole time she didn’t say a word, and nor did he, and nor did Ev. The room was nothing but the click of instruments going from Ev’s hand to hers and from hers to his, and the hiss of the suction Jinx had rigged off a pump, and the boy’s breathing, and Zhao’s. She found the vessel. She found the hole in it, a ragged tear the size of her fingernail in the front wall, and she put her finger over it, and looked up, and he was already there with his own fingers sliding under the vessel above hers, finding the top of it under the ligament where she couldn’t have reached and held the hole at the same time, and lifting it into the light for her in a loop of thread.

She put the clamps on, above and below. The bleeding stopped.

Then she held out her right hand without looking, and Ev put the needle holder into it with the finest thread in the case already loaded, and Elara bent over the vessel with the loupes on that he’d given her four years ago, and began to sew.

Her hand didn’t shake. She felt it not shake. She felt the thread, the tension of it, the exact moment each stitch caught and held in a wall no thicker than wet paper. Across the table he held the vessel perfectly still and watched her hands, and she knew he was watching them, and for the first time since the knife she didn’t care who watched.

She hummed. She couldn’t help it. Three notes, and then the tune that came down, under the mask, low, over the boy’s leg.

He didn’t look up. But she saw his hands, holding the artery, go even stiller.

She let the clamps off, the lower one and then the upper, and the vessel filled, and pulsed, and held, and below it in the boy’s foot, when Ev put her fingers on it, there was a beat.

Ev lifted two fingers off the boy’s ankle. Then she put them down again.

✦ ✦ ✦

They closed together, his hands and hers in the same wound, passing the needle across without a word. The second unit went in. Peng’s colour came back by slow degrees from grey to something nearly yellow, and at twenty past two his eyes found Zhao’s face above him and stopped going round the room.

“Boss,” he said.

“Don’t talk,” said Zhao.

“Sorry.”

Zhao’s face did something none of them had ever seen it do, and he put his hand over the boy’s eyes, gently.

At six, when the light came up grey over the lane, Raiden and Zhao carried him up the three steps on a stretcher to a car going to Crestview, where they didn’t ask questions of people who paid, and Zhao turned on the top step with the light behind him and looked down into the room at the tall man with his sleeves rolled up, washing at the sink.

“Hm. Good,” said Zhao, the second word after a moment.

Xing Yue inclined his head. Zhao looked at Elara. He didn’t say anything to her at all, because the ghost didn’t speak and nobody spoke to the ghost. He touched two fingers to the doorframe, once, where she could see it. Then he went.

✦ ✦ ✦

They drove home in his car with the sky going pale over the harbour and didn’t say anything either.

She sat with her hands in her lap and looked at them. They’d been washed three times. She could still see the night in the lines of her knuckles. Beside her he drove with both hands on the wheel, which he never did, and his face was the face from the theatre, closed and level, and she didn’t know what was behind it and was afraid to ask.

He knew where it was. Thirteen minutes. Gloves two sizes bigger than hers, already laid out. Two units of blood from his own hospital, signed out under his own name in the middle of the night.

At home he went in front of her up the stairs and into the bathroom and turned the tap on, and when she came to the door he held out his hand for hers.

“I’ve washed them.”

“I know.”

“Three times.”

“I know,” he said, and put her hands under the warm water and washed them again, slowly, between the fingers and round the nails and along the wrist, the way you’d wash a child’s hands after a garden, and dried them on a soft towel, and lifted her right hand and looked at the scar on the inside of it in the bathroom light. Then he kissed it.

She waited for him to say something. Anything. How long. Why didn’t you. I knew.

He didn’t. He looked up at her, and his eyes were wet behind his glasses, and he said, “Sleep,” in a voice she’d never heard from him, and took her to bed in his shirt, and lay down behind her with his arm over her and his hand round hers, not on her pulse, not testing her grip, only holding it, and fell asleep before she did.

She lay awake with the morning coming in round the curtains, feeling every finger of his hand round every finger of hers, and didn’t know whether she’d just been found out, or forgiven, or both.

chapters.title: I Know
chapters.desc: The blood bank finds two missing units with his name on them and he’s suspended, and he tells her nothing. She finds the letter, and he tells her he’s known since the pillowcase.
chapters.epigraph: “I never loved you for your hands.”
chapters.content:
The letter came on the second Tuesday in December, in a plain hospital envelope, to his office on nine at twenty to nine in the morning, and he read it standing up.

The blood bank’s monthly reconciliation had found two units of O negative released under his signature at 23:56 on the twenty-eighth of November, with no patient number, no transfusion record, and no return to stock. The auditor had gone back through every release and requisition he’d signed in four years, and found one more thing: an entry in the theatre stock book for March 2023, a surgical set and a box of antibiotics booked against a man with an abscess who had never received either. He was asked to attend a meeting at eleven.

He went. He answered every question they asked about himself. He didn’t blame a junior, or a missing form, or the technician with the headphones. He didn’t pretend either entry had made itself.

“Were these units given to a patient, Dr. Wang?”

“Yes.”

“Which patient?”

“I won’t be telling you that.”

“You understand that without the patient we can’t establish whether they received safe care.”

“I understand.”

“Was there an emergency?”

“Yes.”

“Is the patient alive?”

“Yes.”

“Would you do it again?”

“Yes,” he said, and the auditor stopped writing.

By the afternoon his clinical duties had been suspended pending a full review. Liao called him in at four and shut the door and stood at the window with his back to him, sucking a sweet.

“You’re the best surgeon I’ve had in thirty years. You know what this does,” said Liao, without turning round.

“Yes.”

“Then tell me what happened.”

“I’ve told you what I can.”

“You’ve told me what’s safe to tell. You don’t get to decide the rules stop applying because your reasons are good, Wang. That’s what every one of them says, the ones who end up in front of a tribunal. Their reasons were good.” Liao turned round.

“I know.”

“Do you? Three months, they’ll recommend. Don’t make me regret not fighting it.” Liao looked at him.

He went home at the usual time, and told her nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her nothing for nine days.

He left the flat every morning at seven in his good coat and walked up the hill, and went through the gate, and sat on the bench under the camphor tree in the hospital garden with a coffee he didn’t drink and her student logbooks from 2022 and 2023 in his bag, because he’d taken them off the bottom shelf of the study on the first night and didn’t know what else to do with his hands. He read them under her mother’s window. September 2022: her round upright hand, a list of everything she’d seen on her first week on nine, and beside Mr. Yin’s name, anastomotic leak?, crossed out, and then written in again. He’d been there. He remembered it. He read it four times.

At half past four he walked home and was in the kitchen when she came in from teaching, sleeves rolled up, with the kettle on.

“You’re home.”

“Apparently.”

“Did they cancel your list?”

“Something like that.”

She put down her bag and looked at him. He turned a page of his book.

“You’re very bad at pretending nothing’s happened.”

“I wasn’t aware I was pretending.”

“Your face is doing the thing. The one where you’re listening to a boring lecture.”

She came round the counter and stood between him and the kettle and put the back of her fingers against his forehead. He let her.

“No fever,” she said, and narrowed her eyes, and decided to ask again after dinner, and didn’t, because he made her laugh about Liao and the sweets, and she let it go.

She found the letter on the ninth day, looking for the spare charger he kept in the right-hand drawer of his desk. The drawer stuck, as it always did, and she yanked it, and a white envelope slid out from under a pile of papers with the hospital crest on it and his name.

She read it once standing up, and then sat down on the floor of the study with it.

Two units of O negative. The twenty-eighth of November. 23:56. No patient.

And the stock book, March 2023. She knew that date. A supply room at three in the morning, and her own voice saying don’t ask me, and the instrument set he’d swapped in her bag for a better one, and the antibiotics he’d signed out to a man with an abscess, so that the numbers would match. She’d known he’d done it. She’d never once thought what it would cost him, or that somebody would come looking for it three years later.

Suspended. Three months. Nine days ago. She folded the letter and went downstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was sitting on the floor of the big room with her logbooks round him in a half circle, one of them open on his knee. He looked up when she came in, and saw what was in her hand, and closed the logbook.

“How long?” she said.

“Nine days.”

“Nine days. When were you going to tell me? When the three months were over? When they’d finished? When you’d decided it was safe for me to know?” A short laugh came out of her that wasn’t one.

“That’s not fair.”

“Which part?”

“I wasn’t going to keep it from you for ever.”

“Then what were you going to do? Two units. Your name. No patient. And the stock book from the hill. You told them nothing. You’re taking the whole of it on yourself, on your own, so that nobody ever asks where that blood went, and you didn’t even— You didn’t even let me be frightened with you.” She held the letter up. Her voice cracked.

“I didn’t want you carrying it.”

“You don’t get to decide what I carry. We have a rule about that now. I made it at Christmas over a plate of squares.”

“I know.”

“Stop saying you know.”

He stood up out of the circle of logbooks. “I signed for it. It’s mine. If they ever find out where it went they find out about you, and about Ev, and the room, and your father’s line, and every person who’s ever come down those steps. So they don’t find out. That’s all.”

“That’s all. And you didn’t think I’d want a say in whether you lose your career for me,” she said.

“No, I thought you’d say no,” he said.

“Of course I’d have said no.”

“I know. That’s why.” He looked at her.

She stared at him. He didn’t look away. She put the letter down on the low table carefully, as if it might go off.

“How much do you know?” she said.

His face changed. Slightly. She saw it.

“About what?”

“Don’t. You came down those steps in thirteen minutes. You knew the way. Ev had your gloves out before you were through the door. You didn’t ask me a single thing, not one, not all night, not in the car, not in the bathroom. How much do you know?” Her voice had gone quiet.

“I know,” he said.

The room went silent round them. She could hear the clock, and a bus going down the hill, and her own breath.

“Since when?”

“Since the pillowcase.”

“The pillowcase. That was August,” she said.

“Yes. You were sewing on the floor at two in the morning with your right hand, and you weren’t compensating any more. You tied a knot you couldn’t see. A week later I followed the car. I stood on the bottom step under the lamp. I heard you humming. Nobody spoke. I put my hand on the door, and then I went home and got into bed before you, and pretended to be asleep when you came in.” He didn’t move towards her.

“You followed me.”

“Yes.”

“And you let me lie to you. Every night.”

“Yes. And there’s more, and you’re going to hear all of it, because I promised you everything, and I haven’t given it to you. The boy in the ED in October. I didn’t think he was raving. I told him what would happen to him if he said that name in my building again, and I meant it, and he believed me. I wrote in his notes that his hand had been stitched at a private clinic. In November I went through your bag at three in the morning while you were asleep. I read your notebook. All of it. Even the pages at the back.”

She made a sound.

He said, “And the steel case. The instruments. They weren’t from Ev. I bought them, from the old instrument maker in the old town, with my own money, so that nobody’s stock book would have them. I put them behind Ev’s case and let you thank her.”

She sat down on the arm of the sofa, because her legs had stopped wanting to hold her.

“Why? Why didn’t you just say?” she said.

“Because I knew what it was like to have everyone watching your hands and deciding what they meant before you were ready to tell them. Meng, the therapist, your father, me. Every movement measured. I didn’t want your hand to be one more thing you had to report to me. And because I was frightened. That you were going back before you were ready. That you’d get hurt somewhere I couldn’t reach, and I’d find out from a dot. So I did all of it, everything I’d promised I wouldn’t. I’m not going to tell you it was right.” His voice went down.

She looked at him across the room. “I could feel it. In the garden. In April. The edge of the photograph. I didn’t tell you because I wanted to know it was real first, and because if I told you and then it went away, I’d have to watch your face fall. The wire went silent in May. On Jinx’s rig. My hand stopped shaking in May, and I didn’t tell you that either. I tied off an artery on my father’s kitchen table in July with your loupes on and came home and told you Ah Sim was ill. And every night you kissed my fingers and I could feel every single one, and I pretended I couldn’t, because I was afraid that if you knew my hand worked you’d look at it before you looked at me. And because I was afraid you’d ask me to stop,” she said at last. She looked at her hand.

“I’d have asked you to be careful.”

“You’d have asked me to stop.”

He didn’t deny it.

“The pages at the back. You read them,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Then you know I was frightened you wouldn’t love me if I wasn’t a surgeon.”

He said, “I never loved you for your hands. I loved what you did with them. And I loved you before I’d ever seen you hold anything at all, in a corridor at Harbourside, asking a man you’d never met about your brother’s spleen.”

She put her face in her hands.

When she lifted it again she said, “Now tell me everything else. The meeting. Liao. The garden. Where you’ve been every day for nine days. All of it, in order, and then I’ll tell you mine.”

It was nearly midnight when they’d finished. They went through the months one by one, the way you’d go through a set of notes, sometimes going back because one thing changed the meaning of the thing before it. He told her about the bench under the camphor and the logbooks, and she said, “My first-year logbooks,” and he said, “You crossed out leak and wrote it in again,” and she laughed, badly, with her eyes running.

Then she stood up off the arm of the sofa and took his shirt in both fists and pulled him to her and kissed him, hard, with everything she’d been holding all night in it, the anger and the fear and the relief that he was still standing there.

“That isn’t forgiveness,” she said against his mouth.

“I know.”

“It isn’t permission to do any of it again.”

“I know.”

“Stop saying that.”

“All right,” he said, and she kissed him again, and this time he answered it slowly, one hand at the back of her neck. She felt him pause when her right hand tightened in his shirt, felt him almost look at it, and stop himself. He told her he wasn’t testing it.

“Good. Then hold me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him upstairs. They didn’t hurry, because nothing about that night was going to be made simple by a kiss and neither of them wanted to pretend otherwise. They undressed each other with pauses in it, to look, to say something, to laugh at the indignity of trying to be serious while one of them was still in a sock. He asked before he touched the inside of her wrist. She answered by putting his hand there and holding it. He watched her face, not her fingers, the whole time.

And when she was under him, and then over him, with her hands flat on his chest and his on her hips and the street lamp coming through the gap in the curtain across both of them, she reached down with her right hand and held his face and said, “I can feel you. All of you. I’ve been able to for months,” and he made a sound she’d never heard from him and pulled her down, and she let herself want him without having to prove anything, and it was enough.

Afterwards she lay with her cheek on his chest.

“Are you frightened? About the three months,” she said.

“Yes. About afterwards. What people decide I am.”

“You’re a very good surgeon who made some very bad decisions.”

“That’s a generous assessment.”

“It’s accurate.”

“You’re not going to tell me I’m a good man.”

She thought about it. “You’re the man I love. That’s the one I can give you tonight.”

He turned his face into her palm. “I’ll take it.”

A little after six she woke and touched his cheek, and he woke at once.

“What?”

“Nothing. You’re handsome.”

“That isn’t new information.”

She laughed and kissed him. “Come home for breakfast,” she said.

He looked at her in the grey light. “I am home.”

“Then stay.”

He took her right hand and kissed the fingertips, thumb to little finger, and she felt every one, and told him so.

chapters.title: Rules for a Ghost Surgeon
chapters.desc: They write the ghost’s rules together on the back of his suspension letter. Then he takes her north for New Year, where his grandmother points her stick at everyone.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody does this alone.”
chapters.content:
The suspension letter lay face down on the kitchen table, and she looked at the blank back of it over her tea.

“That’s a waste of good paper.”

“It’s a suspension letter.”

“Exactly. It ought to be useful for something. Rules. For the room. Not your rules and not my father’s. Ours. Write them, your writing’s easier to read when you try.” She took the pen from behind her ear.

He turned the letter over and uncapped his pen and waited.

“One. Nobody does this alone. Not me, not you. Never again,” she said.

He wrote it at the top in his square capitals. 1. NOBODY DOES THIS ALONE.

“Two. Nobody can demand treatment, and nobody can stop a patient going to a hospital. If I say a hospital, it’s a hospital, whoever brought them.”

He wrote it.

“Three. The patient says yes, not whoever carried them in.”

“Four,” he said, “records. Every case. What was done, what was advised, where they went.”

“Kept by me.”

“Kept by you.”

“And you don’t get to read them unless I say.”

He looked at her over the paper, and wrote it, and she watched him write UNLESS SHE SAYS and didn’t comment on it.

“Five. Nothing past what the room can do, or what our hands can do on the night. If it’s past that, they go.”

He said, “Six, nobody hides a complication. Nobody falsifies anything. Not a note, not a stock book, not a release strip. Seven. Neither of us uses anyone’s name or anyone’s stores to get what the room needs. We buy what it needs. In daylight.” The pen stopped at the end of the line. He looked at what he’d written.

“Eight. Ev can stop whenever she likes. Nobody makes her stay because she’s the hands,” said Elara.

He wrote that too. Then she took the pen out of his fingers.

“Nine’s mine.” She bent over the paper and wrote it herself, small and steady, in the hand she’d got back. 9. Neither of us decides something about the other one and calls it protection. We say it out loud, and the other one’s allowed to say no.

He read it twice. “That’s a difficult rule.”

“That’s why it’s a rule.”

She signed under it. Elara Wang. He signed under her. WANG XING YUE. She looked at the two names together on the back of the letter that had taken his work away, and folded it once, and he put it in the drawer where they kept the marriage certificate, and she said, “Don’t laminate it,” and he said he hadn’t been going to, and she said she didn’t intend to be married to a man who laminated a suspension letter, and he came round the table and pressed a kiss into her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening his phone lit up on the counter while he was washing a cup, and she saw her own name beside the small map, the blue dot that had been on his screen since a February night in 2023.

“You can still see me,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Would you turn it off if I asked?”

“Yes.”

“Without turning it back on tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

She held the phone out. He dried his hands and took it and did it, and the dot went, and he gave it back. She looked at the empty map.

“Turn yours on,” she said.

He stopped with the tea towel. “What?”

“Yours. For me. You’re suspended, not dead. You keep vanishing into the hospital garden with my logbooks and I never know if you’re there or at the library or sitting somewhere staring at a wall.”

“I don’t stare at walls.”

“You have a talent for being in a room and somewhere else at the same time. Then turn mine back on. Both. Each of us can see the other, and neither of us goes after the other without asking. If you see me somewhere strange, you ring. You don’t send a car. You don’t ring Baba. You don’t ask Raiden to drive past.” She held out her own phone.

“You’re making a very detailed list.”

“I married a very detailed man,” she said, and he did it, both of them, and put his arms round her waist from behind while she looked at the two dots sitting on top of each other on Banyan Terrace.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father read the rules on the Sunday at the red door, twice, with his reading glasses on, at the end of the long table.

“Who wrote this?”

“Both of us,” said Elara.

“And the last one?”

“Me.”

Lin Jian looked down the table at his son-in-law, and took his old fountain pen out of his breast pocket, and signed under their names in the big careful characters he used for nothing but deeds. Then he held the pen out across the table.

“You call me Uncle. Still. After three years. Don’t,” he said to Xing Yue.

Xing Yue looked at Elara, who was trying hard not to look delighted.

“Baba,” he said.

Lin Jian nodded once, as though a small matter of business had been settled, and put more rice in his son-in-law’s bowl. “Eat. You’re too thin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen came to Banyan Terrace on the Thursday with a bag of oranges and the face of a woman who had rehearsed a conversation all the way over on the ferry and disliked every version of it.

“I wanted to say something. March. The night Zhendong came back. I told Peng to tell you no hospital. Bring everything. No hospital. You’ll know. I knew you were a student. I knew what you’d have to steal and what would happen to you if anyone found out, and I asked anyway, because he was on my kitchen table and I couldn’t think past that. And then it got easier to ask. Every time. And I never once asked what it cost you. I’m sorry. To both of you,” she said in the hall, with her coat still on. She put the oranges on the counter.

Elara put her arms round her. “You don’t have to be sorry for loving him.”

“I’m sorry for making it your job.”

“Ring me when you need me. Not for everything. And ask. Ask first,” said Elara into her sister’s shoulder.

Xing Yue brought three plates of cut fruit from the kitchen and put one in front of each of them. Elowen looked at the plate, and at him.

“He’s become very interested in rules,” said Elara.

“So I see,” said Elowen, and ate a piece of pear, and almost smiled.

Peng came on the Saturday, walking with a stick and a bag of mandarins from his mother’s orchard on the island, more mandarins than any two people could have eaten in a year. He stood in the doorway and held them out to the tall doctor, not to Elara, because the ghost didn’t exist and he’d never seen her face.

“My mother says thank you. To whoever,” he said.

“Tell her whoever says to keep the leg up and do the exercises,” said Xing Yue.

Peng looked past him into the flat, at the small woman in a cardigan at the kitchen counter cutting a mandarin with her right hand, humming. His face changed. He looked at her, and then down at his stick, and then back at the tall doctor.

“I’ll tell her,” he said, and went down the stairs carefully, one at a time, and didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

They flew north on the twenty-ninth, before dawn, on a plane that belonged to his father, because his grandmother had rung three times to ask why she was still waiting.

The house was old, built round a courtyard, with dark beams and stone steps worn smooth and a long dining room with a fire in it. His grandmother was waiting on the top step in a dark red coat with a polished stick, smaller than Elara, with a face like a walnut, and the moment her grandson got out of the car she pointed the stick at him.

“Too thin.”

“Hello, Nainai.”

“Don’t hello me. Look at your face. This one?” She turned the stick on Elara.

“Yes,” said Xing Yue.

“You married him,” said Nainai to Elara. “Why?”

Elara didn’t even try not to laugh. “Because I love him.”

Nainai considered this, and turned the stick back on her grandson. “At least she has a reason. Who chose?” She took Elara’s hand and looked at the rings.

“He chose the star. I chose to keep the band.”

“Good. A woman should choose something. He cried. An hour,” said Nainai, and took her inside by the hand and showed her a photograph on the wall of a boy of seven holding a large fish by the tail and looking.

“Nainai.”

“An hour and a half.”

At dinner his father, at the head of the long table, asked Elara about her hand, and listened to the answer, and then turned to his son. “There’s a department at the northern hospital that needs a head. When your three months are done. You could come home and build it. Get away from all this.”

The table went quiet. Xing Yue put his chopsticks down.

“No.”

“You haven’t heard—”

“I have. I’m not going to run a hospital because I need somewhere to hide. And I’m not going to take a job that belongs to someone else because you can arrange it. I live in the south. With my wife.” He didn’t raise his voice.

Nainai struck the floor once with her stick. “He’s right. You have enough hospitals. Stop giving him things to carry. And you. Don’t look pleased with yourself. Eat.” She pointed the stick at her grandson.

Under the table he found Elara’s hand, and she held it.

Afterwards, in the corridor, his mother caught Elara’s sleeve. She was a quiet, well-dressed woman who had said perhaps eleven words all evening, and she looked down the corridor towards the dining room, where her husband and her son weren’t speaking to each other in exactly the same way, and lowered her voice.

She said, “He has never once said no to his father at that table. Not since he was seven. Not about medicine. Not about the south. He wrote it in a letter, the year he left, and posted it from the airport. He said it to his face tonight, in front of his uncles. With you sitting there.” She looked at Elara with something that might have been envy and might have been relief.

“He’d have said it anyway.”

“No, I don’t think he would,” said his mother. And she pressed Elara’s hand once, quickly, and went back into the dining room to her husband, and Elara stood in the cold corridor among the photographs of a boy holding a fish and found that she was crying, and didn’t know which of them she was crying for.

It began to snow after dinner. She’d never seen it fall like that, big and slow and silent through the courtyard lights, and she stood in the doorway in her coat until he took her hand and walked her out into the garden, where the trees were going white along every branch. Then, without any warning at all, he let go of her and fell straight over backwards into the snow and lay there, and moved his arms and legs, and made an angel with one wing larger than the other.

She laughed until she had to hold onto a tree. “You?”

“Me.”

“Dr. Wang?”

“Not currently,” he said from the snow, and held up his hand, and when she came close enough to tell him his angel looked injured he pulled her down on top of him, and she shrieked, and he laughed, the real one, out loud under the falling snow, and kissed her with snow in his hair until she’d stopped laughing too. At an upstairs window a small shape stood behind the curtain, and a stick lifted.

In his old room that night, under quilts as heavy as a man, with the snow ticking at the cold window and the fire settling downstairs, she lay against him and asked what he’d been frightened of as a boy, and he told her, and he asked what she remembered first about the house with the red door, and she told him: Ah Sim’s ladle, and a dark staircase that went up for ever, and the sound of Baba’s laugh coming up it. He undressed her slowly under the quilts as if they had all winter, and made love to her in the bed he’d slept in at seven because Nainai’s room was across the corridor, with his hand over her mouth at the end and her laughing into his palm.

On New Year’s morning his grandmother gave each of them a red envelope at breakfast. In Elara’s there was a small gold moon on a chain. “Your name’s a moon. So,” said Nainai. In his there was no money, only a note in her shaking hand, and he read it and gave it to Elara across the table. Stop looking so serious. Your wife is here.

That afternoon, in the small study with the snow outside, she opened her laptop and turned it towards him. The surgical training programme. Return after interruption. Occupational health. She’d already filled in the first page.

She said, “I’m going to apply. I haven’t sent anything. I’ll see Meng and the therapist first. I’ll need an assessment. Tell me what you think. Not what I should do.”

He sat down beside her and didn’t touch the keyboard. “I think you should be allowed to want it.”

“I do want it.”

“Then apply,” he said, and she began to type, and when she’d finished the first section she said, “Will you check the dates? Only the dates,” and he leaned over and checked the dates, and nothing else, and downstairs a stick struck the floor twice and a voice called up to ask whether they intended to sit there all day.

chapters.title: No More Pretending
chapters.desc: At Lunar New Year, in the middle of Raiden’s toast, Elara picks up her teacup with one hand. Then she tells the whole table.
chapters.epigraph: “Next time tell me badly.”
chapters.content:
The red door had been open since ten in the morning, and by six on Lunar New Year’s Eve the house was full: shoes in a heap in the hall, coats over the backs of chairs, Ah Sim in command of the kitchen and Lin Jian arguing with Raiden about the fish, and Jun Hyuk told twice not to touch the dumplings before they were served, and touching them anyway.

“That one’s mine,” said Ev, catching his wrist.

“I was checking they’re cooked.”

“You checked six.”

“Quality control.”

Ev looked at him. He put it back.

Elara stood in the kitchen doorway with a tray, laughing. She’d spent the afternoon helping Ah Sim and been told eleven times that she was a guest and should sit down, and ignored it with the confidence of a woman who’d been told the same thing in that kitchen since she was three. Her right hand moved the way it used to. Not perfectly; there were still mornings when the fingers were stiff, and her wrist got tired before the rest of her did, and every so often there was a strange small absence of feeling at the tip of the little finger, like a word she’d forgotten. But she could hold a knife and tie her hair and carry a tray without planning each movement, and she’d stopped hiding any of it.

Her husband came and stood beside her. “You’ve been on your feet for forty minutes.”

“You’ve been counting.”

“Yes.”

He held out his hands for the tray. She looked at him. He looked at her. He put his hands back in his pockets, and she carried it past him with both hands, deliberately, and as she went he bent and said, “You’re very pleased with yourself,” and she said, “Extremely.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eleven chairs that didn’t match, and every one of them taken, and more people than chairs. Her father at the head in the carved one. Elowen and Zhao, home from the hill. Ev and Jun Hyuk by the window. Raiden and Jinx at the end, already disagreeing about the wine. Eliana and Yu Chen with their shoulders touching, pretending they weren’t. Ah Sim, who never sat down, and sat down. A plate of mandarins from an orchard on the island that a young man with a stick had left on the step that morning without knocking.

Xing Yue took the fish off the bone in her bowl without being asked, and she let him, because he liked doing it.

Raiden stood up with his cup. “Before Jun Hyuk eats the rest of the sweets—”

“Too late,” said Jun Hyuk.

“—I want to say something. Another year at the red door. I think we can all agree the last few have been—”

“Expensive,” said Jinx.

“Complicated,” said Yu Chen.

“Full of bad decisions,” said Lin Jian.

Everybody looked at Xing Yue. He lifted his cup. “I’ve been very quiet.”

“Complicated, then. But everybody’s here. To the ones who came home,” said Raiden.

“To the ones who came home.”

Elara picked up her cup with her right hand.

She didn’t think about it. No second hand under the base, no careful set of the wrist first, no small pause to see whether the fingers would hold. She lifted it the way she had before the alley, and drank, and put it down.

Her father’s eyes went to her hand and stayed there. Then Ev’s. Then Ah Sim’s.

Elowen, who’d been up on the hill all autumn with the shop and the dogs and a husband who never told anybody anything, saw them all looking, and looked too, and her face changed. Elara put her palm flat on the table.

She said, “I need to tell you all something. Some of you know some of it. Some of you know all of it. Some of you don’t know any. So I’m saying it once, to everybody, at this table, and then nobody has to keep anything for me again.”

Nobody interrupted. Beside her, her husband didn’t take her hand. He sat with his own on his knee and watched her face.

She said, “My hand works. Not perfectly. It hurts sometimes, and the feeling isn’t all back, and I’ll be doing exercises for a year. But it works. It has since last May. And since August I’ve been using it. There’s a room under the old rope store next to Tai Hing. Baba can ring it, and Mok. People come who can’t go to a hospital. I decide what can be done there and what can’t, and anybody who needs a hospital goes to one. Ev hands me the instruments. I don’t speak, down there, so nobody knows who I am. Some of the people who’ve been there call me Doctor Ghost.” She looked down the table.

Jun Hyuk put his chopsticks down slowly. Yu Chen looked at Eliana, who looked at her plate. Ah Sim’s hand went to her mouth.

Elara said, “Xing Yue’s been suspended since December for three months, because in November I couldn’t do one on my own, and I sent for him, and he brought blood from his own hospital with his name on it, and wouldn’t tell them who it was for. It was for Peng. Zhao knows. That’s what the mandarins are.”

At the far end of the table Zhao said, “Hm,” and nothing else.

“And I’ve applied to go back to training. Properly. In a hospital. They’ll test the hand in April. That’s all of it. I’m sorry it took me this long.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was Elowen who stood up. She didn’t push the chair back hard. She folded her napkin and put it beside her bowl, neatly, the way she’d once folded paper flowers at four in the morning in a shop, and went out through the back door into the yard without a word, and shut it behind her. Elara looked at the door.

“Leave her a moment,” said Ev, low.

“She hates the cold.”

“I know.”

Elara stood anyway. Her husband didn’t stop her and didn’t come with her. She went out into the dark yard, where it had rained in the afternoon and the stones were wet and the little tree by the wall had lost its leaves, and her eldest sister was standing with both hands on the wall and her head down.

“Elowen,” said Elara.

“You told Ev. Ev, who says ten words a month. You told Raiden. You told Jinx. You told Baba. Eliana’s known since the summer, I saw her face. You told Mok. And I sat on the hill all autumn and rang you every Sunday to ask how your hand was, and you said better, and I believed you, and I sent you a book about getting your life back after an injury, and you thanked me for it,” said Elowen, without turning round. Her voice broke.

“It was a nice book.”

“Don’t. I’m the eldest. I’m supposed to be the one you tell.” Elowen turned round. Her face was wet.

Elara said, “You’re the one I couldn’t. Because you’d have asked me to stop. Because you’d have been frightened, and I’d have seen it, and I’d have stopped. Everyone else I told needed me to do it. You were the only one who’d have needed me not to.”

Elowen looked at her.

“I’d have been frightened,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’d have asked you to stop.”

“I know.”

Elowen said, “And then I’d have driven you there myself, and sat outside in the car with a flask. Next time tell me badly. Tell me crying. Tell me at three in the morning. Tell me in the middle of a wedding. Just don’t let me find out at a table with a cup.” She wiped her face with the heel of her hand.

“I won’t.”

Elowen held out her arms, and Elara walked into them, and they stood in the cold wet yard with the noise of the house coming through the kitchen window until Ah Sim opened the back door and said that if either of them caught a chill on New Year’s Eve she would never cook for them again, and they went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ah Sim didn’t sit down again. She stood by Elara’s chair with her ladle and looked at her.

“Show me,” she said.

Elara picked up the teacup with her right hand. Lifted it. Held it out at arm’s length over the table, perfectly still, for a full ten seconds, while eleven people watched. Then she put it down.

Ah Sim, who had fed her since she was three and called her a sparrow and told her every day of her life that she was too thin, put the ladle on the table and covered her face with her apron and cried into it, standing up, with her shoulders shaking. Lin Jian got up out of the carved chair and put his arms round her, which nobody at the table had ever seen him do, and she hit him on the chest with the back of her hand and went on crying.

“Eat. All of you. It’s cold,” said Ah Sim at last, from behind the apron.

It took the rest of the evening for the table to find its shape again. Raiden asked about the room and Jinx answered, the air and the drain and the second door. Yu Chen wanted to know whether the rules were written down, and Xing Yue said they were, on the back of his suspension letter, and Jun Hyuk said that was the most romantic thing he’d ever heard and Ev told him not to encourage them. Eliana looked at Elara across the table and asked whether it hurt, after, and Elara said, “Sometimes,” and Eliana said, “Do you stop?” and Elara said she decided when she stopped, and Eliana looked at Xing Yue, and he said, “That’s correct,” and Jinx laughed.

Later, when the plates had gone and the house had spread itself out over the stairs and the landing and the kitchen, Xing Yue ended up at the window of the front room with Zhao, both of them with their hands in their pockets, the way Lin Jian and the wardrobe had once stood there talking about tides.

“She didn’t know. Your wife,” said Xing Yue.

“No.”

“You could have told her. In November.”

Zhao looked out at the alley for a while. “It wasn’t mine,” he said.

That was all. Xing Yue thought of the kitchen table on the hill in March 2023, and a student with stolen gauze packing an open wound morning and evening for two weeks while this man lay under her hands without once asking her to stop, and of everything Zhao had seen since and said nothing about to anyone, and understood that from this man it wasn’t a small thing. It was nearly the whole of what he believed.

“Thank you,” said Xing Yue.

Zhao glanced at him, and at the woman on the stairs behind them showing Jinx her right hand in the lamplight, turning it over, laughing. “Hm,” he said, and went to find his wife.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven she walked with him down the alley to the place where the stones had been replaced, a little paler than the ones around them, under the noodle stall’s one streetlight. She’d come because she wanted to see it without anybody else there.

She said, “I used to think this was where everything changed. But it had already changed. Everything I wasn’t telling people. Everything you weren’t telling me. I think I spent a year trying to get back to who I was before the knife, and didn’t notice I was turning into somebody else. And maybe I don’t need to be the old one again. Maybe I can just—”

He took her right wrist and turned it over, two fingers on the pulse, and kissed her in the middle of the sentence, the way he’d done in a supply room and on the hospital steps and against the door of her childhood bedroom. She made a small surprised sound and took hold of his coat and kissed him back, with his thumb on her pulse the whole time, under the streetlight, on the new stones.

When he drew back he kept his forehead on hers. “Go on. Finish,” he said.

“You interrupted me.”

“On purpose.”

“I want to be this one. This person. Not the one before,” she said.

“I love this one.”

“Even when she lies?”

“I’d rather she didn’t.”

“Even if she can’t go back?”

“Then we’ll find out what else she wants.”

“And if she can?”

“Then I’ll be in the car park.”

At midnight the sky over the Walled City broke open in red and gold, and everybody went up onto the roof of the house, and her father stood at the edge with his hands in his pockets watching the old piers light up where a lighterage office had once stood. When they came down again he was at the bottom of the stairs by the red door, with his hand on the latch.

“Open it,” he said, and stepped back.

It was a heavy door. It had always needed a good pull, especially in the wet when the wood swelled. She took the handle in her right hand and pulled, and it opened, and the cold air came in smelling of fireworks and rain.

Her father said, “You always opened it before anyone else could. Since you were three. You’d be out of it and three streets away, crying, telling a man at a stall where you lived.”

“I wasn’t lost.”

“You were crying.”

“I was cold.”

He smiled, and stood aside, and she stood in her own doorway with her hand on the latch and the year turning over above the roofs, and nobody came to take the handle off her.

chapters.title: He Goes Back to Work
chapters.desc: The review gives him a warning and his job back. She walks him to the hospital gate in a banana cap, sets the date under her mother’s window, and finds out he’s bought a house without asking.
chapters.epigraph: “Like a very distinguished fruit.”
chapters.content:
The letter came on the first Tuesday in March, and he read it at the breakfast counter once, and then again, while she spread kaya on her toast and watched his face change by about half a degree.

“Good news?”

“Yes.”

“Bad news?”

“No.”

“Then why do you look as if somebody’s told you the hospital’s run out of tea?”

“The review’s finished. A written warning. The three months already served. I’m reinstated from Monday.”

She put down the knife and came round the counter and put both hands on his shoulders. “You’re going back.”

“That’s generally where reinstatement happens.”

“Ward rounds. People asking you things. Somebody bringing you terrible coffee.”

“I’ll survive.”

She kissed him, quickly, and then not quickly, and when she pulled back he was smiling. She took the letter and read the last paragraph for herself: the falsified stock book, noted; the unauthorised release of blood products, noted; the patient’s identity, not disclosed; any further misconduct to be treated with the utmost seriousness.

“You still wouldn’t tell them.”

“No.”

“That isn’t the same as it being right.”

“No,” he said, and didn’t argue, and she’d learned by now that that was what a real apology looked like from him: not a kiss or a promise, but not trying to make her agree.

A second letter came on the Wednesday, from Inspector Song. The police had looked at the two missing units, because a blood bank was obliged to tell them, and had found no evidence that they’d been sold or used for any criminal purpose, and no grounds for proceedings, and had referred the stock book back to the hospital. Underneath the typed lines, in black ink, there was one more in Song’s own hand. Don’t make me write this letter twice.

“Did he ask you who it was for?” said Elara.

“Once.”

“What did you say?”

“That I wouldn’t tell him. He said he’d assumed so, and that he’d grown up next door to your father, and he’d stopped expecting anyone in that alley to tell him anything at about the age of six. I regret the stock book. I regret putting other people’s stock at risk. I regret that you had to live with things you didn’t know I’d done. I’d sign for the blood again.” He folded the letter.

“I know you would. I don’t agree with you.”

“I know.”

“But I understand why,” she said, and it wasn’t forgiveness, and it wasn’t agreement, and they let it stand.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Monday she woke before the alarm. He was already sitting at the foot of the bed doing up his watch.

“You’re nervous.”

“I thought we’d established that.”

She got up and found him a clean shirt and made the tea and inspected his collar and brushed a thread off his shoulder that wasn’t there, and at the door she said, “Wait,” and went back into the bedroom and came out with a scrub cap. Yellow. Covered all over in small embroidered bananas.

He looked at it.

“Your first day back. I had it made,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because you’re a very serious, very frightening man, and you need a banana hat. Your wife once sutured a banana while you watched.”

“I remember.”

“You were extremely impressed.”

“I was,” he said, and took it from her and tied it on, crooked, and she untied it and did it again properly and smoothed it over his hair and stood back.

“How do I look?”

“Like a very distinguished fruit.”

She walked him up the hill to the hospital gate in the cool bright morning, among the porters and the nurses coming in with their coffees, and at the gate she stopped.

“You’re not coming in?”

“It’s your first day back. I’m walking you to school.”

“Are you treating me like a child?”

“A little,” she said, and straightened the cap one last time, and he caught her hand and thanked her, and bent and kissed her at the gate in front of half the morning shift, slowly, with his hand at the back of her neck, and she smiled against his mouth the whole time, and sent him off to be a good surgeon.

He went through the gate. She called after him, “Don’t let anybody steal your hat,” and he turned round on the path and said, perfectly seriously, “I’ll defend it with my life,” and the porter behind him with a trolley of linen nearly walked into a pillar.

She stood and watched him go into the building, and for the first time in a long time she wasn’t watching because she was afraid he wouldn’t come back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ward hadn’t changed. The same smell of antiseptic, the same radiator clicking under the window by bed four, the station crowded with charts and half-drunk tea. Sister Miao looked at him over the top of her glasses and then at the cap.

“Welcome back, Dr. Wang. Nice hat.”

“An unfortunate gift.”

At the third bed a dressing had been changed without anyone looking at the wound first. “Who decided this?”

A first-year resident stepped forward. “I did.”

“On whose instruction?”

“I thought the plan from Friday—”

“You thought?”

It came out the old way, flat and cold, and he saw the girl’s face go. He saw her fingers twist the edge of the chart and her shoulders come in, the way you made yourself smaller in a corridor when the consultant had decided you were stupid. He remembered another corridor, a long time ago, and a registrar who’d sent him a thank-you card at Christmas, and a woman on the floor of their study laughing about a shoe shop and saying poor man, I’ll bring him a sweet.

He asked her to come with him, and took her out into the corridor.

“You should have asked. You were also trying to keep the ward moving with the registrar in theatre. Both of those are true. Tell me what you weren’t sure about,” he said there, more gently.

She told him. He listened without interrupting, and then he walked her through what he’d wanted to see under the dressing and why, and what to write, and when she’d understood he said, “Next time?”

“I ask. Before.”

“Good. Now go and eat something. You look as if you’ve been up all night.”

When she’d gone the registrar beside him said, “That was very nearly gentle.”

“Don’t get used to it,” said Xing Yue, and went back in with his bananas.

At lunch her phone buzzed in the anatomy room with a photograph: the cap, hanging on the hook on the back of his office door.

Xing Yue: It survived the morning.

Elara: did anyone laugh

Xing Yue: One registrar. I told him it was from my wife. He said it suited me.

Elara: I’m proud of you

Xing Yue: I know.

She rolled her eyes at the screen and saved the photograph.

✦ ✦ ✦

She set the date herself that week, at the kitchen counter, with her phone.

“The twenty-ninth of May. A Saturday. Six in the morning, in the hospital garden, under the window. The night staff can come in their scrubs on the way off. Nobody’s ever bled there.”

“Your mother’s window,” he said.

“My mother’s window. Is that strange?” She looked at him.

“No. It’s the only place,” he said.

Within an hour the family chat was impossible. His father wrote from the north that the Wangs would pay for the breakfast afterwards, and when Elara objected, wrote back that they weren’t paying for a marriage, they were paying for a meal for the people who’d kept one alive. Nainai announced that she was coming and that nobody was to seat her more than two metres from the food. Raiden said he’d do the lights in the camphor tree, and Jinx said he wouldn’t without her, and Ah Sim said she was bringing dumplings, and Lin Jian said not too many, there’d be food, and Nainai said there should always be dumplings, and Elara laughed until she had to put the phone down.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday he drove her up the road above the hospital, past the old block and the camphor tree, through a stone gateway, and stopped in front of a big pale old house set back from the road behind a low wall, with a broad veranda and tall windows and a garden going down the hill towards the city, overgrown.

“Whose house is this?”

“Ours,” he said, and took a key out of his pocket.

She didn’t get out of the car. “Since when?”

“February.”

“You bought a house.”

“Yes.”

“In both our names.”

“Yes.”

“Without telling me.”

He heard it then, the whole weight of it, as it came out of his own mouth, and she watched him hear it.

She got out of the car and walked up the path and went in, and he followed her. It had been the old doctor’s house, a long time ago, when the hospital kept a doctor living above it: a hall with wooden floors, a sitting room, a long kitchen at the back with a window over the garden, and through a short corridor a back room with a wide door and good light.

“There’s the kitchen,” he said, “and the back room’s for the rig, Jinx says the floor—”

“Stop.”

He stopped.

“Rule nine. Say it,” she said.

“Neither of us decides something about the other and calls it protection.”

“You didn’t even call it protection. You called it a surprise. You chose it. You agreed a price. You signed the papers and put my name on them, and I found out because you drove me here on a Saturday morning with a key in your pocket.” Her voice was controlled, which was worse than shouting.

“I wanted somewhere that was ours. Not the flat I’d bought before I knew you. Somewhere with a garden for your family, and a room for the rig, and a kitchen long enough. Somewhere that wasn’t the hospital or the cellar or anything that’s happened at Banyan Terrace.”

“Did you think I needed a new house to have a future?”

“No.”

“Then I wasn’t choosing whether I wanted it. I was choosing whether to accept something you’d already decided for me.”

He looked at the floor. “Yes.”

She walked through the empty rooms on her own. The fireplace. The windows. The view of the garden from the kitchen, going down the hill. It was beautiful, and that made her angrier, because she could see all of it: morning light across the kitchen floor, him reading by that window, the whole family in the garden, Nainai’s stick on the veranda boards. She could see all of it, and he’d seen it for her first, without asking.

“Can we sell it?” she said, coming back.

“If you want.”

“Can we keep it and never live in it?”

“Yes.”

“Can I decide?”

“Yes.”

She held out her hand. “Give me the key.”

He put it in her palm. They drove back to Banyan Terrace without speaking, and she went up to the study and shut the door, and he sat down at the kitchen counter and didn’t follow her, and didn’t ring, and didn’t send a message to ask if she was still angry. He waited.

An hour later she came down with her laptop and put it on the counter and opened it, and he saw what it was. The application. She’d filled in every page in the north. Her old training, the interruption, the rehabilitation, the teaching. She read the last declaration twice, with her lips moving, and pressed submit, and the confirmation came up, and she looked at it as if it had surprised her.

She said, “I wanted to do that first. Before I decide anything about the house. This one’s mine. My work, my hand, my decision. I wanted to make it without anyone having built anything round me first.”

“That’s fair.”

“I’m still angry.”

“I know.”

“You can’t buy me a house and make it better.”

“I know.”

She came round the counter and put both her hands flat on his chest. “I love you. I’m still angry,” she said, and kissed him, and it wasn’t gentle, and he didn’t pull her closer until she came.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went back the next afternoon because she asked to. Nothing had been moved in. The kitchen was bare and the sun lay across the floor in long gold oblongs. She stood in the middle of it.

She said, “I like it. I like the garden, and the window, and the kitchen. I don’t like how you bought it. Could we have chosen it together?”

“Yes.”

“Could I have said no?”

“Yes.”

“Would you have let me?”

“Yes. I can put it on the market tomorrow. Or put it in your name. Or leave it empty until you know.”

“Don’t sell it today. And if we keep it, I choose what happens here. Everything. The chairs. The lamp,” she said.

“The lamp.”

“And a plant. Especially a plant. You don’t buy a single thing without asking. Not even a plant.”

“Not even a plant,” he said, and she sat down on the bare floor with her back against a cupboard, and after a moment he sat down beside her, and she leaned her head on his shoulder and said the table should go by the window, and a shelf there for the teapot, and that it would have to be a big table because Jun Hyuk would certainly break a chair, and he said they’d buy two extra, and she laughed. Then she turned and climbed into his lap on the floor of the empty kitchen, in the sun, and framed his face with her hands.

“You’re forgiven,” she said, “for today.”

“Only today?”

“Don’t be greedy,” she said, and kissed him, and this time there was no anger in it at all, and they stayed on the bare boards until the gold had gone up the wall and off the ceiling, talking about which room was whose, and for the first time the house didn’t feel like something he’d bought for her. It felt like somewhere they might choose.

chapters.title: The Skills Test
chapters.desc: A hand surgeon she’s never met tests her strength and feeling, and examiners time her on a model bowel. He isn’t allowed in, so he waits in the car park for three hours.
chapters.epigraph: “Well. You’re here.”
chapters.content:
The examination room at Crestview was cold. Not hospital-corridor cool: cold, so that the steel table under her forearm drew the warmth straight out of her skin.

Ms. Cui was a hand surgeon she’d never met, nearly sixty, with silver hair cut short and the expression of a woman who had spent thirty years being unimpressed by people telling her they were fine. She read the referral without looking up.

“Knife. November 2025. Ulnar artery, flexors, ulnar and median nerves. Dominant hand?”

“Right.”

“Pain?”

“Two or three. More after a long session.”

“Numbness?”

“The little finger, sometimes. The tip. The rest is mostly back.”

“Weakness. Be specific.”

Elara thought. “Grip endurance. Holding a pinch for a long time. Fine control when I’m tired.”

Ms. Cui looked up for the first time. “That’s a better answer than weakness.”

“I’ve had a lot of practice answering questions.”

“Good. You’ll need it.”

She tested everything, and slowly. The range of every joint, against the other hand. Grip, with a gauge. Pinch, with another. Thumb to each fingertip, and again, and again, without helping. When the last two fingers were slow to spread against her hand she asked for it again, and watched the small muscles at the base of the thumb, and asked again. Then a fine nylon filament, and Elara’s eyes shut. Now. No. Now. Once Elara opened her eyes and said, “That was the same place twice,” and Ms. Cui wrote something down and said, “You pay attention.”

“My husband says it’s my best quality.”

“Your husband isn’t examining you.”

“No.”

“Then let’s not give him too much credit,” said Ms. Cui, and the corner of her mouth moved.

At the end Elara’s fingers were white with cold and her forearm ached to the elbow. Ms. Cui went through the numbers on her sheet without expression.

“It isn’t symmetrical. Strength or feeling.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you smiling?”

“Because I didn’t expect it to be.”

Ms. Cui looked at her. “Passing this doesn’t mean your hand is what it was. It doesn’t mean you can do everything you used to do. It means it’s good enough for the next test, with supervision, and I want the deficits written down so that nobody pretends they aren’t there. Including you. You pass this stage.” She closed the file.

Elara sat still.

Ms said, “Thank your therapist. And yourself. You did the work. Your hand’s a good deal better than it has any business being, after what was done to it, and whoever closed it knew what they were doing, and so did whoever’s been training it since.” Cui.

Elara burst into tears on the cold steel table, with her hand in a towel, and Ms. Cui passed her a box of tissues across the desk without any change of expression at all and waited until she’d finished.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been in the car park for three hours. He wasn’t allowed in the room, and she’d told him so twice before they left, and he’d agreed both times, and asked whether she’d like him to wait in the café, and she’d said no, and asked whether she’d like him to go to work and come back, and she’d said no, and in the end he’d looked at her and said, “I’ll be in the car,” and she’d kissed him and gone in.

His phone lit up on the passenger seat. Elara: done.

Xing Yue: How did it go?

There was a pause. Elara: come outside. He was out of the car before she’d reached the bottom of the steps. He looked at her face first, and then at her hand, and then at her face again, which he knew he shouldn’t have done in that order, and she saw him do it and didn’t mind.

“I passed.”

His face didn’t do anything dramatic. It let go of something it had been holding for three hours, round the eyes, and he said, “You passed,” and she said, “I cried on her,” and he took her right hand in both of his, and it was white with cold, and he frowned at it and put it inside his coat flat against his chest under his own hand, and held it there.

“You’ll get cold.”

“I’ll manage.”

“You’re very dramatic.”

“You’ve been in a freezer for three hours,” he said, and bent his head and kissed her, and she smiled against his mouth and told him she’d passed, she’d really passed, and he said he knew, and she asked whether he’d had breakfast, and he didn’t answer, and she said, “Take me home and eat something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday Jinx came up to Camphor Hill with Raiden and a van and two toolboxes and the rig in pieces, because Elara had decided on the Thursday night, lying awake, that she’d keep the house, and had told him so in the morning, at the counter, as a decision and not a question. Jinx looked at the back room for ten seconds.

“The floor’s not level.”

“Good morning to you too,” said Elara.

“Good morning. The floor’s not level.”

“Would you like me to have it levelled?” said Xing Yue from the doorway with a tray of tea.

“No. Don’t agree with me so fast, I haven’t finished complaining.”

They bolted the frame to the floor of the back room by the window. Elara knelt beside Jinx with the drawing and said the forearm cradle would sit two centimetres too high, and Jinx looked at it and agreed, and Raiden leaned over and said, “She’s always right,” and Jinx said, “You’re holding the wrong end,” and he was.

By the afternoon it was in. Elara put her arm in the cradle and went through the set the therapist had written, slowly, with the notebook open, and her husband stood in the doorway with his arms folded and didn’t say anything, and she could feel him not saying it like a hand on the back of her neck.

When she’d finished and took her arm out, he said, “Good,” a fraction too quickly.

“Can we talk,” she said.

Jinx picked up her toolbox. “Raiden. Van.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to go,” said Jinx, and Raiden looked at his sister and at her husband and understood, for once, and went.

“Stop coaching me,” said Elara, when the van had gone down the hill.

“I wasn’t.”

“You were going to. Did it hurt, did you stop, did you keep to the sheet. Every time I move my hand you’re about to ask me something.”

“They’re reasonable questions.”

“Not every time. I know why. I know what it cost to get here. You don’t have to stop caring. You have to stop turning every movement into an assessment. My hand. My way.” She rubbed her forehead.

He was quiet. “All right. Not because I’m giving in. Because it’s yours.”

“And if I want your opinion I’ll ask.”

“I’ll wait.”

She held out the hand. He took it and held it, and didn’t look at the fingers, and didn’t turn it over, and she watched him not do it, and kissed him.

“You’re allowed to kiss me without checking if it’s swollen,” she said.

“I wasn’t checking.”

“You were thinking about it.”

“I was thinking about kissing you.”

“Then do that,” she said, and he did.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the night before the skills test he was at the kitchen table at Camphor Hill at eleven with the assessment criteria, reading them for the fourth time, and she came down in one of his shirts and nothing else and closed the folder on his hands.

“You’re supposed to be asleep.”

“So are you.”

“You’ve read that four times.”

“That’s worse. Tomorrow you wait outside. You don’t ring anyone. You don’t ask anyone anything. You don’t find out the result before I tell you,” she said, and took his hand and led him upstairs, and at the top of the stairs turned and put both hands on his chest.

“I won’t.”

“And tonight’s ours. No hospital. No test. No hand.”

“Just us.”

She stopped him when he reached for the lamp. “Leave it. I want to look at you.” And she did, sitting back on her heels on the bed in his shirt: the line of his nose, the crease between his brows that came when he was thinking, the mouth she’d once been too shy to look at for longer than a second across a ward. He let her. Then she unbuttoned the shirt one button at a time, still looking, and let it fall, and lay down and pulled him down with her, and the night belonged to them, not to the hand that had been cut or the hand that had been mended or the hand that might or might not be ready in the morning, but to the woman who had chosen him and the man who was learning, slowly, that loving her didn’t mean standing between her and every risk in the world. She held him with both hands the whole time. She could feel every inch of him under both of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The skills test was in the training centre behind City Hospital at nine on the Friday, the sixteenth. He parked in the same car park as two weeks before and said, “Three hours,” and she said he could go for a walk, and he agreed that he could, and she said, “Will you?” and he said no, and she laughed and kissed him and went in.

Three examiners. Two assistants. A model bowel on a clean board, a tray of instruments, a digital clock where everyone could see it. She knew one of the examiners: Mr. Zhai, older now, narrow-faced, who’d once watched her first-year knots in the skills lab with the air of a man who’d already decided she was wasting his time.

He looked at her name on the sheet, and then at her. “Elara Wang. Where have you been?”

“Recovering.”

“A long recovery.”

“Yes.”

“Your record before was very good. That means nothing today.”

“I understand.”

“Then show us,” he said.

Knots first, and instrument handling. Then the bowel. The clock started. For one second the room went away and she was in the theatre before the knife, with the weight of the needle holder and the sound of the suction and her hands moving without her having to think about them. Then she was in a hospital garden with the edge of a photograph against her thumb. She breathed out, and began.

She didn’t hurry. The first few stitches were slower than she wanted, and she changed her grip and steadied her wrist and went on. One examiner watched her fingers. One watched the clock. Mr. Zhai watched the line of the sutures. Halfway along she stopped to change the angle of the needle, and someone said “Problem?” and she said, “No, I want a better approach,” and was told to continue, and she did, and she finished with a minute and forty seconds on the clock, and went along the line checking every stitch, and pointed out one she’d do differently, and why.

Mr. Zhai asked for a second technique, and she did it. Then he put his pen down.

“How long can you keep up fine work?”

“Shorter periods reliably. In long cases the fatigue builds and my control’s less consistent.”

“And then?”

“I stop and reassess. I follow the progression my team set.”

“Would you go on operating with a painful hand?”

“Not without finding out why, and whether it was safe.”

“Would you hide a problem to stay in training?”

“No.”

“Even if it cost you the place?”

“Yes,” she said, and he wrote something down.

There was a last timed station, and she did that too. The clock stopped. The three of them leaned together over the sheets and said things she couldn’t hear, while she sat with her hands on the table and felt the edge of the paper under her fingertips, and the small pulse in her wrist, and the ache, and herself waiting.

Mr. Zhai closed the file. “You pass.”

“Sorry?”

“You pass the skills assessment. Where have you been?” He looked at her longer.

This time it was a different question. She gave him a smile. “Trying to get back.”

“Well. You’re here,” said Mr. Zhai, and for the first time in nine years something moved in his narrow face.

✦ ✦ ✦

He saw her before she’d reached the bottom of the steps, walking fast, then faster, then running, and he was out of the car with his arms open before she’d got across the tarmac, and she went into them so hard he took a step back and lifted her off her feet.

“I passed!”

“You passed?”

“Yes. Mr. Zhai asked where I’d been. I said trying to get back. He said you’re here. I did the bowel. I had a minute forty left. They asked about fatigue and I told the truth and—”

He kissed her, and she laughed against his mouth and said “Let me finish,” and he said “Go on,” and she said “And I passed,” and he kissed her again, and this time she didn’t tell him to stop.

They had lunch at the noodle place by the gate where they’d sat at midnight in her final year, and she talked through the whole morning from the beginning, doing all three examiners’ voices, and he listened and didn’t offer a single correction. When she stopped to drink her water she put the glass down and said, “There’s something I need to say.”

His face changed.

“If they ask me whether I’ve operated since the knife, I’m going to tell them the truth. Not in a hospital. But in the room. What I did, what I sent away, what I couldn’t do. If the panel asks me straight out, I’m not going to lie to get the place.”

He was quiet. “You might lose it.”

“I know.”

“Then you’ll lose it telling the truth. And we’ll deal with that if it happens,” he said.

“You’re not going to tell me to keep quiet?”

“No.”

“Even if you think it would be better?”

“More then, not less,” he said, and took her right hand across the table and kissed the inside of the wrist where the scar was, and didn’t look at it at all.

chapters.title: The Board Asks About the Accident
chapters.desc: At her interview they ask about the knife and the year after it. She tells the truth, and when they ask the one question she won’t answer, she says so.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re beautiful at four in the morning.”
chapters.content:
At four in the morning he found his wife in front of the bathroom mirror with a pen torch between her teeth, pulling down her own lower eyelid.

He stopped in the doorway. “What’s happening?”

“Checking.”

“Checking what?”

She took the torch out of her mouth. “My pupils.”

“Your pupils aren’t being interviewed.”

“I know that. I wanted to see if they’re equal.”

“Are they?”

“Yes.”

“Then come back to bed.”

She pointed the torch at him. “Don’t move.” She came across the cold tiles in his T-shirt and shone it into his left eye and then his right, and he stood there and let her, blinking, with his hair flat on one side from the pillow.

“Equal,” she said.

“I was worried.”

“You should be. You never get checked.” She clicked it off. He took it out of her hand and put it on the edge of the basin, and put his hands on her shoulders.

“You’re nervous.”

“No.”

“All right.”

“Don’t do that. Don’t agree with me when you know I’m lying.”

“Are you nervous?”

She let her forehead fall against his chest. “About the questions. About what they’ll think of me when I answer them. About whether anyone sits in that room and believes a person can go away for a year and a half and come back.”

“You’re not going in there to convince them nothing happened.”

“I know.”

“You’re going to tell them what happened, what you can do now, and what you still can’t.”

“And if that’s not enough?”

“Then it’s not enough for that panel, on that day. It doesn’t take away a single stitch you’ve put in.”

She lifted her head. He wiped a smear of toothpaste from the corner of her mouth with his thumb and bent and kissed her, slowly, a warm kiss in a cold room with the whole house asleep round them.

“You’re beautiful at four in the morning,” he said.

“That’s a very low standard.”

“I’ve seen you at three.”

“Rude.”

“And at two. At two you talk about pancreases.”

She put her hand over his mouth. He smiled into her palm, and she took it away and kissed him again and said, “Bed. You first,” and he went, and she switched off the light and followed him, and lay awake until six with her right hand inside both of his.

✦ ✦ ✦

The training committee met in a room on the fourth floor of Harbourside’s education block, with a view of the cranes over the container terminal. Elara had a slim folder on her knee: Ms. Cui’s report, Mr. Zhai’s sheet, her old training record, a year and a half of therapy notes, and a statement about her interrupted residency that she had written six times. The last version was two pages. It didn’t say she was fully recovered, or that the injury had made her stronger. It said what had been done to her hand, and what she’d got back, and what she still didn’t know.

There were four of them. Professor Ying chaired, a small woman with reading glasses on a cord who ran the surgical programme for the whole region and had a reputation for asking the second question. Dr. Xia was a Harbourside general surgeon with grey hair pinned up with a pencil. A consultant from the north side said his name too fast to catch. Ms. Zhuo was the lay assessor, and wrote everything down.

“Tell us what happened,” said Professor Ying.

Elara didn’t look at her hands. “On a Sunday in November 2025, a man attacked my father outside our family home. I put my hand in the way. The blade went through the front of my right wrist.
