It divided the ulnar artery, most of the flexor tendons and the ulnar and median nerves. Dr. Meng repaired it that night.”

“Prognosis?”

“Uncertain. They told me the repair had gone well and that nobody could promise I’d get back the control I needed to operate.”

“How did you respond?” said Dr. Xia.

“Badly, at first. I’d always trusted my hands. I couldn’t open a jar without planning it. I was angry with everyone who helped me, and most of all with my husband.”

“Your husband is Mr. Wang, at City. Associate consultant,” said Professor Ying.

“Yes.”

“Was he involved in your care?”

“As a husband. Not as a surgeon. He didn’t touch my hand except to hold it, and some weeks I didn’t let him do that.”

Dr. Xia’s mouth moved at one corner, and she wrote something down.

They went through the rehabilitation month by month. Then Professor Ying turned a page and took her glasses off.

“Your function was largely back by May last year, according to this. Your application is dated February. That’s nine months. What were you doing?”

Elara had known it was coming since the noodle shop. She had said it to Xing Yue across the table and to Baba in his kitchen. It still took her a breath.

“Training my hand on a rig at home, every day, to a programme my therapist set. Teaching the third-years anatomy two afternoons a week. And treating people.”

The room went still. Ms. Zhuo’s pen stopped.

“Where?” said Professor Ying.

“Not in a hospital.”

“Where, Dr. Wang?”

Elara said, “I won’t lie to you. And I won’t answer that. Not where, not who, and not how many. Ask me about anything I decided and I’ll tell you.”

“You’re refusing to answer the panel.”

“That question. Yes.”

Professor Ying put her glasses back on. “Then let’s do it your way. What did you do?”

“Mostly wounds. Cleaning, closing, deciding. People who wouldn’t go near an emergency department, for reasons that were theirs. When something needed a hospital I said so, and I sent them, and some of them went. Twice I did something that should only be done in a theatre. Both times the alternative was that the person bled to death before anyone else could reach them. Both of them lived.” She kept her voice level.

“Who supervised you?” said the consultant from the north side.

“Nobody. There was someone who handed me instruments. Nobody qualified to stop me.”

“Then who decided what was within your competence?”

“I did. That’s the part I’d do differently. I wrote limits down, and I kept them, mostly. But I was the one deciding whether I’d kept them. That isn’t a safe system, however careful the person is.” She hadn’t planned that sentence. It came anyway, and it was true, so she let it stay.

“Did anyone die?” said Ms. Zhuo, low, as if she was ashamed of asking.

“No.”

“Would you do it again?” said Dr. Xia.

It was the question Elara had been most afraid of, and she found she wasn’t afraid of it at all.

“If I were the only person there, and the choice was the same, yes. Then I’d come into a room like this one and tell you, the way I’m telling you now.”

Nobody said anything. The cranes moved outside the window. Professor Ying wrote a short line and underlined it.

“Do you understand that this may affect your application?”

“Yes. I’d rather not get the place than get it by lying.”

Dr. Xia leaned forward. “If we took you, would you accept a restriction on clinical duties until occupational health and your supervisor were satisfied?”

“Yes.”

“A staged return? Supervised skills sessions, limits on particular procedures, nothing independent until you’d been signed off?”

“Yes.”

“Would you tell us about any pain, weakness or change in sensation that might matter to a patient? Even if it set you back months?”

Elara thought of the back room at Tai Hing at seven in the morning, with the cradle under her forearm, and the first time she’d held a needle without her fingers shaking.

“Yes, I won’t hide a problem to keep a place. I’ve already lost a place once. I know what it costs,” she said.

“Thank you, Dr. Wang. We’ll write,” said Professor Ying.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the far end of the corridor by the lifts with two paper cups of tea, which was as close as he’d agreed to come. He hadn’t rung anyone. He hadn’t asked Liao who sat on the committee this year, because she’d asked him not to, and since the suspension he’d kept the promises she asked for.

He straightened when he saw her. She took a cup.

“Complicated,” she said.

He waited.

“They asked about the knife. Then they asked what I was doing for nine months, and I told them. Not where. They asked where, and I said I wouldn’t lie and I wouldn’t answer, and the chair said you’re refusing to answer the panel, and I said yes.”

“And?”

“And Dr. Xia asked if I’d do it again, and I said yes.”

He looked at her, and something went across his face that she didn’t have a word for: not pride, nothing so simple. Then he said, “Good.”

“They might turn me down.”

“They might.”

“You could pretend to be optimistic.”

He said, “I’m not going to tell you it went well when I don’t know. You told them the truth. That’s what you came here to do. Whatever they write, it doesn’t change that.”

She leaned on him in the corridor, with the tea going cold between them, and he kissed her hair and said, “Come home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Xia rang three weeks later, on a Friday afternoon, while Elara was in the back room at Camphor Hill with her forearm in the cradle and the timer running.

“Elara? Xia, from Harbourside.”

Elara took her arm out of the rig and stood up.

“The panel’s finished. You’ve been offered a training place. Here, with us. Conditional on occupational health and a staged return plan, which I’ll be writing, because you’ll be on my firm. Nobody’s going to put you in front of an open abdomen on your own until you’ve been signed off station by station. The director will send it formally.”

Elara put her free hand flat on the workbench.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me yet. You’re going to hate the staged plan. Everybody does. And Dr. Wang.”

“Yes?”

“I’ve had two people through our emergency department this year with very good temporary closures and no story to go with them. One of them had a square knot I hadn’t seen since I was a registrar on Liao’s firm. I didn’t put a name to it until you sat down in front of me. I know who you are.”

Elara didn’t say anything. She couldn’t.

Dr said, “Your husband is a stubborn man. He was a registrar on my firm for a year. When he wants something badly, he does the opposite of what you’d expect. He goes quiet. He hasn’t rung me once since your application went in. That’s how I knew what it meant to him. But this isn’t his hospital. Your assessments will be yours. Your progress will be yours. He won’t be deciding your duties, and neither will anyone who’s heard of him.” Xia. Her voice changed.

“Good,” said Elara.

Dr. Xia laughed. “That’s what I said to the panel. First of July. Wear flat shoes, the corridors on the old wing are a crime.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t ring him. She drove across the harbour to City and went up to nine in the lift and walked onto Ward 9B.

Sister Miao saw her first. “Mrs. Wang.”

“Sister.”

He was at the far side of the station with a chart, explaining something to a junior. He looked up. He looked at her face, and put the chart down without finishing his sentence.

“Harbourside, with Dr. Xia. First of July,” she said.

He came round the end of the desk without saying anything at all. He’d made a rule, in the autumn of the year they married, the first time a nurse had found them in his office with the door half open: not in the hospital, not where his team were or his patients. He’d broken it himself on New Year’s Eve and said he was allowed to be wrong, and he’d kept it every other day since.

She broke it for him. She held his face, the right one too, and kissed him at the nurses’ station of Ward 9B in front of Sister Miao, the junior, two staff nurses and a porter who stopped his trolley halfway into a bay, and he put a hand at the small of her back and let her, and didn’t hurry it, and kissed her back.

When she let him go the junior was studying the floor.

“Dr. Wang, your patient in bed fourteen is waiting,” said Sister Miao.

“Thank you, Sister.”

“And Mrs. Wang. Congratulations.” Sister Miao’s face did something it had possibly never done on duty.

✦ ✦ ✦

The surgical on-call room on nine was the same as it had always been: the narrow bed, the chair, the sink, the window looking west over the hospital garden to the old block and the fourth arched window on its first floor. She sat on the bed and watched the light go gold on the garden where she was going to marry him again in fifteen days, and he came in at half past five and shut the door and took his watch off and put it on the desk.

“You could have gone home.”

“I wanted you to come in and find me. Do you know what you looked like? At the station?” She stood up.

“Tell me.”

“Like you’d been holding your breath since February.”

“I had. Since February, and before.” He came across the room.

She reached for his tie, and he caught her hand, the right one, out of an old habit two years deep, and she looked at him, and he let it go.

“It’s not always about my hand,” she said.

“I know.”

“Then let me undo your tie.”

He let her. She did it slowly, because she could, because her fingers knew the knot now the way they’d known it before, and then his shirt, every button, and he stood still for it with his eyes on her face. When she pushed the shirt off his shoulders he took her blouse over her head in one movement and put his mouth to her collarbone, and her shoulder, and the side of her neck where her pulse was going hard, and she pulled him down onto the narrow bed that had never been built for two people and had been asked to manage it before.

It was quick, the first part. It had been three weeks of waiting and a year and a half before that. She pulled her skirt up and he got the rest out of the way, and she was ready for him the moment he touched her and said so, against his ear, and he came into her with a sound she felt rather than heard. She held his hips with both hands to keep him there, still, until she could breathe, and then she let him move. He went slowly anyway. He watched her face the whole time, as if he were reading something, and when she began to come apart he put his hand over her mouth, gently, because the corridor was right outside, and she laughed into his palm and bit it and came anyway, shaking, with her heels in the backs of his thighs.

Somebody knocked. He went completely still on top of her. She started to laugh again, helplessly, with her forehead against his shoulder.

“Dr. Wang, you have twenty minutes,” said Sister Miao through the door, perfectly level.

He closed his eyes. “Thank you, Sister.”

“Before the handover.”

“Thank you, Sister.”

The footsteps went away.

“She knows,” Elara whispered.

“She has always known everything.”

“Twenty minutes. Then don’t waste them,” she said, and moved under him, deliberately, and watched his face change.

He didn’t. He moved in her slowly and then not slowly, with his face in her neck and her hands spread on his back, and she held on and felt every inch of him with both hands, until he came with her name said once, rough, into her hair, and lay over her, heavy and breathing, and she stroked the back of his head and looked at the ceiling of the on-call room and thought: I’m going back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter came that evening. She printed it, because she wanted to hold it, and put it on the kitchen table at Camphor Hill beside Ms. Cui’s report and Mr. Zhai’s sheet. Harbourside, not his hospital, not his firm, not under his name.

“I’m really going to do this,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I’ll have to start again.”

“Not from the beginning.”

“Some parts.”

“Some parts,” he agreed.

She turned her hand over on the table and he laced his fingers through hers. “You won’t ring anyone. You won’t ask Dr. Xia how I’m doing. You won’t try to arrange my rotations.”

He looked at her. “Elara. I was a registrar on Xia’s firm for a year. If I tried to arrange anything on her firm she’d put me in the harbour, and then she’d put you on nights for the whole of August to make the point.”

She laughed, and he lifted her hand and kissed the fingertips, and didn’t turn it over, and didn’t look at the scar, and held it the way you hold the hand of someone who is going back to work in the morning, even when the morning is seven weeks away.

chapters.title: The Wedding Under Her Mother’s Window
chapters.desc: They marry again at six in the morning in the hospital garden, with the night staff in scrubs at the back. She talks too long, and he says one sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “Talk as long as you like.”
chapters.content:
At four in the morning Elara Wang was still arguing with her wedding dress.

“It pulls at the back.”

“It pulls because you’re twisting round to look at it. Stand still,” said Sister Miao, who had come off nights at three, gone home, showered, and come back in a blue silk jacket with a sewing kit in the pocket.

Elara stood still. Sister Miao did the last covered button at the nape of her neck. Her sisters had done everything else, in the family room off the old block’s ground-floor corridor, with the garden going from black to grey outside the window: Elowen her hair, pinned low and loose, Ev the sleeves, Eliana her shoes, and Jinx had sat on the windowsill eating a steamed bun and said, every ten minutes, “You look fine. You looked fine an hour ago.” Now they’d gone out to find their seats, and there was only the mirror, and Sister Miao, and a dress that was ivory and plain at the front, with embroidery down the sleeves, light enough to lift her arms in. She’d done every one of the fittings herself. She’d done her own buttons at all of them, with the right hand, slowly, so the seamstress would make them small.

The band and the star sapphire sat together on her left hand. The scar showed at the edge of her right sleeve, pale against her wrist. She didn’t pull the cuff down.

“Nervous?” said Sister Miao.

“About everything.”

“Good. It means you know it matters.”

There was an envelope on the table under the bouquet. Song had brought it to Camphor Hill on Thursday in his long coat and stood on the step and said, “He asked for this to reach you on the day. I read it. You don’t have to.” She opened it now. One sheet of prison paper, one line, in a hand that leaned badly to the left.

My brother would have cried the whole way down the path, and your mother would have laughed at him. — Wenjun

Sister Miao didn’t ask. She handed Elara the bouquet, white camellias cut from the bed under the fourth arched window, and stood back.

“There. Go on,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The garden was blue with dawn. White chairs went down both sides of the old path between the camphor and the pond, and at the end, under the window, there was nothing but a low step of grey stone and a celebrant in a dark jacket. The window itself was shut. It belonged to a store room now. The light was just reaching its arched top, where the bar went across.

Lin Jian was waiting at the gate in the black suit he wore for funerals and nothing else. He’d had his hair cut too short again. He’d been standing there ten minutes pretending to read the plaque about the garden’s history.

“Baba. That’s my bouquet,” said Elara.

He looked down. He’d taken it out of her hands when she reached him, to look at her, and forgotten. He gave it back.

“Your hands are cold.”

“A little.”

“Does it hurt?”

“Not today.”

He nodded. He reached up and straightened her collar, which didn’t need it. Then he said, without looking at her face, “You look like your mother.”

“Which one?”

He looked at her then. He’d known since the winter that she knew everything he’d done in the autumn of 2002, and it was in his face, the whole of it. He didn’t look away from her.

“Both,” said Lin Jian.

Her eyes filled. “Don’t.”

“Don’t you. You’ll ruin your face and Elowen will kill me.”

“You started it.”

“I didn’t. Ready, daughter?” He offered his arm.

“Ready, Baba.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue stood under the window in a dark suit with a white camellia in his lapel, looking like a man about to attend a hospital meeting he’d already decided the outcome of. He’d touched his left cuff three times since half past five. An Yu, at his elbow, had counted.

“You’re nervous.”

“No.”

“You’ve adjusted that cuff three times.”

“Do you have somewhere else to be?”

“Not this morning,” said An Yu cheerfully.

Nainai had arrived at a quarter past five with her stick and was using it to reorganise the front rows. “Not there. You’ll block the view. That chair is too far back. Sit.” A cousin from the north sat. Their father stood beside her and let her. At the back, the night staff were coming out through the old block’s side door in twos and threes: nurses still in scrubs, a porter, two of the juniors from 9B, the registrar who’d shaken his hand on his first round back. Sister Miao came out last and went to stand among them.

The photographer had gone along the back row with the coordinator. Xing Yue watched them, and watched the coordinator lift a hand and start moving the scrubs to one side.

He walked down the path before his brother could stop him.

“What’s happening?”

“We’re arranging the main picture, Dr. Wang. The staff can stand to the side so the families are clearer.”

“No.”

“Of course, but for the main—”

“The main photograph includes everybody who came.”

He turned to the photographer. “You were hired to photograph this wedding. They’re at it. If they’re cut out of a single frame, the rest of your fee isn’t paid,” he said.

The photographer looked at the coordinator. The coordinator looked at the scrubs. “Everyone in. Of course,” she said brightly.

He walked back up to the window. An Yu said, “Threatening the photographer before sunrise. Lovely,” and Xing Yue didn’t answer, and at the back Sister Miao looked at the grass and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The music began at six: a quartet of students from the medical school, playing something Elara had picked because it was quiet. The guests stood.

She saw them all from the gate. Nainai, already wiping her eyes and pretending to inspect a flower bed. His father, upright. Elowen in the second row with Zhao beside her, who had put his hand on the back of her chair and left it there. Ev and Jun Hyuk. Raiden, grinning, and Jinx beside him with sugar on her lip. Eliana, holding Yu Chen’s hand where everyone could see. Uncle Mok trying to make Ah Sim sit down, and Ah Sim refusing. Matron Sima, small, with the red ledger in her handbag. Mr. Yin beside her in a tweed cap, who had been bed fourteen on her first morning and her witness at the old-town registry a year later. And at the back the scrubs, blue and green, people who had known her before the knife and seen her come back.

Lin Jian walked her down the path. At the step he stopped, and the two men looked at each other.

“Look after my daughter,” said Lin Jian.

“I will.”

“Not by deciding things for her.”

“I know,” said Xing Yue.

“Good.” Lin Jian put her hand into his and stepped back.

Xing Yue looked at her. He didn’t say anything about the dress. He lifted her left hand and kissed the ring finger, over both rings, and held his mouth there a second too long, and then, before the celebrant had opened her folder, kissed her on the mouth.

“Not yet,” said Nainai, quite loudly, in the front row.

✦ ✦ ✦

The celebrant spoke briefly: about a marriage already made in the old-town registry on an ordinary Friday, and the years since in which two people had learned what it asked of them; about the garden; about the window. Then she said, “Elara.”

Elara unfolded her paper. There were three pages. Xing Yue looked at them and didn’t change expression at all.

She said, “I used to think the things that were really mine were the things I could remember. Then I found out I’d been loved by people I can’t remember. I had a mother on this ward on nights. I had a father who brought her dinner up the back stairs because the canteen was terrible. I had a name. I found it out from a stranger in a room with a guard at the door, and I didn’t want it, and now I do. My uncle wrote to me this week. He said my father would have cried all the way down the path and my mother would have laughed at him. So I think she’d have liked this. I think she’d have laughed at all of you.” She looked up at the window.

A small sound went through the rows. Matron Sima looked down at her handbag.

Elara said, “I want to thank the people who raised me. And the people who kept me alive, and the people who brought me back, and the people who stayed when I was very hard to stay with.”

She turned to him.

“Especially you,” said Elara.

They laughed. She went on. She told him he’d been there for every version of her: the student who’d told him he was wrong on his own ward, the woman who couldn’t hold a pen, the one who lied to him, the one who came home. She told him she knew he was stubborn, and that he’d rather argue with a wall than admit she had a point, and that he’d made decisions for her he should have asked about. “But you learned to wait. You sat in a car park for three hours. You stood in a doorway with your arms folded and didn’t say anything. I know what that costs you,” she said.

She promised to tell him the truth when it was hard. She promised not to make him guess where she was when she was frightened. She promised to let him look after her without letting him take over.

Then she looked down at the second page and didn’t know where she was.

She looked at the page, and at him, and at the page. She’d had a third point. It had been the best one. She turned the paper over, which didn’t help.

“I also wanted to say something about—”

He leaned in.

“Talk as long as you like,” said Xing Yue.

It was the only thing he said while she spoke. She looked at him with the paper hanging from one hand, and her face went, and she laughed, and the whole garden laughed with her.

After that it came out in no order at all. The first dinner. A banana. The flat on Banyan Terrace. A ring she’d given back and had back. Five weeks at Fig Tree Lane with his car at the bottom of the lane every evening, never once coming up. The first time she’d felt the edge of a photograph against her thumb. “I thought I had to get back into a theatre to be myself again. I don’t think that any more. I think I’m already myself. I’d just like to keep becoming someone new next to you. That’s all. I love you,” she said. She looked at the pages, which were now out of order.

“Xing Yue,” said the celebrant.

He had no paper. He’d written something, she knew, because she’d seen him at the kitchen table at midnight with a pen, and seen him tear it up. He took both her hands.

“I will spend the rest of my life making sure you never have to become someone else to stay next to me,” he said, and stopped there.

Nobody in the garden said anything. They answered together. The celebrant said they were married, which they had been for nearly four years, and nobody minded. He kissed her again, and this time Nainai said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

His gift was on a small table under the window, wrapped in cream paper, and he brought her to it when the photographs were done, all of them, every frame with the scrubs in it.

It was a frame, plain wood, with five documents behind the glass. Qu Lighterage’s licence for four lighters, 1996, with her father’s name and signature. A page from the old block’s night nursing roster for October 2002, in the hospital’s archive since the night wards moved, with S. Y. Shi, Staff Nurse in a column of names. Her own birth registration: Qu Xiaoyue, female, 16 November 1999, mother and father. The page from Matron Sima’s red ledger: the bell girl, about three, from the fire on the piers. And at the bottom, the Lins’ papers from the fourth of November, Lin Elara, with her father’s name in his own hand.

He said, “The originals stay where they are. Matron Sima gave me the ledger page herself. Your father gave me the last one. I asked both of them first.”

She touched the glass over her father’s signature, and her mother’s name in a column of nurses’ names on a night shift, and then the last page, with Lin Jian’s hand on it.

“You put them all together.”

“They’re all yours.”

“I want this somewhere with light. Not in the study,” she said.

“Then it goes on the stairs. Where the afternoon comes in,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The banquet was at noon at the hotel on the waterfront: three hundred guests, round tables, more camellias. Nainai inspected the seating plan and moved two people without asking. Lin Jian sat with Xing Yue’s father, and the two of them talked about shipping for an hour, politely, like two men walking round a minefield together. The 9B table was at the front. Nainai stood up with her stick during the soup and told the room that her grandson had been a difficult child, who refused fish, refused vegetables, refused to sleep, and once put a frog in his father’s shoe.

“I wasn’t born,” An Yu told the room.

“Don’t look at your brother. It was you,” said Nainai.

She raised her glass to Elara.

“Now he has a wife who makes him eat. Keep making him. May you have a long life, a warm house, and enough sense to ask before you do something foolish. You especially,” said Nainai. She looked at her grandson.

✦ ✦ ✦

They got home to Camphor Hill after dark. The house had chairs now, and curtains in every room, and a lamp by the sofa, and the frame was already on the stairs where Mok had hung it that afternoon, while they were at the hotel, under the place where the light would come in.

She stopped in the hall and looked at it, and at the house, and at him.

“We live here.”

“Yes.”

“You look tired.”

“I’ve been standing since five.”

“So have I. Come upstairs.”

In the bedroom she stood in front of him with her back turned, and he undid the buttons one by one, every one of the small ones she’d chosen so that she could do them herself. She could feel him working down her spine, and his breath on the back of her neck, and when he reached the last one he put his mouth to the top of her spine and left it there, and she stepped out of the dress and turned round.

“Sit down,” she said.

He sat on the bed. She took off his tie and his jacket and his shirt and his watch, and knelt and took off his shoes, and he let her, watching her with his hands on his knees.

“You looked after everybody today. The staff. The photographer. Nainai’s chairs. You remembered which junior hadn’t eaten. You do it every day. You forget yourself,” she said.

“It’s my job.”

“Tonight it’s mine. Let me look after you.” She stood up between his knees and put her hands in his hair.

He looked up at her, and he didn’t say anything clever. He just said, “Yes.”

She pushed him back onto the bed and took off everything that was left, slowly, and kissed him everywhere she’d uncovered: the hollow of his throat, his chest, the line of hair under his navel, the inside of his hip where he was ticklish and pretended not to be. He was hard against her stomach and breathing badly by the time she climbed over him and took him in her hand, and she watched his face while she did it, his eyes shut, his jaw tight, and said, “Look at me,” and he did. Then she sank down on him slowly, all the way, and stayed there, still, with her hands flat on his chest, until he said her name like a question.

“Mine. Tonight you don’t do anything,” she said.

She moved. She took her time over it, and he lay under her and let her, his hands on her thighs, gripping and then gentling, as she found the pace she wanted and kept it, rolling her hips until the heat built low in her and she had to lean forward on her hands. He reached up and cupped her breast and ran his thumb over the nipple, and she gasped and caught his wrist and held it there. When she came it went through her in long waves, and she cried out and didn’t care who in the empty house heard, and he held her hips down hard against him and followed her a moment later with his head pressed back into the pillow and her name in his mouth.

She lay on his chest afterwards, sweating, with his heart going under her ear.

“I’m going to look after you. For a long time. You’ll have to get used to it,” she said.

His hand moved down her back. “I’ll manage.”

“You’ll hate it.”

“I’ll learn,” he said, and kissed her hair, and she felt him fall asleep under her before she’d decided whether she was going to argue.

chapters.title: Not Under Her Husband
chapters.desc: Her first day back in surgical training is at Harbourside, under a registrar younger than she is. That night the black phone rings in their kitchen drawer, and they go together.
chapters.epigraph: “Ambulance first. Nothing a hospital should do.”
chapters.content:
At six in the morning she was standing in front of the wardrobe in one shoe.

“You’re missing something,” he said from the doorway.

She looked down. “The other shoe.”

“Good. Your powers of observation are intact.”

She found it under the chair. He came in with one hand behind his back, already dressed for work, his City badge clipped to his pocket, and when she’d got the shoe on he brought the hand round. A yellow scrub cap, printed all over with small bananas.

“Absolutely not.”

“You liked it.”

“I liked it on you. I made you wear it to the gate.”

“This is the spare.”

“Why do you have a spare banana cap?”

“Because you took the original and it’s in your drawer upstairs, folded round your old stethoscope.”

She hadn’t known he knew that. She took the cap and looked at it and couldn’t stop her face doing what it did. “I’m not wearing a banana to my first day at Harbourside.”

“All right.” He folded it and put it in the front pocket of her bag. She narrowed her eyes.

“You expect me to wear it.”

“I expect you to decide.”

“That sounded rehearsed.”

“I had a very good teacher,” he said, and she straightened his collar, which didn’t need it, and then kept her hands on it.

“I’m nervous. My registrar is younger than me. I looked him up.”

“Then he’ll be very surprised when you’re right.”

“What if—”

He tipped her chin up with one finger. “You don’t have to get through the whole year before breakfast.”

She kissed him, hard, standing on her toes, with her bag sliding off her shoulder, and he caught the bag with one hand and her waist with the other and kissed her back until she forgot what she’d been worrying about. At the ferry pier she leaned across the gearstick and kissed him again, as if she were going a great deal further than across the harbour.

“Go, Dr. Wang,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Harbourside’s changing rooms were in the old wing. She’d done her intern year here and forgotten how bad the corridors were. Her locker had a temporary label: WANG, ELARA — SURGICAL TRAINING. She read it twice before she opened the door.

Inside were a clean coat, a shelf, and a small brass hook at the top, where she’d see it, with a ring on the end the right size for a wedding band and a sapphire, and below it, engraved on a plate the size of her thumbnail, E.W. She shut her eyes.

He’d done this once before. Three years ago, at City, a gold hook in a resident’s locker, put in by the porters on a Friday before he’d asked her anything at all.

Elara: Did you have something put in my locker.

Xing Yue: Good morning.

Elara: A brass hook. With my initials. In my new locker. At a hospital that isn’t yours.

Xing Yue: Yes. The porter on the old wing was my patient in 2019. I asked him in June.

Elara: You didn’t ask ME.

There was a pause long enough for her to take her rings off.

Xing Yue: You’re right. I’m sorry. Rule nine.

She read it twice. No explanation of how useful it was. No I only meant. She hung the band and the star sapphire on the ring, one over the other, and they swung and settled, and she shut the locker and went to work without answering, and knew she was keeping the hook.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Jin was twenty-six, narrow and quick, with his sleeves rolled to exactly the same height on both arms. He introduced himself at the ward computer with his name, his grade, and an apology for having read her file twice.

“Jin Yiheng. I’m your registrar for this rotation. I’ve read the reports and the staged plan. I haven’t worked with you, so I’ll assess you the way I’d assess anyone. Do you prefer Dr. Wang?”

“Elara’s fine.”

“Elara. Your duties today are limited to what’s on the plan. If you’re not sure whether something is, ask me. If I’m not sure, I’ll ask Mr. Zhuang.”

She liked him at once. He didn’t know her as the best student in her year, or as the woman whose hand had been opened on a doorstep. He knew she was a returning trainee with a plan in a folder, and that was where they started.

The ward round was long. He asked her the signs that would worry her about a wound and she told him, and he asked a second question, and she answered that too. At the fourth bed a man four days after a bowel resection was holding himself still against the pillows.

“He’s moving less than yesterday,” said Elara.

Dr. Jin looked at the chart. “Pain score’s the same.”

“He’s lying differently. Yesterday he sat up to eat. Today he’s not shifting his hips at all.”

Dr. Jin examined him himself, and came back and arranged a scan.

“Good. Don’t trust the chart,” he said.

“I never have.”

“Then keep never doing it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The hernia was at eleven. Mr. Zhuang, the firm’s other consultant, Dr. Xia being at a meeting in the north all week, was a big soft-spoken man of sixty with a habit of humming between steps. He had read her plan. He went through it with her at the scrub sink.

“You’ll do the steps I give you. I decide how much as we go. If you’re tired you say so. If I say stop, you stop.”

“Yes.”

“Then let’s see your hands.”

The first incision was hers. She’d held a blade on the rig and on a model bowel in front of Mr. Zhai, and none of that was a patient breathing under the drapes. For one second her hand didn’t want to go. Then it went, and the skin opened along the line she’d drawn, and she heard herself breathe out, and Mr. Zhuang hummed two notes and said nothing.

She did the dissection he gave her and gave back the rest. She tied, and her knots were square, and he watched them. Halfway through the mesh she felt the old fatigue start at the base of her thumb, earlier than it used to, and said, “My grip’s starting to tire,” and he said, “Then rest it,” and Dr. Jin took the next three sutures while she stood with her hands folded on her chest, and then she took the last two.

When the drapes came off Mr. Zhuang pulled his mask down.

“Pain?”

“Two. Some fatigue.”

“Loss of control?”

“No.”

He looked across the patient at Dr. Jin. “Keep her.”

“That’s the plan, sir.”

“Good. Don’t make me regret saying so.” He looked back at Elara.

In the changing room she sat on the bench with her phone.

Xing Yue: How was the morning?

Xing Yue: Did you eat?

Elara: I opened a groin. I did the dissection and five sutures in the mesh and stopped when my grip got tired and Dr. Jin did three. Mr. Zhuang said keep her.

Xing Yue: Sensible man.

Elara: I haven’t forgiven you for the hook.

Xing Yue: I know.

Elara: I’m using it.

Xing Yue: I know that too.

She took the banana cap out of her bag, and looked at it, and put it on, and took a photograph of herself in the changing-room mirror with her eyes rolled up to the ceiling, and sent it, and took it off again before anybody came in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was home before her, in the kitchen with his sleeves rolled up, doing something with ginger and a chicken, and he didn’t ask anything. She dropped her bag and told him everything anyway: bed four’s scan, Dr. Jin’s sleeves, Mr. Zhuang humming. He listened with the spoon in his hand. He didn’t ask to look at her hand. He didn’t ask her to show him the grip. When she’d finished he put the spoon down and came across the kitchen and kissed her, with his hand at the side of her throat and his thumb under her jaw where the pulse was, and she laughed into his mouth.

“What?”

“You’ve got that face. The one when you’re pleased with me.”

“I’m allowed.”

“You are,” she said, and kissed him back until the pot boiled over behind him and he swore and turned round.

They ate at the kitchen table. He’d given her too much and said, “Eat what you want,” before she could complain, and he asked once how the hand was, and said she didn’t have to answer, and she said, “Tired. Stiff. No sharp pain,” and he nodded and didn’t ask again.

The bell went at half past eight. Lin Jian was on the step in his old grey jacket, with a paper bag of Ah Sim’s custard tarts in one hand. In the other he had the black phone from the cellar.

He came in, and put the tarts on the table, and put the phone beside them.

He said, “You’re on days now. You’re not down there every night. It shouldn’t be ringing in an empty room under the rope store at three in the morning. It should be where you sleep. If you want it.” He looked at her.

Elara looked at the phone. It was the same: black, old, with nothing on the screen. Only he and Mok had ever had the number.

“Who has the number?”

“Me. Mok. Nobody else. Same as before.”

She said, “After the panel I promised myself I’d stop doing things in that room that a hospital should do. I meant it. Anybody who rings that phone gets an ambulance first. Nobody’s stopped from going. Nobody’s kept back from a hospital because they’d rather not. I don’t go alone. And I don’t decide for him whether he comes.” She looked at her husband.

“I told them. Everyone who knows. Mok said he’d rather do what you say than argue with you at three in the morning,” said her father.

She almost laughed. “Put it in the drawer,” she said, and Xing Yue opened the kitchen drawer by the stove, and moved the takeaway menus and the spare keys, and she put the phone in herself. Then she took a card from the dresser and wrote four lines on it in her right hand, slowly, and taped it inside the drawer above the phone.

Ambulance first. Nothing a hospital should do. Nobody stops a transfer. Nobody goes alone.

Lin Jian read it over her shoulder and said nothing. Then he looked at Xing Yue.

“Look after her.”

“I will.”

“By asking.”

“By asking,” said Xing Yue, and her father nodded and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went up early. She was tired in a way she’d forgotten: not the long grey exhaustion of the year with the splint, but the heaviness of a day spent doing the thing she’d been made for. He undid the buttons at the back of her shirt because she asked him to, and she turned round and pulled his shirt out of his trousers and put her hands flat on his stomach.

“You’re tired,” he said.

“I’m allowed to be tired and want you. Stop asking.” She undid his belt.

He stopped asking. He laid her down on the bed and took her clothes off unhurriedly, as if he’d been waiting all day to do it, which she suspected he had, and kissed the inside of her knee and the inside of her thigh and then between her legs, slowly, with his hands holding her hips, until she was arching off the sheet and pulling at his hair with both hands and saying his name in the voice she used for nothing else. Then he came up over her and into her, and she wrapped her legs round him and held him there, and they moved together slow and deep, her mouth on his shoulder. She came a second time with him, her face pressed into his neck, and felt him shudder and go still inside her and stay there, breathing.

“I liked today,” she said into his skin, a long time afterwards.

“I know.”

“I felt like a trainee. Not the old me. Just me.”

His hand moved down her back. “That’s better,” he said, and she fell asleep before she’d thought of an answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The phone rang just before two. He was awake first. It was a short buzz from downstairs, then another, the drawer rattling against the frame. He sat up, and she opened her eyes and was awake all at once, the way she had been on nights.

“Do you want me to come?”

“Yes.”

He was already reaching for his trousers. It was Lin Jian. A girl of about seventeen, a cut across the palm, broken glass. Ev was with her in the back room, with pressure on it. The bleeding had slowed.

“Has anyone called an ambulance?”

A pause. “Not yet.”

“Call one now. To the front of Tai Hing, not the lane. A girl who cut her hand on a broken windscreen in a garage is a story anyone believes. I’ll be there in twenty minutes. Nobody takes the dressing off.”

He drove. Neither of them said anything on the coast road. Once at a red light he put his hand flat on hers without looking, and took it back when the light changed.

The lane door had its lamp lit. Downstairs, under the low roof, Ev was sitting beside a girl in a plastic chair with the girl’s hand held up in both of hers, a thick pad of gauze over the palm. Lin Jian was by the door. Mok was on the phone on the stairs.

“Hello. I’m Elara. I’m a doctor. What’s your name?”

A hesitation. “Yee.”

“Yee. I’m going to look at your hand, and ask you some questions while I do.”

She gloved. She looked at the gauze before she touched it, and then lifted the edge. The cut went across the palm at the base of the fingers, deeper than it looked from outside, with clean edges. She tested each finger in turn, and the girl flinched at the ring finger, and tried to bend it at the tip, and couldn’t.

“Can you feel this?” On the side of the little finger.

“Sort of. It’s fuzzy.”

Xing Yue was behind her. She said, “Light,” without turning round, and he took the lamp off its hook and held it where she needed it and didn’t say a word.

Flexor tendon to the ring finger, almost certainly. A digital nerve, probably. Six weeks ago she’d have known exactly what she could have done with it, here, with Ev handing her the instruments and the black phone on the shelf. She knew it now too. She took her hands away.

“You need to go to hospital, Yee.”

“No. I can’t.” The girl’s face shut.

“You’re not in trouble. But the thing that bends this finger has been cut, and maybe the nerve beside it. If it isn’t joined properly by someone with a proper theatre and a hand surgeon, you could lose the use of that finger. I can’t do that here. I won’t lie to you about it.” She kept her voice level.

The girl’s eyes filled. Xing Yue crouched down beside the chair so that his face was below hers. He didn’t touch her.

“Going to hospital doesn’t mean you’ve done anything wrong. It means somebody’s going to fix your hand,” he said.

“Will you come?”

“We’ll stay until the ambulance comes. I’ll tell the crew everything I’ve found, so nobody has to ask you twice,” said Elara.

She dressed it again, firm and clean, with the hand splinted in a position that protected what was left of the tendon, and kept it raised. He passed her the gauze before she asked for it. He wrote down the times on the back of an envelope as she said them, his handwriting worse than ever in the lamplight. He didn’t touch the girl’s hand once. When she said, “Tape,” he gave her the tape.

The ambulance came to the front of Tai Hing at 2:41, blue lights turning on the shutters. Mok walked the girl up the lane with Ev. Elara gave the handover on the pavement in her coat and nightdress, as a doctor who happened to be there: the mechanism, the time, the ring finger, the fuzzy little finger, query flexor and digital nerve, needs hand surgery. The paramedic wrote it down and looked at her once, and at her coat, and didn’t ask.

The doors shut. The siren went once at the corner and stopped.

Downstairs she stripped her gloves off and washed her hands at the steel sink. He stood beside it with a clean towel.

“You recognised the limit,” he said.

“I argued with it. I lost. Thank you for coming,” she said. She dried her hands. She looked at the shelf where the black phone had lived for a year, empty now, and at the lamp, and at him.

“You asked.”

She put her forehead against his chest. He put his arms round her and held her there, in the room under the rope store, with Ev’s kettle starting to tick in the corner and her father’s footsteps on the stairs.

At Camphor Hill the kitchen clock said 3:28. He put a cup of warm water in front of her and didn’t tell her to go to bed.

“You didn’t try to take over,” she said.

“You didn’t ask me to.”

“That’s what I want.” She caught his wrist as he turned away, and stood, and took him upstairs, and the black phone lay in the drawer under its card in the dark kitchen.

chapters.title: A Mass Casualty Night
chapters.desc: A footbridge comes down at the lantern fair, and every hospital in the city fills. Across the harbour from her husband, Elara packs a torn liver and closes her first patient on her own.
chapters.epigraph: “Being frightened doesn’t make it less yours.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past eight on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, Elara was in the surgical staff room at Harbourside trying to persuade a vending machine to give up a packet of crackers it had already taken her money for, when the speaker in the ceiling cleared its throat.

“Major incident declared. All available emergency and surgical staff report to your departments. A pedestrian footbridge has collapsed at the lantern fair on the canal. Multiple casualties expected.”

The crackers dropped. She looked at them for half a second, picked them up, and ran.

The emergency department had already changed shape. The waiting area was being emptied into a corridor. Somebody was writing bay numbers on the whiteboard in red, and somebody else was rubbing them out. The doors opened and stayed open: a woman with blood running into one eye, holding a paper rabbit lantern by its stick as if she’d forgotten it was there; a boy with his forearm at the wrong angle, screaming for his mother; an old man in a vest, his shirt cut off him in the ambulance; a girl between two paramedics, her legs dragging.

Dr. Jin was at the central desk with gloves already on.

“You’re with trauma. Dr. Xia’s running the theatres. They’re saying thirty at least, maybe more. The bridge came down while the procession was on it. Some went in the canal, some were under it. Fire service is still cutting.”

“Give me the list.”

He gave her a clipboard and held on to it a second longer than he needed to. “Elara. Don’t try to do three people’s jobs.”

“I won’t.”

“You will. Do two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After that it was faces. A young man with his scalp laid open and a collar on his neck, asking the same question every forty seconds. An old woman who’d been crushed against the railing and kept apologising for the fuss. A man with an ankle pointing sideways who wanted to go back, because his wife was still under the stairs, and who had to be held down by a porter while Elara splinted it. The noise was constant, and frightened, but it never quite tipped. People kept finding room for one more trolley.

At the end of the department a nurse was kneeling by a girl of about twelve who was vomiting into a basin, her festival face paint, a white rabbit and a gold moon, running down her cheeks. The nurse held the basin with one hand and the girl’s hair with the other, and talked to her the whole time in a low, even voice: that’s all right, don’t sit up yet, breathe, I’ve got you.

Elara knew the voice before she saw the face.

“Nuo?”

Nuo looked up. Three years ago she’d been unfolding her exam marks in a bakery on River Bridge Road and reading them four times. Now she was in navy scrubs with a Harbourside badge, and her hands didn’t shake at all.

Nuo said, “Since August. I didn’t tell you. I wanted to see you here first. She keeps vomiting. She says she hit her head on the railing. I don’t know if she was knocked out.” She didn’t look away from the girl.

“Keep her flat. Keep her still. I’ll get her seen now. Find out from whoever brought her if she went quiet at any point.”

“Yes, Doctor.”

When Elara came back that way twenty minutes later with the head-injury registrar, Nuo was still there, talking, and the girl had stopped crying and was holding a corner of Nuo’s sleeve. Elara caught her eye over the trolley, and Nuo gave her one small, serious nod, and that was all there was time for.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ferry clerk came in around half past ten. He’d been found under the collapsed stair section at the canal end, where the bridge met the ferry pier, still in his company shirt. He was grey and damp and his eyes kept going.

“Male, mid-forties. Blunt abdomen. Hypotensive at scene, responded to fluids, then dropped again.”

“Sir. Can you hear me? What’s your name?”

He told her: Chung. He worked the late ticket window. He’d gone up to help an old woman with a walking frame. His abdomen was tight and getting tighter under her hand, and his pressure was falling, and the scan on the trolley showed blood round the liver.

“He’s bleeding. He needs theatre now,” Elara said to Dr. Jin.

Mr. Zhai came down himself. He looked at the screen and at the patient and at her.

“You’re with me. Damage control. You assist until I tell you otherwise.”

“Yes.”

The theatre was already open. They opened him from the breastbone down, and the blood came up to meet them, dark, a great deal of it, and the anaesthetist called a number that made the scrub nurse look up. The liver was torn across the right side, deep, the tissue soft and splitting under their fingers.

“Packs,” said Mr. Zhai.

She gave him packs. He put them above the liver and below it, pressing the torn lobe back together between them, the way you’d hold a broken loaf closed, and said “More,” and she gave him more, and held pressure where he put her hand, and felt the bleeding slow under her palm.

“Don’t chase every millimetre. We’re not fixing him tonight. We’re keeping him alive till tomorrow,” he said.

The anaesthetist said the pressure was coming up. It came up slowly. They stood there with their hands in him and waited, and it held.

Then a runner put her head through the door. “Mr. Zhai. Theatre four. A pelvis, and she’s going off.”

Mr. Zhai looked at the packs, and at the monitor, and at Elara across the table.

“He’s packed. He needs a temporary closure, a vacuum dressing, and the unit. Back in thirty-six hours for the packs. You know how.”

“I’m not signed off to close.”

“You are now. I’m signing it. Do it the way you’d tell me you were doing it. If you’re worried, you call, and I come back. Where have you been?” He was already stripping his gloves. At the door he turned his head.

“Here,” she said.

He went.

There was the scrub nurse, and the anaesthetist, and the patient, and her. She heard herself say, quite steadily, “Count, please,” and the nurse began. She checked the packs. She checked every place the blood had come from. She talked to the anaesthetist, who talked back. She laid the plastic sheet over the bowel and the sponge over that, and sealed it, and connected the tubing, and watched the pressure take and the dressing go flat and hard, and checked the count again. Halfway through, the fatigue started at the base of her thumb, early, the way it always did now. She noticed it and rested her right hand on the drape for ten seconds while she did the next thing with her left, and then went on.

When it was done the anaesthetist said, “Pressure’s holding,” and the scrub nurse said, “Count’s correct,” and Elara stood back from the table with her gloves dark to the wrist, and found that her legs were shaking and her hands weren’t.

Mr. Zhai came back through the door forty minutes later, still in his theatre-four gown. He looked at the dressing and at the chart and at her.

“Hand?”

“Tired. No loss of control.”

“You rested it.”

“Yes.”

He nodded once. “Well done, Dr. Wang. Don’t stand there. There are four more.”

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after one she finally looked at her phone. Seventeen messages in the family chat, which Eliana had named Lins + Strays in 2023, and nobody had ever been able to change.

Eliana: Are you ok

Yu Chen: We saw the news. Which hospital tonight?

Ev: Answer when you can.

Raiden: Jinx says don’t do anything stupid

Jinx: I said don’t do anything UNNECESSARY. There’s a difference.

Jun Hyuk: Ev has been looking at her phone for forty minutes.

Ev: I haven’t.

Elowen: Stay where you are. All of you.

Baba: Elara.

A minute after that, by itself:

Baba: Eat.

She laughed out loud in the staff corridor, a small cracked sound that surprised her. She typed with one thumb. Safe. Harbourside. Very busy. I’ll eat when I can.

Eliana: proud of you

Jinx: Raiden, that means you too. Eat.

Then, separately:

Xing Yue: Are you safe?

Elara: Yes. Corridor. More coming.

Xing Yue: Have you eaten?

Elara: Everybody in my life has decided to ask me that tonight.

Xing Yue: Answer the question.

Elara: No.

Xing Yue: I’ll arrange something.

Elara: Nothing expensive. And not enough for the whole department.

Xing Yue: I make no promises.

It came to the staff entrance twenty minutes later, in two insulated bags carried by a delivery rider who didn’t know who’d sent him: rice boxes, steamed buns, soup in tall cups, cut fruit, enough for the night team and the porters and anyone else who walked past. There was no name on any of it. Underneath, wrapped in brown paper, was a plain tin with no label, and when she prised the lid up the smell came out at her, dark and earthy, the aged tea she’d last smelled in the flat on Banyan Terrace the day his brother came to look at her. A card was tucked under the lid in a careful hand that wasn’t her husband’s.

For whoever is still awake.

Her phone buzzed. An Yu: The tea is mine. Don’t let him take credit.

The nurses fell on the food. Elara made a cup of the tea in a paper cup, and sat down on a plastic chair for the first time in five hours, and ate half a box of rice with her eyes shut.

✦ ✦ ✦

The night didn’t get easier. It changed shape again. A man who’d looked stable at midnight went off at two. Two patients went across the harbour to City because Harbourside’s unit was full, and she wondered which of them would end up under her husband’s hands, and didn’t ask. At twenty to five Dr. Jin found her outside theatre two and pointed at the staff room.

“Ten minutes. I’ll bleep you.”

“I’m fine.”

“That wasn’t a question,” said Dr. Jin, who was twenty-six and had been awake for twenty-two hours.

She went. She sat with the phone in both hands.

Elara: I closed my first patient on my own tonight.

The reply took a while.

Xing Yue: I know.

Xing Yue: I’m proud of you.

She read it, and put the phone away, and pressed the heels of her hands against her eyes until the ten minutes were up.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was light when she came out of the staff door. The canal road was still shut. Helicopters went over towards the fair.

He was at the kerb in his City clothes, coat over one arm, tie loose, the crease between his brows so deep it looked carved. He’d come straight from his own last patient. He took her bag off her shoulder without asking.

“You were meant to go home,” she said.

“So were you.”

He looked at her face and his own went still. “Hold still.” He took a clean folded tissue from his pocket and wiped her cheekbone, carefully, twice, and she saw it come away brown.

“Not mine.”

“I know.” He folded the tissue and put it away, and then he put his thumb where the blood had been, and bent his head and kissed her on the pavement in front of Harbourside, with the ambulances still coming in behind them and a porter going past with a cage of linen, and he didn’t hurry.

“You’re proud of me,” she said against his mouth.

“Yes.”

“I was frightened. I didn’t think I would be.”

“Being frightened doesn’t make it less yours,” he said, and took her hand, and took her home.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d rung the house from his car and Ah Sim had sent Mok up with soup, so there was soup on the stove at Camphor Hill, and the bath was running, because he’d turned the heater on with his phone at the lights. She stood in the bathroom doorway in her scrubs.

“You planned all this.”

“Water. Towels. Soup. Clean clothes.”

He undressed her, because she let him, slowly, peeling the scrub top over her head and kneeling to get the trousers off her ankles, and she stood there in the steam and let herself be undressed like a child, too tired to mind. She washed her face and hands at the basin first, the way she always did after theatre, and then got into the bath and slid down until the water was at her chin.

He sat on the floor beside it with his arm along the edge.

“There was a girl Nuo was looking after. Twelve. Face paint. Nuo was so calm. She’s at Harbourside. She didn’t tell me,” she said, with her eyes shut.

“She wanted you to find out.”

“And a man called Chung. He went up the stairs to help an old woman with a walking frame. He’s in the unit with a sponge in his belly and my dressing on it. He goes back tomorrow. I wasn’t frightened of the operation. I was frightened of what it would mean if I couldn’t do it.” She opened her eyes.

“And you did.”

“Yes.”

“Elara. You don’t have to prove the rest of your life in one night.”

She sat up in the water and kissed him, wet, holding his face, and soaked his shirt down the front, and didn’t care.

“Get in,” she said.

“It’s a small bath.”

“Then get in carefully.”

He got in carefully. It was a small bath. She lay back against his chest with his knees round her and the water slopping at the rim, and his hands moved over her, washing her, her arms, her shoulders, the back of her neck where the gown ties had rubbed, and then not washing her at all. She turned her head and found his mouth. His hand slid down her stomach under the water and between her legs, and she opened her knees for it, and leaned back on him and let him touch her, unhurried, until her breath was coming short and she was gripping the rim of the bath with her good hand and his forearm with the other.

“Upstairs,” she said, when she could.

He carried her, both of them dripping on the stairs, past the frame where the early sun was just coming in, and put her down on the bed still wet, and she pulled him down on top of her. It was slow. Neither of them had anything left for fast. He moved in her with his forehead against hers and his weight on his elbows, and she held his back with both hands and felt every slow stroke all the way through her. The light came across the bed. When she came it was long and almost gentle, and she said his name into his shoulder, and he followed her with a shudder that went through his whole body and a sound like something let go.

Afterwards she lay on her side with his arm under her neck and their legs tangled in the wet sheet, and the city waking outside the window.

“Happy Mid-Autumn,” she said.

He kissed her temple. “We missed the moon.”

“We’ll see it next year,” said Elara, and was asleep before he answered.

chapters.title: Twin Scrub Caps
chapters.desc: A year since the garden. Nearly five years married. Two pagers and a ghost’s phone on the kitchen counter, all quiet, and a pair of silly caps.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve catalogued them.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Elara noticed when she came up the hill and through the gate was that her husband was standing in the road. The second was that he was looking at his phone. The third was that he’d looked up from it and was looking at her. They stopped about two metres apart.

On his screen there was a blue dot. She knew because she had her own phone out, and on hers there was another, almost on top of the first, at the gate of 2 Camphor Hill.

“You’re checking,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I’m standing right here.”

“I noticed.”

“Then why are you checking?”

“To confirm,” said Xing Yue.

She looked at her own screen, and at him, and put the phone in her pocket, and he put his in his, and neither of them moved. Then she laughed and crossed the two metres in three steps and took a fistful of his shirt and kissed him in the middle of the road. He caught her round the waist. A car came up the hill, slowed, and the woman from number six lifted two fingers off the wheel and drove round them.

“Hello, husband.”

“Hello, wife. Did you eat?” He moved a strand of hair off her face.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Food.”

“Elara.”

“You’re not allowed to interrogate me at the gate.”

“Then I’ll do it inside,” he said, and she kissed him again so that he couldn’t, and he let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The kitchen counter at Camphor Hill had become, over the year, a sort of command post. His pager from City lay at one end of the fruit bowl. Hers from Harbourside lay at the other. Between them, on its own folded tea towel, was the black phone, its screen dark. All three were silent. They’d all been silent for six days, which neither of them had said out loud.

She put her bag down on the counter. He was holding a small paper bag behind his back, badly.

“What’s that?”

“What’s in yours?”

“How do you know there’s anything in mine?”

“You’ve been smiling since the car park. Not your usual smile.”

“I have a lot of smiles.”

“I’ve catalogued them,” he said, and she gave up, and took a flat parcel out of her bag, wrapped in pale blue tissue.

“I made something. Open it first.”

His face didn’t change much. It rarely did, all at once. But his eyes went to the parcel and stayed on it, and then came back to her face, and she was aware all at once of how many evenings she’d spent in the back room choosing fabric.

Two scrub caps. One was midnight blue, scattered with tiny silver stars. The other was ivory, with small crescent moons.

He touched the seam with his thumb. “Matching.”

“Obviously. Yours. Mine. Your name’s a star and a moon. Mine’s only ever been the moon. We’re on opposite sides of the harbour all day. I wanted us to have something stupid that matched.” She held the star one against his chest. She held the moon one against her own.

“You made these.”

“By hand. In the back room. Twenty minutes at a time, so before you ask, no, I didn’t hurt it. Will you wear it?” She watched him.

“Yes.”

“Even if your registrars laugh?”

“If they laugh too,” he said, and put the star cap down beside his pager with great care, as if it were an instrument, and held out the paper bag.

Inside was the banana cap. The original, the one she’d walked him to the hospital gate in fourteen months ago, which she’d kept folded round her old stethoscope in her drawer upstairs. It had been washed and pressed. She turned it over, and on the inner band, in small straight letters in yellow thread, it said ELARA WANG.

She looked at it, and then up at him. “You did this.”

“Yes.”

“The stitching is very straight.”

“I practised.”

“Since when?”

He took his watch off and put it by the sink, which was what he did when he didn’t want to answer something. “January.”

“January. Who taught you?”

“You did.”

“I did not.”

He said, “You did every evening for a year in the back room, two metres away from me, talking the whole time. Running stitch, back stitch, keep the tension even, don’t pull. I was listening. I listen to everything you say. You know that.”

She stared at him. “What did you practise on?”

“Your old cloth. The one in the study.”

“Did you ask?”

“No.”

“Xing Yue.”

“I’ll replace it.”

“How many tries?”

He didn’t answer.

“How many?”

“Seven. The first three weren’t usable,” he said.

“Show me.”

“No.”

“Show me.”

He went to the study and came back with a square of calico folded in four, and she opened it on the counter. Three lines of stitching that wandered like a drunk going home. A curve that had been meant as an E. A fourth attempt that was nearly respectable until the thread gave up halfway and went off the edge altogether. She pressed her lips together hard.

“Don’t,” he said.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

She laughed until she had to hold on to the counter, and he stood and watched her with his arms folded and the corner of his mouth going. Then she looked down at the banana cap again, at her name, and stopped laughing.

“You learned to sew to put my name in this.”

“I wanted you to have something with your name in it that you didn’t have to fight anybody for.”

She pulled him in by the shirt and kissed him, slowly, on the mouth and then on the corner of it, and rested her forehead on his.

“Seven,” she said.

“Never mention it again.”

“I’m going to mention it at your funeral.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They were meant to eat at seven. At twenty past she was sitting on the kitchen counter in the moon cap with her hair still damp from the shower, and he was standing between her knees with a hand on the counter either side of her.

“The food’s getting cold.”

“Then heat it.”

“It’s already hot.”

“Then it’ll stay hot.”

“Are you planning to spend the evening up there?”

“Possibly. I like the view.”

He looked down at himself, and back at her. She kissed him before he could say anything, and then took the star cap off the counter and put it on his head. It was crooked. She straightened it, and he straightened hers, and their foreheads nearly touched, and she got down.

He’d made fish with ginger. She’d brought a small cake home from the Harbourside canteen, and he cut it in two before she could suggest the neighbours. The pagers didn’t go. The black phone didn’t go. She looked at them on the counter.

“Four times this year,” she said.

He knew what she meant. It had rung four times since January. A man from a warehouse with a deep cut on his thigh, who’d gone in the ambulance swearing. A woman who’d already been to an emergency department and hadn’t understood a word of what they’d told her, and needed someone to sit at her kitchen table and explain the antibiotics. A dockworker Elara had refused to touch at all, beyond pressure and a phone call, because what he needed was a theatre. A boy with a hand like Yee’s. Four times, and every time the two of them had gone down the hill together at two or three in the morning with her bag on her knee, and come home with nobody hurt by them, and the card in the drawer still true.

“Do you think we’ll ever stop having it?” she said.

“I don’t know.”

“Would you want to?”

“I’d want you to have a life where nobody needed it. That isn’t the same thing. The phone isn’t the important part.” He moved her teacup an inch closer to her hand.

“What is?”

“That you decide what happens when it rings.”

“And that you come.”

“If you ask.”

“Sometimes I don’t ask.”

“Then I come anyway,” he said, and she laughed.

“That’s not in the rules.”

“Eat your cake.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came up after she’d washed the cups and found him perched on the end of the bed with his old stethoscope round his neck, the one he’d had since he was a student, with the tubing gone stiff and the bell scratched.

“What’s that?”

“Your anniversary present.”

“You gave me my present. It’s downstairs with my name in it.”

“That was the first one. This is the examination.”

She laughed. “What’s the indication?”

“It’s been a year.”

“That’s not a clinical indication.”

“It’s a personal one. Sit down,” said Xing Yue.

She sat beside him. He put the earpieces in and warmed the diaphragm between his palms the way he’d been taught to with frightened patients, and then he unbuttoned her shirt, the top three buttons, without asking and without hurrying, and put the cold disc against her skin under her left breast.

“Breathe in.”

She breathed in. He listened, his head bent. She watched his face, the frown he wore when he was concentrating, which had once made a whole ward of residents afraid of him. He moved the disc a little and listened again.

“Anything?”

“Regular.”

“Good.”

“Fast.”

“That’s your fault,” she said, and he took the earpieces out and put the stethoscope on the bedside table and kissed her, with his hand still flat where the disc had been, and her heart going under it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The anniversary night was slow, because neither of them had anywhere else to be and nothing was ringing. She undid the rest of her own buttons and let the shirt fall off her shoulders, and he looked at her the way he had at four in the morning in a cold bathroom a year ago. She took his clothes off him one piece at a time and folded none of them. He lay back and pulled her down over him, and they kissed like that, her hair falling round both their faces, his hands moving up and down her back.

When he turned her over, he went slowly. He kissed her breasts, the hollow of her stomach, the old fine scar on her hip from a fall off Raiden’s bicycle when she was nine that only he had ever asked about. When he came into her she sighed against his mouth. They moved together without any hurry at all, his weight on his forearms, her hands spread on his back, the bed creaking in a way they kept promising each other they’d fix. He watched her face. She watched his. When it built in her she held his gaze through it and didn’t close her eyes, and came with a long shaking breath and his name, and felt him follow, his forehead dropping to hers, his breath going out of him all at once.

Afterwards she lay on his chest with the sheet tangled round her knees.

“One year since the garden. Nearly five since the registry,” she said.

“Nearly.”

“Is that a long time?”

“Not enough.”

“Greedy.”

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was nearly asleep. She could tell from his breathing and from the way his fingers had slowed on her back.

“Do you remember the first time you saw me?”

“The lift. Harbourside. You asked me about your brother’s spleen.”

“Not that one. On the ward. My first morning.”

“Yes.”

“What did you think?”

“That you were very young. That you were looking at the scan request when everyone else was looking at the monitor. That you’d be difficult.” His eyes stayed shut.

“Excuse me.”

“Very difficult. You were right about the join.” He caught the hand she’d hit him with and kissed the palm.

“I’m usually right.”

“You are,” he said, which she hadn’t expected, and she put her head back down on his chest and began to talk.

She told him about the new registrar on Dr. Xia’s firm who’d mistaken her for a consultant because she was standing next to Mr. Zhuang and looked as if she knew what she was doing. About Nuo, who’d moved to resus and had already made two junior doctors cry, kindly. About a man on Ward 6 who’d tried to pay her with a bag of oranges for explaining his discharge letter, and how she’d taken one so as not to offend him and then had to carry it round all afternoon in her pocket. About nearly sewing the crescent on the moon cap upside down. About how she’d wanted the stars on his to be small enough that he could wear it on a ward round without dying of embarrassment.

He made a small sound.

“You’re awake.”

“Mostly.”

She told him she liked the house more than she’d thought she would, when he’d bought it without asking and she’d been so angry she couldn’t speak. That she liked the plants on the kitchen windowsill, and the frame on the stairs, and his shoes by the door when she came in. That she liked the pagers being quiet. That she liked knowing the black phone was in the drawer, and sometimes wished it would stay there for ever, and sometimes didn’t.

“Are you listening?”

“Yes.”

“You’re falling asleep.”

“No.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

He made a sound that might have been a laugh. His hand had stopped on her back.

“I love you,” she said.

His fingers moved, once. “I love you.”

She kept talking, quieter. About the first time he’d given her the banana cap, and how she’d thought it was ridiculous, and worn it to the gate anyway, and how the porter had stared. About the seven tries. About how glad she was that he’d learned. About the noise the house made at night, which she’d been afraid of at first, the pipes and the wind in the camphor at the bottom of the garden, and which she’d started to like.

He didn’t answer. She lifted her head. He was asleep, with his mouth a little open and the crease between his eyebrows gone smooth for once, and she looked at him in the light from the landing.

Downstairs, on the counter, two pagers and a black phone lay in a row on a folded tea towel, saying nothing. On the peg behind the bedroom door, where she’d hung them on the way up, a cap with stars and a cap with moons hung side by side, and under them, the banana, with her name inside.

She pulled the blanket up over his shoulder and settled back down against him, and under it, without waking, his hand turned over and found hers.

chapters.title: The First Time He Saw Her
chapters.desc: At the end of a twenty-six-hour shift he’s sent to look at a young man’s ribs, and a medical student in a T-shirt stops him by the lift to ask about her brother’s spleen.
chapters.epigraph: “Observation is a decision.”
chapters.content:
At the twenty-sixth hour of a twenty-four-hour shift, Wang Xing Yue had stopped believing in time.

The clock over the nurses’ station on the surgical floor at Harbourside said 8:43 on a Saturday morning in June. His coffee had gone cold twice. He was fairly sure he’d had dinner, but not certain, and the crease between his eyebrows had been there so long that a nurse on nights had asked him if he was angry with her. He’d been at Harbourside for four months of a six-month rotation, a senior registrar from City lent across the harbour to a trauma service that was always short, and he was halfway through signing a discharge summary when the sister put her head round the door.

“Dr. Wang. Bed nineteen. The young man from the van last night. He says his ribs are worse.”

“Imaged?”

“Last night. Three cracked on the left, a broken wrist, a knock on the head. The report says query small splenic bruise, for observation. He’s very uncomfortable. He says.”

He took the chart and went.

On the way he passed a woman coming the other way along the corridor from the far end of the floor, walking fast, head down, with long black hair that looked as if she’d ridden through a gale to get there and a dark T-shirt with something black worked into the creases of her knuckles. She looked up at him once as she passed, sharp and furious and frightened all at once, the look of somebody who was somewhere she would never explain. Then she was through the stairwell door and gone.

He didn’t stop. It wasn’t his business. Bed nineteen was sitting up against three pillows with his wrist in a cast and a dressing over one eyebrow, looking a great deal better than a man who’d made the whole night staff worry about him.

“You’re the new one. Raiden. Good morning,” said the young man.

“Where does it hurt?”

“Everywhere. Here mostly.”

Xing Yue examined him: the cracked ribs on the left, low down, where they lay over the spleen; his breathing; his belly, soft; his pulse and pressure on the chart, steady all night. Raiden swore at him when he pressed the ribs, inventively and at some length.

“You’re exaggerating.”

“I’ve been hit by a van.”

“You’ve been hit by a van and cracked three ribs. You’re very lucky that’s all.”

“Lucky,” said Raiden, and grinned, and then winced, and grinned again.

There was a second chair by the bed, pulled close, and on it a woman’s grey cardigan, much too small for anyone in the room. A paper cup of tea on the locker had a lipstick mark on the rim. Xing Yue wrote his note and didn’t ask.

“You’ve had visitors.”

Raiden’s face did something careful. “Family.”

“Tell your family not to disappear before the nurses have finished asking them things,” said Xing Yue, and went out, and didn’t mention the woman on the stairs to the sister, or to the chart, or to anyone at all, then or later. Two years afterwards, at Elowen’s wedding in the flower shop, he was introduced to his wife’s new sister-in-law and looked across a bucket of peonies at Jinx and she looked back at him, and they both understood that he’d seen her on the stairs that morning, and that he had kept it to himself. Neither of them ever said so.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lift was slow. He pressed the button twice, which he knew did nothing.

“Excuse me. Doctor?”

He turned. A girl in a white T-shirt and jeans, with her hair tied up anyhow and a canvas bag over one shoulder, and a sheet of paper folded small in both hands. Twenty, perhaps. A student, certainly. She had a small crease between her own eyebrows, which made him want to laugh for the first time in twenty-six hours.

“Are you one of the surgeons? On nineteen?”

“Yes.”

“I’m his sister. Elara. Lin Elara. Can I ask you about his spleen?” She held up the paper. It was a photocopy of a page from a textbook, covered in her handwriting in the margins, small and slanting, with three things underlined twice.

“You’ve read about it.”

“All night.”

Her hands shook a little on the paper. Not from nerves; he could see that at once. It was a fine, steady tremor that she was holding down by pressing her thumbs hard against the page, the way someone does who has had it a long time and has stopped expecting it to go.

“The report says query small splenic injury, for observation. I’m in fourth year. I know what the words mean. I want to know what they mean for him,” she said.

He looked at her properly then. He said, “Most small splenic injuries don’t need an operation. If he’s stable, and he is, they watch him. Pulse, pressure, his belly, his blood count, and a repeat scan if anything changes.”

“And what would make you operate?”

He told her: if his pressure fell and didn’t come back, if his blood count kept dropping, if his belly changed under their hands. She listened without interrupting, and wrote one word in the margin.

“And if they took it out? He’d get infections more easily?”

“Some infections. He’d need vaccines, and antibiotics with a fever. It’s manageable. Don’t learn a rule for this. There isn’t one. It depends on him.” He watched the pen.

She looked up at him and smiled, all at once and completely.

“I’ll remember that.”

The lift came. The doors opened. Neither of them moved.

“Thank you,” she said, and got in, and then turned round with her hand on the door. “One more thing. If they say they’re going to observe him, that doesn’t mean they’re doing nothing. Does it?”

He put his own hand on the door so it wouldn’t close.

Somebody had told her once, he thought, that watching was the same as not caring. Somebody had watched her, maybe, and done nothing, and she’d been left with the shaking hands.

“No, observation is a decision. It means someone’s decided that watching is the safest thing for him right now. They keep looking, because things change,” he said.

Her face let go of something. “Good.”

He took his hand off the door. The doors shut on her. He stood in the corridor looking at them until his pager went.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t leave until nearly ten that night. He sat in his car in the staff car park at Harbourside for an hour without starting the engine, and then, at eleven, did something he had never done in his life. He rang his brother.

An Yu answered on the fourth ring. “Who’s dead?”

“Nobody.”

“You don’t ring me. I ring you. On Sundays. To tell you that you work too hard.”

“I know.”

A pause. “What’s happened?”

“Has anybody studied it? Love at first sight. Is it in the literature?” said Xing Yue.

There was a silence on the line so long that he thought the call had dropped.

“Oh. Oh, brother,” said An Yu.

“Forget it.”

“Who is she?”

“It’s a theoretical question.”

“At eleven o’clock on a Saturday night, from a car park. I can hear the car park. There’s a paper. Several. Mostly about how people remember it afterwards, not whether it happens. I’ll send them. Go home and sleep.” Another pause, and when An Yu spoke again his voice had changed.

“Don’t send them.”

“I’m sending them,” said An Yu, and rang off, and in the morning there were four papers in his inbox, which he didn’t open for two years.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home, in the flat he hardly lived in, he emptied his pockets on the kitchen counter. Car park ticket, pen, wallet. He opened the wallet to put the ticket away, and stood there with it open.
