He found a pen. He tore a corner off the back of a pharmacy receipt and wrote on it, in his own handwriting, which nobody could read:

L. Elara — spleen.

He looked at it. Then he added, smaller:

Fourth year. Asked the right question.

It was unnecessary. He knew that. She was a patient’s sister he’d spoken to for four minutes by a lift, and he’d go back across the harbour to City in August, and he’d never see her again. He slid the scrap behind his licence anyway, where it stayed. He moved it to a new wallet in 2022 without reading it. Fifteen months later he walked onto Ward 9B on the first Monday in September and a final-year student turned round from the scan request she’d been reading and looked straight at him with a small crease between her eyebrows, and he knew her before she opened her mouth.

He didn’t call it anything, that night in June. He wasn’t that foolish. He was twenty-nine and had never once in his life been tempted to believe in something he couldn’t examine. He went to bed and slept for eleven hours, and dreamed about nothing at all, and woke with her question in his head.

That doesn’t mean they’re doing nothing. Does it?

chapters.title: Before She Had a Family Name
chapters.desc: On the morning of her wedding, Lin Jian sits at his kitchen table before dawn and remembers the autumn of 2002: a schedule sold to the wrong man, a fire he watched from across the water, and a children’s home on Plum Steps.
chapters.epigraph: “Everything has a name.”
chapters.content:
Lin Jian woke at a quarter to four, before the alarm he hadn’t set, and lay in the dark in the big bed he had slept in alone for twenty-four years.

The house behind the red door was quiet. The kitchen clock downstairs hadn’t struck. Today his second daughter was getting married to a man she had already been married to for nearly four years, at six in the morning in a hospital garden, under the window where her mother had sat on her breaks with a cup of tea. The registry had been the real one. The garden was for everybody else, and for her mother. She had always needed to do a thing properly before she believed it.

He got up and dressed in the dark, in the black suit, and went down and sat at the kitchen table without turning on the light.

There was a photograph on the table. He’d taken it out of the drawer last night and not put it back. A small girl on this kitchen floor in November 2002, in a pale yellow jumper that had been Elowen’s, holding a wooden spoon in her fist and looking up at whoever held the camera with an expression of the deepest suspicion. Mama had taken it, the first week. On the back, in Mama’s round hand: Elara, who doesn’t trust the soup.

He put his finger on the edge of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the autumn of 2002 he owed Zuo Hanlin for most of what he had. He had thought, for twelve years, that a man could keep his hands clean if he made sure other men did the work. He’d never killed anyone himself. He’d only said where people would be.

Zuo wanted the Qu berths off the old piers, and the ship contract that went with them, and Qu Mingde wouldn’t sell, because his were the only honest boats on the piers and he was proud of it. On a Thursday in October, in the back room of a tea house on Pier Road, Zuo had poured Lin Jian’s tea himself and asked which nights the Qu boats were out at the anchorage and the office was shut.

Lin Jian knew. He knew everybody’s nights. He’d told him. Friday. After midnight.

He went down to the piers on the Friday night. He didn’t know why, then. He told himself, afterwards, that he’d meant to stop it, and he knew that wasn’t true; he’d gone because he wanted to see what he’d bought. He stood in the dark under the ferry awning across the basin with his collar up and watched the low building with QU LIGHTERAGE painted over its door, and the flat above it, where a light was on in one window that should have been dark. That was the first thing he saw. The light.

Two of Zuo’s men came along the quay at ten to one with cans, unhurried, like men delivering something. One of them went round the back. The other poured along the front step and up the outside stair to the flat, all the way to the top, and came down again, and lit a match, and dropped it, and stepped back.

The fire went up the stair like water running the wrong way.

The lit window went orange. Somebody inside shouted, a man, one word, a name. Glass went. A woman’s voice, high and sharp and then not. Lin Jian stood under the awning across the black water with his hands in his coat pockets and didn’t move, and Zuo’s men walked back along the quay the way they’d come, not hurrying, and got into a car at the end of it, and the car went. The shouting stopped before the fire engines came. He heard the engines from the bottom of Pier Road, and turned, and walked up it the other way with his collar up, and didn’t look back, and so he didn’t see whatever happened on the outside stair at the back of the building in the smoke.

The paper the next day said two dead. The owner and his wife. Fire set. No one charged.

✦ ✦ ✦

Four days later a policeman he paid every month to tell him things told him something else. There’d been a child. A girl, nearly three. A neighbour from the next building had got up the outside stair at the back before the smoke took it, and put her in the laundry basket under wet towels, and carried her down, and she hadn’t a mark on her. The police had taken her up to the children’s home on Plum Steps.

He didn’t go home that night. He sat in the car with Mok at the wheel outside the iron gate on Plum Steps until it was light, and didn’t get out.

He went back on the Saturday. He didn’t go in. He stood at the gate in the cold and listened, because there was a girl’s voice in the yard, a small loud voice that didn’t stop, asking somebody something. A young man was up a ladder against the wall of the building, doing something to the roof, and she was at the bottom of it with her head tipped all the way back.

“Does it have a name?”

“What?”

“Your ladder. Does it have a name?”

“It’s a ladder, little sister.”

“Everything has a name. Mine’s Xiaoyue,” said the child, sure.

He went home. He couldn’t give her parents back. He had sat across the water and watched them burn. He went back on the Monday with an envelope of cash for a matron in a cardigan who looked at him as if she knew exactly what sort of man he was, and paid for the whole of the roof that had leaked for six years and that the government had never paid for. He paid for new windows. He paid a clerk at the welfare office to put a file at the top of a pile instead of the bottom. Then he went home to the red door and told his wife that there was a little girl from a fire on the piers who had nobody, and could they.

He never told her which fire. He never told her what he’d done. She was tired all the time that autumn and wouldn’t say why, and Elowen was seven and Ev was four and Raiden was far away on the farm in the borderland, where he’d be safe, and Mama had every reason in the world to say no.

She said, “Bring her to me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went to fetch her on the fourth of November. Mama came in the car with a blanket and a cloth rabbit she’d sewn the night before. The matron brought the child to the gate in a coat too big for her, holding a paper bag with everything she owned in it, which was a toothbrush and a pair of socks.

The child looked at Mama’s face, and then at him. Mama knelt down on the wet step in her good coat and held out the rabbit.

“Hello. Would you like to come and live with us?”

The child considered the rabbit. She took it by one ear. Then she looked up at him, the man who’d watched her mother’s window go orange from across the water, and held out her other hand to him without being asked.

He took it. He didn’t know what else to do. They went down Plum Steps together, the child holding his hand and talking the whole way down, about the rabbit and the steps and the roof and the ladder, which didn’t have a name, which she thought was sad, and he didn’t say a single word. He couldn’t. Mama walked behind them with her hand on the rail, slowly, and watched his face.

At the bottom, in the car, Mama took the papers out of the envelope the matron had given her and read the name on them. Qu Xiaoyue.

“Little moon,” she said.

She looked at the child on her knee, who was explaining the rabbit to Mok.

“Then she’s Elara. It’s a moon too. She’ll keep a piece of it without knowing,” she said.

That night in the kitchen, with the girl asleep upstairs in the room next to Ev’s and the soup she hadn’t trusted untouched in its bowl, Mama put her hand on his arm.

“Jian. Love her more than the others.”

He looked at her.

“Not because she’s worth more. Because she’s lost more, and she’ll know it one day even if nobody tells her. Don’t ever let her feel she has to earn her place at this table. Promise me.” Mama’s face was tired and fierce in the lamplight.

“I promise,” said Lin Jian, who had sold the child’s parents for a debt and watched them burn, and Mama believed him, and was dead three and a half months later, in February, without ever knowing.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the spring of 2003 Zuo Hanlin went for a walk along the West Basin wall after dinner, as he did every Thursday, and Lin Jian was waiting for him by the bollards with Mok and two other men.

Zuo saw him and smiled and opened his mouth to say something reasonable. Lin Jian hit him in the face with a length of iron pipe before he could say it, and then again, and Zuo went down on the stone with his hands up. Lin Jian didn’t stop. When it was done, Mok and the other men wrapped him in chain and rolled him off the wall into the black water, and he went down without a sound, and the bubbles came up for a while and then didn’t. Lin Jian stood on the wall in the dark and threw the pipe in after him.

It didn’t change anything. He had known it wouldn’t. He did it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty-four years later, at the kitchen table behind the red door, the kitchen clock struck four.

He’d told her. All of it but the awning, a year and a half ago, at this table, with the splint on her arm, and she’d said Don’t when he moved towards her and walked out through the red door past Ah Sim. At New Year the table had gone to her, up Fig Tree Lane, because she couldn’t face the door. She’d come back through it in the end. She’d never said she forgave him, and he’d never asked. She’d only kept coming to Sunday lunch, and called him Baba, and asked him to walk her down a garden. He had never in his life been given anything he deserved less.

A light came on in the passage. Ah Sim came in, dressed for the wedding in a dark red jacket she’d bought for Elowen’s, with her hair done and her handbag already over her arm.

“You’re up.”

“I couldn’t sleep.”

She looked at the photograph under his hand and didn’t ask. She’d been in this kitchen in 2002. She’d made the soup.

“She’ll be nervous,” he said.

“She’ll talk all the way down the path and lose her place. And you’ll cry, and she’ll tell you not to, and you’ll say you’re not.” Ah Sim put the kettle on, because she couldn’t be in a kitchen without doing it.

“I won’t cry.”

“Mok has a handkerchief for you. I gave it to him. Come on. Mok’s got the car out. You’re walking your daughter down a garden.” She came and straightened his collar, the way Mama used to, which nobody else in the house was allowed to do.

He put the photograph in the inside pocket of the black suit, over his heart, where she couldn’t see it and he could feel it.

“Yes, my daughter,” said Lin Jian.

chapters.title: A Cafeteria Lunch, Narrated
chapters.desc: Twenty minutes on the mystery meat in the hospital canteen, while the chief resident eats his and the next table watches him listen.
chapters.epigraph: “Now you’ve had some.”
chapters.content:
By the seventh minute of Elara’s investigation into the canteen’s meat of the day, three people at the next table had stopped pretending not to listen.

Wang Xing Yue was the fourth. He was also the only person at their own table who’d actually started eating.

“Look at this,” said Elara.

“I’m looking.”

“Properly.”

He put his chopsticks down and looked properly. It was a brown slab in a shallow pool of brown gravy, beside a scoop of rice and some greens that had given up some time ago. The board by the till called it Chef’s Braise, which told nobody anything, and was the point.

“What am I looking for?”

“The texture. It’s too smooth outside to have been roasted, but inside there are fibres. So it was an animal. Once.” She lifted the edge with one chopstick.

“That’s encouraging.”

“Don’t be sarcastic. This is a hospital. We feed this to the people who keep other people alive. I think it’s beef.” She narrowed her eyes at it.

“Then eat it.”

“That’s exactly what you’d say if you wanted me to stop asking questions.”

He picked up his own piece and ate it, looking at her.

She stared. “You don’t even know what it is.”

“I know what it is.”

“What?”

“Lunch,” said the chief resident.

At the next table a junior from orthopaedics put his spoon down to hide his face.

“Chief Resident Wang. As a medical professional, you ought to be concerned about what’s served to hospital staff.”

“As a medical professional, I’m concerned about how long you’ve spent looking at something you could have eaten.”

“Eight minutes.”

“Thank you for the update.”

“You’re welcome. Do you think it was boiled first? Because if it was boiled, the gravy could be hiding—” She picked her spoon up and put it down.

“Eat your greens.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the eleventh minute Rao arrived with a folder under his arm and the face of a junior who has been sent.

“Sorry, Chief Resident. Bed twelve—”

“Have you looked at the observations since the round?”

“I was going to ask whether—”

“Have you looked at them?”

Rao hesitated a fatal second.

Xing Yue said, “His pressure’s been drifting down since nine. You have the chart. You have the nursing notes. You have this morning’s bloods. Read them, decide what you think is happening, and then come and tell me, and I’ll tell you if you’re right. Don’t ask me to read you what’s already written down.” He didn’t raise his voice. He never did; he didn’t need to.

“Yes, Chief Resident.”

“And don’t come to a table where people are eating unless he’s getting worse.”

Rao looked at the table. Then, possibly against his better judgment, at Elara, who was holding a piece of the braise halfway to her mouth and watching with great interest.

“Understood.”

“Go.”

Rao went. Xing Yue picked up his chopsticks. Elara put the braise down, uneaten.

“That was frightening,” she said.

“He needed to read the chart.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

“Because you were very handsome while you did it.”

His chopsticks stopped halfway to his mouth. Elara smiled into her rice. At the next table somebody had a coughing fit.

“Finish your lunch,” he said.

“You’re ignoring a compliment.”

“I heard it.”

“Then say thank you.”

“Thank you.”

“That was terrible.”

“Then don’t compliment me in the canteen.”

“Fine. I’ll do it after lunch,” she said, and leaned back, extremely pleased with herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the fourteenth minute he took a small pudding pot out from behind his water bottle, where it had been hiding under a folded napkin the whole time.

She was explaining the greens. Frozen, she thought, not fresh, because fresh greens didn’t lose their structure all at once like that unless— She stopped.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s clearly something.”

He peeled back the lid. “It’s a pudding.”

“Where did you get a pudding? There weren’t any puddings.”

“There was one.”

“Why didn’t I get one?”

“You were looking at the meat,” he said, and picked up his spoon.

She gave him a look of profound betrayal and went back to her greens. He let her, for about twenty seconds. Then she leaned over, took the spoon out of his hand, and ate a mouthful of his pudding.

“Oh,” she said.

“Good?”

“That’s very good. Why didn’t you tell me it was this good?” She took another.

“Elara.”

“Hm?”

“That’s mine.”

She looked down at the spoon in her hand as if it had been put there by somebody else, and gave it back. “Sorry.”

She went back to her lunch. A minute later, still explaining the greens, she reached over without looking, picked up the pot, and finished it with her own spoon, and put it down empty beside his tray, and went on talking.

He looked at the empty pot. Then at her.

“Was it good?” he said.

“Very.”

“You’re welcome.”

She glanced up, saw his face, and smiled at him. “Thank you, Chief Resident.”

At the next table a staff nurse leaned over to her neighbour and whispered something, and the neighbour looked at the chief resident of general surgery and put her hand over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the eighteenth minute their knees touched under the table. It happened when she moved her chair to reach her water, and she didn’t move it back, and neither did he.

She’d gone on to argue that the canteen ought to be required by law to state the animal. He leaned an elbow beside his tray and listened, and every so often asked a question. He didn’t care about the meat. He asked because she lit up whenever he did, and he had discovered, in the seven months since a final-year student had turned round on his ward and told him he was wrong, that he would do quite a lot for that.

“Suppose it is beef,” he said. “Why does it taste like that?”

“What does beef taste like?”

“Beef.”

“An excellent definition. You’re not taking this seriously.” She nudged his knee with hers.

“I’m listening.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Can’t I do both?”

She looked at him. His face was calm. The corner of his mouth had gone up. She knew that look by now. It was the one that made her forget what she’d been saying, however sure she’d been.

“You’re distracting me from my investigation.”

“An unfortunate loss to science,” he said, and left his knee where it was, and at the next table the staff nurse gave up on her lunch entirely and watched.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the twentieth minute she stood up. “Pharmacology. Ten minutes.”

He took her tray off her and stacked it on his. She looked at the empty pudding pot on top.

“Next time get two.”

“Next time don’t spend twenty minutes interrogating lunch.”

“That’s not a promise.”

“No,” he agreed.

He walked her out past the queue and round the corner into the corridor by the service lifts, which was empty, and smelled of floor polish, and had a broken trolley parked against one wall. She stopped. He’d gone a step further before he noticed and turned.

“What?”

She came up to him, took the front of his white coat in both hands, and pulled him down, and kissed him. It was quick and warm, and entirely unbothered by the fact that they were standing in a hospital corridor in the middle of the day with a broken trolley watching.

When she let go he stayed where he was, close, his eyes on her face.

“What was that for?”

“Now you’ve had some.”

“Some what?”

“Pudding.”

His eyes went to her mouth. “I didn’t know it was served that way.”

“Only if you share.”

“I seem to remember you ate most of it.”

“Exactly,” said Elara.

He laughed, low, the laugh nobody on the surgical floor had ever heard, and took her hand and kissed the knuckles once, quickly.

“Go to your lecture.”

The lift came. She got in, and turned round with her hand on the door.

“I still think it’s beef.”

“I’ll inform the kitchen.”

“And Xing Yue. Two puddings.”

The doors closed on her face. He stood in the corridor looking at the doors. Behind him the canteen door banged and Rao came round the corner with his folder open, half running.

“Chief Resident. I read the chart. His pressure’s down twenty since nine, his urine’s dropped off, and I think—”

“Walk. Tell me,” said Xing Yue.

Rao told him, all the way back up to the ward in the slow lift, with the folder open against his chest, and he was right, and Xing Yue told him so. On the way past the canteen he looked once through the door at the refrigerated counter by the till, where the puddings came out at noon, and worked out how early he’d have to come down tomorrow to get two.

chapters.title: Perfect Squares
chapters.desc: On Christmas Eve, a month after the knife, he cuts her dinner into exact squares. She tells him what she thinks of that, and then she makes him do a dumpling.
chapters.epigraph: “You killed it twice.”
chapters.content:
The rice had gone cold. Elara stood with her forehead against her husband’s shirt in the kitchen at Banyan Terrace and listened to his heart, which was going much too fast for a man who was standing still, and thought: he’s been like this for eleven days. She lifted her head.

He didn’t let go of the back of her head until she’d stepped back, and then he did it at once, the way you take your hand off something hot. His eyes went to her right arm in its splint, strapped to her chest in the sling, and away, and back.

She sat down on the stool again and looked at her plate. Squares. A centimetre and a half, she’d have bet her hand on it, in rows, with the greens beside them in a pile so neat it might have been sutured.

“Did you measure them?”

“No.”

“You’re lying.”

“Not with a ruler,” said Xing Yue.

She took a square on her fork in her left hand. It went in her mouth on the second try. He watched the fork the whole way, and she watched him watch it.

“I can cut chicken,” she said.

“You can’t hold a knife.”

“I can hold a fork in my left hand and tear it. I can pick it up with my fingers. I’m not a fledgling. Every night for three weeks. Every night you cut it at the counter with your back to me, so I can’t see you doing it, and you bring it over cut, and I eat it, and I don’t say anything because I’m not saying anything. I hate them.” She put the fork down. She looked at the squares.

“The food?”

“The squares. Every time I look at them I’m back on that trolley with Dr. Sha’s hands in my arm.”

His face didn’t move. That was how she knew she’d hit something.

“I’ll leave it whole.”

“That isn’t what I want.”

“What do you want?”

“I want you to stop looking at my hand every time I pick something up with the other one.”

He didn’t answer. He was choosing his words, she could see him doing it, carefully, the way he’d been choosing everything for a month, every sentence handled as if it might go off. She was so tired of careful she could have screamed.

She got off the stool and came round the counter, and took his collar in her left fist, and pulled.

He came down because he wasn’t expecting it. His hands landed flat on the counter on either side of her plate to stop himself falling into her dinner, and she kissed him. It wasn’t kind. She was angry, and she’d missed him for eleven days while he slept a foot away, and she wanted to be his wife and not his patient, and he had been looking at her for a month. She kissed him until he made a sound against her mouth and his hands came off the counter.

She let go of his collar.

“Was that an answer?” he said. He sounded as if he’d run up the stairs.

“No. I’m still angry. That was a reminder.”

“Of what?”

“That I can still pull you about by the collar with the wrong hand. Sit down. Eat your dinner. It’s cold.” She went back round to her stool.

He looked at her. Then he sat.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were dumplings. He’d made them in the afternoon, she’d heard him through the bedroom door: a bamboo steamer of them, each one pleated with the same number of folds, so alike they might have come off a machine. He put the steamer on the counter between them.

She took one in her fingers and looked at it. Then she put it on the chopping board in front of him.

“Cut that into eight.”

He looked at it. “Why?”

“Because I want to watch you do it.”

“That’s unnecessary.”

“So were my carrots.”

He looked at her a while longer, and then he picked up the knife.

He cut it in half, cleanly. Then in quarters, less cleanly. Then he tried to halve each quarter, and the filling, which was soft and hot and full of cabbage and ginger and chicken and didn’t care how good a surgeon he was, began to come out. One piece fell over. One slid off the board onto the counter. The last cut produced a flap of pastry and a smear.

He looked at what he’d done. He counted with the tip of the knife. “Eight.”

“That one’s just cabbage.”

“It was part of the dumpling.”

“Was.”

He looked at her, and she looked at him, and the laugh got out of her before she knew it was there.

It was small at first, and rusty. Then it was bigger. She put her good hand over her mouth and it came through her fingers anyway, and her shoulders shook, and it hurt her arm in the sling and she didn’t care. She laughed until her eyes ran.

He didn’t move. He’d heard her cry, in the weeks since the alley, and swear during therapy, and go silent when her fingertips couldn’t tell silk from sandpaper. He hadn’t heard this since November.

“What’s funny?” he said.

“You. You did it like a post-mortem.”

“It needed eight pieces.”

“You killed it twice.”

She was still laughing when she saw his face change. Not much. Something went across it and stayed.

The squares had never been for her. He saw that, standing there with the knife and the wrecked dumpling, at the same moment she did. He’d stood on a pavement with her blood on his hands, in a corridor for four hours while Dr. Meng worked inside her arm. He’d stood at the end of a trolley while somebody else held her artery shut. There had been nothing in any of it that he could do. So every night he’d stood at the counter with his back to her and cut her dinner into something exact and equal, and he’d told himself it made things easier for her. It made something easy he could hold.

He put the knife down.

“I thought if I made everything simple, you wouldn’t have to struggle. I don’t know what to do with my hands when I can’t help,” he said.

She stopped laughing. She reached across the counter with her left hand and put it over his right one, flat, and left it there.

“You can sit next to me. You don’t have to fix anything. You can let me be cross. You can let me take too long. You can let me drop things. I don’t want to be frightened of my own hand because you’re frightened of it.” She held on.

He turned his hand over under hers, so that they were palm to palm. “All right.”

“You’ll forget.”

“Then remind me.”

“I’ll use your collar.”

“I know,” said Xing Yue.

✦ ✦ ✦

He warmed the dumplings again and came round and sat on the stool beside her, not opposite, for the first time in three weeks. He put the wrecked one in a small bowl, all eight pieces of it, because she insisted. Then he picked up a piece with his chopsticks and held it in front of her mouth. She looked at it, and at him.

“You’re feeding me.”

“Would you rather tear it with your fingers?”

She thought about saying yes. She opened her mouth instead. He fed her the piece, and a drop of sauce ran down the chopstick onto his thumb, and before he could reach for a napkin she caught his wrist with her left hand and put her mouth to his thumb and licked it off. He went completely still.

“That’s unhygienic,” he said, after a moment.

“You’re a surgeon. You washed.”

“I did.”

“Then we’re fine. More.” She let go.

He fed her another, watching her face this time and not her arm. When she caught him looking at the sling she said, “Eyes,” and he lifted them to hers and kept them there.

“Better?” he said.

“Much.”

She ate the whole wrecked dumpling that way, and two whole ones, and some of the cold rice with the squares, because she was hungry, which she hadn’t been since the thirteenth. Then she put her left hand on his collar again.

He was ready this time. He leaned across the corner of the counter and let her pull him down, and his hands went to her waist, careful but not hesitating, and he kissed her back, slowly, and she let him, and held on to his shirt.

“I’m still angry,” she said against his mouth.

“I know.”

“Tomorrow you make them again. All of them. And you leave the chicken whole.”

“All right.”

“And you don’t cut anything.”

“How should I cut it, then?”

“Don’t,” said Elara, and kissed him again, and behind them on the chopping board the cabbage and the flap of pastry and the bit that had slid off the counter lay where they’d fallen, and neither of them tidied them up.

chapters.title: The Cousin Who Wants Emergency Medicine
chapters.desc: Yu Chen comes to Banyan Terrace to ask his mentor about emergency medicine, and about something harder. Elara walks in talking.
chapters.epigraph: “It gets complicated when people won’t say what they mean.”
chapters.content:
Yu Chen had been on the sofa at Banyan Terrace for eleven minutes with a cup of tea he hadn’t drunk, and Xing Yue had noticed three things.

His cousin had come without ringing first, which he never did. He’d brought the blue folder with his elective reports and his portfolio in it, which meant this wasn’t a social call. And he had been looking at the same point on the rim of the cup for long enough that the tea had certainly gone cold.

“You’re not here about your results,” said Xing Yue.

“No.”

“Wei Long?”

“He’s fine. He sends his regards and says you’re to eat.”

“Then what?”

Yu Chen looked at the folder on the coffee table. “I’m thinking about emergency medicine.”

Xing Yue sat back. “Why?”

“I like not knowing what comes through the doors. I like having to decide before I know everything. I think I’d be good at it.”

“Thinking you’d be good at something and being good at it are different.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Yu Chen gave him a slightly wounded look. Xing Yue went on as if he hadn’t seen it.

“It isn’t surgery without a theatre. You’ll spend your life recognising who’s dying among forty people who all feel terrible, stabilising what you can and handing them on to somebody else, and most nights you won’t find out how it ends. Very little of it is satisfying. If you want it because you like being the person who arrives when something’s gone wrong, don’t.”

“That isn’t why.”

“Then do it. Spend your elective in the department. Do nights. Talk to the consultants at four in the morning, not at a careers fair. Find out what it looks like after the excitement’s gone.”

Yu Chen turned the cup round. “How did you know you wanted surgery?”

“I didn’t. I liked the work, I kept doing it, and in the end I was difficult to get rid of.”

“That’s your career advice?”

“Don’t be difficult to get rid of. Be useful enough that they’d rather you stayed.”

Yu Chen stopped smiling and took a pen out of his pocket and wrote it on the back of his hand.

“Don’t quote me in your application.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were. Wang,” said Xing Yue, and his phone went on the arm of the chair. City. He answered it.

It was the medical registrar on call, a young voice, too fast. “Mr. Wang, sorry, it’s about your lady in bed six on 9B, the day-four colectomy. She’s more breathless than this afternoon, but her sats are only—”

“What’s her respiratory rate?”

“Twenty-eight.”

“Can she finish a sentence?”

A pause. “Not really.”

“Is she using her neck to breathe?”

“…Yes.”

“Then why are you telling me her numbers are reassuring?”

“We were waiting for the repeat gas before we—”

“Don’t wait for a gas to tell you somebody’s getting worse when you can see it from the end of the bed. Get her on oxygen, get a second line in, get the outreach team to her now, and ring the medical consultant. Then ring me back and tell me what you see, not what you’re hoping the next result will say. And don’t leave her on her own while you do it.”

“Yes, Mr. Wang.”

He put the phone down. Yu Chen was looking at him.

Xing Yue said, “That’s emergency medicine. The part nobody puts in the brochure. Acting before you’ve got every answer, and asking for help before you think you need it.”

“That’s what I want,” said Yu Chen.

“Then you’ll have to get comfortable being uncomfortable.”

“I think I can.”

“You’ll find out.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a different kind of silence after that. Yu Chen drank some of the cold tea, made a face, and put it down.

“Can I ask you something else?”

“You came here to ask something else.”

Yu Chen rubbed his thumb along the handle of the cup. “There’s someone.”

“Of course there is.”

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you know already.”

“I don’t. Go on.”

“What do you do,” said Yu Chen slowly, “when someone you care about won’t let you help? She isn’t careless. She’s brilliant. She looks after everyone, all the time, she fixes things for people before they’ve noticed they’re broken. But when it’s her, she just goes. She says she’s fine. She changes the subject. She makes a joke and everybody laughs and lets her off.”

“Have you asked her what she needs?”

“She says nothing.”

“Then believe her a little. And watch,” said Xing Yue.

“That’s all?”

“What did you want?”

“Something more useful than watch.”

“You can’t make someone take care by deciding for them what it is. You can tell her you’ve noticed. You can offer something small and specific, so it’s easy to say yes to. You can stay where she can find you. And if she says no, and she’s not in danger, you let it be no.” He heard himself say it and felt it land somewhere under his own ribs.

“Even if she’s hurting.”

“Especially then. If she’s spent her whole life looking after everyone, your worry is one more thing she’ll feel she has to look after. Don’t make it her job.”

Yu Chen looked at him. “How do you know that?”

“Because I’ve done it wrong.”

“With Elara.”

“Among other things,” said Xing Yue, and didn’t go on, and Yu Chen didn’t push.

Then Yu Chen said, so low it was nearly lost, “I think I love her.”

Xing Yue looked at his cousin, whom he’d known since Yu Chen was a skinny eight-year-old in the Wang house next to the Lin estate, climbing the wall between the two gardens to look at the Lin girls’ rabbits.

“Ah,” he said.

“That’s it?”

“Does she know?”

“No.”

“Then tell her.”

Yu Chen laughed helplessly and put his face in his hands. “You make everything sound so simple.”

“It gets complicated when people won’t say what they mean. What’s her name?” Xing Yue picked up his own tea.

Yu Chen took his hands away. He looked, for a second, about fourteen.

“Eliana.”

“Then stop calling her someone,” said Xing Yue.

✦ ✦ ✦

The front door went.

“I’m back. I bought custard buns, and I have a serious complaint about the bakery by the hospital gate, because they’ve changed the filling, and I think it’s a mistake, and I told the woman so—”

Elara came in with a paper bag in one hand and her City lanyard swinging against her coat, and stopped.

“Oh! You’re here.”

Yu Chen stood up. “Hi, Sister-in-law.”

“Why are you sitting so straight? Has he been interrogating you?”

“No,” said Xing Yue.

“Not exactly,” said Yu Chen.

“That’s what people say when they’ve been interrogated. Six. She said they were fresh, but I saw another tray behind the counter, so I don’t believe her.” She put the bag on the coffee table and took the buns out. Two in front of Yu Chen. Two in front of Xing Yue. Two in front of herself.

“You’re keeping two,” said Xing Yue.

“I paid.”

“Fair.”

She sat down next to him and took a bun and kept talking. The new pineapple bun, which she didn’t recommend; the custard, which was better but only warm; the woman at the counter, who’d said it was a traditional recipe, which didn’t excuse anything. Then she stopped, because Yu Chen was smiling into his tea.

“What? Did he say something embarrassing?”

“No.”

“Did you ask him for advice?”

“Mostly about work.”

“Mostly? What else?” Her eyebrows went up.

“It’s not my story to tell yet.”

She considered him with her head on one side, a custard bun in her hand, and nodded. “Fair enough.”

There was custard at the corner of her mouth. Xing Yue wiped it off with his thumb without looking, and she went straight on talking. “—and if you advertise custard the custard should be the point, not a little surprise in the middle you have to dig for—”

Her lanyard had twisted round on itself. He took it between two fingers and straightened it.

“—and she said it was her mother’s recipe, which isn’t a reason—”

He tugged it, gently, and she stopped in the middle of a word and looked at his hand, and then at his face, and he drew her in by the lanyard, slowly enough that she was coming of her own accord by the end, and kissed her. His hand went to the side of her neck. Hers, still holding half a custard bun, came to rest on his chest.

Yu Chen looked with great care at the pattern on the coffee table.

“I was talking,” said Elara, when she could.

“I noticed.”

“I hadn’t finished.”

“Go on, then.”

She looked at Yu Chen, who was now studying the coffee table. “You’re embarrassing me in front of your cousin.”

“He’s eating,” said Xing Yue.

Yu Chen choked on his bun.

✦ ✦ ✦

She walked him to the door when he left, with his blue folder under his arm and two buns in a napkin for later.

She said, “If you do go into emergency medicine, remember to eat. Nobody in a hospital remembers to eat. And don’t let him frighten you. He’s worse at home.”

“I can hear you,” said Xing Yue from the sitting room.

“Good!”

Yu Chen laughed. Then he looked at her, and at the sitting room door, and back. “How do you know when somebody wants you to stay?”

Her face changed. She thought about it properly, the way she thought about a case.

“Sometimes you don’t. Sometimes you have to ask. And if they say they don’t need you, you let them know you’re still there. But you don’t stand in the doorway waiting for them to change their mind. They’ll feel guilty instead of loved. People are bad at asking for what they need. That doesn’t mean you get to decide it for them.” She leaned on the door frame. She smiled a little.

He nodded, slowly, and thanked her, and went down the stairs.

When she came back Xing Yue was collecting the cups.

“You gave him advice.”

“Maybe. About Eliana?”

He looked at her. “He told you?”

“He didn’t need to. You were both very obvious. That’s for giving him good advice.” She broke the last custard bun in half and gave him the bigger piece.

“Is that how it works?”

“Yes,” said Elara, and sat on the arm of the sofa beside him and started on the bakery again, and he sat back and ate his reward and listened to the whole of it.

chapters.title: Banned From Trivia Night
chapters.desc: The hospital social club bans Elara from the Tuesday quiz after four weeks of her team winning. She appeals, and Xing Yue, on the other side, gets every question wrong.
chapters.epigraph: “One for each right answer.”
chapters.content:
Elara Wang was banned from the Tuesday quiz at the Harbourside staff social club in February, in the middle of her intern year, which she regarded as a disproportionate response to intellectual excellence.

“They can’t ban me.”

Xing Yue looked up from his phone at the kitchen counter. “They can.”

“It’s a social club. It isn’t a government.”

“It can still ban you.”

“On what grounds?”

He held out his hand, and she gave him the notice, printed on club paper with the club’s crest of two crossed scalpels and a teapot. “Repeated disruption of competitive balance,” he read.

“That isn’t a real offence.”

“It is now.”

She took the paper back and smacked it down on the counter. Four Tuesdays. Four wins, with a team of herself, two house officers from medicine and a pharmacist who knew every river in South America. And now the committee had decided that her presence was bad for the recreational wellbeing of its members.

“Mr. Tu said I was making the other teams feel inadequate.”

“Were you?”

“I was answering the questions.”

“Quickly.”

“That’s how a quiz works.”

“You also corrected his pronunciation of the capital of Kyrgyzstan. In front of the whole room.”

“He was wrong.”

“And you challenged the answer about who invented the telephone.”

“The question was badly worded. It’s a contested— Don’t.” She saw his face.

“Anything else?”

“He said I wasn’t allowed to bring my own reference book.”

“You brought a reference book.”

“A small one. A pocket atlas. It was in my bag anyway.”

He looked at her, and the corner of his mouth went.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re laughing on the inside.”

“Probably,” said Xing Yue.

She folded her arms. “I’m appealing. And I need someone to come with me and say I’m reasonable.”

“You aren’t.”

“Represent me.”

He looked at her for a while. “All right.”

She leaned across the counter and kissed him on the cheek. “Best husband.”

“I know,” he said, and picked up his phone again, and when she’d gone upstairs to look up the inventor of the telephone, he scrolled to a number he’d been given on a committee for operating theatre scheduling two years ago and had never once rung, and rang it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The appeal was the following Tuesday in the small seminar room next to the library, with six chairs in a half-circle and a plate of biscuits that looked as if they’d been chosen to make nobody stay. Mr. Tu sat in the middle, with a folder squared to the edge of the table. He was the social club’s secretary and the hospital’s head of medical records, and he had the air of a man who’d been waiting four weeks for this.

“Mr. Wang. Dr. Wang,” he said.

“We think the ban is unfair,” said Elara, before anybody could sit down.

“Dr. Wang, you won four weeks running.”

“Because I knew the answers.”

“You answered before the questions were finished.”

“Because I knew the answers.”

“That, is precisely the problem,” said Mr. Tu.

Elara turned to her husband. “Say something.”

“She’s very knowledgeable,” said Xing Yue.

“Nobody disputes that. The problem is that nobody else is enjoying themselves. The committee proposes one appeal round. You and Mr. Wang against myself and two members of the committee. Ten questions. If you win, the ban is lifted. The committee chooses the questions. No reference books. No correcting the host.” Mr. Tu put his hands together.

Elara opened her mouth. Xing Yue put his hand on her knee under the table, and she shut it.

“Agreed,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first question was the capital of Mongolia. Elara took a breath, and Xing Yue pressed the buzzer.

“Ulaanbaatar.”

“Correct,” said Mr. Tu, surprised.

The second was the chemical symbol for tungsten. Xing Yue got there first again. “Tin.”

“Incorrect. It’s W.”

Elara turned her head and looked at him. He looked back, mildly interested.

The third was the author of Pride and Prejudice.

“Charlotte Brontë,” said Xing Yue.

“Incorrect,” said Mr. Tu, and something in his face was nearly joy.

The fourth was the number of bones in the adult human skeleton, and he said two hundred and six, and was right, and she relaxed. The fifth was the distance to the moon, and he was out by a factor of ten. The sixth was the periodic table again, and he swapped two noble gases. The seventh was a treaty, and he put it in the wrong century with the calm of a man reading out a blood result.

By the eighth question Elara wasn’t looking at the scores. She was looking at her husband. He sat straight with his hands folded, listening to every question with the face he used at handover, getting every answer wrong. Not carelessly. Precisely. He was beating her to the buzzer every time.

“Are you feeling well?” she whispered.

“Perfectly.”

“You know who wrote Pride and Prejudice.”

“Do I?”

“Mr. Wang, question nine. The author of Great Expectations,” said Mr. Tu.

“Charlotte Brontë,” said Xing Yue.

Elara shut her eyes. They lost seven to two. Mr. Tu was generous enough to call it close.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Charlotte Brontë, twice,” she said in the lift.

“An understandable mistake.”

“It is not.”

“She was a writer.”

“That isn’t the point. You did it on purpose.” She turned on him.

He looked at the floor numbers. “Did what?”

“Got them wrong. You knew all of them. You were faster than me.”

“I answered the questions.”

“Xing Yue.”

He looked at her then. His face was composed. His eyes weren’t.

He said, “I rang Mr. Tu on Wednesday. If you won the appeal, you’d be back on Tuesday, and you’d win again, and by March you’d be banned for good and the committee would put it in the minutes. If you lost the appeal badly enough, with me, the committee would feel it had been fair. He agreed that you could come back next week. On one condition.”

She stared at him. “What condition?”

“That you’re on my team. And I’m on it.”

“You fixed my appeal.”

“I participated in your appeal.”

“You went behind my back to Mr. Tu.”

“Yes,” said Xing Yue. “I should have asked you. I’m asking now. Would you like Tuesdays back?”

The lift doors opened. Neither of them got out. The doors closed again.

“Yes,” she said.

“Then it’s done. And I’m sorry about the asking. I’ll ask first next time, even when I already know what you’ll say.”

She looked at him in the lift with her mouth open, her coat half off one shoulder, and then she started to laugh, and laughed until she had to lean on the wall of the lift, and he pressed the button for the car park and waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car he didn’t start the engine until she’d done her seatbelt. She was still smiling.

“You’re terrible.”

“I’ve been told.”

“I’d have won that round. By a lot.”

“I know. That was the problem.”

She leaned over the gearstick and kissed his cheek. “Thank you. For the Tuesdays. Not for the Mr. Tu part.”

“Noted.”

“How many did I get right? On my own sheet. I was writing them down.”

He picked up the sheet from her lap and looked at it. “Nine.”

“Nine out of ten.”

“You got Great Expectations wrong.”

“I did not— That doesn’t count.” She snatched it. She’d written Charlotte Brontë, out of pure fury, in capitals.

“Nine,” he said, and leaned across and kissed her. Once.

She blinked. He kissed her again, and again. By the fourth she’d understood, and was smiling against his mouth. By the sixth her hand had found his collar and was holding on. By the eighth she’d forgotten what she’d been about to say. The ninth was slow, and he took his time over it, his hand at her jaw, until a car’s headlights went across them in the car park and somebody hooted.

“That was cheating,” she said.

“One for each right answer.”

“What if I’d got ten?”

“Ten.”

“And twenty?”

“Twenty.”

“Then I’m going to answer every question there is,” said Elara, “next Tuesday,” and he started the engine.

✦ ✦ ✦

The following Tuesday she went back to the quiz with her husband, two house officers and the pharmacist who knew the rivers. He answered nothing. He sat beside her with his arm along the back of her chair and let her answer everything, and when she began to correct the host’s pronunciation of Reykjavik he put his hand flat on her knee under the table, and she stopped mid-word and looked at him, and didn’t.

They came second, by one point, to a team from the laboratory who’d been losing every week since September and nearly wept. Mr. Tu wrote it in the minutes, and underlined it.

In the car park afterwards he kissed her eleven times, and she’d counted, because she’d got eleven right, and she said so, and he said, “I know. I was counting too.”

chapters.title: Doctor’s Orders: Nap
chapters.desc: After three nights in a row he writes her a prescription for a nap. She complies, loudly, like an operation note, and falls asleep in the middle of a sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to earn the right to lie down.”
chapters.content:
At a quarter to seven on a Sunday morning, after three nights on call in a row, Elara Wang was cleaning the kitchen at Banyan Terrace.

This wasn’t in itself unusual. What was unusual was that she’d come in at half past eight the night before, slept for four hours, got up at a quarter past six, and was now polishing a section of the counter that had nothing on it, with the concentration of a scrub nurse laying out a tray. She was humming. It was the tune she hummed when she was tired, or thinking about something she didn’t want to think about, the one she’d never been able to tell him the name of.

He stood in the doorway in his T-shirt and watched her do the same circle three times.

“Elara.”

“Hm?”

“Why are you cleaning?”

“Because it’s dirty.”

“It’s clean.”

“Not this bit.”

He came and looked. There was nothing on it. “How many hours did you sleep?”

“Enough.”

“How many?”

“Four.”

“Friday?”

She did another circle. “Three.”

“Thursday?”

“Why is this an investigation?”

“Because you’re polishing an empty counter at a quarter to seven on a Sunday,” said Xing Yue, and took the cloth out of her hand.

“I’m making breakfast.”

“I’ll make breakfast.”

“You don’t know where the good pan is.”

“I live here.”

“That doesn’t mean you know where anything is.”

He held the cloth out of her reach. She looked at it, and at him, and gave up, and walked out of the kitchen with enormous dignity. Three seconds later he heard a cupboard door in the hall.

“I’m getting a towel!”

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past seven he found her in the study, reorganising his journals by year. He took the one out of her hand and put it on the desk.

“Bed.”

“I’ve got things to do. There’s laundry.”

“I’ll do it.”

“The plants.”

“I’ll do them.”

“The fridge needs—”

“It can wait.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re enjoying this.”

“Very much.” He pulled a sheet of paper out of the printer tray, sat down at the desk, uncapped a pen and began to write.

“What are you doing?”

“Writing you a prescription.”

“For what?”

“Your condition.”

“I haven’t got a condition.”

“Chronic refusal to lie down,” he said, and signed it, and folded it once and held it out.

She opened it. It was in his handwriting, which the pharmacy on four had once sent back to the ward with a note that just said Please telephone, and which she had been able to read since the first note he ever left her.

Patient: E. Wang. Dx: three nights on call, complicated by domestic overactivity. Rx: Sleep. Dose: ninety minutes. Route: supine, eyes closed. No cleaning, reading, cooking, journals, or arguing with prescriber. Repeats: as needed. — W. X. Y.

She read it twice. “Supine?”

“You’re welcome to sleep prone if you’d prefer.”

“You’ve prescribed a position.”

“I’ve prescribed a route.”

She folded it with great care and put it in the pocket of his shirt, which she was wearing, and gave him a bright smile so insincere that he narrowed his eyes.

“Don’t use that face.”

“What face?”

“The one that means you’re going to do what you want.”

“Understood, Doctor,” she said, and went upstairs.

Loudly.

“Patient proceeding to bedroom under protest,” she announced from the landing.

“Patient is non-compliant,” he said, following her.

“Patient disputes the diagnosis.”

“Patient has a long history of disputing diagnoses.”

“Prescriber has a long history of being a control freak.”

“Patient is sleep-deprived and therefore an unreliable witness.”

“Prescriber is handsome but very irritating. Patient is supine. Eyes closed. Patient requests water,” she said, and got into bed and pulled the duvet up to her chin and lay flat on her back with her arms by her sides like a patient waiting for the anaesthetist. She closed them.

He gave her the glass from the bedside table. She drank and gave it back without opening her eyes.

“Patient requests a kiss.”

He bent and kissed her temple.

“Patient requests a better kiss.”

She opened one eye. He kissed her properly, slowly, with one hand on the pillow beside her head, and when he drew back she said, “Prescription accepted,” and closed the eye again.

“Sleep.”

“Prescriber may leave.”

He’d nearly got to the door.

“Xing Yue?”

“Hm?”

“Stay until I’m asleep.”

He came back and sat down on the bed and put his hand on the duvet over her hip.

“Patient would like to report,” she said, “that the prescriber’s handwriting is—”

And that was all. Her mouth stayed a little open on the next word. Her breathing changed. He sat there and watched it change, and waited until he was sure, and then took the prescription out of the shirt pocket before she could roll on it, and put it on the bedside table under her phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past eight his phone went in his own pocket. He took it out onto the landing.

“Wang.”

“Mr. Wang, sorry, it’s the house officer on nine. It’s about one of Dr. Fei’s patients from Friday, bed eleven, I’ve got a question about his—”

“Is he deteriorating?”

“No, but—”

“Have you examined him?”

“Yes.”

“Have you bleeped Dr. Fei?”

“She’s not answering. I thought, because you’re—”

“I’m not on call. Dr. Fei is. If she doesn’t answer in ten minutes, bleep her again. If she still doesn’t, you ring the consultant on call, who isn’t me, and you give them what you found when you examined the patient, not what you think Dr. Fei would say. And if you ring this number again on a Sunday morning about somebody who is not getting worse, you’ll spend the whole of next month on Dr. Fei’s nights, and she’ll know why,” said Xing Yue, low, because the bedroom door was ajar.

There was a silence on the line.

“Yes, Mr. Wang.”

He put the phone on silent and left it on the landing windowsill, and went back in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at twenty past nine, in full sun, with the curtains open because he’d forgotten to close them. She didn’t know why she was in bed in the daytime. Then she saw the paper under her phone, and at the bottom of it, under his initials, a line that hadn’t been there before, in the same disaster of a hand:

Taken as directed. Repeat as needed.

He was in the armchair by the window with a journal on his knee.

“Morning,” he said, without looking up.

“Did you sleep?”

“Enough.”

“That’s my answer.”

“I learned from you. How do you feel?” He turned a page.

“Better.”

“Headache?”

“No.”

“Good.”

She pushed the duvet back and got up and went over to the chair, and bent down, and kissed the side of his neck under his ear.

His hand came up to her waist. “That wasn’t in the prescription.”

“It’s an adjunct.”

She did it again, lower, just above his collar, and felt him swallow.

“Is it effective?”

“Very,” said Elara, and took the journal out of his hands and put it on the floor, and pulled him up out of the chair by the front of his T-shirt, and walked backwards to the bed with him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the slowest she could remember. There was nowhere either of them had to be, no pager in the room, no phone, the sun across the sheets and the noise of somebody’s radio from a window across the terrace. She lay on her side facing him under the duvet and undressed him by touch, his T-shirt over his head, his shorts, taking her time, and he did the same with his shirt she was wearing, one button at a time, kissing each place as it came open: her collarbone, between her breasts, the soft skin under her ribs. When he got to the last button she pulled him in by the shoulders and wound her leg over his hip and held him there, close, without doing anything else, just to feel the whole length of him against her.

“You’re supposed to be resting,” he said into her hair.

“I am. This is restful.”

He kissed her, deep and unhurried, and ran his hand down her back and over her hip and between her thighs from behind, slow, until her breath caught and she pressed her forehead into his throat. When he finally came into her it was like that, on their sides, face to face, her leg still over his hip, so slow that it was hardly moving at all, and she felt every bit of it. She kept her eyes open. So did he. It built in her slowly, a little at a time, like the sun coming across the bed, and when she came it was long and quiet and shook her right through, and she held his face in both hands and said his name into his mouth, and he followed her a moment later with a sound she felt in her chest.

They lay there afterwards with the duvet half off and her head on his arm.

“Sometimes I only notice how tired I am when I stop,” she said.

“Then stop more often.”

“You make it sound easy.”

“It isn’t. You don’t have to earn the right to lie down.” He moved her hair off her face.

She didn’t answer that. She turned her face into his arm and stayed there, and after a while he said, “Another ninety minutes?” and she said, “Repeat as needed,” already halfway gone, and this time he lay down beside her and slept too.

chapters.title: The Machine
chapters.desc: Jinx builds the rig at night in the workshop at Tai Hing, from calipers and graph paper and a hand she measured at Ev’s kitchen table. Then she doesn’t watch.
chapters.epigraph: “These she can do herself.”
chapters.content:
Jinx measured her sister-in-law’s hand at Ev’s kitchen table on Fig Tree Lane at New Year, with the oranges pushed to one end and the canvas roll undone between them: two pairs of calipers, a steel rule, graph paper, a pencil sharpened with a knife.

It was the second time. The first had been in 2021, in the back room at Tai Hing, when Elara was twenty-one and her hands had shaken for three years and nobody had been able to stop them. Jinx had measured her wrists without saying a word and built her a brace out of aluminium and leather that she’d worn under her sleeves through her last two years of medical school. Elara remembered the stool. Jinx remembered the numbers.

“Relax your fingers.”

“They’re relaxed.”

“You’re holding them like you’re going to stab me.”

Elara looked down. Her fingers were curled a little, the way the scar had taught them. “That’s how it rests now.”

“Then let it rest like that. I want the hand you’ve got. Not the one you think you should have.”

Across the table Raiden was eating a sesame biscuit and watching. “She’s measuring it. She’s not cross-examining it.”

“Don’t distract my problem,” said Jinx, without looking up.

“Your problem?”

“Engineering problem. Thumb.” She closed the calipers on the width of Elara’s palm and wrote the number down in small neat figures.

Elara held it out.

Jinx measured everything. The span from thumb to first finger, the length of every finger to every joint, how far each one went before the scar pulled and where it stopped feeling anything at all. She had Elara pick up a coin, turn a key, hold a pen and put it down. She didn’t say anything when the fingers hesitated. She just wrote, and said “Again,” and wrote.

“Does it hurt?”

“Not now.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Elara looked at her. “Sometimes, if I stretch too far. And it gets tired before the rest of me does.”

Jinx wrote that down too, and underlined it. Then she rolled the graph paper up and put a rubber band round it.

“Get me your therapist’s sheet. I build to that and I stop.”

“How long?”

Jinx shrugged. “Till it’s right.”

Raiden reached across and took the last biscuit off her plate, and she slapped his wrist without looking, and he ate it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

She built it at night, in the workshop at Tai Hing, after the last car had gone and the shutter was down.

The first night she drew the frame on graph paper on the long bench and looked at it for two hours. The second night she cut steel. On the third she threw away the whole of the finger mechanism, because she’d checked it against the numbers and the first version would have asked the wrist to turn further than the therapist’s sheet allowed. She tore the drawing in half.

“Stupid.”

“Talking to yourself?” Raiden was in the doorway with two coffees.

“Talking to bad engineering.”

He put a cup by her elbow and looked at the drawing, at the measurements in every margin, the little sketches of a hand in six positions. “That’s a lot of work for something she says she doesn’t need.”

“She needs it.”

“I know.”

He sat down on the low stool by the bench with his own coffee. His hands had healed from the fire the summer before, but they still went stiff in the cold, and he wrapped them round the cup.

“You know she doesn’t expect you to fix it,” he said after a while.

Jinx tightened a bolt. “I can’t fix it. Somebody opened her wrist on a doorstep. I can’t do anything about that. I can make something that means she doesn’t have to ask anybody for help to get it back.” She tightened it again.

Raiden didn’t say anything. He drank his coffee and watched her work, and at one in the morning he put his chin on her shoulder from behind and said, “Bed,” and she said, “Ten minutes,” and he pointed out that she’d said that forty minutes ago, and she offered five, and he took her hand and she went.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took three weeks. A steel frame that would bolt to the end of the long bench in the back room, with a cradle for the forearm padded to the shape of the numbers, and a row of small pulleys, and a turntable, and a fine steel wire, and a set of pieces for the fingers that could be changed one at a time. She tried three kinds of adjustment on the resistance before she was satisfied. Screws first, which needed a screwdriver. Then thumb wheels, which needed a pinch Elara didn’t have yet. Then knobs, big ones, ridged, set where the left hand could reach them, each one turning exactly a quarter with a click.

She turned one with two fingers. Click. Another. Click.

“What was wrong with the screws?” said Raiden from the doorway.

“Nothing.”

“Then why change them?”

“Because if she has to ask somebody for a screwdriver every time she wants to change it, she’ll stop changing it. These she can do herself.” Jinx turned the last knob.

He looked at her with an expression she pretended not to see.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Monday she bolted it to the end of the long bench in the back room, and swept the floor, and put a lamp on the shelf at the right height, and a notebook beside it with the therapist’s sheet clipped inside the cover. She left the shutter down and the back door off the latch, because Tai Hing didn’t open until seven and Elara had said she’d come at five.

She came at five, in a taxi, in her coat over pyjamas, with her right hand tucked inside her sleeve.

She stopped in the doorway of the back room and didn’t come in.

Jinx was at the other end of the bench pretending to sort a drawer of washers. She didn’t look round. She’d decided in the second week that she wasn’t going to stand over it and explain every part, and she wasn’t going to watch Elara’s face while she looked at it, because Elara would feel she had to have the right face.

“The cradle comes up and down with the big knob underneath. The wire’s set to the lowest on the sheet. The finger pieces are in the tray. Each knob turns a quarter. You do it. I’m not touching it,” she said to the washers.

Elara walked in, slowly, and stood in front of it. She put out her left hand and touched the cradle, and then one of the knobs. It turned under her fingers. Click. She didn’t say anything.

Jinx put a washer back in the wrong compartment and took it out again. It had gone quiet in the back room, and she couldn’t stand it. She picked up the big spanner off the bench, held it at arm’s length over the concrete, and let go.

It hit the floor with a crash like a car door.

“Fuck,” said Jinx, loudly and sincerely, to the spanner.

Elara laughed. It came out of her all at once, cracked and helpless, and she put her good hand over her face, and her shoulders shook, and when she took the hand away her eyes were wet and she was still laughing.

“You did that on purpose.”

“I dropped a spanner.”

“You held it out.”

“It slipped. Go on. It’s yours. I’m going to get the van out.” Jinx picked it up and put it back on the bench and didn’t look at her.

She went through to the workshop and shut the door behind her and didn’t come back for an hour. She stood in the cold among the cars with her back to the door and listened, and after a minute she heard it: the cradle settling, the wire beginning to whisper on its pulleys, small and steady, and a click, and another click, as Elara changed the resistance herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night Raiden brought her dinner in a tin at the workbench, Ah Sim’s chicken and rice, because Ah Sim had heard, because Ah Sim heard everything. Jinx sat on the end of the bench and ate it with a spoon.

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m eating.”

“You’ve been eating for ten minutes.”

She scraped the bottom of the tin. “She changed the resistance herself. Twice. She went up a quarter after twenty minutes, and then she went down again.”

“I know. She texted me.”

“She texted you?”

“Tell your wife she’s a genius and that I know about the spanner.” Raiden held out his phone. Jinx didn’t take it.

He sat down on the low stool, and she slid off the bench sideways onto his knee without being asked and put one arm round his shoulders, and he put his arms round her waist and kissed her hair, where her hair was full of steel dust.

“You’re proud of yourself,” he said into it.

“Don’t make it a thing.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He kissed her hair again. She put her cheek down on his head and closed her eyes, and in the back room behind them, under its lamp, the machine stood bolted to the end of the long bench, with every one of its knobs turned to where Elara had left it.

chapters.title: Handwriting Nobody Else Can Read
chapters.desc: Nobody can read a word he writes except Elara. Pharmacists ring her to translate, and some of the notes are only for her.
chapters.epigraph: “Here is the rest of your name.”
chapters.content:
The first person to tell Elara that Wang Xing Yue’s handwriting couldn’t be read was a pharmacist. The second was a staff nurse. The third was his own registrar. By then Elara had already decided that the problem wasn’t his handwriting. It was that he had no interest in anybody reading it but her.

✦ ✦ ✦

October 2022

The first note was on the back of a pharmacy leaflet, folded into the book she’d left on the arm of his sofa. Two lines. She unfolded it on the bus home and turned it sideways, and then upside down, and then sideways again, and rang him from the back seat.

“What does this say?”

“Which?”

“The note. In my book.”

“Thursday. Seven. Old Bian’s. And the name of the paper you wanted on the gut microbiome.”

“That’s what you wrote?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

“Normally.”

“It looks like a heart trace someone took during an earthquake.”

There was a pause on the line in which she could hear him deciding to be amused. “Can you read it?”

She looked at it again. Now that she’d been told, she could. The T of Thursday was a lightning strike. The B of Bian was a lowercase b that had lost its nerve. “Yes.”

“Good,” said Xing Yue, and rang off.

She kept it. She told herself it was evidence that he needed lessons. It went into the back of the book, where it stayed for years.

✦ ✦ ✦

February 2023

On a Wednesday in February, at a quarter to twelve, the ward phone on 9B rang, and Sister Miao answered it and listened and then held the receiver out across the station to the final-year student who was writing up a clerking at the end of the desk.

“Pharmacy. For you,” said Sister Miao.

“For me? I’m a student.”

“You’re the one who can read him.”

Elara took the phone. “Hello?”

“Sorry, it’s pharmacy. We’ve got a chart from the chief resident and we can’t make out the instruction under the dose. The drug’s fine. It’s the bit after.”

“Can you send a photo?”

It came through on the ward computer. His writing, at speed, interrupted, slightly annoyed. She could tell all three from the angle of the letters.

“Twice daily. After food,” said Elara.

“You’re sure?”

“Completely.”

“Thank you. You must know his writing very well,” said the pharmacist, with great feeling.

Elara looked at the screen. “Unfortunately.”

That evening, in his flat, he was taking his watch off at the chest of drawers when she told him.

“I wrote it clearly.”

She looked at him. He looked back. Then the corner of his mouth went.

“Apparently you could read it.”

“I can read anything you write.”

“Then it’s useful,” he said, and kissed her before she could start on the subject of professional standards.

✦ ✦ ✦

August 2023

By the time she was his wife she was 9B’s unofficial interpreter, even from the other side of the harbour. Nurses at City rang her at Harbourside. City’s pharmacy rang her. In the third week of her intern year, a Harbourside registrar came and found her in the doctors’ room with a transfer letter from City held out in front of him as if it might go off.

“Dr. Wang. Sorry. It’s from Mr. Wang. Your Mr. Wang.”

She read it. She gave it back.

“Repeat his bloods at six. If the white count’s up, ring City and ask for him.”

The registrar stared at her. “How did you—”

“Exposure. Don’t tell him. He’ll get worse,” said Elara.

✦ ✦ ✦

November 2023

At Banyan Terrace the notes began turning up in places that had nothing to do with medicine.

On the fridge: Milk. Eggs. Tea.

By her shoes at the door: Rain. Umbrella. Taxi.

Inside her lunch box, tucked under the lid: three words she couldn’t make out at all, even after a minute. She photographed it at her desk and sent it to him.

Elara: What does this one say.

Xing Yue: You can read it.

Elara: I want to hear you admit your handwriting is a disaster.

Xing Yue: Eat. Properly. Please.

Elara: I already ate.

Xing Yue: What?

Elara: Your note.

He rang her. She answered laughing.

“Have you eaten?” he said.

“Your handwriting.”

She could hear him smiling. “Come home,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

June 2024

The first time she found I love you on the fridge she nearly missed it.

It was at the bottom of the shopping list. Milk. Rice. Washing powder. Dish soap. And squeezed into the last bit of paper, below dish soap, where there was hardly room, smaller than the rest: I love you.

She stood in front of the fridge with the door half open for so long that he came in behind her with the teapot.

“You’re letting the cold out.”

She pointed.

He looked. “Oh.”

“You wrote that between dish soap and the edge of the paper.”

“There wasn’t much room.”

“That’s your explanation?”

“Would you rather I wrote it somewhere else?”

She turned round and put her hands on his collar and kissed him, with the fridge open behind her.

“No, I like it there. And we need more milk. And I love you too,” she said.

The list stayed on the fridge for three weeks. She didn’t let him take it down. When he finally bought the milk he wrote a new list and stuck it beside the old one instead of over it.

✦ ✦ ✦

November 2025

After the knife he stopped leaving her notes. He wrote things down, because somebody had to. Tablets and times. The therapist’s exercises. Dr. Meng’s appointments. The questions she wanted to ask at the next review, which she dictated to him in the car because she couldn’t hold a pen. His handwriting didn’t get any better. She could still read it.

Some days she couldn’t bear to. Every line was in the hand that had held her arm shut on the stones, and it reminded her of the one that couldn’t. He noticed. So he stopped leaving them where she’d find them. When she asked, he wrote, and turned the page round to face her, and pushed it across the table, and took his hand away. He never once reached over to point at a word for her. He never took the pen back to correct one. He waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

May 2027

The card was on the dressing table in the family room off the old block’s corridor at four in the morning, propped against the mirror beside the brushes Elowen had laid out. Cream, heavy, folded once. On the front, in that hand, one word.

Elara.

There was a brown envelope beside it from An Yu, and inside that a photograph of her husband aged about seven with a haircut so terrible that she had to sit down. She’d put that in her bag, for later, for blackmail. She opened the card.

Qu Xiaoyue. Lin Elara. Wang Elara.

Here is the rest of your name.

She read it twice. Her birth name, in his writing, the one she’d only found out at twenty-six from a pencilled ledger. The name the Lins had given her on the fourth of November. The one she’d taken at the old-town registry on an ordinary Friday. He’d written them in a row.

She didn’t hear him come in. He’d been told to stay in the garden. He was in the doorway in his dark suit with a camellia in the lapel, and he looked at her face and came straight across the room.

“What’s wrong?”

She held up the card.

“You wrote this.”

“Yes.”

“By yourself?”

He looked offended. “Who else would?”

She laughed with her throat tight, and stood up and put her arms round him, carefully because of the dress and the hair and Elowen, and pressed her cheek against his shirt.

“Your handwriting’s still terrible.”

“So I’m told.”

“Nobody else can read it.”

“I know.”

“But I can.”

He kissed her hair, where it wasn’t pinned. “That’s why I write it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning they sat at the kitchen table at Camphor Hill among the wedding cards, a hundred and something of them, opened and half-opened, in drifts. She’d taken every pin out of her hair and her hair was a mess. He was sorting cards into piles in his white shirt with the sleeves rolled up, and when he reached for the next one she caught his wrist.

“Wait. Give me your pen.”

He gave it to her. She took the cap off with her teeth. She turned his left forearm over on the table, palm up, the pale inside of it where the veins showed blue, and held his wrist still with her right hand, the one with the scar across the front of it.

He watched her face, and then her hand, and then the pen.

She wrote, slowly, in her own hand, which the knife had made worse and Jinx’s machine had made better and which would never again be quite as neat as it had been. Three words, across the inside of his arm.

I can feel.

He didn’t move at all.

She put the cap back on the pen. “There. Something you can read without me.”

He looked at the words. He knew what she meant. Not only the pen, and the skin, and the scar. The months when she’d had it back and hadn’t told him, because she’d wanted it to be hers first. Every one of the things he’d tried to fix that weren’t his to fix.

“Can you?” he said.

“Yes.”

He put his thumb on the scar on her wrist. “Does it hurt?”

“Sometimes. But it’s mine. All of it’s mine.” She turned her hand over under his thumb.

He leaned across and kissed her hair, and then her cheek, and then the corner of her mouth, so carefully that she lost patience, and took the front of his white shirt in her fist and pulled him straight across the table. Cards went everywhere. His hand came down flat beside hers on a congratulations from Nainai’s bridge club, and the pen rolled across the table and stopped against the cream card with her three names on it, and he laughed against her mouth.

“Your handwriting,” he said, when she let him go, looking at his own arm, “is not much better than mine.”

“Can you read it?”

“Every word,” said Xing Yue, and didn’t wash it off for three days.

chapters.title: The Stitches Competition
chapters.desc: At the trainees’ skills night Elara takes on her husband and his cousin with a chicken thigh each. She wins, and he asks for a rematch at home, in writing.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not made of glass.”
chapters.content:
The trouble with inviting Elara Wang to the surgical trainees’ skills night was that nobody had considered she might take it personally.

It began innocently. The second-years had organised it in the skills lab after the Thursday evening teaching: knot tying, suturing on a pad, instrument handling, and a final round on a chicken thigh, which had been Yu Chen’s idea. He was in his last term of medical school and had been allowed in because he’d carried the chicken.

“One thigh each. Judged on tissue handling, spacing, tension, apposition, and time,” he said, putting the trays down.

“Why chicken?” said Elara.

“Because it’s cheap.”

“That isn’t a surgical reason.”

“It’s a practical one,” said Xing Yue beside her, with his sleeves rolled to the elbow. He’d been asked to judge. He’d declined, and said he’d compete instead, and the second-years had gone pale and then excited.

She turned and looked up at him. “You’re taking his side?”

“I’m taking the side of cheap teaching materials.”

“Traitor.”

“Are you in, Sister-in-law?” said Yu Chen.

Elara looked at the chicken, and at her husband, and back at the chicken. “Yes.”

“Are you sure?” said Xing Yue.

She smiled at him sweetly. “Completely.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first round was knots. Three pairs of hands, a timer, a row of trainees leaning over the bench. Yu Chen was quick. Xing Yue was exact. Elara was both, and put her instrument down first.

“Done.”

The second-year running it pulled on the knot and wrote something. “Secure.”

Yu Chen finished. Xing Yue finished a breath after that, which had never happened in front of witnesses in his life.

“Need more time, Mr. Wang?” Elara murmured.

“Don’t distract me.”

“You’re losing.”

“I’ve finished. One round,” he said, putting his down.

“One round,” she agreed, and held both hands up for the room, which cheered.

The second round was suturing on a synthetic pad, and he won it. Clean, even, every bite the same depth, tension you could have measured with a gauge. She bent over his pad and studied it.

“Annoyingly good.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t get comfortable.”

He glanced at her pad. “Your spacing drifts at the far end.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little.”

Yu Chen came third, and stared at his pad in disbelief. “I thought that was better.”

“It is. Your tension’s more even than last month,” said Elara.

“Your last knot’s loose,” said Xing Yue.

“Thank you, Cousin,” said Yu Chen, and looked at his phone under the bench, and smiled at it, and put it away before anybody could see who’d sent him whatever it was. Elara saw. She saw the thin plaited cord on his wrist, too, blue and copper wire, the kind of thing a girl who rewired walls might make out of offcuts. She didn’t say anything. She’d find out soon enough.

So it was one each. The chicken would decide.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Shall we make it interesting?” said Yu Chen.

“No,” said Xing Yue.

“Yes. Winner chooses dinner for a week,” said Elara at the same moment, and they looked at each other.

He thought about it. “Fine.”

“What if I win?” said Yu Chen.

“Then we’ll be very proud of you,” said Elara, and patted his shoulder.

The timer started, and her face changed. All the play went out of it. She laid the thigh flat with the cut towards her, chose her angle, and began, and the room went quiet round her the way rooms did. Beside her Xing Yue worked with the economy he brought to theatre, his hands doing exactly what was needed and nothing extra. Yu Chen was quick and took a bite too near the edge, and swore under his breath.

“Don’t pull so hard,” Elara told him without looking up.

“Concentrate on your own chicken.”

She laughed, and kept going, and tied her last knot, and put the needle holder down.

“Done.”

Xing Yue tied his. Yu Chen tied his. The judges bent over the three thighs. One was neat, with its spacing a little uneven at one end. One had perfect apposition and too much tension on two stitches. The third, everybody agreed afterwards, was almost annoyingly beautiful.

“First. Dr. Wang. The other Dr. Wang. Elara,” said the second-year.

“Again?” said Elara.

“Again.”

Xing Yue was looking down at his own thigh with an expression she knew. It was the face he wore over a scan he didn’t like.

“Something wrong, Mr. Wang?”

“No.”

“Would you like to inspect it again?”

“No. Congratulations.” He looked up.

“Thank you, darling,” said Elara, in front of a room full of surgical trainees, and one of them dropped a needle holder.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came and found her by the sinks afterwards with her certificate, a sheet of printer paper with a chicken drawn on it in biro.

“Rematch,” he said.

“What?”

“At home. Best of three.”

“That was best of three.”

“Tonight was a preliminary round.”

“That isn’t how competitions work.”

“It is now. In writing.” He held out a sheet of lined paper torn from somebody’s notebook, and a pen.

She took it, laughing, and wrote across the top, leaning on the edge of the sink: THE WANG HOUSEHOLD SUTURING CHALLENGE. Three rounds. Equal materials. No outside assistance.
