Winner chooses the reward. No appeals. She signed it. He signed underneath. Yu Chen, drying his hands, read it over their shoulders.

“You’re actually going to do another one.”

“Would you like to take part?” said Xing Yue.

“No. I’ve got somewhere to be,” said Yu Chen, and went red, and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they got back to Banyan Terrace she opened the fridge for milk and stopped.

There were two packets of chicken thighs on the middle shelf. Six thighs.

“Xing Yue.”

He was taking his watch off. “Hm?”

“Why are there six chicken thighs in our fridge?”

“Preparation.”

“For what?”

“The rematch.”

She looked at the packets and at the date on the label, and at him. “You bought these yesterday.”

“Yes.”

“Before tonight. Before you’d even competed. You knew you were going to lose.” She shut the fridge.

“I knew you’d agree to a rematch. Whether I’d lose remained to be seen,” he said.

She came across the kitchen and pulled him down by the shirt and kissed him, and when she let him go he said, “Is that part of the competition?”

“It’s a victory celebration.”

“You’ve already celebrated.”

“Not properly,” said Elara.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next evening he set it out on the kitchen counter like a theatre tray: three thighs each on two boards, a needle holder, forceps and scissors each, packets of three-nought and four-nought. She looked at it and laughed.

“You’ve been planning this all day.”

“I like to be prepared.”

The first round went to him. He was faster, and his tissue handling was beautiful; he didn’t touch the chicken one more time than he had to. She looked at it with her lips pressed together.

“Acceptable.”

The second went to her. Her stitches were cleaner and her edges met better, and he studied it and said, “Yes. Fine.”

One each.

On the third she watched him instead of the chicken. She couldn’t help it. The crease between his brows. The way his thumb shifted on the needle holder before each bite. The tiny pause before the final pass, when he looked at the line as a whole. He was enjoying himself. He was enjoying himself more than she’d seen him enjoy anything outside theatre in months, and it made her want to laugh, and it made her want something else entirely.

He tied his last knot. “Done.”

Hers had one stitch left. She knew exactly how she’d do it. She put the needle holder down on the board.

He looked up. “You’re not finished.”

“I know.”

“You’ve got one knot left.”

“I know,” she said, and took the front of his shirt in both hands across the corner of the counter and kissed him, with the suture still hanging out of her chicken and his forceps still in his hand.

He went still for half a second. Then the forceps went down on the counter and his hand went to her waist.

“Congratulations, you won,” she said against his mouth.

“You stopped.”

“Did I?”

“Elara. You threw the round.”

“Maybe. You looked very handsome concentrating.” She smiled.

“That isn’t a judging criterion.”

“It is in my competition. I wrote the rules.”

He pulled the agreement out from under the fruit bowl, turned it over, and wrote on the back in his terrible hand: Winner: W. X. Y. Reward: to be determined. She took the pen off him and wrote under it, Subject to negotiation. He signed it.

Then he lifted her onto the counter between the two boards, and she yelped and laughed and caught his shoulders.

“There’s chicken—”

“There’s chicken everywhere,” he agreed, and kissed her, and she stopped worrying about the chicken.

✦ ✦ ✦

He carried her upstairs because she’d wrapped her arms round his neck and announced that the winner was entitled to collect his prize in person. At the bedroom door he stopped.

“Terms?”

“One. No chicken for a week. Two. You make breakfast. Three. Stop talking.” She kissed him.

“That one may be difficult.”

“Try.”

He tried. He put her down on the bed and undressed her without a word, every button, every hook, watching her face as he did it, and she lay back and let him look. Then she sat up and pulled his shirt over his head and undid his belt and pushed everything down at once, impatient, and he laughed, and she said “Talking,” and he stopped.

He kissed her all the way down. Her throat, her breasts, the soft skin of her stomach, the inside of her knee. When he put his mouth between her legs she gripped the sheet with one hand and his hair with the other and arched up off the bed, and he held her hips down and took his time, all the time in the world, until she was saying his name in a voice that had nothing to do with chicken or rules or who had won. When he came up over her she was already reaching for him, and she guided him into her herself and wrapped her legs round him. He moved slowly at first, watching her, and she wouldn’t have it. She pulled him down by the back of his neck and said, “I’m not made of glass,” and he stopped being careful. She came hard, clutching at his back, her heels digging into him, and he followed her with his face buried in her neck and her name broken in half against her skin.

Afterwards she lay on his chest, sweating, with the sheet somewhere on the floor.

“Who won?” she said.

“I did. It’s in writing.”

“Technically.”

“Signed by both parties.”

She kissed his jaw. “I’m the better surgeon.”

“Debatable.”

“Debatable?”

He kissed her cheek and pulled her closer and didn’t argue, and after a while he said, into her hair, “I’ll buy more chicken,” and she laughed into his chest until she fell asleep.
